docs/adding-content.html.title: Adding content: what is data, and what still needs code | The Last Fleet
docs/adding-content.html.summary: Adding content: what is data, and what still needs code So you want to add a new gun, a room, an enemy? Good news: most things are data! That means a new entry in a JSON file under content/defs/, plus art under content/ if it needs a model. None of it needs a programmer or a build. You can edit the data in LastFleet Studio (the Studio reference) or by hand. Studio picks up hand edits as soon as you save them, so use whichever you like. In Studio, every list has a + New button. It adds an entry at the end of the list, copied from the one you have selected (or the first one), so every field is already filled in. Give it an id and a name, then change whatever makes it different. Too easy! Not sure what something does? The text above the fields says what the list is for, and hovering over a field tells you what it does. Fields that point to other entries (a rarity, a maker, a frame) are picked from a list, so you can't make a typo. The tables below go area by area: what you can add, where it lives, what to set, and anything else it needs. Guns and loot (content/defs/loot/) To add Where What to set Anything else? A maker Armory > Makers (manufacturers.json) id, name, color (its paint), models (the model names it sells for each frame it makes), bias (stats applied to all its guns), signature (its trait), weight, minRarity Optional: give it its own parts (set their manufacturer to the maker's id). Loot tables can favor it under manufacturers. A part Armory > Parts (parts.json) slot, mods, rarity, weight; manufacturer to limit it to one maker; archetypes to limit it to some frames; model for the model it shows as Its model goes in the frame's file in content/weapons/ (weapons.md). The model field opens a 3D picker with icons for that slot's models. The 3D panel's Part models shows every model and which parts use it. An affix Armory > Affixes (affixes.json) kind (prefix or suffix), rarity, weight, mods, traits A frame (archetype) Armory > Frames (archetypes.json) model (its models file), firing (hitscan, pellets or projectile), frameStats (rate of fire, magazine, damage, spread...), base stats, clamps; sound, kit, sidearm and grip (how a body holds it, animation-graphs.md); soldier (how an enemy soldier fights with it: damage and range scales, how long it holds the trigger, its squad role) Its models go in content/weapons/<model>.gltf, made in Blender (weapons.md). Frames can share a file. A maker has to list models for the frame before it makes it, and a loot table has to name the frame before it drops. Enemy variants carry it once their weapons list it. Its shot sound is the cue gun_<model> (content/defs/sounds.json, sound.md), unless sound names a different one. A rarity Loot > Rarities (rarities.json) color, weight, perLevel, affixes, statBonus, mods Tiers rank in file order, lowest first. A relic Loot > Relics (relics.json) archetype, manufacturer, five parts, traits, affixes, flavor It never drops unless a loot table entry names it ("relic": "<id>"). A loot table Loot > Loot tables (tables.json) entries (frames, other tables, relics; weights and item levels), rarity and manufacturers bias Something has to roll on it: a mission's loot settings or another table. Never change a table that has shipped, because guns are rebuilt from their table. A trait's strength Armory > Trait rules (traits.json) The numbers for each trait A new trait (a new effect) needs code. An item (a medkit, an ammo pack, a fleet supply, a raw material...) Items > Items (items.json) id, name, model (file/Object in content/props), paint, color, stack; flags: consumable (useSeconds, and the effect it runs), fleetSupply, refinable (a raw material), weaponPart (fitSeconds), carried (held in both arms, like a crate) Put it in item tables so players can find it lying around. There's a limit of 64 items, and the order matters (it's how items are sent over the network), so add new ones at the end. An item that does something the game can't do yet needs code (see below). An effect (what an item does: healing, armor, a shield, a stat change for a while, refilling ammo, calling a pod, or a mix of these) Items > Effects (effects.json) id, name, trigger (use: from a quick slot; passive: while its item is held), actions in order. Each action is a do: heal with amount; giveArmor with amount, max; shield with amount, delaySeconds, perSecond; changeStat with stat, by, seconds; refillAmmo with magazines; callPod; placeDevice with fuseSeconds, blastRadius, blastDamage; sound with cue; flash with color, brightness, radius, seconds A consumable item names a use effect in its effect. Any item can name a passive effect in its passive. Try one out with --give <item>. A fleet supply's rules (how much a jump uses, what happens when you run short or have enough, its stations) Items > Supplies (supplies.json) item (an item with fleetSupply), use (each one a per: jump, ship, damagedShip, people with people and round, shipAlive with ship, contact; plus its amount), short (each one a do: peopleLost, morale, shipWorn, message), stocked (morale, repairShips, produce), jumps, boarders, startJumps, stations Every fleet supply item needs rules. A new supply's crates come from item tables, and its stations get added to the star map. Whether a station keeps it in tanks is the mission's (tankKinds and the reservoir's supplies). A kind of tank, or the fittings for the reservoir or the airlock A model in content/props (in Blender, see docs/blender/props.md: station.gltf's Tank, with Hose, Gauge and Gauge_Top), then Missions > tankKinds (station_raid.json) model, supplies, radius, height, weight; for reservoir: model, outlet, valve, radius, height, supplies; for airlock: intake and chute Collision is boxes only (..._CollisionOnly). Whatever the tank kinds hold is everything a station keeps in tanks. Run the gate tests, since a solid fixture in the way can break a seed. An item table (what a supply pile, a footlocker, a case or a cargo crate holds) Items > Item tables (items.json) entries: an item (by id), its weight, count and perDeck A mission names it in its loot (pileTable, footlockerTable, caseTable, cargoTable). A cargo crate only holds fleet supplies. A grade of refined material (Mk I...) Items > Grades (crafting.json) id, name, itemLevel (the item level that things made from it roll at), color Lowest first. Recipes make it, refinery tiers unlock it, fabrication spends it. A refinery tier (the fleet's refinery upgrades) Items > Refinery tiers (crafting.json) cost (fleet supplies, by item id), grades it can make, batches per jump Lowest first. A fleet starts at the first tier and upgrades from the needs board. A refinery recipe Items > Recipes (crafting.json) inputs (raw materials, by item id, and how many), grade, gives The refinery makes the best grade it can first. Something the armory fabricates Items > Fabrication (crafting.json) makes (a weapon from a loot table, a part for a slot, or anything), grade, cost Players drag it at the armory bench on the ship. It rolls at the grade's item level. Missions (content/defs/missions/) To add Where What to set Anything else? A mission template Missions > + New mission (a copy) (a new file) Decks, rooms, loops, soldiers, stories, built rooms, and its loot tables The game plays station_raid.json and ship_raid.json (campaign.json says which a star map target uses). You can make and check a new template in Studio, but playing it needs code (see below). A station's tanks and deep reservoir Missions > the template (station_raid.json, ship_raid.json) tanks, tankAmount, tankFill, hoseLength, pumpRate; reservoir: chance, amount, junctions (valves along the way), valveSeconds, pumpRate The reservoir sits deeper in than the hose can reach, and it's piped to an outlet near the airlock. A ship raid (a mission laid out by a plan) Missions > ship_raid.json > laid out by a plan (plan) plans (weighted), zones, routeLength, keycard (rooms by tag, offRoute, detourChance), objective (kind: hack, data or destruct, rooms, archetype, seconds, countdown, sealEvery) or objectives (several, each with a weight), insertion and extraction (exits: hangar, airlock), pods (perZone, seats), closets, threat (zones, districts, rooms, reinforcements: everySeconds, size; sources) The game plays one as --level frigate:<seed>, carrier:<seed> or any plan's id (accreted_station:<seed>). Run the gate tests (-class "*GateSeeds*") after a change. The lobby can force an objective kind (-o<kind> in a level's settings). Levels (content/defs/procgen/) To add Where What to set Anything else? A tag (a room type, a style, a zone) Levels > + New tag (tags.json) Its dotted name (room.storage.cold) and what it means Rules that use tags come with the next phases of the procgen revamp (plans/procgen-revamp.md). A room archetype (a kind of room built from the seed) Levels > Archetypes > + New archetype (archetypes.json) Its shape (a kind with its ranges, or a stamp drawn on the grid), tags, roles, style, furniture (a furnishing in rules.json), cut corners, pillars, weight and roomDoor (its doors in a ship's level: auto or interact). Set vertical for a tall room: the stories slider goes up to 4. Each story above the ground gets a gallery, mezzanine, catwalks, landing or nothing, 2.5 to 8 m deep. Stairs are generated, either straight or switchback, running up from the nearest floor below where they fit and through any open stories in between. A room with a floor that needs stairs has to be at least 4 cells each way. A template builds rooms from the archetypes it lists (Missions > the template's archetypes). A template never draws an archetype taller than its own stories. A room in a biome's kit (a room every level in the biome has: a corridor, the insertion bay, a hangar to extract from) Levels > Archetypes > + New archetype, with kit (archetypes.json) The same as an archetype, plus kit (the biome: station). For a rectangle of a fixed size, also doors (each one a side, a cell and a level; one-cell sides are allowed). It can also take the mission's roles (insertion, corridor, closet, key, objective, extraction). Set vertical with a landing for a stairwell. Nothing else. The kit is built once from each room's id and offered to every level. If a role needs a spot in the room, the room gets it from its roles (the insertion's spawns, the extraction's spot) or from a prop its furnishing places (a terminal's marker). If a furnishing's required rules can't be met in any of six footprints, the kit stops and names the room. A surface style (how rooms or halls look) Levels > Styles > + New style (styles.json) Its id, its base, and what's different from the base: walls, floor, ceiling, trims, duct, pipes, lights, and how a hall built in it looks (hall) A deck theme builds its halls in the style it names (style under the template's hallThemes). Rooms built from the seed use their archetype's style. In later phases, rules will pick styles for kit rooms. A prop (something rules place) Levels > Props > + New prop (props.json) Its kind (furniture, footlocker, case, cargo, supplies, ammo, keycard, tank) and size. For furniture: a model (picked from content/props, and its size comes from the model) and its paint, or its color, what it breaks into and its piece's name, and which mission spot it stands for (marker: terminal, extraction or key; markerAhead is how many meters in front of it) A rule that places it (Levels > Rules). A tank's size and model come from its kind in the mission template. A furniture model (a table, a chair, a rack) A recipe in content/props/forge.json, edited in Levels > Props > Its recipe, or a model in a new content/props file (docs/blender/props.md) Its parts and materials, its solid boxes, Socket_<Group>_<n> empties where loot sits, and Attach_<Group>_<n> where another piece stands A prop that uses it. Then on the prop, set sockets (each group's loot table, chance and count) and attach (what stands at each group, and how far it's pulled out). Collision is boxes only, and a piece that breaks is one box. A placement rule (what goes where in rooms) Levels > Rules > + New rule (rules.json) What (props and weights), where (a tag query), anchor and fallback, count, clear space, spacing, priority, blocks, interaction, required. Set arrange for a row or grid (gaps, aisles of 1.1 m or more, back to back). Nothing else. The level's rules apply to every station level. You can see how a rule did in a room on the Missions mode map. A furnishing (how a built room is furnished) Levels > Rules > + New furnishing (rules.json) Its rules (with no where, since they apply to the room being furnished) An archetype that names it (furniture), or built rooms that draw one. A loot assignment (what loot a kind of room gets) Levels > Loot > + New assignment (loot.json) Where (a tag query: role.*, deck.*, layout.*, or the content's tags), and any of these: a cache (table, count), a stash weight (per room deeper, per soldier carrying it; table), the tables its piles, footlockers, cases and cargo roll from, and added item levels Its tables have to exist in the loot data (Checks will tell you). Order matters: the first cache and table win, while weights and levels add up. A recipe step (how a mission's decks grow) Missions > the map's Recipe view > + side rooms or + loot rooms (the template's recipe) How many per deck, how often a side room is two deep, and which decks (leave it out for every deck). Move it with < Earlier and Later >. The main path and the keycard steps stay as they are. The node shows the mission's graph after the step runs. A typing rule (what mix of rooms a level has) Levels > Typing > + count, + adjacent or + distance (typing.json), or a tick in the Adjacency table A count (where, per deck or level, min and max), an adjacency (rooms a and b are never connected) or a distance (min and max steps between rooms a and b), all by tags; plus the kit's share If a rule set can't be satisfied, the level stops and tells you why. Try a few seeds in Missions mode (Types). A network's costs (where a pipe runs) Levels > Networks (networks.json) What its route pays for each direction it can run and each bend, its open span and service cells, and its pipe's look The generator lays reservoir_feed. A new network only gets laid once code asks for it. You can see its route on the Missions mode map. A level plan (a ship's or a station's shape) Levels > Plans > + New plan (plans.json) Its parts (a hull, boxes, arms, rings, painted cells), its halls (spines, cross passages, rings, service ways) and its sections; its decks (names, districts) and stair cores; parts and halls name their decks Its rooms come from its sections' districts; its mission comes with the next phase of the structure-first plan (plans/structure-first.md). A pin (a set piece held in place on a plan) Levels > Plans > Its pins > + room pin or + boarding pin, then drag it on the preview (plans.json) pin (room or boarding, the squad's airlock; one boarding pin a plan), archetype for a room, on (the part), at (along it, 0 to 1), across (cells off its line) or offset (cells from a ring's center), deck A room pin's room is cut round where it's pinned (the bridge at the bow). A boarding pin picks the airlock or hangar nearest it. A district (what a section's rooms are) Levels > Districts > + New district (districts.json) Its anchor and its rooms: archetypes with widths, weights, runs and private A plan's sections name it. Enemies and their behavior (content/defs/ai/) To add Where What to set An enemy variant (a new kind of soldier) Behavior > Enemies, + New (enemies.json) behavior (which behavior file it thinks with), body and model (what it's drawn as: an animation graph in content/anim and a model in content/characters; see rigs.md), faction (hostile or choir), health, damageScale, grenades, runSpeed, sprintSpeed, dropsLoot, weapons (frames and how often each is used), spawns (how often this variant shows up in the level's squads, reinforcements, the director's patrols or the Choir), clips (its own clips in place of the body's, animation-graphs.md) A behavior (how a kind of soldier thinks) Behavior > Behaviors, + New behavior (a new file next to soldier.json, named after its id) Its tree, built from the palette (right-click the canvas), and its scoring if the tree picks an intent. Then pick it as a variant's behavior. And inside a behavior's scoring: To add Where What to set A personality Behavior > Behaviors > Scoring (right-click the graph background) share (how many squads get it), flankers, cohesion (how many meters its soldiers stay within each other), and a scale for each intent A term, factor or condition Behavior > Behaviors > Scoring Right-click the canvas for the palette (or drag from an input and let go on empty canvas), then wire it to an intent's or term's pin Art Art has its own guides (start at the artists' start page if you're new). Here's which one covers what: To add Guide Part models and frame receivers weapons.md The ship's hub (rooms are archetypes: see the table above) hub.md Creatures creatures.md Characters on a rig, their clips, and new rigs rigs.md How a body type's clips are blended (its animation graph) animation-graphs.md Props: loot, containers, crates, the cargo pod props.md Surface materials (how every model takes light), and which ones a model uses materials.md The skies windows show, one a sector (content/defs/skies.json) Studio, Look mode, Skies How windows break and what a breach does (content/defs/breaches.json) Studio, Missions mode, Breaches How rooms' own doors behave (content/defs/doors.json) Studio, Missions mode, Doors What the fleet raids on the star map: stations and ships (content/defs/campaign.json) Studio, Missions mode, Campaign Still in code: ask a programmer We're not all the way there yet. These are the places where adding or changing content still needs code, so grab a programmer for these. Each one is on the list to move into data. What Where it is Why it's still code A new way of firing (beyond hitscan, pellets and a flying round) WeaponHandling, WeaponFiring It's new behavior. Any frame that fires one of those ways is data. A new trait (a new effect) WeaponTraits, WeaponTraitSystem It's new behavior. Its strength is data (traits.json), but its card text is still in WeaponCard. An effect that does something new (an action beyond the ones above, or a new stat to change), or a fleet rule beyond what a supply's rules cover (a new kind of use, shortage or bonus) a record under LastFleet.Simulation/Effects (EffectAction), EffectRunner, EffectReader.Actions and Studio's LootGlossary.Variants; a record under LastFleet.Simulation/Supplies, FleetSim, SupplyReader It's new behavior. Any effect built from the existing actions, and any supply rules built from the existing parts, in any order and amounts, is data. What a soldier drops besides its gun SoldierLoot Not moved yet. Which mission template a mission plays (the lobby uses the station raid; the star map the station or ship raid) Levels, StarMap Levels loads each template by name. Bark lines (what soldiers shout) BarkLines Not moved yet. The reasons shown over a soldier's head IntentReason A term can only give one of the reasons the game already knows. How a gun's power number is worked out, and how tall a loot beam is for each rarity WeaponRoller, GameView Not moved yet. The horde's and the director's tuning HordeTuning, DirectorTuning Not moved yet. (The soldiers' tuning is data: content/defs/ai/tuning.json, one per side, edited in Studio's Behavior mode, Tuning tab.)

docs/animation-graphs.html.title: Animation graphs | The Last Fleet
docs/animation-graphs.html.summary: Animation graphs A soldier is running, crouching, leaning out of cover and reloading, sometimes all at once. Which clip plays? That's the job of a body type's animation graph: it decides how its rig's clips get blended into a pose, based on what the body is doing. If you've used Unreal's anim graphs, this'll feel familiar. The graph is a file, content/anim/<id>.json (the humanoid's is humanoid.json), shared by every model on the rig. It sits next to the clips it plays (content/anim/<rig>.gltf; see rigs.md), and it's part of the plan in plans/animation.md. Soldiers and the Choir's lancers use it: each enemy variant names its body (the graph) and its model in content/defs/ai/enemies.json. The game and the graph only talk through two things: Parameters: numbers the game sets for each body every frame from its state (how fast it's moving and which way, crouched, leaning, dead). Actions: what the graph plays when the game says the body does something (a reload, a throw). That's it! The behavior that decided to crouch never names an animation, and the graph never knows why the body crouched. The code that sets the parameters is the body type's bridge (the humanoid's is HumanoidBridge). If the graph doesn't declare a parameter, it just doesn't get set. The file Key What it is id, name The graph's id (the file name) and its display name. rig The rig it poses. Its clips and masks have to belong to that rig. clips The file with the rig's clips, in content/anim (humanoid.gltf). parameters Each one has a name, a default (0 if not given) and a description (about). Flags are numbers: 1 is on, 0 is off. min and max (default 0 and 1) and flag are only for Studio's sliders and checkboxes; the graph accepts any number. targets The points its IK reaches for, each with a name and about. The game supplies them while the graph plays (for example, the humanoid's leftGrip is where the gun's fore grip is). capabilities What a body of this type can visibly do: fire, reload, throw, crouch, lean, blindFire (the humanoid has all of them). An enemy variant's behavior can only need these. A behavior's needs come from its tree (Hold cover needs crouch, lean and blind fire; Throw grenade needs throw). If a variant's behavior needs more than its body can do, it gets flagged (in Studio's Enemies tab and in the game's log). fire, reload and throw also need a graph action with the same name. actions One-off things the body does on top of everything else, played into the graph's slot node (below). Each has a name (the game's name: reload, throw, fire, use), the rig clip it plays, the mask it covers (the whole body if not given), fadeIn and fadeOut (seconds, default 0.1), about, and events. Events are moments in the action, each with a name and an at value from 0 to 1 giving how far through the action it happens. For example, the humanoid's throw has release at 0.55, when the grenade leaves the hand. Because it's a fraction, the event stays in the right place however long the action lasts and whichever clip a grip plays for it. groundSpeed The parameter that holds the body's speed over the ground, in meters per second. Clips played by stride use it. root The node at the top of the tree. Its output is the pose the body is drawn in. pos, loose Only Studio uses these; the game ignores them. pos (on the graph or any node) is where the node sits on the graph editor's canvas. loose holds nodes that aren't plugged into anything, each as { "node": ... }, until you plug them in or delete them. A value in a node is either a number (0.5) or the name of a parameter ("leanLeft"). Nodes A graph is a tree of nodes, with poses flowing up from the leaves to the root. Each node is an object with exactly one of these keys. Node Keys What it does clip clip (its name), loop (uses the rig's setting if not given), time, stride, rate, normalized, events Plays a clip. time says where the clip's time comes from. "clock" is the default: it starts from the beginning each time the clip starts playing, then runs with real time, multiplied by rate. "stride" uses the ground covered: one loop every stride meters, so the feet keep pace. "end" holds the last frame. A value means seconds into the clip, or with normalized, a fraction from 0 to 1 regardless of its length. blend1d blend1d (a value: the axis), points (each with an at number and a node, in order along the axis), sync Blends the two points on either side of the value, weighted by how close it is to each. For example idle at 0, walking at 1.8, running at 4.5, by speed. blend2d blend2d (two values: across and up), points (each with an at of [across, up] and a node), sync Blends points on a plane, for example a stride in each direction, by which way the body is moving. Between two neighboring points, only those two count. select select (its states, each with a node and a when), fade (seconds, default 0.2) Plays the first state whose when is true, fading from the previous one when it changes. The last state can leave out when, so it's picked when none of the others are. when can be dead (flag on), !dead (flag off), speed > 2 or speed < 2. layer layer (the node underneath), over, mask, weight (a value, default 1), fade Plays over on top of the node underneath, only on the rig's mask. For example, a reload from the spine up on top of running legs. The weight eases toward its value over fade seconds. While the weight is 0, the over node isn't played at all (a clip on its clock restarts the next time). slot slot (the node underneath) Where the body's actions play, like Unreal's slot node with montages played into it. On top of the node underneath, it plays the clip of the action the body is doing, on the action's mask, from the clip's start to its end as the action goes from 0 to 1. So the clip lasts exactly as long as the action: a reload gets stretched to the gun's reload time. An action fades in when it starts and fades out when it's done. If another action replaces it, the current one fades out first and then the next one fades in. A graph has only one slot. additive additive (the node underneath), add, reference, weight, mask Takes the difference between add and reference (for example leaning out, compared to standing) and adds it on top of the node underneath, scaled by weight. IK nodes Clips get the pose close, but they don't know the floor is uneven or where your gun's fore grip ended up. That's where IK comes in. IK nodes bend the pose underneath them after it's been blended. They use the rig's chains (content/rigs/<id>.json). A chain is a run of bones from root to tip, plus its pole, which is the direction its middle joint bends. IK nodes ask the game where things are in the world, so when there's no world (Studio's preview, a test) they do nothing. Node Keys What it does reach reach (the node underneath), chain (three bones: two plus the tip), target, socket, weight, fade, swing Bends the chain so its tip, or the rig's socket on it, lands on the target. The middle joint bends the way the clip had it, or toward the chain's pole. The tip keeps its rotation (a hand stays the way it was held). The weight eases over fade seconds. If the target is out of reach, the bone the chain hangs from (a shoulder) turns toward it, up to swing radians (default 0). look look (the node underneath), chain, pitch, yaw, shares, weight Turns each bone in the chain up by pitch and left by yaw (in radians), each by its share (shares, root first; split evenly if not given). This is how the spine and head bend toward the aim and carry the arms and gun with them. ground ground (the node underneath), chains (the legs, three bones each, all hanging from one pelvis), weight, range, ease Checks how high the ground is under each foot and moves the foot up or down by that much from where the clip had it on flat ground (at most range meters, default 0.4). The pelvis drops by the lowest foot's amount so the legs can reach. Each foot's height follows the ground at one meter every ease seconds (default 0.25). Works with two feet or up to eight. Sync Ever seen a character's feet shuffle weirdly as it speeds up from a walk to a run? That's two strides out of step. A blend with sync keeps the strides under it in step. They share one phase, advanced by the ground covered divided by their blended stride, so a walk blending into a run keeps the feet together. A stride clip outside a synced blend keeps its own count of the ground. Events Events are moments on a clip: "events": [{ "at": 0.53, "name": "footstep" }], in seconds into the clip. You place them in Studio on the clip timeline under the Bodies preview, by dragging them to the right frame. An action's events fire the same way when the action passes them (every time it's done), and they're reported with the action's clip. An event (on a clip or an action) can also say what it does, like Unreal's notifies. It can have: sound: a cue in content/defs/sounds.json, played where the event happens; gain: how loud (default 1); effect: dust kicked up, sparks; socket: the rig socket it happens at, like Grip.L (the feet if not given). So a footstep looks like { "at": 0.333, "name": "footstep", "sound": "step", "gain": 1.2, "effect": "dust" }. The game plays and shows these for every body drawn from the model. A couple of gotchas: Blended strides don't double up. When several blended strides pass the same event, it only counts once, and a stride weighted at less than a quarter of the pose is left out. Events replace distance footsteps. A body whose events play step makes footstep sounds from those events instead of from the distance it walks (sound.md). Studio catches typos. It flags a sound that isn't a cue, or an effect the game doesn't show. Each frame, a body reports the events it passed along with how much of its pose that clip made up (so a footstep from a walk that's half blended away is half as heavy). Clips chosen by who plays it The graph is one template for every body of its type. But a soldier holding a hand cannon shouldn't hold it like a rifle, right? So whoever plays the graph can swap the clips it names, without needing a graph of their own. This works like Unreal's per-weapon animation layers (Lyra gives each weapon its own). The gun's grip. Each weapon frame has a grip (content/defs/loot/archetypes.json; in Studio: Armory > Frames, the frame's grip). rifle is the default and plays the rig's own clips. pistol (the hand cannon) plays the rig's Pistol_ clips instead, wherever the rig has one: Pistol_Idle for Idle, Pistol_Reload for Reload, Pistol_Fire for Fire, and the rig's normal clips for everything else (the strides). A new grip is just clips, not code. Name them <Grip>_<Clip> on the rig (Heavy_Idle) and frames can pick it (Studio offers every grip the rig has clips for). The enemy variant. A variant's clips (content/defs/ai/enemies.json; in Studio: Behavior > Enemies) swaps in its own clips for the body's: "Idle": "Lancer_Idle". The grip is applied first, then the variant. So to change how a variant holds a pistol, swap Pistol_Idle, not Idle. A clip name the rig doesn't have is never played (Studio warns you). The choice is made once per grip and variant and then kept (AnimPlayer.Choose, a ClipChoice set on the body's AnimInstance.Clips), so it costs nothing per frame! Studio's Bodies mode plays it the same way the game does: the gun picked under Holding plays its grip's clips, a Variant plays its own, and the parameters panel lists which clips are being played in place of the graph's. The humanoid's graph Want to see how it all fits together? Here's the one we ship. At the top, a select picks between dead, downed and alive. Alive is built from these pieces: The legs' locomotion: a select between crouched and standing. Each is a blend1d by speed, from standing still to a synced blend2d of the four strides by movement direction. The arms holding the gun the way Idle holds it, layered on top. So a grip's own Idle (a pistol held out) is also how the arms hold the gun while walking and running. The rig's strides already hold a rifle the same way its Idle does, so for a rifle this changes nothing. Blind fire, layered on top from the spine up. The slot where actions play (a reload, a throw, a shot's kick). Leaning, added on top of all of it. Then IK runs: the feet are set on the floor, the spine and head bend toward the aim, and the hands go on the gun (its grips are markers on its receiver, see weapons.md). Other players' guns hang from their right hands, pointed along their aim, and the left hand reaches for the fore grip. Your own gun, in first person, is wherever the view holds it, and both hands reach for it. If the fore grip is out of reach, the left hand slides back along the gun toward the magazine well, and the shoulders swing forward to reach. Your own body Look down in first person and you'll see your own body: the player model (content/characters/player.gltf), under your eye, playing the same graph as everyone else. The camera is still the simulation's eye; the body is moved to sit under it. The head (the rig's firstPersonHides mask) isn't drawn, otherwise you'd be staring at the inside of your own face. The body and gun are drawn in front of the world, so neither one clips through a wall you're standing against. --floating-gun shows just the gun, the old way. Parameter Set from speed The simulation's horizontal speed. moveForward, moveRight The direction the body's feet move from frame to frame, in the body's own axes (a unit direction; kept when it stops). crouched Crouching or sliding. leanLeft, leanRight How far it leans around cover (the simulation's Lean, fully out at 0.45 m). blindFire Firing blind over cover. downed Down and waiting for a revive. dead, deadSeconds Dead, and for how long. aimPitch How far up the view is aiming (radians). It's 0 while firing blind, so the head stays down. leftHandOnGun 1 unless reloading, throwing, using an item or downed. Otherwise the left hand lets go of the fore grip so the clip can move it. A gun whose frame has step-by-step reload (content/defs/reloads.json) keeps it at 1 during the reload, and the hand follows the steps instead of the clip. rightHandOnGun 1 for your own body in first person: the gun is where the view holds it, on the aim, and the right hand reaches for its grip (rightGrip). Other players' guns hang from their right hands. Whatever the hands are doing plays the graph action with that name, at how far through it is: reload during the reload (stretched to the weapon's reload time), throw during the throw, fire for 0.3 s after each shot (restarting with every shot), and use while an item is being used (the humanoid has no use action, so only its left hand lets go). The humanoid's actions are reload, throw and fire, all on the upper body. A gun's grip can play its own clip for one of them (Pistol_Reload). The host sends what other players' hands are doing (reloading, throwing, using an item, firing) as one byte with each character, so a client that joins sees every body the same way the host does. One byte, too easy! Seeing it Studio's Bodies mode (the Studio reference) plays a graph on a model on a turntable, with its parameters as sliders, and can draw the bones and IK targets. Its Graph tab lets you wire the graph's nodes on a canvas, like Unreal's anim graph, with poses flowing left to right into the Output Pose. Every change plays right away, with the parameters as sliders beside it. Its Rig tab edits the rig, and Reloads edits the reloads' steps. Studio reloads the files when they change on disk. Checking The game reads a graph when it loads the body and reports every problem it finds: a clip or mask the rig doesn't have; a parameter or target that's used but not declared; a node with no kind, or two kinds; a blend whose points are out of order, or that has only one point; a stride clip with no stride; a state after one that has no when; a reach or leg that isn't a chain of three bones; legs that don't hang from one pelvis. dotnet test tests/LastFleet.Content.Tests checks the shipped graph and plays it (AnimGraphTests).

docs/architecture.html.title: Architecture | The Last Fleet
docs/architecture.html.summary:
Architecture This is the tour of the code: how it's organized, the rules that keep it testable and deterministic, and (most importantly) why we made the big decisions the way we did. Projects and dependencies flowchart BT Core[LastFleet.Core
random, hashing, timestep] Ecs[LastFleet.Ecs
GameWorld, ISimulationSystem] Sim[LastFleet.Simulation
components, systems] AI[LastFleet.AI
navigation, soldier AI, horde] Content[LastFleet.Content
glTF, models, rigs, animation, materials] Physics[LastFleet.Physics
Jolt characters, ray casts] ProcGen[LastFleet.ProcGen
mission grammar, layout, assembly] Loot[LastFleet.Loot
loot data, weapon rolls, drops] Platform[LastFleet.Platform
window, input] Rendering[LastFleet.Rendering
Vulkan renderer] Audio[LastFleet.Audio
OpenAL sound, cues, placeholders] Net[LastFleet.Networking
transports, snapshots, sessions] Client[LastFleet.Client
main loop, camera, HUD, menu] Studio[LastFleet.Studio
designers' tool: the game's data] Shaders[tools/LastFleet.ShaderCompiler
Slang to SPIR-V, build time] Forge[tools/LastFleet.WeaponForge
part files from forge recipes] Friflo[(Friflo.Engine.ECS)] Brutal[(BRUTAL packages)] Ecs --> Friflo Sim --> Core Sim --> Ecs AI --> Core AI --> Ecs AI --> Sim Loot --> Core Loot --> Ecs Loot --> Sim Content --> Core Content --> Brutal Physics --> Sim Physics --> Content Physics --> Brutal Platform --> Brutal Rendering --> Platform Rendering --> Content Rendering --> Brutal Audio --> Brutal Client --> Audio Net --> AI Net --> Sim Net --> Brutal Client --> Net Client --> Sim Client --> AI Client --> Content Client --> Physics Client --> ProcGen Client --> Loot ProcGen --> Content ProcGen --> Core Client --> Platform Client --> Rendering Client --> Core Client -. runs at build .-> Shaders Studio --> Client Studio --> Loot Studio -. runs at build .-> Shaders Shaders --> Brutal Forge --> Content Arrows point from a project to what it depends on. The big idea here is that Core, Ecs, Simulation, AI, Loot, Content, Physics and ProcGen are headless. They never reference windowing, rendering, audio or UI. Why bother? Because it keeps gameplay testable in CI without a GPU, and it lets a host run the simulation without a window later. We don't just trust ourselves on this one either: ArchitectureTests in the Simulation, AI, Loot, Content, Physics and ProcGen test projects enforce it by checking assembly references. Content stays headless so the host, the tools and physics can all load the same meshes the renderer draws. The client is the game's composition root. It's the only place in the game that knows about both the simulation and the renderer. Rigs (LastFleet.Content.Rigs, content/rigs/.json; docs/blender/rigs.md, docs/plans/animation.md) are the skeletons bodies are modeled and animated on. They're data, so a new kind of body is just a new file! Rig.Parse reads a rig and names every problem it finds. A rig has: bones, with their rest pose, each listed after its parent. Each bone has a RigTranslation that says where its offset comes from when a clip plays on a model. sockets (RigSocket): the eye, the grips. IK chains (RigChain): a run of bones, a pole and a RigChainTarget. masks (RigMask): from some bones down, minus others. One mask is the one hidden in first person. the body the simulation uses (RigBody), with the same numbers as MovementSettings and HitVolumes. Shots never hit the animated mesh. The mesh is held to these shapes instead. its clips (RigClip). Rig.SkeletonProblems checks a model's joints against the rig. RigFit.Problems checks that and also the model's eye at rest: a model's bones can be longer or shorter than the rig's, but its eye can't move. The Blender add-on (tools/blender/lastfleet_rigs.py) builds the armature from the same file and checks models and clips (bones, weights, 30 fps, in place, loops closed). Here's how the files fit together: A model (content/characters/.gltf) is its meshes plus the armature. A rig's clips (content/anim/.gltf) are the armature and its actions, and every model of the rig shares them. The sources are Blender files in content/raw/characters/ (Git LFS): a .blend for each model and a _clips.blend for each rig's clips. You export them with the add-on's buttons, or all at once with tools/blender/export_characters.py (export_source checks a file, then writes it). The starter files (the grey-box soldier, the lancer, the player and the 22 clips) were written by tools/blender/generate_soldier.py, which won't overwrite them unless forced. The skeletal runtime (LastFleet.Content.Skeletal) plays them: SkinnedModel reads a model's skinned meshes as flat triangles in the bind pose (SkinnedVertex: position, face normal, color, four joints packed in a uint, weights), plus its Skeleton (joints ordered parents first, rest pose, inverse binds). ClipSet binds a rig's clips to a skeleton by joint name. A ClipChoice swaps the clips a graph names for the ones that fit a gun's grip, for example Pistol_Idle for Idle based on WeaponArchetype.Grip, and then for an enemy variant's own EnemyVariant.Clips. AnimPlayer.Choose makes one per grip and enemy variant, and it's set on AnimInstance.Clips. SkinnedBodies and Studio's BodyStage pick them from the held gun and the variant (docs/animation-graphs.md). The rig retargets the clips to the model (docs/plans/animation-2.md). A Skeleton joint's translation keys are dropped, so it keeps the model's offset. A Scaled joint's keys are scaled by the model's rest offset divided by the clips' rest offset. ClipSet.Problems names any joint that's rotated at rest compared with the clips' armature. A SkeletalClip can be sampled at any time between its keys, looping or held. NodeChannel is shared with AnimatedModel's bake. A Pose holds every joint's JointTransform. Poses can be blended (Blend, with a mask of joint weights from Skeleton.Mask, which gives you a layer), added to (Add: an additive clip's difference from a reference pose), and turned into the matrices that skin the mesh (Skin: inverse bind, pose, placement). None of this allocates per frame. The renderer skins on the GPU. AddSkinnedMesh uploads a body's vertices once (SkinStore). Each frame, FrameGeometry.SkinMatrices (at most MaxSkinMatrices) go into a storage buffer, one per frame in flight. Each SkinnedDraw is one draw of its mesh, and its first instance is the index where its matrices start (content/shaders/skinned.slang, lit the same as the level; skinned_shadow.slang draws into the shadow maps). Animation graphs (LastFleet.Content.Skeletal.Graph, content/anim/.json; docs/animation-graphs.md) are data too. AnimGraph.Parse reads a body type's parameters (AnimParameter) and its tree of nodes, and checks them against the rig. The node types are: clips (ClipNode): looping or held. A clip's time comes from its clock, from the ground covered at a given stride, from a parameter, or runs to its end. Clips can have events. blend spaces (Blend1DNode, and Blend2DNode using gradient bands). A synced blend keeps the strides under it in phase. selects (SelectNode): picks the first state whose AnimCondition holds and fades to it. layers on a rig mask (LayerNode), with the layer's weight eased. the slot where a body's actions play (SlotNode). It plays the graph's AnimActions, such as a reload or a throw. Each action is a clip played by the action's progress on its mask, faded in and out. A body's AnimInstance.Play says which action is playing, by name, from the bridge's HandActionKind. additives (AdditiveNode). IK on the rig's chains: ReachNode moves a two-bone chain's tip or socket to a target, LookNode turns a chain toward an aim, and GroundNode sets each foot on the ground under it, drops the pelvis to the lowest foot and moves it by the instance's BodyOffset, and keeps the feet planted. IK nodes ask an IAnimWorld (passed to the player) for targets and the ground, and solve with PoseIk in model space. JointPoint is a rig socket placed on a skeleton, at the same distance from its model bone's head as the rig has it from the rig's bone. An AnimPlayer binds a graph to a skeleton and a clip set, and poses any number of bodies into a Pose. Each body is an AnimInstance: its parameters, plus what the nodes keep for it from frame to frame (clocks, phases, the chosen state and its fade). It keeps a pair of scratch poses per depth, so a frame allocates nothing. The events a body passed during the frame are in AnimInstance.Events. Drawing bodies. The client draws soldiers and the Choir's lancers this way. With --box-soldiers, or when a body doesn't load, it falls back to CharacterModels' boxes. ModelBody loads each body type and model pair once (an enemy variant's Body and Model). GameClient uploads every variant's mesh. SkinnedBodies keeps each character's instance, which way its feet are going, and any reload or throw still playing between the host's messages about it. HumanoidBridge is the one place where the simulation's state becomes the graph's parameters: MovementState, Health, the aim's pitch and BodyActions. Body actions play as the graph's action with the same name (HumanoidBridge.ActionName). They come from a HandAction, which is what the hands are doing: reloading, throwing, using an item or firing. HandActions.Of works it out from the weapon, grenades and items, and it's sent to clients in two bytes that stay the same while the action lasts: its kind and length, and the tick it began. BodyWorld answers the IK queries from the level's collision and the held WeaponModel. The gun hangs by its GripRight from the right hand along the aim, with the left hand on its GripLeft. In cover, the body is held to the hit volumes. Here's the problem. Shots hit HitVolumes, which are built from the simulation's eye. CoverSystem puts the eye wherever the cover needs it (ducked below low cover, raised to see over it, leaned round an edge)... but the clips only have a crouching eye and a standing one. So what do we do about the gap? Each frame SkinnedBodies compares the drawn eye (the rig's Eye socket) with the simulation's eye and moves the body by the difference (AnimInstance.BodyOffset, eased, limited to half a meter down, a third of a meter up and under half a meter sideways). HumanoidBridge draws a crouched body in cover with the standing clips once its eye is closer to standing height. Out of cover, the offset eases off and the clips set the pose. When firing blind, the gun sits on the line the simulation's shots leave along (CoverSystem.Muzzle, held a little out along it) and the hands reach for it (BodyWorld.PlaceHolding): Over low cover it uses the held-up BlindFire clip. Round a right-hand edge it uses both hands. Round a left-hand edge it uses the left hand only, because the right arm can't reach across. The first-person gun goes out to the side by the same amount. F3's Hit volumes option draws every other character's capsule and head sphere over its body. Other players are drawn the same way, with the players' body (ModelBody.Players, player.gltf). Your own body in first person (SkinnedBodies.AddSelf, off with --floating-gun): It's the players' body under the camera, which is the simulation's eye. The body is moved sideways under it and held down with BodyOffset (feet kept planted), so its eye is never above the camera. Why? Without that, the camera drops to a crouch and dips on landing faster than the clips fade, which puts the shoulders around the camera. Not a great look! Its head is shrunk to a point (the rig's FirstPersonHides). Nothing within OwnCutRadius (0.2 m) of the eye is drawn (SkinnedDraw.CutRadius: skinned.slang and ray_prepass_body.slang discard it, but its shadow stays whole). In the poses the clips hold, nothing in view is that close, so this is a guard for what the animation does while moving between them. The gun is where ViewModel holds it (ViewModel.Held, at a nearer hip, HeldByBody), and both hands reach for it (BodyWorld.PlaceHolding: the graph's rightGrip target and rightHandOnGun). The left hand slides back toward the magazine well when the fore grip is out of reach, and a reach's swing brings the shoulder forward. It's a SkinnedDraw.Near, drawn with the view model in the near end of the depth range. The gun is then seen through the world's projection (FrameGeometry.ViewModelInWorld) so the hands and gun line up. Studio's Bodies mode (BodiesMode, BodyStage) plays any body type's graph on a model of its rig, driven by sliders over its parameters (AnimParameter.Min, Max, Flag). It can also play it on a second model beside the first that follows it (BodyStage.Follow: Compare). Under the stage is the ClipTimeline, where you drag, add and remove a clip node's or action's events and give them a sound, effect and socket. The body can be posed in that clip alone with BodyStage.Solo. The body is skinned on the CPU (SkinnedModel.Skin) into a ModelStage, and its IK gets a held gun (BodyWorld without collision) and a floor with a step. The shapes shots hit for the current stance (BodyHitShapes) are drawn over the stage on top of the body (ModelStage.ToScreen), and you can pick and drag them there (HitShapeEditor, which writes the rig's body). Animation events reach the game. Each ClipEvent can name a Sound, Gain, Effect and Socket. SkinnedBodies collects the events each body passed (BodyEvent; with strides blended, each one counted once; placed at the socket or the feet), along with the characters whose graph plays step (Stepping). On the next frame GameView.PlayBodyEvents hands them to ImpactEffects.AddEffect and GameAudio.PlayBodies, which then leaves out those characters' distance-based footsteps. The Graph tab edits a graph's file as a tree (LastFleet.Studio.Bodies): GraphTree reads the JSON into GraphTreeNodes, each with its GraphSlot. GraphCanvas draws them the way Unreal's anim graph does, with poses flowing left to right into the Output Pose and each node's named inputs as a GraphPin. GraphWiring connects them: plugging in and out, keeping loose nodes in the file's loose list, storing positions in each node's pos, and never putting a node under itself. GraphInspector edits a node's fields, offering the rig's and the graph's names (GraphVocabulary). GraphEdits wraps and unwraps nodes, and adds and moves points and states. The Rig tab edits a rig's file (JsonEditor) beside its skeleton (RigPreview). Both are data workspaces like the loot's (RigWorkspace, GraphWorkspace; each graph is read against its rig as the rigs currently are in Studio), so they can be saved, undone and reloaded from disk. Their files are written in a compact layout (DataDocument.Compact: an object or list goes on one line where it fits). LastFleet Studio (LastFleet.Studio, docs/studio/reference.md) is a second executable: the designers' tool. It ships and runs separately from the game. It references the client for its view code (GameView, LocalSession, UiLayer, the Loot Lab), so the range it fires a weapon on is the game's own, and it builds the same shaders (src/Shaders.targets, shared by both projects). It edits the loot data files in the repository. Each file is a DataDocument: its JSON as a node tree. The comment block at the top of the file is written back as it was, and the rest is written the way System.Text.Json indents it, which is the layout the files are kept in (LastFleetStudio --format restores it). LootWorkspace holds all of them and tracks what isn't saved. Every edit rebuilds the game's LootCatalog from the documents' text (LootCatalog.Parse), with an in-memory loot table, studio.preview, that rolls the frame, maker and rarity you picked. A few things make this nice to work with: If a rebuild fails, Studio keeps the last catalog that built and shows the problems. A catalog built from the saved files is kept alongside it, so you can compare a roll with it. LootContent.Use hands the new catalog to the client's code (and clears its rolls and the guns WeaponModels has kept), so the HUD's cards, the gun models and the range all follow the data as you edit it. The forms are generated from the JSON itself (JsonEditor), so a new field in the data needs no Studio code. Too easy! Every data folder Studio edits is a DataWorkspace: LootWorkspace, AiWorkspace (which builds every behavior, SoldierBehavior.Parse, and the EnemyRoster), and the workspaces for rigs, graphs, missions, procgen data, materials, skies, doors, breaches, colliders and the campaign. DataWorkspace.Create and Delete add and remove a file, which is written or deleted at the next save. Behavior mode's sandbox. Sandbox is a LocalSession of the range with no fight of its own. It's drawn by a GameView whose Spectator camera stands apart from the player. The player's body is drawn like anyone else's, with no gun in hand and no HUD, and it's driven by PuppetCommand (standing still, or strafing), so it's a target that can't be hurt. Squads (SoldierSpawner.SpawnHunting, of the picked variant, with their personality and any behavior you're trying out set on their brains) and hordes (HordeSystem.CallHere) spawn where a click's ray (CameraMath.ScreenToRay) hits the level. Every AI edit goes straight to the session's SoldierAiSystem.Behaviors. The scoring graph. A behavior's scoring graph (UtilityGraph) is rebuilt from its file's nodes every frame, so it never gets out of step with an edit or a revert. Each node is a JSON object (a term, a condition, and so on), and every edit in the graph changes that object and then calls DataWorkspace.Changed. With a soldier picked, the graph shows that soldier's TacticalInputs run through the built UtilityModel (UtilityModel.Values, then each rule's terms and factors in the order the file lists them). It's drawn with ImGui's draw lists, with no node-editor library. So where does the layout go? Right on the objects themselves: Where the designer places a node is written on its object (x, y; the inputs and the choice are in the root's layout). So is the route a wire takes: via on the item the wire leaves, or inputVia on the item an input's wire reaches. These are ids of reroutes, stored once in the root's reroutes so wires can share them and branch from them, or bare points. Nodes added from the palette but not yet wired in go in the root's loose list, each marked as term, factor or condition. The graph lays itself out in columns until the first such edit, which pins every node where it is (Freeze). Won't all that extra stuff slow the game down? Nope. The game's parsers skip all of these keys (System.Text.Json ignores members the file type doesn't have), so they cost nothing at run time. A test scores the shipped scoring with all of them added and without them, and gets the same result. The tree editor (BehaviorGraph) works the same way. It's a card for each node in the file's flat list, rebuilt from the JSON every frame and wired parent to child. Every edit changes the nodes' objects and then calls DataWorkspace.Changed, so the soldiers run the edited tree on the next tick. The edits are: connecting (which refuses a cycle), moving (which sorts the parent's children by height, since they run top to bottom), adding from the palette, and deleting. The tree shows the picked soldier's last run: SoldierAiSystem.TracedSoldier makes RunTree keep each node's result (Trace) for that one soldier. The picture beside the editor is the sandbox's own view, drawn with a camera that follows the soldier (BehaviorMode.PipCamera). How do we fit it in the picture without a second render target? Its projection is shifted (CameraView.Shift, added to the projection's third column) so its center falls inside the picture. It's the same view drawn off center, undistorted, with no second render target. The rest of the screen behind the editor is painted over. CameraMath.ScreenToRay removes the shift again, so clicking in the picture picks a soldier there. The sandbox's TestCover boxes are added to physics as static meshes (JoltWorld.AddStaticMesh). A moved box becomes a new body, and the old one is put away with SetSurfaceSolid. They're drawn through GameView.ExtraBoxes and taken out of the navigation grid with NavGrid.SetObstacle. That's an overlay on the walkability the grid was built with, and the pathfinder, its path smoothing and the cover map all read it. When obstacles might close the corridor the pathfinder's clusters chose, it searches every cell. After that, SoldierAiSystem.RebuildCover finds cover again and makes every soldier choose again. An edit becomes solid when it ends, not while you're dragging a box. Flow mode (FlowMode, LastFleet.Studio.Flow) reads the loot files themselves, not the catalog, into a FlowChart. That's FlowNode boxes in columns and lanes, and FlowLink arrows with a FlowLinkKind and an amount. A name that doesn't exist becomes a Missing box, and its links are Broken. FlowLayout lays it out: each column is ordered and placed by the boxes its arrows come from, sweeping right, then left, then right. FlowView draws it with ImGui's draw lists. It's rebuilt whenever DataWorkspace.Edits changes (every edit, undo and reload, whether or not the data then builds), and the selected box's entry is edited beside it with the mode's SectionEditor (DrawSelected). The frame Here's what happens every time the client draws a frame: sequenceDiagram participant Loop as Client main loop participant Input as InputState participant Step as FixedTimestep participant World as GameWorld participant Renderer as VulkanRenderer Loop->>Input: BeginFrame, then PollEvents Loop->>Step: Advance(frame time) Step-->>Loop: n ticks (0 to 8) loop each tick Loop->>World: write PlayerCommand from input Loop->>World: Step(): systems in fixed order Loop->>Loop: remember the eye position before and after end Loop->>Loop: camera: eye lerped by Alpha, view angles plus unapplied mouse movement Loop->>Loop: hit results into CombatFeedback (markers, impacts, tracers, target flashes) Loop->>Loop: effects into an EffectBuilder, part tints, HUD and hit marker into an OverlayBuilder Loop->>Loop: ImGui frame: developer overlay, menu when the mouse is free Loop->>Renderer: RenderFrame(camera, FrameGeometry with ImGui draw data) Fixed ticks, smooth frames. The simulation always advances in whole 60 Hz ticks. The renderer runs as fast as the display allows and draws the eye position interpolated between the last two ticks with FixedTimestep.Alpha, so motion is smooth at 144 Hz. The mouse. Mouse movement accumulates between frames and is applied by the first tick of a frame, so a frame that runs two ticks doesn't turn twice. The camera also adds the movement no tick has applied yet (InputState.PeekMouseDelta), so the view follows the mouse every frame, not every tick. Recoil comes from the simulation's view angles, so it's never lost. View feel (ViewFeel) is presentation only, and it always decays back to what the simulation says. It's all the little stuff that makes moving feel good: Eye height glides between stances. A step's vertical snap is eased in (a vertical move in one tick that's steeper than any walkable slope counts as a step). Hard landings dip the view on a damped spring. Aim is interpolated between ticks and eased for the zoom and the gun. The gun sways against turning and bobs with speed, and the reticle opens quickly and settles more slowly. While aiming, look speed is divided by the zoom (times the aim sensitivity setting), so the zoomed view moves the same distance on screen for the same mouse movement. The model library (ModelLibrary, Content) holds every model made in Blender for the game's things. That's each top-level object of each .gltf in content/props/ and content/weapons/, named file/Object (ModelId: items/Medkit, auto_rifle/Receiver), so a file dropped into either folder is picked up with no code! A file that doesn't load is kept, empty, with the reason, and the rest still load. Each model lists its paint slots (PaintSlots): materials named Paint_. The data picks the color of each slot for each thing that uses the model, and the default is the material's own color. A few names are the game's own colors and are reserved (PaintSlots.ReservedForProps: Glint, Rarity, Supply, Light; ReservedForWeapons: Body, BodyDark, BodyShade, Accent, Reticle, Lamp). PaintSlots.Problem says what's wrong with a misused one, the same way the Blender add-ons' Check does. The prop and weapon part libraries below are read through it. Icons (IconRenderer, IconAtlas, ModelIcons, Client) are drawn from the models, never by hand. Each model is seen from a fixed three-quarter angle (right side and front, a gun's muzzle pointing right, a little from above), orthographic and as large as fits, lit by lights fixed to the view, on a transparent background. Why not draw them on the GPU? They're rasterized on the CPU (3 × 3 samples per pixel, sRGB, straight alpha), so icons are the same on every machine and can be drawn in tests without a GPU. ModelIcons keeps one icon per model and paint colors in an IconAtlas: one picture with square cells that doubles in height when it's full. Its Version changes whenever its pixels do, so the GPU copy knows when to update. An icon is only drawn again when its model is reloaded or its paint changes. A prop is drawn the way it looks lying around, and a weapon part in gunmetal. The HUD's icons (GameIcons, in the ViewShell) are drawn the same way from the things themselves: A weapon's icon comes from the gun as rolled (WeaponModels.Of: its frame and parts, its maker's paint, its rarity's glow) and is kept by its roll and frame. An item's icon comes from its model as it lies around (CharacterModels.ItemVertices) and is kept by its kind and rarity. At most two are drawn per frame (about 3 ms each). The 96 least recently used make room for new ones, and all of them are redrawn when the loot data, the items or frames in play, or the part models change. The weapon card, the inventory and the quick bar show them, and IconTexture copies the atlas to the GPU after each frame. Weapon models (WeaponModels, WeaponPartLibrary, Client; ModelParts, Content) are forged from recipes (content/weapons/forge.json, LastFleet.Content.Forge: ForgeRecipes builds each part from its shapes, ForgeShapes builds the shapes, and ForgeFile writes the glTF; run it with tools/LastFleet.WeaponForge, or from Studio's armory with its recipe editor, ForgeEditor; docs/plans/weapons.md phase 5). Where a part has no recipe it's made in Blender instead (docs/blender/weapons.md, the add-on tools/blender/lastfleet_weapons.py). There's one glTF file of parts per frame in content/weapons/, plus shared.gltf for parts any frame can use. A forged part has a Detail child mesh (rail ridges, vents, bolts; only on your own gun) and a Far one (no bevels or detail, round parts with six sides), which other players' guns and dropped guns use (WeaponModels.Of(weapon, detail: false)). That's about 1,000 to 2,400 triangles in your hands, and 250 to 500 in anyone else's. A gun is the frame's Receiver with one part for each slot at each of its sockets (empties): Each rolled part shows as the model its data names (WeaponPart.Model, WeaponModels.ModelOf). That's either a full name or the end of a shape name, for example Drum for Magazine_2_Drum, so a part can name its look on every frame. If the frame has no such shape it uses the frame's first, None means nothing in the slot, a part that names nothing gets one picked from its id, and a stock weapon gets the first. The optic is the optic part's kind (iron, red dot, holographic, scope; WeaponModels.SightOf), but a gun that magnifies 2× or more always carries a scope, whatever is fitted. A part's paint slots take its data's colors (WeaponPart.Paint). Barrels stretch with range and magazines with capacity. Materials named Body, BodyDark and BodyShade take the maker's finish, and Accent takes the rarity's color. Each gun is put together once and kept. The view model, soldiers' guns and weapons lying in the world all draw from it. The starting files are the old box guns exported box for box (tools/greybox/generate_weapon_parts.py). Characters are only drawn in rooms that can be seen (RoomVisibility). Prop models (PropLibrary, PropModel, Client) are made in Blender too (docs/blender/props.md, the add-on tools/blender/lastfleet_props.py). The files are: content/props/items.gltf: each item lying around. containers.gltf: the supply case, the footlocker's inside, and their lids, which hinge at the body's Hinge empty and swing up to open. cargo.gltf: the crate, the cargo pod and its lid, and the drone and its rotor blade, which spins at each Rotor empty. Every top-level object of every file there is a prop, found by its name (or by file/Object). Each is baked once into flat-shaded vertices. Each vertex records whether it keeps its own color or takes one the game gives it (PropMaterial: Glint, Rarity, Supply and Light, from a PropPaint), and its paint slot, which is colored by the colors passed to PropModel.AppendTo (or its color in the file when none is passed). CharacterModels draws the props from them, and ViewModel draws the crate in your arms. What if a prop is missing from the files? It's drawn from the boxes in code, so a missing file costs looks, not the prop. The starting files are those boxes exported (tools/greybox/generate_props.py), and PropModelTests checks every prop against the sizes the game's rules use and against its markers. The weapon in your hands (ViewModel, Client) is the gun's model, placed each frame and drawn in the renderer's view-model pass. It takes the view feel's sway and the aim from ViewFeel. It sits low and right at the hip, turned in towards the reticle, and comes up until its sight is on the eye line when you aim. It drops and cants for sprinting, sliding and swapping, and kicks back for 0.14 s with a 60 ms muzzle flash. Reloads. For a reload it dips and rolls while the magazine follows its frame's reload steps (content/defs/reloads.json, ReloadLibrary, built into LastFleet.Content; ReloadHands; docs/plans/weapons.md phases 3 and 4). Picture it step by step: the left hand goes to the magazine's grab point, the magazine slides out along its well with the hand and is dropped, the hand goes to the body's pouch (the rig's Pouch socket), a new magazine is lined up under the well and pushed home, the charging handle is pulled after the last round, and the hand goes back to the fore grip. Each step takes its share of the simulation's reload progress, so a faster reload speeds up all of it (the host never animates). The points come from the gun's parts (WeaponModel): the fore grip: a fore grip module's Hand.L, or the grip itself, else a barrel's Hand.L, else the receiver's Grip.L; the magazine: its Grab, else low on its front; the well: at Socket_Magazine, out along its -Y; the charging handle: the receiver's Charge, else high on its right side. So the same steps fit any gun! Your own body's left hand goes where the view model's magazine is (BodyWorld.Reloading). Soldiers and other players follow the same steps (without knowing whether it's an empty reload), with their magazines moving along (SkinnedBodies.Magazine). Meanwhile the bridge keeps the hand on the gun (HumanoidBridge.HandOnGun), and the Reload clip moves the rest of the upper body. A frame with no steps (the shotgun, hand cannon, grenade launcher) works the old way: the hand comes off the gun with the clip, and the magazine drops out and comes back. Studio's Bodies mode plays reloads with its reload action (Actions: Play reload, or held part way) and "reload from empty", and edits them in its Reloads tab (ReloadEditor), playing changes at once. The armory draws a rolled gun's hand points on its turntable. Sights. When you aim, you look through the sight, not at it (ViewModel.SightKind): the optic's Sight marker is on the eye line. Iron sights are a notch with a post, and the post's tip is the aim point. A red dot and a holographic sight are frames on a mount around a pane of sight glass (WeaponModels.AddSightGlass, which replaces the model's own Reticle triangles; the materials sight_dot, sight_ring and sight_chevron, SurfaceMaterial.Sight). The glass is clear except for its reticle, which world_shading.slang's sightGlass draws on the aim point whatever the gun is doing, the way a real one sits at infinity. The glass sways and kicks around it, and the shots go where the reticle is (shots go where the camera points; the gun's sway is only visual). The sight line runs through the window, clear of the barrel, and is held closer to the eye for bigger optics. A gun with 2× zoom or more has a scope: a tube on rings that, once raised, gives way to its lens. The tonemap draws the lens over the zoomed frame (ScopeLens in FrameParameters, GameView.ScopeLensOf; tonemap.slang's scopeLens). It's a round window that opens as the scope comes up. The scene inside is pulled in a little towards the rim and fringed there, and darkened towards it. It's shadowed on the side the gun's sway moved it away from (the "eye box"). The screen around it is blurred and dark, and its reticle (ScopeReticle: duplex, mil-dot or chevron) sits on the aim point. An optic part's reticle picks the reticle for either kind (WeaponModels.ReticleOf), and Studio's armory previews it with "Through the sight" (ReticlePreview). The HUD's own reticle disappears once the sights are up. Want to look at a particular gun? --weapon [,...] gives you a rolled gun of a frame with the given parts fitted (ChosenWeapon), and a smoke camera's ,aim aims it. ViewModelTests casts rays from the eye to check that only the reticle is on the line of sight and the view around it is clear. Long stalls. After a long stall the timestep runs at most 8 ticks and drops the rest, so the game hitches briefly instead of spiralling. Smoke runs. --smoke runs exactly one tick per frame with scripted input, so a smoke run is the same on every machine. It shows the splash for its first 30 frames, then plays with the developer overlay open. Before gameplay the loop shows the BRUTAL splash and runs no ticks. Gameplay starts, and the mouse is captured, when the splash ends. Input, settings and UI Bindings. InputBindings maps each InputAction (move, jump, sprint, crouch, dash, fire, aim, reload, grenade, weapon slots and swap, interact, drag, ping, flashlight, quick slots, inventory, zoom, lean, fire mode) to two InputBindings, each a key or mouse button. Binding something that's already in use takes it away from its old action. Escape, F3 and F11 (full screen) are reserved. InputMapper reads actions, not keys, to build the PlayerCommand. Settings. GameSettings holds sensitivity (and aim sensitivity), invert Y, field of view, overlay visibility, the toggles for aim, crouch and sprint, the display and video settings (window mode, vsync, shadows, antialiasing, bloom, ray tracing and its quality, the renderer, path tracing and DLSS), difficulty, sound and subtitles, and the bindings. It saves as JSON (System.Text.Json, source-generated) to the application-data folder whenever the menu changes it, by writing a temporary file and moving it into place. Loading never fails the game: out-of-range values are clamped, bad entries are skipped with a warning, and unreadable files are replaced by defaults. Smoke runs ignore the file. Dear ImGui. UiLayer owns the ImGui and ImPlot contexts and feeds them GLFW events itself, so the BRUTAL GLFW/OpenGL backends aren't used. While the mouse is captured, ImGui gets no mouse input, so an overlay can never swallow a shot. The renderer draws ImGui's output (see Renderer) and handles ImGui 1.92's texture requests, so the font atlas lives in the same texture store as the logo. Interpolated strings passed to ImGui (ImGui.Text($"...")) are formatted into BRUTAL's per-frame arena, so the overlay allocates nothing per frame. The menu, which is only open while paused, does allocate. Simulation rules These are the rules that keep the simulation deterministic, cheap and testable. Break one and something downstream (snapshots, checksums, co-op) breaks with it. Components are plain unmanaged structs with public fields: no references and no behavior. That makes them cheap to copy, checksum, snapshot and send over the network. Systems hold queries, not state. They implement ISimulationSystem and run in the order they were added to the GameWorld. That order is part of the determinism contract. No allocations per tick. Iterate with query.Chunks and spans, not ForEachEntity with a capturing lambda. SimulationTests.Step_DoesNotAllocate measures it. Input is a command. PlayerCommand is the only way input reaches the simulation. In co-op, clients send commands to the host. Randomness and seeds. Use DeterministicRandom.ForStream(runSeed, "stream.name") so each consumer gets its own independent stream. Turn content IDs into numbers with StableHash.Fnv1a64, never GetHashCode, which is randomized per process. Profiling. GameWorld times every system with Stopwatch each tick for the developer overlay. The times are only read for display and never feed back into the simulation, so they can't break determinism. Checksums. SimulationChecksum.Compute fingerprints the world. The same commands give the same checksum on the same platform. Windows and Linux can differ in the last bit of trigonometric functions. Is that a problem? Not for us: the design doesn't need cross-platform equality, because the host is authoritative. Player controller and weapons Each tick the systems run in this order. feet and MovementState Its own history, for rewinding shots The logic is in pure static functions. PlayerController.Update, Mantle and WeaponHandling.Update take ref structs and know nothing about the ECS, so the tests drive them directly, tick by tick. The systems just fetch components and call them. Buttons are held state. PlayerCommand carries which buttons are down, not which were pressed. Why? The simulation keeps last tick's buttons in MovementState and WeaponState and works out presses itself. That keeps commands idempotent for the network, and a lost packet can't swallow a press. The client latches taps, so a press shorter than a tick still reaches one tick. Weapons are data. A WeaponProfile (archetype plus 0–100 stats, and scales on the frame's damage, magazine and zoom) is resolved once by WeaponStatsResolver into WeaponStats with physical units. Procedural loot produces profiles, never raw stats (see Loot). Frames (WeaponArchetypes) are the loot data's archetypes in archetypes.json. Each has an id, a Model file, Firing (hitscan, pellets or projectile), a shot Sound, Kit and Sidearm flags, Soldier use and frameStats. WeaponArchetypes.Use puts them in play when LootContent loads the data, so the stock kit and soldiers' guns follow them too. WeaponArchetypes.Shipped keeps the built-in ones, and an archetype with the same id starts from the built-in one. A weapon's WeaponStats.Frame is a WeaponFrame: the frame's index among those in play, sent as a byte (protocol version 38). Loadouts are saved by frame id. The frames are: auto rifle and hand cannon (the starting loadout), pulse rifle, SMG (950 RPM, short falloff), shotgun, marksman rifle (3.5× zoom, a head shot drops a soldier), grenade launcher and machine gun (a hundred-round belt at 720 RPM, a round a little lighter than a rifle's, slow to aim and wide from the hip, a 4.2 s reload; protocol version 16). A shotgun round is eight pellets (Pellets, from the frame's frameStats). Each pellet is its own ShotRecord with the round's ShotIndex, in a fixed pattern (one in the middle, and rings around it at the golden angle) rotated by the round's hash. It's the same every time for the same weapon and round, so a client can predict it. A launcher round is a shot with a ProjectileSpeed. Hitscan skips it, and the grenade system launches it as a Grenade marked Impact. It falls with a third of a frag's gravity and bursts on the first wall, floor or body it meets (within 0.45 m of the segment from a character's knees to its eyes, not counting its shooter), dealing the frame's damage at the center of its BlastRadius. Grenade carries its blast, so the snapshot does too (protocol version 8). Shots are events, not entities. WeaponSystem appends a ShotRecord to the ShotLog for every shot: origin, direction, spread and damage profile. The log is cleared each tick and preallocated, so firing allocates nothing. Hitscan runs in the tick. ShotResolutionSystem casts every shot up to 300 m, right after the weapon fires and before anyone moves, so the shot leaves from where the shooter stood. Each result goes into the HitLog (HitRecord: point, normal, distance, surface, target, precision, damage, kill), which the client reads for feedback and co-op will send to clients. Targets are level parts. A Target names a body surface and an optional precision surface. A ray hit carries the surface (level part) it struck, so the system matches it to a target without any extra collision. Damage is DamageProfile.DamageAt(distance, precision). A destroyed target stays down, blocking shots but taking no damage, until TargetSystem stands it back up healed. Enemies will get their own hit volumes; the matching stays the same. Characters are hit through HitVolumes: a body capsule a little narrower than the collision capsule, and a head sphere for precision hits. Both are built from the character's stance, so crouching makes a smaller target. They're exact ray math in the simulation, never physics-engine queries. Their sizes are a HitShape (the head sphere's radius, how far it sits above the eye standing and crouched, and the capsule's share of the collision radius), stored in HitVolumes.Shape. It comes from the humanoid rig's body (content/rigs/humanoid.json, RigBody). The client puts it in play at startup (HitShapes.Load, with host and clients reading the same file), and Studio does it as the rig is edited (RigWorkspace). Otherwise it's HitShape.Default. The drawn bodies keep their eye where the simulation has it. A rig's clip marked with an eye (RigClip.Eye: standing or crouched) keeps the Eye socket near the simulation's eye (checked by HitShapesTests through the graph, and by the Blender add-on's Check), so the head gets shot where it's drawn. A shot stops at whichever is nearest: the level or any living character. A character on the shooter's side stops it without taking damage. Health (Health) regenerates Destiny-style after a delay without damage (players only, for now). LifeSystem clears a dead character's commands and removes its collision body so the corpse doesn't block anyone. Players with a SpawnPoint respawn after three seconds; soldiers stay dead. Recoil is eased, not instant. A shot adds its kick to WeaponState.RecoilPending, and each tick moves most of what's pending into the view (a 25 ms time constant), so the view climbs over a few ticks. WeaponState.LastRecoilStep is how far recoil moved the view on the last tick. The camera subtracts the part of it the frame hasn't reached yet, so recoil is smooth between ticks too. Recovery starts once a shot interval and a quarter has passed and the kick has fully landed. Bloom recovers every tick, at 15% of its rate while firing, so sustained fire settles below the maximum. Aiming down sights scales bloom down to 30%. Items as data (ItemDefinition, Items, ItemKind, ItemRoles; protocol version 34). Every item is data, in one list in content/defs/loot/items.json (LootCatalog.Items, put in play by Items.Use; without data it's Items.Shipped, which matches the repository's list). Each item has an id (snake_case), name, model (file/Object in content/props), paint (colors for the model's paint slots), color, stack size, and flags for what it's for (ItemRoles). Each flag turns on its own fields: consumable: used from a quick slot.
