It has useSeconds and the effect it runs, effect (see effects, below). fleetSupply: one of the fleet's supplies, used by the needs board, the hold and pods. refinable: a raw material for the refinery. weaponPart: a loose part, fitted in fitSeconds. carried: held in both arms as a cargo crate, never in the pack. One laid down by SimulationSetup.SpawnItemDrop is a crate. In play, an item is its index in the list (ItemKind, a byte starting at 1), and that's how it's stored and sent (ItemPile, Inventory.Using, CargoLoad, SupplyTank.Supply, FleetHaul by item; at most Items.Max, 64). Host and clients must play with the same items. So how does code find, say, a medkit without hard-coding a name? By what its effect does (Items.FirstThat(): the starting kit's medkits, ammo pack and beacon, a soldier's drop) or by what it's for (Items.WeaponPart, Items.FleetSupplies), never by name. What the fleet does with each supply is data too (see supplies, under the fleet). Effects as data (LastFleet.Simulation/Effects: EffectDefinition, EffectAction, EffectRegistry, EffectRunner; EffectSystem, PlayerEffects; protocol version 36). What an item does is an effect, defined in content/defs/loot/effects.json (LootCatalog.Effects, read by EffectReader and put in play by EffectRegistry.Use; without data it's EffectRegistry.Shipped). An effect has an id, a name, a trigger and a list of actions. The trigger is EffectTrigger.Use (used from a quick slot) or Passive (active while its item is held, in a quick slot or the pack, once per kind of item). Each action is a record with its own numbers: HealAction (amount) GiveArmorAction (amount, up to max) ShieldAction (amount, delay, recharge per second) ChangeStatAction (a PlayerStat: move speed, damage taken or reload speed, by a fraction, for some seconds) RefillAmmoAction (magazines, LoadoutSystem.AddAmmo) CallPodAction PlaceDeviceAction (fuse, blast radius and damage) SoundAction (a cue in sounds.json) FlashAction (color, brightness, radius, seconds) A passive effect can only shield and change stats. A consumable item names its use effect (ItemDefinition.Effect), and any item can name a passive one (ItemDefinition.Passive). The reader rejects an item that names the wrong kind. InventorySystem only uses a quick slot when EffectRunner.IsUseful says at least one action would do something: you're hurt, armor is below its max, a shield would be fuller, a stat change (always), a weapon has room, a mission is going. No wasting a medkit at full health! Then EffectRunner.Apply runs the actions in order. Anything that needs the world comes back as EffectRequests for InventorySystem to carry out: a pod set down in front of the player; a device placed on whatever the player is looking at within 1.6 m, or else on the floor ahead (InventorySystem.DeviceSpot). It's a resting Grenade marked Placed with the action's fuse and blast, so it goes off like a grenade does (enemies and the player who placed it get caught if they're in the open, and DestructionSystem breaks what's in reach), and it's sent, drawn (a flat blinking charge) and warned about like one; sounds and flashes, logged as EffectCueRecords (EffectCueLog, passed to SimulationSetup.CreateWorld). Each names the effect by its index in EffectRegistry and the action by its own index. They're sent with the tick's events (the bark count says whether any follow, so a tick without any costs nothing extra) and played by GameAudio (the cue, if the sound library has it) and SceneLights.RecordCues. What lasts is kept in the player's PlayerEffects: up to eight timed stat changes (using the same one again renews it) and the shield a used effect gave. EffectSystem (after LifeSystem, before movement) counts them down, adds the passive effects of whatever is held (EffectSystem.Held), and writes the totals, each clamped from -75% to +300%, to where the game reads them: MovementSettings.SpeedChange (ground and air speed, so the client's prediction has it), Health.DamageTakenChange and PlayerEffects.ReloadSpeedChange (for WeaponHandling.Update's reload). The shield is the stronger of the used one and the held ones, and it recharges after its delay without damage. Damage always goes through the same layers. Health.TakeDamage scales damage by the damage-taken change, then the shield absorbs it, then armor (which doesn't come back), then health, so every source of damage goes through them. Going down ends all of it. PlayerEffects is sent raw to its own player next to Health. The HUD draws shield and armor as thin bars over health, and lists the running changes and the held items with what they give (EffectsHud). --give [,...] puts items in the inventory when a solo mission starts. Inventory (Inventory, InventorySystem; protocol version 21). Besides the two weapons, a player carries four quick slots and a pack of twelve. Each holds a pile of one item (ItemPile: medkits stack to 3, ammo packs to 2, supplies to 10). Quick slots only take things used in a fight (Items.IsConsumable). Everything else goes in the pack, except things carried in both arms. An item lying on the floor is an ItemDrop entity (a pile and a yaw). Holding Interact at it, the same as at a weapon (WeaponPickupSystem picks what the player is looking at: see Looking at things below), takes what fits and leaves the rest. What a player does with the inventory is an op in their command (PlayerCommand.Op: two slot bytes and a serial). The ops are drop, move (onto a pile of the same item, otherwise swapping where both fit), use from a quick slot, and put down the weapon in hand (never the last one). How do we make that safe over a lossy network? The client sends each op for six ticks under one serial and the host applies each serial once, so a lost packet loses nothing and a repeated one doesn't happen twice. When downed or dead, ops are used up and not carried out. Using an item takes its useSeconds (1.4 s for a medkit, 1 s for an ammo pack) with the weapon down, and only works when it would do something: healing when hurt (a medkit's 60 health), refilling ammo when a weapon has room (an ammo pack's three magazines), or calling a pod while the mission is still going. A player who dies drops every pile in a ring where they fell and comes back with an empty inventory. Levels place supply piles in their rooms (SupplySpot: the position, the item table, the deck and the item level). The level's rules place them (StationPlacements), and designers can put them on furniture's sockets (FurnitureLootRolls). They're rolled when the fight is set up (LootCatalog.RollPile, from an ItemTable: items by id and weight, a count, and more per deck). LevelRolls seeds each one from the level's seed, its position and the run, so Studio's Missions mode can show what the fight will spawn. A soldier that dies leaves something that heals or refills ammo one time in five (SoldierLoot.ItemChance). The snapshot carries items lying around in their own section, and the recipient's inventory in its own player's section. Raw materials and crafting (ItemRoles.Refinable, Client/Fleet/Refinery; protocol version 34). Raw materials are items with the refinable flag (scrap, ore, ...). They're found wherever item tables name them and brought back like the fleet's supplies (by pod, the hold or the dropship), and counted in the haul by item. After a mission the fleet keeps them in its stores by item id, along with its supplies (FleetState.Stores, FleetSim.Deliver). Each jump, the refinery runs as many batches as its tier allows (RefineryTier: what it costs from the fleet's supplies to reach, by item id, the grades it can make, and its batch count). It runs the recipes for those grades, best grade first (RefineryRecipe: inputs by item id, a grade, how many), and produces graded material (MaterialGrade: Mk I to Mk IV shipped, each with the item level of what's made from it; FleetState.Graded). The needs board shows the stores and the upgrade (RefineryPanel). Drag at the armory bench on the ship opens the fabricator (FabricatorScreen), which spends a grade on whatever the data offers (Fabrication: a weapon rolled from a loot table, or a part for a given slot or any slot, made by LootCatalog.Fabricate at the grade's item level and seeded from the fleet's seed and how many it has made). The result is laid on the bench. All of it is edited in Studio's Items mode. Containers (Container; protocol version 23). Rooms have footlockers and supply cases to search, placed by the level's rules (see Placement rules): A loot room gets a footlocker or two against its walls, and about one room in three of the others gets one (not corridors, closets, the insertion bay or the extraction). There has to be room in front to open it, and none go where a soldier stands. The footlocker's body is built into the level (LootLocker_ parts), so it's solid and the soldiers' grid goes around it. A quarter of rooms (most loot rooms) also get a case on top of something (ContainerSpot). The fight fills each one fresh every run from the mission's item table for its kind (FightSession, LevelRolls.Container: medkits, ammo packs, weapon parts and supplies). Holding Interact at a closed one opens it, the same as a pickup (WeaponPickupSystem weighs containers alongside weapons and items). Its contents are laid out on top along its length as items to take, and it stays open. The snapshot carries each container's kind, yaw and whether it's open (its own section, 16 in all), but not what's inside, which stays on the host until it's lying in the world. The airlock and the haul (Airlock, AirlockLayout, FleetHaul; protocol version 24). The squad starts in an airlock built into the insertion bay (Airlock.Build). It's a chamber around the player spawns, against a bay wall with no doorway: the hull (Airlock.HullSide). The outer hatch the dropship docked at is in that wall. The inner wall's door (Airlock_Door) is lock 0 of the mission, and it opens on a timer (MissionLockPlan.OpensAt, MissionTuning.AirlockSeconds = 5) rather than with a keycard. The HUD counts the cycle down. The layout keeps the two cells beyond the hull empty on every story (LayoutSolver, the dropship's berth), so the hatch always backs onto space. When the hack starts, the dropship casts off (with a notice), and the extraction is where it picks the squad up ("DROPSHIP"). Getting out counts the haul (MissionState.Haul, MissionSystem.CountHaul): the fleet supplies in the packs of everyone standing at the point, the crate in their arms, and every crate set down within the extraction's radius plus 2 m. The banner and the lobby's line show it. How the fleet keeps it is covered under the fleet. Cargo (CargoCrate, CargoSystem; protocol version 24). Crates of a fleet supply stand against the walls (CargoLoad: which supply and how much, rolled from the mission's cargo item table when the fight is set up, fuller deeper in; most of it is whatever the station was chosen for). The level's rules place them: in two loot rooms out of five and one other room in ten, times the template's cargoShare, and half as often on the first deck. Holding Interact at a crate picks it up in both hands (WeaponPickupSystem, into Inventory.Carried). Carrying one is meant to hurt a little: CargoSystem (after the rescue and ping systems, before movement) keeps the weapon down and takes Fire, Aim, Grenade and Reload out of the command. The controller allows no sprint, slide or dash, and 70% of normal speed (MovementState.Carrying). You can't use items, fit parts, or revive or drag anyone. Drag (F) puts it down in front of you. Fire drops it at your feet and the weapon comes up 0.35 s later. When downed or dead, it falls where you are (LifeSystem handles that too). Crates lying around have their own snapshot section (17 in all). The crate being carried is in the player's own inventory, and other players see a bit in the character's flags and draw the crate in its arms. Cargo pods (CargoPod, PodPhase, CargoPodSystem; protocol version 26). Every player starts with a pod beacon (the first consumable whose effect does CallPodAction, usable only while a mission is still going). Using it sets a pod down in front of you (InventorySystem.PodSpot: 1.1 m out, stopping short of a wall). While it's loading, holding Interact at it (WeaponPickupSystem.LoadOrCall, which weighs pods with everything else) moves every fleet supply in your pack into it. If your pack has none and the pod has some, the same hold calls the drone (PodPhase.Called). A crate put down with Drag within 2.5 m goes in (CargoSystem). CargoPodSystem (a command system after the mission's and the Director's) then starts the defense: The drone is 30 s out, plus 12 s for each deck the squad has opened (not counting the airlock; from the hack on, all of them plus one more: CargoPodSystem.DefenseSeconds). A Director patrol of two, plus one per deck (up to six), comes out of the closet nearest the pod (MissionSystem.SendPatrol), and another two come halfway through a defense of 40 s or more. A horde (out of the floor 14 to 32 m away by walking distance, HordeSystem.CallToPod) comes only if the mission's hordes are due now by the run's pacing (HordeSystem.Coming), so the pod never draws anything the level doesn't have yet. With an enemy within 6 m and no standing player within 8 m, the pod counts toward being overrun (5 s; it counts back down while held). Once overrun, it's smashed open and what it held is lost. If it's held until the drone lands, the drone takes it (PodPhase.Launched) and its contents are added to MissionState.Delivered, which goes to the fleet whatever happens in the mission (FleetSim.AfterMission takes what reached the fleet: on a win the haul plus the delivered; on a loss or abandon, just the delivered). A launched or overrun pod stays for 6 s (the drone lifting it away, or the wreck) and then it's gone. Pods have their own snapshot section (18 in all), with the component sent raw. The HUD marks each pod, counts the drone in with a bar and warns while it's being overrun. --pod sets a loaded pod down in front of the player when a mission starts. Fuel and water tanks (StationTanks, TankSpot, SupplyTank, TankPhase, TankSystem, TankPumpSystem; protocol version 27). Fuel and water aren't carried out in crates anymore (the station's cargo table holds neither). They're in big octagonal tanks built into the level's mesh (Tank_: the sides and tops take rays, so the navigation grid sees them, and there's a body to bump into). The level's tank rule places them against the walls of rooms off the main route (not corridors, closets, the insertion, objective, arena or extraction), clear of doorways, breaches and anything else in the room, with space in front of the valve, one per room. They're only placed where the way back to the dropship's port, doorway to doorway, is within four fifths of the hose length and before the gate the hack opens (StationPlacements, StationTanks.Stamp). They're prop models (Phase 5's station props: content/props/station.gltf, made in Blender, docs/blender/props.md; StationProp, StationProps). The generator sets them into the level's mesh (LevelGenerator takes the props' ModelLibrary alongside the room kit) as a room's furniture. Each mesh object becomes a part named after the instance (Tank__Shell, Tank__Valve). What's solid is the model's collider in content/props/colliders.json (StationProp.Collider): the shipped fixtures are their meshes, so a tank's octagonal shell, valve and gauge are solid as drawn; given authored, each object is drawn only (_NoCollision), solid only (_CollisionOnly, a box) or both (a box); given box or cylinder, one solid part (Tank__Solid) is around everything drawn. Supply and Light materials take the supply's color and the coupling's glow. The model's empties place the hose (Hose), the gauge's window (Gauge, Gauge_Top: TankSpot.Gauge, SupplyTank.GaugeBottom and GaugeTop, protocol version 37), the reservoir's valve and riser, the outlet's pipe, each valve's wheel and stand, and the airlock's port and chute. The template names the models. Tank kinds (tankKinds, TankKind) each have a model, the supplies they can hold, a radius and height, how much room their spot takes (a smaller kind stands just as close to its wall), and a weight against other kinds for the same supply (only used when there's a choice). The template also names the reservoir's model, outlet, valve, size and supplies, and the airlock's intake and chute (airlock, AirlockModels). What the kinds and the reservoir hold (MissionTemplate.TankSupplies) is everything a station keeps in tanks, and it's never in its crates. A template that names a model that doesn't exist, or one that's missing an empty, or has a solid that isn't a box, is rejected with every problem named (StationProps.Problems; Studio's Missions mode picks the models in 3D). The template also says: how many tanks (tanks, 1 to 2); how much a full one holds (tankAmount, 30 to 50 on the first deck, a tenth more per deck); how full they are when found (tankFill, a quarter to full; empty with tankEmptyChance, 15%, which means its valve is dark and there's nothing to take). A gauge over the valve shows it: a bar of the supply's color as high as the tank is full, and a red lamp blinking when it's empty (SupplyTank.Center, protocol version 30); the hose length (hoseLength, 150 m); how fast it pumps (pumpRate, 1.5 per second). A station chosen for fuel or water has one more tank, holding only that supply. The airlock has the dropship's intake beside its hatch (AirlockLayout.Port). So how do you actually get the fuel out? Holding Interact at a tank's valve takes its hose (TankSystem.Take). It's dragged the way a crate is carried (slow, no sprint, weapon down; Drag puts it down, Fire drops it so you can fight, and it falls if you go down). It's laid behind the player every 2 m (walking back along it picks it up again; past 24 bends, the straightest one is removed), and at full length it's pulled out of your hands. A hose lying on the floor is picked up again where its end is. Brought within 1.6 m of the port, it couples and pumps (TankPumpSystem, a command system after the mission's). What's pumped goes to MissionState.Delivered right away, like a drone's pod. Of course the station doesn't just let you: it sends a patrol (two, plus one per deck, up to five) and a horde if hordes are due now. An enemy within 1.4 m of the hose for 2.5 s cuts it, and nothing pumps until a player fixes it (hold Interact at the cut). When the hack starts and the dropship casts off, every tank that isn't empty yet is left as it is (TankPhase.CastOff). The tanks belong to the mission (MissionPlan.Tanks, spawned and restarted with it) and have their own snapshot section (19 in all), with the component sent raw along with its hose. The hose is drawn from the valve along its bends (to the hands of whoever is dragging it). Pulses of the supply's color run along it while it pumps, and a cut glows. The HUD marks a hose that's lying or cut, the pumping progress, and the port while you're dragging one. Studio's Missions mode marks the tanks. Looking at things (Interaction; protocol version 33). Everything you use with Interact is used by looking at it, not just standing next to it. You're looking at a thing when the line of sight from the eye (MovementState.EyeAt, with the view's yaw and pitch) passes within its size, treated as an upright column (Interaction.LooksAt). The sizes are: a weapon or items lying around, 0.45 and 0.4 m; a container 0.5; a crate 0.55; a pod 0.7; a tank's valve wheel, a hose's end, a reservoir's valve wheel and the hold's chute 0.5; the terminal 1.2; the hatch 1.1. It also has to be within 3.2 m along the line of sight, and within reach (1.6 m) of where it's used from. If there are several, the one most squarely in view and nearest is used, and the HUD's card only shows that one, so walking past things shows nothing. Starting the hack and leaving early work this way too (MissionSystem, TerminalSight and HatchSight). The gate tests' bot turns to face the terminal to start the hack. Deep reservoirs (StationReservoirs, ReservoirSettings, TankPhase.Sealed, PipeValve; protocol version 32). A station has deep reservoirs at the template's chance (reservoir.chance, one in two), or always when the template requires them (reservoir.required). How many is drawn from reservoir.count ([fewest, most], 1 by default, at most 4). Each is in its own room with its own outlet and feed (feeds bundle together where they share a route). If a template requires reservoirs and the level can't place the fewest, the level is generated again from seeds drawn from its own seed, up to six times, keeping the one that places the most (LevelGenerator, GeneratedLevel.Remade). Each reservoir is a big tank in a room further from the port than a hose reaches (walking distance, doorway to doorway). The room has one doorway, so it's never on the way through. The furthest of three candidates is picked, as long as it fits on the floor the other rules left free and the floor in front of its valve can be reached. It's placed after everything else in the level, from its own random stream, so it doesn't change anything else a seed produces. Its pipe is a network (see Networks), the reservoir feed. It's routed along the walls and ceilings to an outlet on a wall of a room on the way back to the port, with a clear stretch a short walk away (half the hose length; the first such place the pipe reaches, counting from the port's side). Along the way there are valves on the walls under the pipe (junctions, 1 to 2, at most 3; spread along it, where the squad can stand to turn them), plus the reservoir's own. It's a SupplyTank at the outlet (the gauge there shows the reservoir's level) holding the reservoir's contents (amount, 120 to 200). It's Sealed with its valves (SupplyTank.Valves, at most 4) until each one is opened. Holding Interact at a valve for valveSeconds (3 s; let go and it starts over; WeaponPickupSystem.NearestShut) opens it: the wheel turns and its lamp goes from red to green. While a valve is turning the station hears it (noise for the alert), and once the last one is open the station sends a patrol to the reservoir (TankPumpSystem). Then the outlet's hose is taken, dragged and pumped like a tank's, but faster (reservoir.pumpRate, 4 per second). The HUD marks shut valves within 20 m and tells you as each one opens. All of it is set in the mission template and Studio's Missions mode. The dropship's hold (MissionState.Hatch; protocol version 28). While the dropship is docked (until the hack starts), holding Interact while looking at its cargo chute in the hull next to the hatch (AirlockLayout.Chute, MissionState.Chute; protocol version 33) unloads the fleet's supplies from your pack into it (WeaponPickupSystem.Unload). A crate put down with Drag within 2.5 m of it goes in too (CargoSystem). It works like a pod but with no defense: what goes in is added to MissionState.Delivered right away (HoldLoads counts how many times). So a squad has three ways to bank its finds, each with a cost: going back to the airlock (which costs time, and the station's alert is counting); calling a pod where it stands (which means a fight); or carrying them to the extraction (lost if the squad wipes). The hold belongs to the mission (MissionPlan.Hold, the floor in front of the chute). It has no entity of its own, so a level's entity numbering doesn't change. The HUD marks it while the player is carrying a crate or fleet supplies, and says when something has gone in. Leaving early (MissionSystem.LeaveEarly, MissionPhase.LeftEarly; the template's earlyExtraction). While the dropship is docked and its lock has cycled, the squad can leave: everyone alive within 4.5 m of the hatch (MissionState.Door) leaves when one of them holds Interact while looking at it for holdSeconds (5). Looking at the chute instead only unloads. What they carry and set down there goes aboard (MissionState.Haul). It counts as a success (Succeeded, with MissionState.Early set) when what the fleet got, banked plus carried, meets the mission's requisition (MissionState.Required and RequiredTotal, MissionState.Meets). The requisition is set when the mission starts, from the fleet's stores (FleetSim.Requisition: each supply with fewer than reserveJumps jumps of reserve is made up to that, at most mostPerSupply each, and minimumHaul in total). If it falls short, it's LeftEarly: the squad keeps the weapons it carried out and the fleet keeps what it brought, but the run's streak ends (LoadoutStore.Finish). While docked, the HUD shows the requisition against what's banked, and near the hatch it shows how to leave. Weapon parts (PartFit, FittedParts, PartFitSystem; protocol version 22). A loose part is an item (one with weaponPart, Items.WeaponPart; one per slot, in the pack) that names its part by the hash of its id and carries a quality byte: each of the part's ranges sits at that fraction between its worst and best. A rolled weapon's WeaponIdentity carries the fitted parts that replace the ones it rolled, one per slot. LootCatalog.Roll(identity) rolls it as before and then rebuilds it with them (WeaponRoller.WithParts: same maker, rarity, affixes and name, with the stats worked out again), so a weapon a player has modified still travels, saves (loadouts.json) and draws from those bytes. Fitting is an inventory op, and works any time, anywhere. PartFitSystem lives in LastFleet.Loot because it needs the loot data, and it's a command system that runs before the inventory system. It checks that the part goes on that weapon (rolled, not a relic, the right maker if it's a maker's part, any rarity), takes the item's fitSeconds (2.5 s) with the weapon down, and stops if the player takes damage. Then it puts the part on and puts the replaced one in the part's slot (LootCatalog.FitOf: the rolled part at the quality its ranges came out at). The magazine and reserve keep what they hold, up to the new sizes. Parts are found in rooms (one item pile in eight) and dropped by soldiers (one in sixteen), and rolled by LootCatalog.RollPart: first a rarity, the same way weapons roll one (better deeper in), then a part that rarity allows. Stock weapons don't take parts. Loadouts. A player carries up to two weapons (Loadout). The one in hand is the entity's WeaponStats and WeaponState, so everything that reads a weapon stays the same. PlayerCommand.WeaponSlot asks for a slot by number (absolute, so a repeated command can't switch twice). LoadoutSystem stows the weapon in hand into its slot (magazine, reserve, shot counter) and draws the new one, which isn't ready until its swap time is up (0.3–0.55 s depending on handling). A reload in progress is lost. Ammunition. Reloads draw from WeaponState.Reserve (the frame's reserveMagazines: four for the rifles and the grenade launcher, five for the hand cannon, SMG, shotgun and marksman rifle, three for the machine gun). Soldiers' reserve is unlimited (MaxReserve 0). Characters with an AmmoDrop leave an AmmoPickup where they die, which lasts 30 s. Crates (SimulationSetup.SpawnAmmoCrate) come back after being taken. A player within 1.2 m takes a pickup if any carried weapon has room, and gets its magazines' worth for every weapon. Flinch. A damaging hit kicks the victim's view up and to alternating sides: 0.3° plus 0.03° per point of damage, 1.4 times that for headshots, at most 3°. It throws off a player's aim and, because soldiers aim through the same view, a soldier's too. Stagger (soldiers only, in SoldierAiSystem, based on the drop in health since the last tick). A hit of at least 15% of a soldier's health (a headshot, or a hand cannon, shotgun or marksman round; not a rifle body shot) staggers it for 1.2 s per share of its health, at most 0.6 s. While staggered it can't fire, it stumbles away from the shot, its aim gets knocked up and to the side, and then settles again from further off. Each hit builds poise (three times its share, at most 0.8, wearing off at 0.6 per second), and the stagger lasts (1 - poise) as long, so sustained fire knocks a soldier around without pinning it in place. Why not players too, and why the threshold? Players are never staggered: their movement is predicted, and a host-side stagger would force a correction. As for the threshold, letting every hit stagger cost soldiers over a quarter of their damage in the room benchmark; with the threshold, it costs nothing. Shot randomness comes from StableHash(weapon seed, shot index), so every peer computes the same spread and recoil without sharing random state. AI How do you make soldiers that feel fair to fight? Our answer is to not let them cheat. Soldiers are characters exactly like the player (same components, controller, weapons and collision), plus a SoldierBrain and a SoldierTag. SoldierAiSystem runs first each tick and writes each soldier's PlayerCommand, so the AI can only do what a player could: move at the same speeds, turn at a limited rate, and fire the same weapons with the same spread. Perception is honest. A soldier sees an enemy that's inside its view cone (130°, or within 3 m in any direction) and in range, with a clear line to the enemy's eye or chest. It hears enemy gunfire within 40 m, knows who shot it, and gets told about spotted enemies by squadmates within 25 m. It acts on the last known position, never the enemy's true position once it loses sight. No wallhacks! Enemies are anyone on another side: players, the Choir's Lancers and the horde (a swarmling is seen by its head and aimed at low). Only the nearest six in view get a line-of-sight check (SightChecks), so a horde in view costs no more rays than a squad. States: Idle: watching. Alerted: the reaction delay, 0.35–0.55 s. Engaging: aim, fire bursts, keep to 8–26 m, strafe unpredictably. Hunting: walk to the last known position. Searching: where the tree has Search for the enemy, check the squad's guesses about where he went; then look around, and stand down once there's nothing left to check and SearchSeconds have passed, or after MaxSearchSeconds whatever is left. Fair aim. Each burst gets an aim error that starts at 6° and settles to 1.6° over 2.5 s of tracking, plus 0.5° per m/s of the target's speed, so moving players are harder to hit. Soldiers only fire once their (rate-limited) turn has brought the aim close. Taking turns shooting to kill. Ten rifles all trying to hit you at once isn't fun, it's a death sentence. So at most two soldiers (MaxShootersPerTarget) aim to hit any one player at a time, each for 3 s, then they rest 2.5 s before asking again, so the pressure moves around the squad. The others still fire, but at a deliberate near miss 4–5.6° off (to the side or over the head). That's suppression you can see and hear, without the damage of ten rifles at once. Anything else (the horde, the Choir's Lancers) they just shoot at. Spawn protection. A respawned player takes no damage for 3 s (Health.ProtectedSeconds), and the outpost's start is behind a wall that hides it from the courtyard. Difficulty is data (SoldierTuning, read from content/defs/ai/tuning.json by SoldierTunings.Parse): reactions, aim, ranges, hearing and turn rate, following the design doc's difficulty table. It's per side. The file's soldiers values are shared, and its factions can change any of them for the station's soldiers (hostile) or the Choir's lancers (choir). SoldierAiSystem.Tunings holds them, and the system thinks for each soldier (and each squad, and each soldier hearing a callout) with its own side's values (SoldierTunings.For). TuningFields lists every value with its key, label, group, slider range and description. The file, the F3 overlay and Studio all go through it, and a test checks that it covers every SoldierTuning property. Soldiers' weapons do a third of normal damage; the threat is numbers and tactics. Navigation is a layered grid (NavGrid, 0.25 m columns) sampled with rays through ICollisionWorld, so it sees exactly what characters collide with. Each column keeps every floor in it (ground, mezzanine, catwalk, stair landing). A ray down finds the top surface, restarts just under it and passes out of the solid without hitting anything (faces are one-sided) to find the next one. Below the top, a surface only counts as floor if an upward ray hits the underside of whatever is above before it gets back to the surface. Seeing nothing means it's inside a solid, such as the ground under a wall. So does seeing only the surface above itself (Jolt shows a ray the inside of a face it starts behind, so the ground under a wall that runs up to the slab of the next story sees the slab's underside right where the wall's top was). A cell (one floor of one column) links to the floor within a step in each of its eight neighboring columns. It's walkable when it's floor, flat enough, has headroom, and every column within the agent radius can be reached through those links. So walls, cover and ledges block, and stairs and ramps don't. The last walkable cell before a ledge gets one-way drop links to walkable floor up to 2.6 m below, as long as nothing is in the way at knee, waist or head height (a lintel over a catwalk's edge isn't a way down). Pathfinder is A* over links and drops (eight-connected, no corner cutting; climbing and dropping cost their height) with string-pulling. It doesn't allocate after construction. Why two steps? On a big level, a search over cells alone fills everything within reach before it finds a way around (half the searches between random spots in a station raid ran out of their 40,000 cells, at 5 to 10 ms each). Ouch. So it searches in two steps. NavClusters splits each 4 m square of each floor into the parts connected inside it (a few thousand clusters per level), and joins clusters wherever a link or a drop crosses between them. A search over clusters finds the corridor (or finds right away that there's no way through), and the cell search stays inside the corridor's cells, heading for the middle of the next cluster along it plus the corridor's length from there. What never changes is built once per grid and shared (NavGrid.Topology, a NavTopology): each cell's column coordinates and the cluster map, of the floor as built (NavGrid.WasBuiltWalkable), so obstacles placed later don't cut it. Each Pathfinder (the soldiers', the Choir's, the mission bot's) and its corridor search (CorridorSearch) hold only their search memory, Pathfinder.BytesPerCell (41) bytes a cell; that's also what a search thread would need. Shut doors. Shut doors and obstacles aren't on the cluster map, so each pathfinder also labels the level into the parts that still connect with its doors as they are (Reachability), again only when they change: A cluster with nothing shut in it is one part, a cluster with a shut door or an obstacle is split cell by cell, and parts any move joins are joined (a union-find; the moves into a cluster that have no way straight back, drops mostly, are kept in the map for this). A search between parts that don't connect is no way at once, without searching a cell (on a station behind its locked doors: 0.002-0.03 ms, where it used to flood every reachable cell, 7-8 ms). Labelling after a door changes takes well under a millisecond. When a corridor's search fails, the search over every cell runs only if a cluster of the corridor has a shut door or an obstacle in it; otherwise nothing would get round it. A soldier going after someone where it can't follow (on a crate it can't climb) goes to the nearest place within 3 m it can reach (Pathfinder.ReachableNear: the clusters it can get to, drops only downward, past its shut doors), not a search for no way. String pulling doesn't cut through shut cells either (NavGrid.HasClearLine with the pathfinder's marks), so a way round a shut door isn't smoothed back through it. So did it pay off? Over 400 random pairs of spots up to 80 m apart on one station raid, every path was found (the old search found half within its budget, and needed 8 to 16 ms per search without one), taking 1.5 to 2.5 ms on average and visiting 2 to 4 thousand cells. Paths were 1% longer than the shortest on average and 13% at worst. A shut door the bot has blocked (SetBlocked) isn't on the cluster map. When it closes off the corridor, a search over every cell decides. NearestWalkable prefers walkable floor at the point's own height within 1.5 m, so someone at a catwalk's edge is on the catwalk, not the floor under it. Cell numbers run column by column, bottom floor first. Deterministic. Random choices hash the soldier's seed with a draw counter, and the brain is plain data. The same seeds and commands give the same fight, which SameSeeds_GiveTheSameFight checks. Tactics (LastFleet.AI.Tactics, and the SoldierAiSystem.Tactics partial): Cover map. At load, every other walkable cell is probed with horizontal rays at crouch height in eight directions. A hit within 0.95 m makes it a cover point facing the obstacle. A second ray at standing height marks it as low (crouch to hide, stand to shoot over) or full height (step out to a precomputed peek spot to shoot). Points are thinned to one per meter per facing, keeping the snuggest first. The room has a few hundred. Safe routes to cover. Soldiers never pick cover that's more than 95° around the enemy from the soldier's side (behind the player, from the soldier's point of view), or cover whose straight route passes within 7 m of the enemy (or 60% of the current range, when closer). Soldiers don't run past you or at you to reach cover. Cost. Cover is where the AI spent most of its time, so this one's a long list of the tricks that keep it cheap: Cover points are filed in 8 m squares (CoverMap.Near), so a search only looks at the squares within 22 m, not the five thousand points of a station raid. A soldier with no cover available fights in the open and looks again after 0.5 s rather than every tick (that search, with its ray tests, was 90% of the AI's time on big levels). Path searches are capped at four per tick across all soldiers, and by a budget of cells searched: a balance that each tick tops up to 4,000 (ExpansionsPerTick, never banking more), which a search may start while it's above nothing and pays for with the cells it searched, so one long search makes the next ticks wait instead of a tick taking several. The rest wait a tick with the path they have (counted in LastSearchesDeferred), and a search that found no way isn't repeated for 2 s. A path goes stale when its goal has moved by a meter close by, or by a fifth of the way when further off (RepathDrift): someone 40 m away taking a step doesn't change the way to him, only its end, which is found again nearer. A safe-route check for cover searches at most 6,000 cells: a route to cover needing more is no route to cover. It searches into scratch memory, so a route it turns down doesn't cost the soldier the path it has. Covers ruled out (an unsafe way, or none) are kept on the brain (SoldierBrain.CoverRejects, up to four) for 3 s or until the enemy is known 3 m from where he was, so a choice put off to the next tick, or made again soon, doesn't search for them again. Soldiers scattered by a grenade pick cover again a little apart, by their seeds, over a quarter second. Choosing cover scores every point within reach without a ray (points facing away from the threat are left out first, CoverMap.Faces), then ray-tests them best score first and stops once none left could win: the same pick as testing them all, for a few tests (8 a choice on the range, 113 on a station, from 56 and 308). Other soldiers' claims are checked only within reach of the search and 4 m past it. Each cover point keeps its last ray tests' answers (the threat asked about, and whether it protects or can be fired from) until the level's geometry changes (ICollisionWorld.GeometryVersion, which a world whose geometry changes bumps; rays hit only the level, so nothing else changes them): on a station about two ray tests in three are answered so, mostly every soldier's tick-by-tick check that its cover still protects it while the enemy is where he was last seen. SoldierAiSystem.LastCoverWork counts the choices, points, claim checks and ray tests a tick. Looking for an enemy goes over only the soldier's side's living enemies, gathered once a tick in candidate order, not every character in the level; LastSightWork counts the looks, the enemies in view and the sight lines cast. A soldier that saw its enemy last tick looks every tick (it aims and fires by it); one that didn't casts its sight lines less often the further off the nearest enemy in its view is (LookInterval: every second tick within 15 m, every third within 30, every fourth beyond), spread over the ticks by seed. Why is that okay? A few ticks later to notice someone far off is nothing beside its reaction time, and most of those lines end on the wall he's behind. At most four cover choices are made a tick (MaxCoverChoicesPerTick); the rest decide a moment later, so a squad that all wants cover at once (scattered by a grenade) spreads its choosing over a few ticks. To see where the time goes, every search is counted by what it was for (PathPurpose: chase, cover, cover route, room, search, roam) in SoldierAiSystem.PathSearches, with the cells it searched, whether it found a way, whether it fell back to the whole grid, and its time, which the developer overlay's AI section shows for the last second. The AI's tick is also timed in parts (AiSection: preparing, perception, cover choice, path searches and the rest), shown beside them. --headless --soldiers plays the level as the game does (a LocalSession: mission, doors, director, horde), adds n soldiers in squads of four around an invulnerable player where they have a way to him, and prints each system's time a tick, the AI's parts and the path searches; --level range is an open fight, a station seed one with doors. Roles rotate every roleSeconds of the squad's scoring (data, 6 s). While one of the squad's flankers is still on its way round (it hasn't called out its flank, which it only does when it moves to a new spot, or hasn't reached it), the rotation waits, up to 12 s. Tactical position system. Whether a point gives protection is decided at runtime against the threat: the cover has to face the threat, and a ray from the threat's eye to the hidden head has to be blocked by something next to the point. A point also needs a line of fire from its firing position. Scores add up travel cost, the role's preferred range band, loyalty to the current point and a pincer angle for flankers, and they exclude points claimed by squadmates or near grenades. Only points that could still win get the expensive ray tests. Squad coordinator. Each squad has a blackboard (SquadBoard): the shared target and last known position, strength (alive against peak), and covering-fire and grenade timers. Roles are reassigned every six seconds and rotate: one suppressor, one flanker once there are three, and the rest riflemen. A squad down to half its peak retreats. A squad's machine gunner is always its suppressor, and a soldier with a shotgun or SMG is always its flanker. Soldiers' guns (SoldierArms; how each frame changes the way a soldier fights is set by its archetype's soldier, a SoldierUse). Each soldier carries a gun picked by its seed: a pulse rifle (30 in 100), auto rifle (22), SMG (15), machine gun (13), shotgun (10) or marksman rifle (10). The client draws it in their hands, and their shots sound like it (riflemen keep the soldiers' own rifle sound). With an automatic gun the trigger is held for a burst (an auto rifle 0.3 to 0.55 s, an SMG a little longer, a machine gun 0.55 to 1 s). In the open, a shotgun or SMG fights at about half a rifleman's distance and a marksman at 1.4 times it. Indoors, the room sets the distance for everyone. Each gun's damage is scaled (SoldierUse.DamageScale) to hurt about as much as a pulse rifle alone. On the room-fight benchmark (ten stations), mixed squads take about 25% more health off a player clearing rooms than squads of pulse rifles do, and about the same off a player holding a room. Behavior. Soldiers move to cover (sprinting on long moves and flanks), then alternate between hiding and exposing themselves. Where the cover system has them in cover, exposing means peeking the way a player does: crouched at low cover and rising just over it, or leaning out around a wall's edge. Elsewhere they stand up or step out to the cover point's peek spot. They only shoot once they've peeked out. Calm soldiers peek to fire. When pinned down by near misses, or shaken by their squad's losses (SquadBoard.Fear: the share of the squad lost, higher for 10 s after each loss), they spend stretches ducked, firing blind at where they saw the enemy in the last 3 s, and peek out less often. Hits, reloads and near misses send them down. The suppressor stays exposed longer and fires at the last known position even without sight, which lets riflemen bound to closer cover. It only does this if a line from its position reaches that spot (the squad shares where you are, not where each of them can shoot from; this is checked four times a second), so nobody fires into a wall or floor at someone they've never seen. Near misses within 1.5 m suppress a soldier for 1.6 s. A squad that knows where you are but hasn't seen you for 2.5 s may throw a grenade (one per squad every ten seconds). It's aimed with GrenadeSystem.PitchToHit, a little short to allow for the roll, and only thrown if its arc is clear (GrenadeArc: eight rays along it; a ceiling, a lintel or a wall more than 3.5 m short of the landing spot stops the throw). So soldiers don't throw into walls anymore, and under a station ceiling they lob no further than about 17 m. Soldiers run from any enemy grenade within 7 m. Indoors (SoldierAiSystem.Rooms, generated levels only). The level's rooms and doorways reach the AI as a RoomMap: which room a point is in, the doorways of a room, the route between rooms with the fewest doorways, and whether a doorway is shut (found by a ray across it and cached for a second). Soldiers placed a room apart are joined into fire teams of up to four (FireTeamSize), so a station's one- and two-soldier rooms fight as squads. A sighting alerts soldiers up to two rooms away by doorways, as well as anyone in earshot, and a squad learns where the enemy is from what its members hear. Within 14 m indoors, cover and fighting distances shrink to fit the room (4 to 11 m for riflemen), and soldiers stop backing off across it. A squad that loses the enemy in another room takes that room by plan instead of trickling through the doorway. It holds the doorway he went through from spread-out spots out of line with it, aimed at it, for 4 to 7 s once in place (whoever comes through gets shot at with the aim already settled). Then it stacks up on both sides, throws a grenade in, waits for it to go off and goes in together, with its flanker coming through another doorway if one can be reached without crossing the room. Squads taking the same room stay in step and go in through different doorways. The plans cost a few room-graph searches when the enemy changes rooms, and a handful of rays per soldier per step. Going in isn't always right. A squad placed in the station contains first (holds the doorway 20 s longer, ContainSeconds), while one sent in as reinforcements goes in right away. A squad of fewer than three, or one that has lost anyone during the plan, holds the doorway and keeps him in rather than assaulting. Soldiers have no keycards. A locked door that's still shut (or a closet's) isn't a way through for their paths (ShutDoors, refreshed whenever a door opens or shuts; the mission bot uses it too), so nobody crowds against one. A squad that knows the enemy is on the other side lies in wait instead: the same spread spots, on its side of the door and with a view of the door itself, aimed at it, flashlights off unless it's dark, for up to two minutes (AmbushMemorySeconds). It never stacks or breaches, and when the door opens whoever walks through is shot at once. If nobody comes through within 6 s of it opening, the squad makes a new plan through it. Bounding (SoldierAiSystem.Tactics). A squad moves cover to cover a few at a time. At most a third of it (at least one) is moving while the rest stay in cover and put fire on where the enemy was, seen or not (with longer exposures while someone is moving). A soldier claims the bound and the spot the moment it picks them, so two never start in the same tick or head for the same spot. Falling back, a bound is at most 10 m (BoundDistance), and spots past the squad's rearmost soldier score better. Advancing, the squad leapfrogs. Only a soldier at the back of those taking turns (within 2 m of the rearmost, or any of them when they're level) may bound (AdvanceTurn). The ones taking turns leave out the suppressor (the base of fire, which stays back), a soldier that recently found no cover ahead, and anyone pushing or falling back (MayBound, SquadBoard.BoundFarthest), so one soldier that can't move never holds up the rest. A bound goes to cover near the lead's line or up to 3 m in front of it (LeadSlack), or 4 m or more to catch up. It's up to 16 m (AdvanceBoundDistance), or as far as it takes to come up to the lead, with travel costing in the score so nearer cover wins. The squad's ranges from the enemy (SquadBoard nearest, next nearest, farthest and next farthest) count each soldier at where it's going, its cover, so one in the middle of a bound already counts as being where it's bounding to. Cohesion (Personality.Cohesion, data). Every cover pick except a fall back keeps a soldier within the cohesion distance of the rest of its squad, towards the enemy or away. The lead's line, and 3 m in front of it, always counts as within, since where a soldier bounds to has to be somewhere it can hold. A soldier that has cover within it won't leave it for a spot outside. One that has none (at the start of a fight, or after a push) or is already outside weighs the distance against the spot (and still takes cover: it keeps cover that protects rather than fight in the open). Spots within 4 m of a squadmate score worse, and soldiers keep 2 m apart. A spot is only taken if the path to it (not the straight line) stays clear of the enemy, so nobody runs down the corridor he's in, or past him, to reach a flank. A squad hunting an enemy more than 7 m away bounds the same way. Whether a spot protects is a short ray from it towards the enemy, so cover still counts when he's gone to ground behind his own cover. Measuring it (RoomFightTests, LASTFLEET_ROOM_SEEDS=N, about five minutes for 40 seeds). So do the tactics actually make soldiers harder? On generated stations, a bot that shoots whoever is in view (with a human reaction time and a wandering aim) holds a room next to a squad's, or clears rooms toward the nearest soldier, for 75 s. The damage it takes is compared with and without the indoor tactics. The surprise: the tactics alone came out about even (a few percent either way: soldiers mostly meet a player one or two at a time and are dead within about five seconds of fighting, so how they go in matters less than how they shoot). What made them harder was the duel itself: shorter pauses between bursts (0.5 to 0.95 s), tighter aim (4° on first sight, settling to 1.1°) and quicker reactions (0.4 to 0.65 s). Those raised the damage taken by 34% when clearing rooms and 22% when holding one, compared with the AI before this change. LASTFLEET_AI_TUNING="Name=value;..." tries other tuning against the default. Behavior trees (LastFleet.AI.Behavior). What a soldier does from moment to moment is its behavior's tree (SoldierBehavior: content/defs/ai/.json; the shipped soldier.json is built into the AI as SoldierBehavior.Default). Every tick, after perception and the awareness transitions (idle, alerted, engaging, hunting, searching, which are still code because they follow what the soldier sees and hears), SoldierAiSystem runs the whole tree from its root. It's a reactive tree: no node keeps running from one tick to the next, so a soldier never stays in a branch after its reason is gone. The node types: Composites are selector, sequence, all (runs every child, for things done alongside the main choice) and not. Conditions are awareness, intent, check (compares one of the scoring's inputs), hasCover, squadAlive, distanceToEnemy and seesEnemy. Actions are the soldier's own code (BehaviorAction): roam, watchEnemy, chooseIntent, holdCover, boundForward, pushEnemy, fallBack, fightFromCover (the four in one, picked by the intent), fightInOpen, clearRooms, goToEnemy, searchForEnemy, lookAround, topUpMagazine, throwGrenade and dodgeGrenades. An action node's value is its setting, and only searchForEnemy has one. chooseIntent only sets SoldierBrain.Intent (every reconsiderSeconds). The shipped tree branches on it with intent conditions to the four cover actions, each a FightFromCover with its own mode. boundForward fails without doing anything when it isn't the soldier's turn or PickCover finds no spot ahead (AdvanceBlockedSeconds, 3 s), so the selector falls through to holdCover. The scoring sees both cases as advanceBlocked (which gates out advance in the shipped file). A change of intent to hold keeps the cover a soldier has or is heading to; any other change looks again right away. A soldier on its way to cover it picked doesn't pick again until it gets there (and 1 s after), whatever its role, intent or timer, unless that cover stops protecting it, it gets stuck (2 s without progress gives up the cover) or it falls back. The shipped advance is gated on range > 12, so when they're close enough to fight from where they are, the squad holds. The file is a flat list of nodes with ids and children (plus x, y and a note for Studio), compiled to arrays (BehaviorTree) so a tick allocates nothing. Loose nodes that can't be reached from the root are kept but not checked. The shipped tree started as a branch-for-branch copy of the hand-written state machine it replaced. A behavior's scoring sits next to its tree in the same file, and a behavior whose tree never chooses an intent doesn't need one. SoldierAiSystem.Behaviors holds them all, the soldier first, and SoldierBrain.Behavior is a soldier's own (BehaviorIndex(id)). The game loads every behavior file in content/defs/ai (AiContent). A behavior's Needs (BodyAbility: fire, reload, throw, crouch, lean, blind fire; worked out from its tree's actions by BodyAbilities.For) must be in the capabilities of its variant's body type's graph. After all, a behavior that throws grenades on a body that can't throw would look silly! BodyNeeds (client) names any variant where they aren't (logged by AiContent, and shown as a problem in Studio's AI workspace), and any capability in a graph that isn't an ability or is missing its action (docs/plans/animation-2.md, phase 4). Enemy variants (LastFleet.AI.Enemies, content/defs/ai/enemies.json; the shipped file is built into the AI as EnemyRoster.Default). Each variant is a kind of enemy soldier: the behavior it thinks with, its side (hostile, or the Choir), health, damage scale, grenades, run and sprint speed, whether it drops loot, the frames it carries by weight, and how often a squad from each source is that variant (EnemySource: a level's squads, the mission's reinforcements and closets, the director's patrols, and the Choir's squads sent with the horde). A squad is all one variant, picked by the roster in play (EnemyRoster.InPlay, set by AiContent on load and by Studio while editing) from the squad's seed, so it's the same on every machine (SoldierSpawner.SquadVariant). Its soldiers' guns are picked from the variant's weights by their seeds (EnemyRoster.PickWeapon, the same draw the old kit used). SimulationSetup.SpawnSoldier takes the variant's body (SoldierBody). The brain keeps its variant (SoldierBrain.Variant), and SoldierAiSystem.BehaviorOf resolves a variant's behavior by id (a behavior set directly with SoldierBrain.Behavior wins; Studio uses that to try one out). The shipped soldier and Choir Lancer are the soldiers the game already had, number for number. A variant's Body (an animation graph) and Model (content/characters) are what the client draws it as, and each soldier's variant is sent with it (SoldierVariant on a client's replica). Intent (UtilityModel, content/defs/ai/soldier.json; TacticalUtility scores with the shipped model). Every half second, an engaged soldier scores four intents from what it knows (TacticalInputs: its health, the target's health and whether it's reloading when visible, range, time since the squad saw the target, being pinned, the suppressor's covering fire, and its role). The scoring is data: Each intent (IntentRule) starts at its base (or its base for the soldier's role). It adds its terms (UtilityTerm: a weight times a curve over one input, or a weight by role, each only when its conditions hold). A curve (UtilityCurve) is a from-to line, or keys joined by straight lines. It's multiplied by its factors (UtilityFactor). An intent whose gates fail scores 0. The current intent gets a stickiness bonus (0.1) so soldiers don't dither, and the term that added the most to the winner is kept as its reason (IntentReason). The shipped file is built into the AI assembly (UtilityModel.Default), so a world without the content folder plays the same, and a test proves it scores the same as the hand-written code it replaced over 20,000 inputs. Every squad gets a personality (Personality) by share, from its number and the level's seed (UtilityModel.PersonalityOf). A personality is a scale on each intent's score, plus how many of a squad of three or more flank: Steady (half of squads) uses the scores as they are. Aggressive moves up and pushes more and falls back less. Cautious holds, falls back early and sends nobody round the side. Flanking sends two. The game reads the file at startup (AiContent) and falls back to the shipped model if it has problems. The AI debugger shows a soldier's squad personality. Intent Raised by Effect Hold The default; being pinned; the suppressor role Keep the current cover, retargeting every 6–9 s Advance Covering fire; the enemy beyond 20 m; the enemy hidden for a while (weakened by being pinned or hurt) Next cover at least 3 m closer, retargeting every 3.5–5.5 s: bounding overwatch Push The enemy reloading or below 60% health, in sight and within 22 m; much less when a squadmate is already pushing Leave cover and close to 11 m, firing Fall back Own health below 50%; a broken squad Cover at least 6 m farther away, firing positions not required Searching for a lost enemy (SoldierAiSystem.Search, the tree's searchForEnemy). If you duck out of sight, where should a soldier look? Not where you were, but where you probably went. SquadBoard keeps how he was moving when last seen (LastHeading, from his velocity; a heard position has none) and, once a member starts searching, its guesses (SearchLeads, eight at most). The guesses are: straight on along his heading, as far as he'd get in a couple of seconds; a point 2.5 m past each open doorway of his room and, out to the node's value in rooms (2 by default), past the doorways beyond. Each is weighted by how well it lines up with his heading (sharper the faster he was going; with no heading, away from the squad), with nearer ones counting more and each room further out counting half as much; where he was. Each guess is moved to the nearest walkable floor, close ones are merged, and the weights are turned into shares. A searching member takes the best free guess for it (the likeliest, with the nearer one winning near-ties; a guess whose taker hasn't worked on it for ten ticks is free again), walks there (aiming once within 8 m), and looks around it for 1.5 s. Then it's checked. An unreachable guess is checked right away. The action fails when every guess has been checked, and the shipped tree falls through to lookAround. A sighting (Share) ends the search, and a heard shot (Hear) makes the guesses again from where it came from. The searchLeads input (unchecked guesses) lets a check node branch on it. Barks (BarkLog, like the ShotLog). Soldiers say what they decided or what happened: contact, lost contact, searching, all clear, flanking left or right, covering fire, moving up, pushing, the enemy reloading, falling back, reloading, frag out, grenade, man down, pinned. A soldier speaks at most once every 2.5 s except for urgent warnings, and a squad doesn't repeat a bark within 2 to 10 s depending on the kind. The client (BarkFeed) shows barks within 40 m as text over the speaker's head and as subtitles. The words, with variants, live in the client (BarkLines); the simulation only says which bark. AI tuning (F3, AI tuning). Pick a side to tune (the station's or the Choir's), then use the sliders for every SoldierTuning value (TuningFields, grouped the same way as Studio's Tuning tab). Changes apply on the next tick. Copy gives you what the side changes from the file's shared values, the way tuning.json writes it, and reset goes back to the file's values. AI debugger (F3, AI section). A table of soldiers with their state, role and intent. Click one to see its intent scores, the reason, its inputs, its cover and its last bark. A timeline shows every soldier's role and intent over the last 20 s, and Labels writes each soldier's id, role and intent over its head. Destruction (DestructionSystem, Destructible). Level parts named Break_* (found by BreakableLayout) become props with health based on material: glass 1, wood 90, metal 140. A shot that hits a prop's surface damages it (and stops there, glass included). A grenade damages every prop within its radius at 1.5 times its damage to people. A broken prop's collision is switched off, so it stops blocking movement, sight and shots (the AI's cover checks and sight lines update at once), and a BreakRecord tells the client to hide the part (with a negative tint alpha) and throw debris. DestructionSystem.RestoreAll repairs everything for a restarted fight. Drops lying on a prop that breaks (weapons, piles, crates, cases: DropFallSystem) fall onto whatever is under them; the snapshot already carries their position. One gotcha: the navigation grid is only built once, so the floor under a broken crate stays unwalkable for soldiers. Levels (Levels, EncounterLayout). Each level module has an .encounter.json next to it with the player's spawn, the squads (each one its own squad for the AI) and the ammo crates. The client plays a station raid from a random seed by default (Levels.Choose), and the outpost with --level slice. Smoke and headless runs use the grey-box room (--level range), so their numbers stay comparable. FightSession owns a fight on the client: it spawns squads, crates and props, turns breaks into debris, shows AREA CLEAR when every soldier is dead, restarts the fight, and keeps a PlaytestReport for each attempt. Grenades live in the simulation (GrenadeSystem), so players and soldiers share them. A fresh press of the grenade button throws one along the view at 16 m/s. Grenades bounce off the level and explode after 2.2 s for up to 110 damage within 6 m. They need a clear line to the body (so cover works), and never hurt the thrower's side, except the thrower. Explosions go to an ExplosionLog for the client. Characters block each other in CharacterBodySystem, in the simulation rather than in Jolt: velocity into another capsule is removed and overlaps are eased apart, using start-of-tick positions so the order doesn't matter. Each character only looks at the bodies in its square of a grid (as wide as two capsules) and the eight around it, in the order they were gathered, which gives the same result as looking at every body. Physics The simulation never calls Jolt. Instead it talks to an ICollisionWorld: add a character, move it with a velocity, switch its capsule between standing and crouching, ask whether it can stand, cast a ray. There are two implementations: Implementation Where Used by FlatGroundWorld LastFleet.Simulation Unit tests and anything that needs no level: an endless floor at height 0, exactly reproducible JoltWorld LastFleet.Physics The game, --headless and the physics tests: the grey-box room Characters are Jolt CharacterVirtuals: kinematic capsules standing on their feet, 0.35 m radius, 1.8 m tall standing and 1.2 m crouched. The controller decides the velocity, and JoltWorld.MoveCharacter works out where it goes with ExtendedUpdate. That slides along walls, walks up steps up to 0.4 m, sticks to the floor going down stairs and slopes, and refuses slopes steeper than 46°. A couple of details keep movement honest: On walkable ground the requested velocity is first turned along the slope (JoltWorld.AlongGround: horizontal velocity kept, vertical speed added to stay on the surface), so walking up a slope at an angle keeps the line you're walking instead of sliding along the slope. The velocity handed back is what was asked for minus what the level blocked, never more, so stepping up a stair or being pushed out of a wall can't add speed. A character is only grounded when Jolt reports OnGround and it isn't moving up, so the tick a jump starts never counts as standing. Crouching swaps the capsule. Shrinking always works; standing up fails if the taller capsule would overlap the level. While crouched, the body system asks every tick whether the character could stand, and MovementState.CeilingBlocked keeps the controller crouched (at crouch speed) until it can. Mantling (Mantle, MantleSystem) only uses rays, so it works against any ICollisionWorld. It needs a wall at knee height in front, a flat top between 0.45 and 1.6 m above the feet (found by a ray cast down from above), and room to stand on it. The climb goes straight up, then level over the edge. Cover and peeking (CoverSystem, the way Red Orchestra does it) works the same for players and soldiers. It only uses rays, runs every fourth tick per character (spread across ticks), and never changes mid-peek or mid-burst. A character is in cover automatically when something is within 0.8 m in front of its body at waist height and it's facing it within 60°. No cover button needed! If the view over it is clear at standing eye height, it's low cover, and a crouched character is in it (CoverKind.Low; the top is found by a ray down onto it, 0.8 to 1.6 m). The character ducks so its eye is 12 cm under the top (no lower than 0.7 m). Otherwise it's a wall, and the character is in cover beside its edge (Left or Right) if there's room to lean 0.5 m to that side and the view straight ahead from there is clear (it checks the side it's looking towards first). Holding aim peeks (MovementState.Peek, out in 0.2 s, back in 0.15 s, eased). For low cover it rises until the eye is 22 cm over the top (so the shots clear it, without standing up). For a wall it leans the eye 0.5 m out around the edge (MovementState.Lean). The eye is MovementState.EyeAt(feet). It's where shots leave from, where the head's hit sphere is (the top of the body capsule leans 70% as far and the hips stay behind), where the camera is, and what soldiers see and aim at (the chest when it's showing, otherwise the head). Firing without aiming while in cover fires blind (BlindFire, for the rest of a burst too): from over the top, or 0.5 m out around the edge, with the body hidden and 8° more spread. While peeking a character moves at 30% speed. Moving 0.5 m from where it took cover, standing up from low cover, sprinting, sliding, mantling or being downed takes it out of cover. The HUD draws a small half circle beside the crosshair on the side aiming will peek to (above it for low cover), fading as the peek comes out, and orange while firing blind (CoverHud). The gun goes up over the cover or out around the edge along with the shots, on your screen and on everyone else's. Other players see the cover and peek as a byte in each character's entry (since protocol version 17) and work out the lean from the facing. The predicted player runs the same system. Static geometry comes from the same MeshData the renderer draws. Each part (glTF node) with a body becomes one static Jolt body in its MeshPart.Shape (StaticBodies): a box fitted exactly with its rotation (walls, floors, ramps: the default), its triangles as they are (Mesh), or an upright cylinder around them (Cylinder). Placed furniture gets its shape from its model's entry in content/props/colliders.json (ModelColliders, ColliderKind; see docs/plans/model-colliders.md): a desk is collided with as its drawn mesh, a barrel as a cylinder, and the part's triangles are what rays hit, so movement, shots, sight, cover and the navigation grid agree. Parts can opt in or out by name and usage: A part whose name ends in _NoCollision is drawn but not collided with or hit by rays. One ending in _CollisionOnly is collided with but not drawn (MeshPart.Usage). Generated levels also use PartUsage.Rays (hit by rays but with no body: a face that doesn't have to be a box, such as a ceiling, which rays only see from the side it faces) and PartUsage.Body (a box characters bump into that rays pass through). Stairs use both: drawn steps over an invisible ramp, as most shooters do, so walking up them is smooth from any angle and the camera doesn't jolt on each step. Ray casts run against the mesh's triangles through TriangleRaycaster, a bounding-volume hierarchy that's deterministic, allocation-free and ignores back faces, like Jolt's own mesh shapes. Breaking parts. ICollisionWorld.SetSurfaceSolid switches a level part's collision off or on. JoltWorld removes the part's box body (but keeps it, so a repaired prop can go back) and tells its TriangleRaycaster to skip the part's triangles. Worlds without parts ignore it. Debris (DebrisWorld) is cosmetic and client-side. It's a second Jolt physics system with its own copy of the level's bodies (the same StaticBodies), stepped at frame rate on its own thread with Jolt's thread pool (up to four workers). Each frame finishes the step started the frame before, draws it, and starts the next one, so the step runs in parallel with the rest of the frame and the pieces are drawn a frame late. Every other call waits for any step in flight first. A broken prop splits into a grid of box fragments (thin shards for glass) thrown in the direction of whatever broke it. They tumble, bounce and settle, then shrink away after six seconds. At most 160 are live at once. The pieces go to the renderer separately from the other moving triangles (FrameGeometry.Debris). They're drawn normally, in the ray prepass and in shadow maps, but never built into the ray-traced scene. Why leave them out? So a burst of them doesn't force a ray structure rebuild every frame (they cast no traced shadows and don't show in traced reflections). F3 shows the pieces, the step's time and how long the frame waited for it. Surfaces. JoltWorld.AddStaticMesh returns the surface number of the mesh's first part. Part i is surface first + i, and every RayHit reports the surface it hit (RayHit.NoSurface for the flat-ground world). Gameplay uses it to find targets, and later destructibles and hit materials, from level parts by name (TargetLayout in LastFleet.Content). Gaps in BRUTAL's Jolt binding (2026.10.2) So why all the workarounds above? The managed binding declares 3,246 native functions, and 774 of them were missing from its native library. These are the ones that shaped this design. Good news since then: 2026.10.4 exports the mesh, convex hull and cylinder shapes and the NarrowPhaseQuery casts, and builds hulls without crashing (MeshColliderTests, docs/plans/model-colliders.md), so level pieces can now be meshes and cylinders. Rays still go through TriangleRaycaster. Missing or broken Effect Workaround NarrowPhaseQuery casts (all) No Jolt ray or shape queries TriangleRaycaster Indexed MeshShapeSettings constructor; the triangle-list one passes no triangles No mesh collision One box per node ConvexHullShapeSettings crashes when a body is created from it No hull collision Non-box nodes are rejected at load with their name PhysicsSystem.GetDefault*Filter, SetSupportingVolume Null filters crash ExtendedUpdate Jolt's base filters (BroadPhaseLayerFilter.Create() and friends), which accept everything; Jolt's default supporting volume Jolt's ray queries could now replace TriangleRaycaster behind the same interface; nothing needs them yet. Procedural levels LastFleet.ProcGen turns a seed and a mission template into a level, in the design doc's three passes. It's headless, has no physics, and is deterministic: one seeded random stream per pass (DeterministicRandom.ForStream), modules in id order, and no decisions in the layout that depend on dictionary order or floating point. Why so strict? Because the same seed, template and module library have to give the same mesh on every machine. That's how a co-op client builds the host's level itself! The procgen revamp (plans/procgen-revamp.md) moved rooms from hand-drawn modules to designer data, in phases. Since its last phase, every room is built from an archetype. Its foundations (Phase 1) and its structure and styles (Phase 2) didn't change any level; rooms in any shape (Phase 3) change them on purpose. So how do we know when a change alters levels? GoldenLevelTests holds the fingerprints of the station raid's first hundred seeds, made with the repository's procgen data the same way the game makes them. A change that alters levels records the new values and says why. Procgen data (Data/ProcGenData) is what designers author for generation, in content/defs/procgen. It's read once and shared by every level built from the same content. That's the content's tags (tags.json), surface styles (styles.json), room archetypes (archetypes.json), props and placement rules (props.json, rules.json), networks (networks.json), loot assignments (loot.json), room typing (typing.json), plans (plans.json) and districts (districts.json). Every problem is reported at once, by file, and a file the generator doesn't read is an error. LevelGenerator takes it (or just the built-in tags and styles if none is given). The client loads it from the build, and Studio generates with it while it's being edited. Plans (Plans/) are the start of structure-first levels (plans/structure-first.md). The idea is to build a level from the outside in, its envelope first: the envelope, then the halls, then the rooms. The envelope. A LevelPlan (from plans.json) is a list of parts: a HullProfile, BoxModule, ArmPart, RingPart or PaintedMask, each adding cells or cutting them out in order. Envelope.Build makes the cells inside for a seed, each part drawing from its own stream (GenerationStage.Envelope, keyed by the part's index) in whole cells and plain arithmetic, so a seed makes the same envelope everywhere. Each part also records the shape it was drawn at (PartShape: a line with its length and half width, or a ring's radius and width). Halls and sections. PlanStructure.Build then: carves the plan's halls (SpineHall, CrossHall, RingHall, each laid on a part and following its shape; corridors first, then service ways); cuts the envelope into sections (SectionPlan: bulkheads across a part, or each part its own); puts pressure doors where corridors cross bulkheads and hatches where service ways do; stubs a hatch from each section's service way onto a corridor; counts the compartments, and lists its problems. The stubs and the bulkheads' jitter draw from GenerationStage.Circulation. Rooms. PlanLevel.Build goes on to the rooms: the cells between halls in each section are plots, cut across their length into rooms from the section's DistrictProgram (districts.json: an anchor and rooms, each an archetype with widths, weights, runs and whether it's private), with slivers a cell deep merged into a neighbor. Each room's door faces the hall it has the most frontage on; a room between two halls gets a second (usually if shared, rarely if private); a room with no hall gets a suite door. A section's anchor can span up to 16 cells each way (PlanLevel.MostAnchor, ParametricRoom.MostCells: a carrier's hangar), other rooms 8. Halls are cut into stretches within 8 by 8 cells (one two or more cells across only along its length, so each stretch is its whole width: PlanLevel.HallBlock), joined by openings as wide as the hall (ParametricRoom cuts a doorway as wide as its connector says). Every piece is then built as a room module with exactly its doorways (so none goes unused), cached by archetype, shape and doors per set of procgen data, and placed. A stretch of a hall that names a style (HallPart.Style) is built in it; one two or more cells across also gets its style's hall structure (RoomFinish.Frames, ParametricRoom.HallFrames: frames, arches, a colonnade or pillars at every cell boundary along it, frames if the style has none, each with a lamp up its faces toward the hall as a module light), never in a doorway or across the way through (ReachGrid.TryBlock). Its pressure doorways through a bulkhead, side by side, become one connector its width (PlanLevel.WidenBulkheadDoors), and the assembler builds one door across them (DoorSpans: a pressure door or a gate, its frame, reader and sign at its edges); the doorways it spans get none. Layout() and Mesh() give the LevelLayout and mesh. PlanPicture draws one for --plan-png. Decks and stairs. A plan of several decks (LevelPlan.Decks) gets a structure per deck, its bulkheads lined up through them, and PlanLevel builds it deck by deck on one grid, pieces and doorways carrying their deck and placements their story. Stair cores (PlanCore, PlanPieceKind.Stairs) are placed before the halls are cut into stretches: a two-story stairwell turned to fit near its frame, clear of both decks' halls, its foot and landing joined to corridors by short passages. Pins. Pins (PlanPin, LevelPlan.Pins) hold set pieces in place on a part, as cores do, or round a ring as cells from its center scaled with its radius in whole numbers (PlanPin.CellOn, and MovedTo back for Studio's drag). A room pin's room is cut round the plot cell nearest its cell (PlanLevel.Pins, Pinned): the plot's strips stop short of it and it starts about its middle on the pin (round a ring, the wedge reaching it is it), the anchor if it names its district's anchor's archetype. The boarding pin makes the insertion the exit of the recipe's kind nearest it (PlanLevel.Boarding, MissionEmbedder). A plan without pins builds as it did. Hangars. A district's anchor may be a tall archetype (flight_hangar, two stories, vertical floor none), built its full height where no deck is over it (PlanLevel.StandsTall); Layout() puts its upper story in the envelope and its outward walls on the hull, so the skin wraps it. An archetype with bay gets a ship entrance (Modules/ShipBay, RoomFinish.Bays) in each wall wholly on the hull with no doorway, a pair across from each other if it has one (flown straight through). For each entrance, ParametricRoom: leaves the wall open on every story but a post at each end; adds the field (BayField_, PartUsage.Body: characters bump into it, rays and shots pass) and a lit frame; faces the dropship's nose to the first entrance; and keeps its pad and the lane in from each entrance clear (RoomModule.KeepClear): out of the furnishing's floor and, in the level, blocking every placement rule (RoomFloor.Blocks) and reserved in its reach. The assembler cuts the skin and any wall dressing at each entrance (LevelAssembler.Outside); hull breaches skip those walls, and pod bays skip the hangar.
