The client draws the field's shimmer (BayFields), and a dropship's hold is roofed so it stands in a hangar of any height. Smooth halls. A ring hall (RingHall) is built smooth (Modules/AngledHall, Modules/HallArc): the structure carves it on every cell its band (across meters) touches and remembers its bend (PlanStructure.BandAt); its stretches are cut apart from any other hall's and built round the bend, the walls straight sides of at most 1.5 m, each a box turned to its side (MeshBuilder.AddTurnedBox), clipped to the stretch's cells. A room's door onto it gets a throat in to the wall (a room only counts a ring cell as frontage where the bend is within a cell of its door, AngledHall.Reaches); a narrow doorway across the band (a pressure door) gets jambs so its door seals. The module carries its band (RoomModule.Band, a HallBand: a HallArc round a ring or a HallLine on a slant), so the dressing hangs its panels along it, turned to it, and leaves its cells' edges without trims or services. A bridge part (BridgePart) runs out from a center at any angle; a spine on it is built smooth along its line (PlanStructure.CarveBridge), meeting the rings' halls either end; where smooth halls overlap, each one's walls stop on the other's floor. A ring part's plots are cut into wedges round its center (PlanLevel.CutRound). Plan missions (Plans/MissionEmbedder, Plans/ExitPlanner, Missions/PlanRecipe): a template with a plan block (ship_raid.json) is laid out by a plan. LevelGenerator.LayOut picks the plan from the seed and builds its PlanLevel with the mission read in after the doors are placed and before the rooms are built (GenerationStage.Embedding), trying seeds made from the level's own (at most PlanAttempts) when it can't be. Here's how the embedder fits a mission into the ship: It makes an airlock vestibule (a small room on the hull with one door onto a corridor, ExitPlanner.Vestibules) piece 0, the insertion, built against the hull side it found (RoomFinish.Hull, RoomModule.Hull). Zones are runs of the fewest bulkheads crossed to get somewhere from it, so every door and hatch from one zone to the next is a gate (the deeper zone's lock id, every door of a gate its own Lock__ part). The objective goes in the zone before the last (a room tagged for it, or one made into its archetype, of the kind picked by weight from the recipe's objectives: a hack, a download or a self-destruct, with a terminal set up in whatever room it is), finishing it opening the last gate. Extraction is at the deepest exit of the last zone (a hangar the dropship lands in, or else an airlock it docks at: a vestibule's hull side, a room's side wholly on the hull, or any wall of a room on the hull with no doorway in it, ExitPlanner.Dock, PlanMission.Dock; the room keeps the floor before it clear, the squad stands 1.8 m in from it, and the assembler builds the outer hatch in its docking collar with an amber lamp over it, Airlock.BuildDock). Each other keycard goes in the zone before its gate, off the way through. Spawn closets are cut from void cells, or the corners of big rooms, beside the halls. The result (PlanMission) gives every piece its zone and role, every doorway its lock, and a MissionGraph in which each piece is the node of its own index, so the assembler, placements, the Director and the bot read it as they read a solver's. The client plays one as : (frigate:7), with generation settings after a slash as a station's (carrier:41/s150-cfuel-k150). A recipe can board by a hangar instead (Levels/Airlocks/Dropship: the dropship built on the hangar's pad, its hatch, intake and chute standing in for an airlock's, AirlockLayout.Landed), and give rooms on the hull escape pods (Levels/Pods/EscapePods, MissionLayout.Pods; the mission's EscapePod hatches and EscapedTag players). The insertion only cycles once every client has loaded (MissionSystem.Boarding). When extraction would rather leave by a hangar, the squad boards at the end farthest from it, and extraction in a hangar gets a dropship landed to take the squad off (PlanMission.Pickup, the pickup tag: its pad kept clear and the extraction point in its hold; Dropship.BuildPickup builds it with its hatch open). A vestibule's airlock goes on the hull side across from its door, or on one beside it only with the door two cells along, clear of the chamber. Tags (Tags/) are dotted names that nest (room.storage.cold is in room.storage and room). They're the vocabulary every rule uses. TagRegistry numbers them in name order and adds every parent a name implies. TagSet (what a room, marker or prop carries) and TagQuery (any, all, none) match hierarchically. The generator's own tags are built in (BuiltInTags): role.* for what a room is for, deck.1 to deck.6 for the deck it's on, and layout.main_path, layout.dead_end and layout.on_loop. Content can use them in rules but can't define them again. Room tags (Layouts/RoomTags, GeneratedLevel.RoomTags) give each placed room its role and where it sits: its deck, on the mission's main path, a dead end (one doorway), or on a loop (found from the layout's bridges). Spawn closets only get their role and are left out of the graph. Streams (Seeding/Streams) are random streams per stage, per room and per rule, keyed by fixed names. Why bother with so many? So a change to one rule changes nothing else. Code written before them keeps its own named streams, so its levels don't change. Rooms and structure (Rooms/Footprint, Structures/). A footprint is a room's grid cells, in any connected shape (RoomModule.Footprint: every cell of a kit module's bounds, or any shape within them for a built room). The layout places, overlaps, joins and finds rooms by it, and a doorway can be on an edge where the outline steps in (ModuleConnector.Inset). FineGrid is one story of it at half a meter, where shapes are carved and walls are found. StructureMarkers each have a MarkerFrame (a point, the direction into the room, and the direction along it). MarkerFrame.OnWall runs along a wall with the wall on its right as seen from its room, so up is always up. Walls are built from frames and props are placed in them; nothing is rotated by hand. EdgeClassifier finds a footprint's structure: a floor and a ceiling marker for each piece of the rectangles that cover its outline (FineRect), and along its outline a wall marker for each run between corners and doorways (WallOpening), a doorway marker for each opening, and a corner marker at each inner and outer corner (corner.inner, corner.outer; a run of three cells or more is wall.long). Surface styles (Styles/, Data/StyleReader, content/defs/procgen/styles.json) say how a room is built and how it looks, so no designer has to model a wall. StyleBuilder builds a room's floor and walls from its markers in its style. StationDressing dresses every room in its style (RoomModule.Style): its ceiling, upper walls, lintels, baseboard and stripe (TrimStyle, a fixed color or the room's deck or role color), duct, pipes and ceiling light panels. It follows the room's shape: trims run along each straight run of wall (WallRun), broken at doorways; the duct and pipes run along the longest run in each direction; and the ceiling and its panels cover each rectangle of the room (RoomRects), each rectangle lighting itself. A hall's style says what stands along it, what its floor and floor light are, and its accents (HallLook). A style only lists what differs from its base, which eventually is SurfaceStyle.Station. The station style and a style for each default deck theme are built in (SurfaceStyle.Builtins), so they exist whether or not the file lists them. Sizes the rest of the game relies on (a wall's thickness and height, a doorway's height, a panel's size) belong to the layout: a style decides how a room looks, not where people and shots can go. Colors are numbers or "#rrggbb". Modules (RoomModule, ModuleLibrary) are the rooms a level is laid out from. They're all built, never drawn: the kit's rooms and a level's own rooms from room archetypes (ParametricRoom), and the halls between them (ParametricHall). The footprint is in 4 m cells, and the height is the number of stories it stands through (Grid.StoryHeight, 3.8 m: a 3.6 m wall plus the 0.2 m slab of a room above). A built room describes itself as a scene of nodes, the way a glTF file would: Door at each connector (a 2 m doorway in the middle of a cell edge, on the floor of one of its stories), spawns, the key, terminal and extraction markers, item spots, and a Module node with its role tags. ModuleReader reads that into the module and checks the kit's rules, failing with every problem by name: whole cells, doors on the outline, a clear lane inside each door, every colliding piece a box (BoxFit, shared with physics), markers inside the room, and each role's markers present. It also finds each room's spawn spots in its geometry (RoomModule.SpawnSpots): ground-floor points on a meter grid, clear of anything a standing soldier would touch, of the walls and of every doorway's approach, two meters apart, next to cover first, each facing its nearest doorway. Item spots are where weapons, keycards, cases and supplies can lie (the onTop anchor's spots, and the key marker too). The climb marker is the foot of a ramp or stairs up from the ground floor, and whatever gets placed keeps it clear. Every connector is open in the module, and the assembler walls up the unused ones. The kit (Modules/KitRooms). A biome's kit of rooms is the archetypes whose kit names it (the station has 23, in archetypes.json): the insertion bay, four corridors, the stairwell, the spawn closet, the security office (a keycard room), the data vault and server room (objectives), the hangar (extraction), and rooms large and small: the atrium, the concourse, the cargo bay and catwalk hall (two stories), the reactor hall (5 × 5 cells, with a gallery around its core), crew quarters, the mess, the lounge, hydroponics, the lab, the office and storage. KitRooms.Build builds each one once, from a seed taken from its own id, so the kit is the same in every level and on every machine, and offers it to every level of the biome (LevelGenerator.ForKit). If a room's furnishing's required rules can't be met in its first footprint, it's tried in up to six, and a kit that can't be built throws an InvalidDataException naming the room. A kit archetype can specify its doorways exactly (doors: a side, a cell and a level each, for a rectangle of one size, with one-cell sides allowed: a corridor, a closet). Otherwise one is drawn on each side. Its set pieces are props placed by its furnishing's rules. A prop can stand in for a mission spot (PropDefinition.Marker, markerAhead meters in front of it), so the vault's terminal is wherever the vault rule put the terminal. The roles do the rest (ParametricRoom): an insertion bay puts its squad's four spawns by the wall with no doorway, facing in, and keeps the airlock's 5.6 m clear of furniture; an extraction room's marker is the free floor nearest its middle; a key room's marker lies on its first top; a passage (all of its roles are corridor) and a closet get no crate, items or guards of their own, and a closet gets three soldiers at most; a stairwell's upper floor is a landing (across its north end, with its doorway a story up). Its stairs climb from the foot to it, and the floor under the landing is kept clear first. Rooms aren't drawn in Blender anymore. Only the hub is (docs/blender/hub.md), read by GltfNodes and HubLevel. Room archetypes and shapes (Rooms/RoomArchetype, Data/ArchetypeReader, content/defs/procgen/archetypes.json; Rooms/ShapeBuilder, ShapeRecipe). These are the kinds of room built from the seed, as designer data. Each has: a shape recipe: a rectangle, an L, a T, a U, a cross, or a blob of rectangles run together, within a fewest and most number of cells and how much a cut takes; or a stamp, cells drawn in Studio and built as drawn; the content tags it carries (into GeneratedLevel.RoomTags) and the roles it can play; the surface style it's built and dressed in, and its furniture; whether its corners are cut at 45° (chamfer, 0.5 or 1 m) and whether pillars hold up its ceiling; its second story if it's two tall (vertical, a VerticalSpec); a weight. A template names the archetypes its rooms can be typed as (archetypes; see Room typing), and never a tall one in a one-story template. With none, its built rooms are rectangles of parametricRoomSize, offered alongside the kit's. A corner is cut where the room is on one side only and neither wall has a doorway (Levels/CornerChamfer). The cut is a wedge: a box rotated 45° (MeshBuilder.AddTurnedBox; boxes, rotated or not, are the only solids level collision accepts), with its back inside the walls. The wall runs that everything is laid along (WallRun: trims, the duct and pipes, lockers) stop short of it. Do shaped rooms make layout harder? Barely: LayoutBudgetTests keeps the layout's attempts with shaped rooms close to what rectangles took (1.53 per level with rooms typed, against 1.56, over the first hundred seeds). Room typing (Typing: RoomTyper, TypingRule (CountRule, AdjacencyRule, DistanceRule), RoomTyping; content/defs/procgen/typing.json, read by TypingReader). Before the layout, each room of the mission graph gets a type: the kit's own (built once for every level) or one of the template's archetypes, so a level's room mix follows the designers' rules. A room's domain is only the kit's type where the mission's markers are needed (the insertion, keycard rooms, the objective, extraction, transit: these are pinned). Otherwise it's the kit's at kitShare and the archetypes that play its role for the rest, by weight. Rules work on each room's tags as each type would give them (its role, its deck, layout.main_path, and the archetype's content tags or type.kit). There are three kinds: a count: the fewest and most rooms of a kind each deck, or the level, has; an adjacency: no room of A joined to one of B (a room and the one it's reached from); a distance: rooms of A no nearer than so many steps along the mission's routes to rooms of B, and each within so many steps of one. The search is wave function collapse over the graph. The rules narrow the domains: pairs of rooms are kept arc consistent for adjacency and least distance; a count's scope rules its rooms out once it's at its most, or forces them at its fewest; a distance's most rules out a room of A with no room of B in reach; and the level's budget of archetypes (parametricRooms drawn) rules out others once it's spent. Then the room with the lowest entropy (ties broken by node id) gets a type drawn by weight from the typing stream, backing up when a domain empties, within 4,000 steps. A rule set that can't be satisfied throws a RoomTypingException whose trace describes each contradiction (the rule, and the room or scope). Each room's typing is kept (GeneratedLevel.Typing, NodeTyping: what it could have been and at what weight, and what ruled out each type it isn't). One room of each archetype used is built, from a stream keyed by its id, and the solver places that module for each room typed as it (tried 24 times at a doorway, versus 8 for the kit's). An archetype whose furnishing can't be met is left unbuilt, and its rooms use the kit's. Kit rooms are tagged type.kit. The station raid's rules: never two cargo holds on a deck, no offices joined, labs three steps apart. About one mission room in six is built (for one in four of those an archetype is allowed), and a level takes about 145 ms. RoomTypingTests checks that a thousand seeds never break a rule, that typing is the same each time, that a contradictory rule set explains why within seconds, and that the layout builds each room as typed. Built rooms (ParametricRoom, finished the way a RoomFinish says: look, furniture, cut corners, pillars). A template can ask for rooms made from the level's seed (parametricRooms; station raids build from three to five archetypes). Each is built once for the level (LevelGenerator) and placed for every room typed as its archetype. A template that names no archetypes gets rectangles offered alongside the kit's rooms for rooms on the way and side rooms. Each built room fills its footprint, with a doorway on its outline facing every direction (now and then two on a long side) and a post filling each corner that juts into the room. It's furnished by the rules of a furnishing (rules.json: offices, a warehouse, a lab, a plaza; the archetype's own, or one drawn at random), placed the same way as the level's rules (see Placement rules) on a half-meter map of the floor (ParametricRoom.FloorPlan: inside its shape, clear of its walls, cut corners and pillars), from the room's own stream. The shipped furnishings try seeded pieces anywhere, and each piece is only kept if it: stays 1.2 m from every other; stays clear of every doorway's approach (a lane in from the doorway and inside the room, never on the doorway's far side, where a shaped room's bounds have no space); and leaves every doorway connected to every other with no open floor cut off. If a room's furnishing's required rules can't be met, it's built again in another footprint, up to four times, and left out if none work. The room is then built as boxes and markers (soldiers on open floor facing the nearest doorway, items on furniture) and read by ModuleReader like a drawn module, so the kit's rules and the spawn spots work the same way. Over 30 levels, about three rooms in ten are built. Tall rooms (RoomFinish.Vertical, Rooms/VerticalSpec, Rooms/StoryFloor, Modules/TallRoom, Modules/UpperFloor, Modules/Climb). A built room can be up to four stories tall (VerticalSpec.MostStories, the most a mission allows), with a floor, or none, on each story above the ground (StoryFloor). Each floor is planned on the half-meter grid inside its shape: a gallery around the walls, open in the middle; a mezzanine across the end with the most wall; catwalks along the two long walls with a 3 m bridge between them; a stairwell's landing; none (the story is open from the floor below). Each is as deep as the archetype says (2.5 to 8 m). Only the largest connected piece is kept, and nothing goes behind a cut corner, whose wedge runs up every story. A room of open stories is just tall. One whose middle story has no floor goes from its ground floor to its top floor with nothing in between. TallRoom plans the floors from the ground up. Each floor is reached from the nearest floor below where its stairs fit, otherwise from one further down, with the ground last. Stairs (Climb) climb one story at a time, either as one 7 m flight or as a switchback's two half flights with a landing. To go up more than one story they stack: either turning back at a landing a story up (two lanes wide), or running on straight, end to end with landings between (one lane wide, for a narrow room). The kind asked for is tried first, then the other. A flight is a box tilted up its slope (28.5°, within the character's and the navigation grid's limits). Stepped blocks fill in under the first story's flights (higher ones have a story's headroom over the one below, and railings on their sides). A stair position is only kept if: it's a cell clear of the walls; its column is open on every story it climbs through and arrives at, and each landing a story up is open on its story; it's clear of other stairs on the stories they share; from the ground, the doorways below stay connected and its foot can be reached (furniture keeps off it); from an upper floor, its foot can be reached from where that floor's own stairs arrive, and so can everything else on that floor (doorways only where their lane is). Stairs arrive on the floor or, if no such place works, on a bridge a story up across open space to a full row of the floor, which then becomes part of it. A floor whose stairs don't fit anywhere is left out, and a room where none of the floors can be reached is built one story tall, as it always was. Railings (1 m) stand on every edge over open space, except where stairs arrive. Each floor has a doorway on each side where it reaches the wall (ModuleConnector.Level), so the layout joins it to rooms on that story, and two soldier spots. Each climb from the ground has its foot marked (Marker_Climb, RoomModule.Climbs), which later placement keeps clear. Floors and stairs use their own random streams, and up one story the plan is exactly what a two-story room always had, so rooms of one and two stories build the same as before. How do we know every floor can actually be reached? The tests build the navigation grid with no drops at all, so every floor has to be reached by its stairs from every doorway, in rectangles, Ts, Us, Ls and crosses. They also check 2 m of headroom over everyone standing, and walk a character up both kinds of stairs in Jolt. Light panels hang under every floor (see Station dressing), clear of the pillars under it. The station raid draws a galleried hall, a maintenance bay with catwalks, and stacked stores with a mezzanine. archetypes.json also has a mall's atrium (a U of galleries, three stories) and a light well (a mezzanine two stories over its ground floor, with nothing between) for missions of three stories or more. A mission only draws a tall room if it has that many stories. Placement rules (Placing/ and its subfolders: PropDefinition, PlacementRule, RulePlacer, RoomFloor, LevelPlacer; Levels/Dressing/StationPlacements; content/defs/procgen/props.json and rules.json, read by PlacementReader). What goes in rooms is designer data. A prop is a kind (furniture, a footlocker, a case, cargo, supplies, ammunition, a keycard, a tank) and a size. Furniture also has a color, what it breaks as, and its piece's name. A rule places props (one drawn by weight for each place) in the rooms its tag query matches (role.*, layout.*, the content's tags), at an anchor: the floor (places drawn at random on the half-meter grid, rotated a quarter turn or not), against a wall, in the middle of a long enough stretch of wall, in a corner, as near the middle as it fits, beside a doorway, on top of something (the module's item spots and low furniture already placed), or under the ceiling. It also has a fallback for a prop its anchor has no place for. It says how many a room gets (a chance of between a fewest and most, or so many per cell), the clear space kept around each and the spacing between its own props, its priority, whether it blocks the way, whether it needs space in front to use it from, and whether it's required. Furniture models (FurnitureModel). Furniture can name a model from the library (content/props/furniture.gltf, forged from forge.json), and the model's bounds are its size. ParametricRoom and StationPlacements stamp its solids as parts (one box each, keeping Break_ names for pieces that break; what's drawn is a name/Shape part that BreakableLayout groups with its owner). Its Socket__ empties take designer loot (SocketLoot, rolled by FurnitureLootRolls on its own stream in LevelAssembler, only for sockets within pickup reach of walkable floor), or are tops that other rules place things on. Its Attach__ empties hold other props (Attachment: chairs under tables, pulled out and turned a little, each checked against walls, the room's routes through and the arrangement's aisles). A rule's arrangement (Arrangement, ArrangementLayout) places its props as a row or grid with gaps and aisles, all or nothing. The aisles are kept clear (RoomPlacements.KeepClear) and reserved in the ReachGrid, so every doorway can still reach every other. Keycards (one per lock, in its zone) and tanks (the template's count, within reach of the hose) are counted by the mission and only placed by their rules. Each placed room's floor (RoomFloor) is its module's geometry transformed into the level (ModuleFloor, computed once per module, exactly from its boxes, rotated or not), with whatever was built after the rooms counted as solid (LevelPieces). It's a grid of half-meter cells a soldier's middle can stand on (ReachGrid). The lane in from each doorway and a square around the foot of each of its stairs (Marker_Climb) are reserved before any prop, and its doorways' ways in must stay connected. A place is only kept if: the prop is entirely on the floor, no higher than 0.6 m under the ceiling (its ducts and lights), and clear of the room's pieces, of other props by its clear space, and of the mission's spots (spawns, weapons, soldiers, the floor under a hull breach), and spaced from its own kind; if it blocks the way, it leaves every way in connected, cuts off no open floor, and stays off the lanes; if it's used from the front, that floor is open and reachable (and then kept that way); otherwise, wherever it's reached from is kept that way: a thing on a top has to be within pickup reach (1.2 m) of open floor. Each rule draws from its own stream for each room (Streams, the placement stage), and is tallied (RuleTally, GeneratedLevel.Placements): how many it wanted and placed in each room, and why each place it tried didn't work. The shipped rules keep a station as full as the placement code they replaced (over the first hundred seeds: 25 footlockers, 14 cases, 1.6 tanks, 6 crates of cargo, 51 piles and 55 ammunition crates per level), in the same time (140 ms per level). PlacementGuaranteeTests checks the first hundred seeds: no solid prop in a lane, and every required rule met. Networks (Networks: LaneGraph, NetworkRouter, PipeBuilder, NetworkSpec; Levels/Supplies/ReservoirFeed; content/defs/procgen/networks.json, read by NetworkReader). Pipes are routed, not drawn. A level's lanes (LaneGraph) are straight edges along its axes: along every room's walls, a band at 3.2 m (over the doorways' 3 m lintels), a lane at 3.5 m (under the ceiling, or up a tall room's wall), and a standoff lane 0.6 m off the wall at 3.5 m (past a room's duct and pipes); risers between them, and up a story on tall rooms' walls; spans straight across a room's open ceiling from wall to wall; ways through the walls rooms share (at a wall's middle, and beside a doorway), and the lintels of their open doorways, and up through the floor between rooms stacked in line; the empty cells walled in by rooms (service cells, found by flooding the outside), entered through their walls. No lane goes out through the hull, through a doorway's opening, or up a wall where there's a doorway. Each lane is checked against the level as built so far (LevelObstacles, exact against triangles, bucketed by cell). A fitting in it (anything built after the rooms: light panels, ducts and pipes, alarm lamps, props) leaves it out. A room's own structure along a wall (a hall's rib, a column) makes it a way through. A network (NetworkSpec, in networks.json) has integer costs for each kind of lane (per meter, or once for a wall or lintel passed through) and for each bend, the longest open span it can cross and the most service cells it can run through, a kind (networks of the same kind bundle side by side on a lane, LaneUsage; a lane taken by another kind can't be used) and its pipe's look. NetworkRouter finds the cheapest route by A* over (node, the axis it came in along). Its estimate is the distance along the axes at the cheapest rate, with ties broken by node number. A route through more service cells than allowed is found again with none. PipeBuilder builds it from boxes: a square tube for each stretch, a collar at each bend, brackets to the wall every 2 m, and a sealed duct (drawn only) through a service cell, with a part for each room's run. The reservoir feed connects each end to the nearest lane of its room that the other room reaches (by a way up and across that nothing is in the way of), and its valves along the way stand on the walls under the route, where the room's floor (LevelPlacer) reaches the floor in front of them. Each level records the networks it laid (GeneratedLevel.Networks, LaidNetwork: the route, what each stretch runs along, its cost, and the cheapest route it didn't take, found the first time it's asked for). Over the first sixty seeds with a reservoir always wanted, 49 have one (the rest have no deep room it fits in, or no outlet the pipe reaches). A level with a reservoir takes about 55 ms longer to generate. StationReservoirTests checks that the feed stays on walls and ceilings, over the doorways, inside the station and within its open span, and the gate seeds walk to every valve. Loot assignments (Looting: LootAssignment, LootData, RoomLoot; content/defs/procgen/loot.json, read by LootReader). Where a level's loot goes is designer data, by tag (role.*, deck.*, layout.*, the content's tags). An assignment, for the rooms its query matches, can give: a cache of weapons (its table and count, or the template's); a weight for holding one of the deck's stashes (more for each room further off the main path and each soldier holding it, two at most; its table, or the template's); the item tables its supply piles, footlockers, cases and cargo are rolled from; item levels added to its caches, stashes, piles and containers. Every assignment that matches a room applies, in the file's order (RoomLoot.Of). The first cache and the first of each table win, and stash weights and item levels add up. stashesByDeck gives decks their own stash counts. The lobby's loot share scales the counts the assignments give, the same way it scales the template's (LootSettings.Share). The built-in assignments (LootData.BuiltIn, and the shipped loot.json, which says the same) put the loot exactly where the template always did: the first hundred seeds' weapons, piles, containers and cargo are unchanged, draw for draw. Deck themes and their halls (DeckThemes, HallTheme, ParametricHall; the template's themedHalls, on unless turned off, and hallThemes, hallsPerDeck and hallShare, tuned in Studio's Missions mode). Each deck gets a theme from the seed, never the same as the deck before. The themes are the template's own, by name, and it can use any it likes; a stock theme with the same name fills in whatever it leaves out (HallTheme.Defaults, also used by a template that names none). A theme says how big and how open its halls are, and names the surface style they're built and dressed in (style), which says how they look (a theme that uses one of the old look keys is rejected, with a pointer to styles.json). The themes are: service ways: one or two cells wide, low, ribbed, no ceiling panels, lit amber from a grated channel down the floor; a public concourse: two or three cells, a third of them two stories tall, columns down the middle with glowing bases, light strips along the walls and runway dashes down the lanes; cargo halls: two or three cells, half of them tall, arched frames, sodium light, hazard-yellow floor strips; labs: one or two cells, slim ribs, cyan strips. Four halls in the deck's theme are built per deck (hallsPerDeck), two to four cells long, and the layout picks one of them for a corridor on that deck six times in ten (hallShare), otherwise the kit's. A hall two or more cells wide is open across its ends (ModuleConnector.Width and Shift: an opening wider than a kit doorway, centered on the hall), so two halls end to end read as one. Where openings of different widths meet, the way through is the part both are open over (Openings.Passage). Whatever either has beyond that is walled up in that module's own wall (Openings.Fill, which walls up unused openings too), the lintel spans the way through, and the room portals use it. Frames' beams and haunches have no top face for rays and their own body, like lintels. Floor light is drawn only, flush with the floor, with its own low lights (RoomModule.Lights) lighting the room the same way the panels do. What stands along a hall is ribs, arches, columns down the middle, or pillars against both walls. Its style's accents (HallAccents) add bands of light along the foot or the top of its long walls, and strips etched into (or the whole of) every face of a post, column or pillar that isn't against a wall. Every piece of glowing glass is its own rect light, facing out from what it's on, so a strip or band broken at a doorway leaves no light across it (ParametricHall.Lights.cs). The Missions mode's map names each deck's theme. Pass 1, MissionGraph: production rules on the template build a tree from the insertion: the main path, locks on steps before the objective (regions count the locks crossed), a key branch before each lock, and loot rooms. A template with zones (the station raid has four) builds a chain of zones instead. Each zone is a small mission and its own region: its first room (the insertion, or a transit set piece behind a gate locked by the previous zone's keycard), rooms on the way through, dead-end side rooms (sometimes two deep), loot, and the keycard for the next gate on a branch. The objective and the arena are in the second-to-last zone. The gate to the last zone is the HackLock, which the hack opens instead of a keycard (LockedDoor.OpensOnHack), and extraction is at the far end of the last zone, so the squad fights its way out through a deck it hasn't seen. Counts, soldiers and loops are per zone. How the zones grow is the template's recipe (LevelRecipe, recipe; a template without one grows by exploreRooms, sideRooms and lootRooms, LevelRecipe.Of). It's a list of steps applied in order to each deck in turn: the way through first (MainPathStep: rooms on the way, and the last deck's share of them), one keycard step (KeycardStep: its detour chance), then any side-room and loot-room steps (SideRoomsStep, LootRoomsStep), each on every deck or only on the decks it lists. The reader rejects a recipe that doesn't start with the way through, or that has anything other than exactly one keycard step, so every level can still be finished. The station raid's recipe draws the same numbers its counts did, so its levels are unchanged. MissionGraph.Build can stop after any step, for Studio's step-through. A level of one zone keeps its own rules (locks on the way through), with the recipe's counts and no side rooms. Pass 2, LayoutSolver: works zone by zone, each with its own search and up to 12 tries starting from where the previous zone left off. Why zone by zone? So a dead end deep in one zone redoes that zone, not the whole level. Within a zone it's depth-first, with undo. Rooms off the way through (side rooms, loot, the keycard's branch) try their own parent first and then any room in their zone with a free doorway. Each room is tried (16 times) at a random free connector of its parent, after up to two corridors, as a random module of its role rotated a random quarter turn. It's kept if its cells are free on every story it stands through and its doorways are within the template's stories, then the solver moves on to the next room. Stairwells are corridors with a doorway a story up, so levels climb wherever one is drawn (about half of station raids). A step budget and up to 60 fresh attempts bound the search. Loops come last: First come pairs of free connectors in the same region and story that face each other (directly, or across up to three free cells filled with straight corridors), joining rooms at least three apart in the tree. Then, while the zone wants more (two or three each in a station raid), any two free doorways of rooms at least four apart on one story, joined by the shortest corridor across empty cells that turns corners (corridor_straight and corridor_corner pieces, six cells at most), longest way round first. A station zone has about 2.3 loops (it used to have 1). The recipe's loop rules (LoopRules, the template's loopRules) say how far apart a loop's ends must be and how long its routed corridor can be, and set targets: a share of the rooms on a loop, and the most that can be dead ends. While a layout falls short, more loops are added (from dead ends first, for the dead-end target), and a layout that still falls short is tried again (up to half the attempts). They also give one-way shortcuts across each gate (oneWayPerGate): a doorway between rooms in neighboring zones, joined directly or across a straight gap, with its own locked door that opens for whoever stands at it on the deeper zone's side (Doorway.OpensFrom, LockedDoor.OpensFrom, MissionLockPlan.OpensFrom; MissionSystem opens it without a keycard, and the HUD says "Shortcut opened"). So it's the short way back once you're through a gate, never a way past one: LinearityReport.SkippableLocks floods the layout with each gate shut and finds no room beyond it reached. Spawn closets, the insertion, the objective, the arena and extraction never get one. Each level's linearity (LinearityReport, GeneratedLevel.Linearity) covers the share of its rooms on a loop and the share that are dead ends, the longest chain to a dead end, and how long the mission's route is (insertion, each keycard, the objective, extraction) and how much of it is walked twice. The station raid asks for two rooms in three on a loop and at most one in ten a dead end (it was about 0.6 and 0.12 before), and up to one shortcut per gate. LoopRulesTests checks that a thousand layouts meet it, and that two hundred with shortcuts at every gate skip none. GridDoor (a doorway in half-cell coordinates, the side it faces, and its story) is how connectors meet. Placement transforms module points, directions, yaws and connectors into the level. Pass 3, LevelAssembler: module meshes are rotated and moved into one MeshData (part names kept, so Break_ props still break), with Plug_ boxes in unused doorways and Lock_ doors across locked ones. It also builds the encounter (players at the bay, a squad per room within the soldier budget, the objective and arena first) and the MissionLayout (keys, locks, objective, extraction, and reinforcement points just inside the arena's doorways, except the one the squad comes in by, so the escalation arrives from the way out). Station dressing (StationDressing, part of pass 3) is what makes the rooms look like a station rather than boxes under the sky. A ceiling over every room's top story wherever no room is above it. It's a face looking down, hit by rays from below (PartUsage.Rays), with an invisible slab for characters to bump their heads on (PartUsage.Body), so the navigation grid, which looks down each column, never finds a floor on a roof. Light panels every two cells in each direction, set into the ceiling and drawn only. A panel is never placed over a piece that reaches up to the light, such as a column: it moves along or across the room to a clear spot, or is left out, because a light inside a column is shut in and shadows everything around it. Each has a LevelLight colored by what the room is for (cool white in corridors, amber in arenas, red at the objective, teal at extraction) that only lights the inside of the room. Six in a hundred are dead and six flicker. In a room taller than a story, panels also hang under every overhead floor (a thin, wide piece at least 2 m up and a meter below the ceiling: catwalks, landings), one every 3.5 m along it, the first one always working, each lighting only what's below it. Every lit panel is its own part, Break_Glass_Light_: a glass prop (one shot or a nearby blast breaks it, and the light goes out, leaving its dark housing). Rays hit its underside and sides but it has no top (the navigation grid would take a top for a floor), and the client dims it as it flickers. A baseboard and a stripe of the room's color at 2.4 m around its ground story, broken at every doorway, so you can see the way through at a glance. A duct under the ceiling along one long wall (drawn and bumped into, but not seen by rays: it can run over a tall prop, and its underside there would look like headroom over a floor) and two pipes along the other. A lintel over every doorway, leaving a 3 m opening, except for locked and closet doors, whose slabs fill the doorway (a lintel's underside inside one would open a way through the lock for the navigation grid). Notice a theme? Things that hang from a ceiling and are seen by rays have no top face, for the same reason as the ceiling. Hull breaches (HullBreaches, part of pass 3) are weak spots in the station's outer hull for the horde to blow open. Candidates are the middle of every ground-story wall cell with no room beyond it and no doorway in it, and every roof cell (no room above) that's clear of the light panels (where each lit one ended up) and over clear floor (nothing standing under it to catch a body dropping through: a container, a shelf, a column, a frame's beam). Rooms other than the insertion and closets qualify. Walls and roofs are picked in turn from a seeded shuffle, at most one per room, 14 m apart, one for every three rooms up to ten. Each breach is a patched plate (Breach_, 1.5 by 1.8 m on a wall starting 0.3 m up, or 1.6 m square in a roof; standing 6 cm off, seen by rays from the front and sides only) over a ragged black hole (BreachHole_, drawn only, 3 cm off). When the plate is blown away, the hole shows. It's in the MissionLayout as a HullBreach (plate, center, which way is in, wall or roof, room, zone). The session makes each one an unbreakable Destructible with a Breach component (MissionSystem.Spawn), replicated like closet doors through the broken-surface list. (The new parts renumber a station's surfaces, so peers must build the same thing: protocol version 18, and 19 with the gates' dressing.) Decks and their gates (Decks, GateDressing, part of pass 3). A station's zones are its decks (a room's region; deck 1 is the insertion's). Each deck has its own color (blue, amber, green, magenta, yellow, teal) that every room's baseboard takes (dimmed), so the color at your feet tells you which deck you're on. Each gate between two decks (a locked doorway between regions) is marked on both sides in the color of the deck beyond it: a bulkhead frame around the doorway (hazard-striped posts, a header in that color); a sign beside it with that deck's number in blocks (on whichever side has wall for it; if neither does, as in a corridor, the number is painted on the floor in front of the doorway); and a band of that color across the floor. These are drawn only (Gate__). The HUD (DeckHud) shows the deck you're on in its color at the top right, and a banner as you go through a gate: "ENTERING DECK 3", or "BACK ON DECK 2" going back. A room several stories tall whose walls stop short of its ceiling (the reactor hall, cargo bay and catwalk hall have 5 to 6 m walls under a 7.4 m ceiling) has its walls filled up to the ceiling above the ground story, 2 cm behind the module's own face, with doorways left on the upper stories. These are only seen by rays on their sides, because a bottom face set into the module's wall looks to the grid like headroom over the floor inside the wall (which gave paths through walls; the gate's bot found it). The assembler records which room each part belongs to (GeneratedLevel.PartRooms; a doorway's parts belong to both its rooms), for the client's culling. In the client, a level named grown: is generated this way from grown_raid.json (Levels.Load), a developer level since station raids moved over to plans (docs/plans/structure-first.md, Phase 12): station: is now laid out by a station plan from station_raid.json, as a ship raid is from ship_raid.json. The name is sent in co-op's welcome message, so a client generates the host's level itself. Missions MissionSystem (LastFleet.AI.Missions) plays a generated level's mission: infiltrate, hack, escalate, extract. It runs with the command systems, after the soldiers' AI, so it reads this tick's Interact. MissionPlans.From (in the client) turns the generated MissionLayout into a MissionPlan, finding each lock's Lock_ part. A level without a plan (the range, the outpost) has no mission, and the fight ends when the area is clear, as before. Keycards are hidden. The keycard rule puts each one on top of something in a room on its side of its lock, in a room its where allows (rules.json: security offices and crew quarters, room.security, room.crew.quarters; its own keycard room two times in five, otherwise any of them; on the room's floor if nothing is free), within reach of open floor. The HUD has no marker for them, so the squad has to search! A level's keycard rooms are the kit's rooms playing key (archetypes.json: the security office and crew quarters), so the rule always has its own room to fall back on. If a designer narrows its where to exclude them, the card is left where the key room's module keeps it (the rule's tally shows the shortfall). Spawn closets. After the loops, LayoutSolver attaches up to six 1 × 1 closet modules behind unused doorways where there's room: one per room, with the ones by the arena and extraction first. A Closet_ part is the closet's door. Players can never get in. The starting squads use each room's designer spawns and found spawn spots, shuffled. State is one MissionState entity: the phase, keycards held and locks open (a bit per id), the hack's progress, waves sent, and the extraction hold. Keycards are MissionKey entities. A locked door is a MissionLock on the same entity as a Destructible with infinite health, so shots can't break it. Its keycard opens it: the system marks it broken and switches its collision off. Why piggyback on destruction? It means doors travel in the snapshot's broken-surface list, so clients' collision and drawing follow along the same way they do for broken props, and DestructionSystem.RestoreAll shuts them on a restart. No new networking needed! The host builds the navigation grid with the locked doors open, so soldiers can follow players through once they're open. Nobody can be behind a door until it opens. Compartments and pressure doors (a plan's level; LevelLayout.Bulkheads and Compartments, BulkheadDoor, BulkheadPlan, SealableDoor). Rooms are in compartments, parted where a corridor or a service way goes through a bulkhead. Each corridor's pressure door (Seal_, or the gate's door where it's one) is a SealableDoor on its door's entity. Pressure doors stand open (broken, collision off, open for the navigation grid too). MissionSystem.Seal(compartment) shuts them all, gates too, until both sides are unsealed; a sealed gate ignores its keycard and once unsealed is as its lock left it. ShutDoors blocks sealed doors for soldiers' paths, and the horde's field counts pressure doors after the locks and closets. Service ways' hatches stay open: the way round a sealed door. The developer overlay seals the compartment you stand in (LocalSession.SealCompartmentAt) and unseals them all. Where a bulkhead crosses a smooth hall (BandCrossing: a ring's quarter, a bridge on the slant), the hall's walls run on through it and its door stands square across the hall at its middle, wall to wall, built of turned boxes; the doorway's passage (Openings.Passage, which room culling projects) is the whole crossing of the grid line. Breaches (docs/plans/structure-first.md, Phase 10; WindowBreaches, owned by MissionSystem; BreachTuning from content/defs/breaches.json; the plan's breaches, BreachRule). Every window onto space (HullWindowSpot, MissionLayout.Windows, WindowPlan) is a HullWindow on its pane's Destructible, which Holds (damage wears it down to nothing but doesn't break it). Its parts (_Pane, _Crack1, _Crack2, _Shards, _Shutter) are shown and hidden through the broken-surface set, so clients see the same. So what happens when you shoot out a window? Here's the sequence: The cracks show at the tuning's shares of its toughness. At nothing left, it's a breach (BreachPhase.Venting): the pane goes, the shards show, the alarm sounds, and a HullPull entity drags everyone in sight of it toward it (HullPulls.Drift, added to the character's move in CharacterBodySystem, falling off to nothing at its reach), hurts anyone in its core, and pulls out dropped weapons and items near it. After the seal timer the compartment seals (MissionSystem.Seal). Whether it's for good is rolled from the level's seed against the plan's permanentChance, and is allowed only if the compartment isn't in a never district and MissionWalk.Finishes (the mission can still be finished from insertion, through the doorways of the compartments left, to the keycards, the objective and an extraction) without it and every compartment already lost: then Lost, otherwise the shutter closes (Shuttered), the air comes back and the doors unseal (Closed). The latest breach is in MissionState (its phase, timer, place, pull and reach), replicated whole, so a joined client's prediction keeps a HullPull of its own (PlayerPrediction.FollowBreach) and feels the same pull. The HUD shows the countdown and a marker; the developer overlay's Blow out window breaks the nearest (LocalSession.BlowOutWindowNear). A breach in a room with a door of its own on every doorway but a closet's (MissionPlans.RoomsSealedAlone, WindowPlan.RoomSeals) seals that room alone (MissionSystem.SealRoom, MissionState.BreachRoom), unless one of its doors is wrecked; any other seals its compartment. A room is lost for good as a compartment is (MissionWalk.Finishes(lost, lostRooms)), and only with nobody of the squad in it as it seals (its bounds, WindowPlan.RoomMin/RoomMax); otherwise the shutter closes. What it looks like (BreachEffects, client only, from the mission's state and the window parts every machine sees): mist and frost streaming to the breach while it vents (look.mist a second), the doors it seals flashing amber over both faces (red once lost, and for rooms lost earlier: a window whose shards show and whose shutter never closed), steam from their edges as they seal. Sealing doors slide shut (DoorVisuals), and the shutter slides down (ShutterVisuals, look.shutterDrop), each keeping its part hidden (ApplyTints) until it's home. Sounds: breach_vent loops at the breach while the air goes, door_seal, shutter_close and door_slide play where they happen (GameAudio.PlayAt). Rooms' own doors (a plan's level; RoomDoorSpot, LevelAssembler.RoomDoorPrefix, RoomDoorPlan, RoomDoorState, RoomDoors owned by MissionSystem, RoomDoorTuning from content/defs/doors.json). Every doorway from a room onto a hall (or into another room) that isn't a gate, a pressure door, a one-way shortcut or a spawn closet's gets a door, DoorKind.Auto or DoorKind.Interact as its room's archetype says (roomDoor; by hand between two rooms if either says so). A sliding door opens for anyone on its own floor within its reach (the swarm too) and shuts a moment after, never on someone in its doorway. One opened by hand toggles on a player's press of Interact looking at it (Interaction.LooksAt, from its own floor: MissionSystem.AtDoor), opens for a soldier who stands at it a moment, and is battered by swarmlings at it until it's Wrecked: open for good, and it can't seal. Open is broken, replicated through the broken-surface set; PropVisuals and RayParts know the prefix. The navigation grid is built with them open; ShutDoors blocks only sealed ones; the horde's field bars a shut one (HordeField.SetBarred: the way through, but nobody steps in until it opens) and shuts a sealed one. The HUD prompts for one opened by hand and says when one's sealed; the gate bot taps Interact at one in its way. The kinds look apart: a lit strip across a sliding door, a handle up the seam of one opened by hand, both under a cold white lamp. Doors look like doors (StationDoors, DoorLayout, DoorKind; MissionLayout.Doors). Every door the mission opens (the locks, the spawn closets' doors, the airlock's inner door) is a slab filling its doorway (its part, solid as before), with both faces plated as two leaves (StationDoors.Plates, a part /Leaves that belongs to it, so they go together). The paint depends on the kind, so a door tells you what opens it: a keycard gate is grey with a red band and a keycard reader on its bulkhead's post; the lockdown (the gate the hack opens) is striped yellow and black under an amber lamp; a one-way shortcut has a no-entry sign on the side it can't be opened from, and a green band and release lever on the other; a closet is grey over a hazard kick plate; the airlock's door is in hazard paint; a pressure door through a bulkhead (a plan's level) is grey with a red seal band and a white stripe under it. A lamp over each door (and on each panel) is red, or amber where it's waiting on the hack or on a hand at the release. Inside it is a green one (Door_, which stays) that shows once the door is gone, along with the transom over the leaves. The client slides the leaves apart into the walls as a door opens (DoorVisuals, StationDoors.OpenSeconds, drawn with the moving models; a door that's already open when first seen doesn't slide). At a shut door, the HUD says why it's shut (MissionHud.DrawShutDoor: needs this deck's keycard, opens when the hack is done, sealed from this side, or step up to the release). The airlock's outer hatch is two leaves with ports inside a docking collar striped yellow and black, under a docking lamp that the client lights green while the dropship is docked and red once it casts off (AirlockLayout.DockLamp). The rules. Keycards: anyone standing (not downed) picks one up by walking over it, for the whole squad. Doors: a door opens when someone standing comes within 3 m of it holding its keycard. Starting the hack: hold Interact for 1.5 s within 2 m of the terminal. The hack: 60 s, counted only while someone standing is within 7 m of the terminal and on its floor. Reinforcement waves: three waves, 4 s after the hack starts and then every 18 s, of two soldiers plus one per player. A wave's soldiers wait (MissionState.Pending) until a spawn closet can take them: the escalation's closets first, nearest the terminal, with the door shut, nobody inside, and nobody standing within 15 m. They appear inside out of sight (SoldierSpawner.SpawnHunting, hunting towards the terminal), the door (ClosetDoor and an unbreakable Destructible, like a lock) opens, and it shuts again once the closet and its doorway are empty. A level without closets falls back to points inside the arena's doorways, but never one that anyone can see or is within 15 m of. Each wave is its own squad, numbered from MissionSystem.ReinforcementSquadBase. Extraction: once the hack is done, everyone alive must stand within 5 m of the extraction point for 3 s, with nobody downed. Objective kinds (MissionPlan.Objective, an ObjectivePlan; MissionState.Objective; protocol version 45). The hack is one of three, all started and held at the terminal the same way, for the kind's own Seconds: a download (ObjectiveKind.Data) leaves a drive on the terminal. It's carried like a keycard, but by one player: whoever standing walks over it (MissionState.DataCarrier, DataAt), dropped where its carrier goes down or dies. Extraction waits for it to be within the extraction's radius too, and an escape pod gets it off only with its carrier aboard (DataOut); otherwise a pod is leaving early. The client draws it where it is (GameView.AddDrive) and the HUD marks it through walls. a self-destruct (ObjectiveKind.Destruct) is armed. Countdown runs from the plan's seconds, the alert is held at lockdown (DirectorSystem), and every SealEvery seconds a compartment seals (MissionSystem.SealOneAhead): the one farthest from extraction (MissionWalk.Hops) that isn't the squad's or extraction's, nor on anyone's way down to it (MissionWalk.WayDown), with the gates already open. At zero the mission fails, unless someone got off in a pod first. The HUD counts it down. Failure: nobody left standing. Playing alone, dying is enough. The numbers are in MissionTuning. The Director (DirectorSystem, LastFleet.AI.Director) runs after the mission and paces the fight, the way Left 4 Dead's does. The idea is that a fight should breathe: build up, peak, then give you a moment before the next push. Stress: each player's Stress rises with damage (a whole health bar is 1.2) and with going down (0.5), and fades (0.08 per second) once they've been safe for 3 s and no soldier is fighting. The squad's stress is that of the most stressed standing player. Phases (DirectorState): building up; a peak at 0.85, held for 5 s; then a breather of 15 to 30 s (it ends early once the squad is calm). Roaming: while nothing is happening, 45% of the station's soldiers (not patrols or reinforcements) wander around their post (SoldierAiSystem.Roam). They walk to a walkable spot 3 to 11 m from where they were placed, on its floor, at 45% of full speed, look around for 3 to 9 s, then pick the next spot. Seeing or hearing anything works as before. Patrols: while building up, a squad that's gone 35 s without a fight gets a patrol out of the nearest usable spawn closet, in a zone it has opened, by MissionSystem.SendPatrol, under the same closet rules as the waves. It's two soldiers plus one per extra player, at most one patrol per minute, and at most three patrol soldiers alive plus two per extra player. Threat (a plan's level whose recipe has a threat block; MissionPlan.Threat, a ThreatPlan). Each room's threat is its zone's, rising evenly from the first zone's to the last's, scaled by its district and by the highest scale of its room tags, never over 2 (ThreatRule.Of, PlanMission.Threat). The threat where the squad is (DirectorState.Threat, the hottest room a standing player is in, MissionSystem.ThreatAt) sets the patrols before the alert speeds them (DirectorTuning.Threatened): the time between them and their size, each along the line from threat 0 to threat 1 (reinforcements.everySeconds, reinforcements.size), and as many more of them alive at once as a patrol is bigger. The wait for the next patrol is never longer than the time between them where the squad now is, so walking somewhere hotter brings one sooner. The stress phases still decide when. Where patrols come from: a source closet (ClosetPlan.Source: on a service way, or off a hall with a doorway into a room with one of the recipe's sources tags, security offices by default; PlanMission.Sources) counts as half as far (MissionSystem.SourceFavor), and no closet is used whose compartment or room is sealed, or whose only way to the squad's compartment crosses a sealed one (over the walk's doorways, MissionSystem.Unsealed). When no closet will do, a patrol comes out of the nearest source room instead (MissionLayout.PatrolRooms, MissionPlan.PatrolRooms: its soldier spawns and found spots), while nobody is in it, within 15 m of a spot or can see one, under the same zone and seal rules. The station's alert (MissionState.Alert, 0 to 1, and AlertStage; AlertTuning, the template's alert; protocol version 29). It rises with time on the level (0.05 per minute), with fighting (0.003 per second for each soldier fighting), with noise (0.002 per second for each tank pumping or pod drone inbound), and at once when the hack starts (0.15). It only falls while everything is quiet and calm (0.01 per second), and never below three quarters of its highest value. The Director reacts to it (DirectorTuning.Alerted): at full alert its waits are 2.5 times shorter (on top of the run's pace), each patrol has two more soldiers and three more can be alive, and in lockdown (0.9) a patrol comes without waiting for quiet. From 0.6, the run's hordes can come during infiltration no matter how few decks are open (HordeSystem.AlertHordeAt; never on a mission of the run without hordes). Its stages (0.35 alert, 0.65 high alert, 0.9 lockdown) are shown in the station, not on the HUD. There's an alarm beacon over a doorway in every room except the closets (two in a big room; StationAlarms, GeneratedLevel.Alarms). It's dark red glass while calm, and then lights up and turns: amber, then deep amber, then red and faster, lighting its room in its own color while the panels stay as they are (SceneLights.AlertStage; beacons cast no shadows). The PA also chimes and speaks (MissionHud). The developer overlay shows the number. Hunting (DirectorSystem.Hunt, the way Alien: Isolation's director handles its alien: it knows where the squad is, but its soldiers don't). A patrol is told to look in the middle of the squad's room within 20 s of the last fight, a room next to it within a minute, and two rooms away after that (one step closer at high alert, and the squad's own room in lockdown). It doesn't know where anyone is standing (DirectorSystem.Guess, by the level's RoomMap). After looking and finding nothing, a patrol soldier sweeps on to a neighboring room, two times in three the one nearest the squad's, two rooms when calm and sweepRooms more at full alert (SoldierBrain.Sweeps). From the first alert stage, every nudgeSeconds (three times as often at full alert) the nearest idle garrison soldier within three rooms of the squad goes to look in its room or the one next door. And when hunters who aren't fighting have spent backOffSeconds in total within 12 m of a player, the Director pulls them two rooms further away and sends nothing for 30 s. A hand-built level has no rooms, so patrols go straight for the squad as before. The starting population (LevelAssembler.Populate). Each zone's budget rises from the template's fewest soldiers in the first zone to its most in the last. Rooms take soldiers by threat (objective and arena 1, key room 0.8, loot and transit 0.7, extraction 0.5, rooms on the way through 0.6, side rooms 0.35), with the objective and arena first, and no room over its cap. Then come squads for a second, third and fourth player (SquadLayout.MinPlayers), each about a third of the zone's budget (soldiersPerExtraPlayer), in the spots that are left. FightSession spawns the squads for the players who are there at the start. When a player joins, each waiting squad turns up once nobody is within 30 m of it. Stashes (LevelAssembler.PlaceLoot, after the soldiers): stashesPerZone weapons (or the deck's own count, in loot.json) from the stash table in each zone, at most one per room, among the rooms the loot assignments allow, drawn by their weight (see Loot assignments). By default that's a dead-end side room 1 (plus 0.5 for each room deeper down its branch), a key room 0.6, a room on the way through 0.25, plus 0.25 for each of the level's own soldiers holding it (two at most). A stash guarded by two or more of them rolls guardedLevels item levels higher. Over 40 seeds, a side room holds one about one time in five, and a room on the way through one in thirteen. Waves: during a peak or a breather, the hack's waves wait (MissionSystem.HoldWaves), but never longer than 10 s. The numbers are in DirectorTuning. The developer overlay's AI tab shows the phase, the stress and the patrols. Replication. The snapshot ends with the MissionState, raw (protocol version 5), and the replica keeps it on an entity. MissionHud draws the same HUD from either world: the objective line, markers through walls, the hack and extraction bars, notices, and the end banner. Positions come from the MissionLayout, which every peer generates. FightSession ends the playtest report with mission complete or mission failed. The gate (Phase 3: every seed can be completed). How do you prove every seed is beatable? You play every one! MissionBot (LastFleet.AI/Bots) plays a mission the way a player would, writing the same PlayerCommand a keyboard does: the lowest keycard still lying around, then the terminal (holding Interact), then extraction. It plans on the soldiers' NavGrid with the shut doors blocked (Pathfinder.SetBlocked: a lock whose card it doesn't have, and every spawn closet; only the floor around the door's sill, so a story above stays open). It replans every second and sprints when lined up. When it's not making progress it jumps (to mantle a lip), fires ahead (to break glass) and backs off to one side. It doesn't fight: GateTests make it invulnerable and clear out the soldiers, since the question is only whether the level can be finished. Ten classes of ten seeds (1 to 100) run in parallel in CI, taking about two minutes on two cores. A seed fails when its phase, keys and locks stop changing for four minutes of game time, and the failure reports where the bot was and what it was doing. Bonus: the gate found two navigation bugs that soldiers had too: the ground inside walls under an upper story counted as floor, and drop links passed under lintels. The level map (F3, "Level map", generated levels only; DevOverlay.LevelMap.cs). The Layout view shows the rooms of a story from above, colored by role, with doorways, locks, keycards (greyed out once taken), the terminal, extraction, weapons lying around, and players and soldiers live. The Graph view shows the mission graph as an indented tree, one room per row, with the way through down the left edge, side branches hanging off it, and locks on the links they close. Loot LastFleet.Loot makes weapons (design doc, "Procedural weapons and loot"). Like the rest of gameplay, it's headless and deterministic. Data. content/defs/loot/*.json holds rarities, archetypes (a simulation frame, base stats and clamps), manufacturers (a stat bias and model names per archetype), parts (a slot, an optional maker, a lowest rarity, the archetypes they fit, and stat ranges), affixes (prefix or suffix), relics, and loot tables (weighted archetypes, nested tables and relics, each between item levels, with rarity and maker biases). The same folder also holds the items, effects, traits, fleet supplies, crafting (crafting.json, CraftingReader) and how a round's push moves what it hits (impact.json, ImpactRules), each covered where it's used. Any file can hold any of the lists, and the catalog merges them. LootCatalog.Load checks every reference and range and fails with every problem listed. The roll (WeaponRoller). One generator, seeded by (seed, table, item level), drawn in a fixed order: down the table to an archetype or relic; a rarity (weight × (1 + per-level shift × (level − 1)) × the tables' biases); a maker of the archetype at that rarity; a part per slot from the pool its maker and rarity allow (rarer parts favored when allowed, and a maker's own parts favored on its guns); the parts' ranges; then affixes (two means a prefix and a suffix). Stats are the base plus the rarity's bonus, then every addition, then every multiplication, then the archetype's clamps. A relic is fixed, with every range at its best. The result is a RolledWeapon (name, parts and what they rolled, affixes, power, and a WeaponProfile). A weapon is its seed, so its roll never changes. Here's the catch with that: a player's weapons are saved as their identities and rebuilt from the loot data, so adding to the data must not change them. Imagine logging in to find your favorite rifle rolled into something else... heck no. So how do we add new parts safely? Each part records the data generation it was added in (since, 0 for the first), and each weapon records the generation it was rolled in (WeaponIdentity.Generation, the newest part's generation in the catalog when it was rolled; 0 for weapons saved before this existed). A weapon only rolls from the parts of its generation and earlier. The muzzle and grip slots (added after the first five) roll after everything else, each from its own generator (the seed hashed with the slot), so the first five slots, the affixes and the name roll exactly as they always did. A weapon of generation 0 gets the bare muzzle and the standard grip, which change nothing. WeaponGenerationTests checks a set of seeds against the weapons they rolled before the slots were added. Suppressors. A part's traits (a suppressor's suppressed) are added to the weapon's. A suppressed gun's shots carry the flag (ShotRecord.Suppressed, on the wire too). A soldier only hears one in the room it's fired in (its RoomMap; without rooms, within SoldierTuning.SuppressedHearingRange), the horde only within HordeTuning.SuppressedHearRange, and clients play it quieter, with a smaller flash. Parts that do something. A laser sight's part has the laser trait (hip, moving and airborne spread at WeaponStatsResolver.LaserHipSpread). The client draws its dot where the middle of the view meets the world, and a faint beam to it from the module's Laser marker (only on your own gun). A light module's lamp becomes your flashlight's origin when you carry one, with a tighter beam that reaches further (Flashlights.GunReach). An optic's secondZoom (a variable scope, or a magnifier behind a red dot) is a second zoom level that the zoom key (B, InputAction.SwitchZoom) switches to. It's client side only, since zoom belongs to the camera. ViewModel.Magnified multiplies the gun's zoom, and where that gives 2x or more the sight becomes a scope's lens (a magnified red dot uses ScopeReticle.Dot). A new gun in hand starts unmagnified. A hostile soldier whose frame zooms 2x or more (a marksman) glints from its scope when it points within about 11 degrees of you, brighter the more directly it points (GameView.GlintOf). It's a cue drawn by the client, and no soldier's awareness uses it. In the simulation a weapon carries its WeaponIdentity (seed, table hash, level and rarity rank) in its WeaponSlot, so it travels as resolved stats plus a few bytes, and any machine with the data can rebuild its card. A stock weapon's identity is empty. A WeaponDrop entity is a weapon lying in the world. WeaponPickupSystem gives it to a player who holds Interact by it for 0.5 s: into a free slot, or in place of the weapon in hand, which is left where the new one lay (one hold takes one weapon). Where weapons come from. Generated levels put two or three on item spots in each loot room, and the Director also hides one to three stashes in each zone (MissionTemplate.Loot, LootSpot; see the Director's population), at an item level that rises by one per zone. FightSession rolls them fresh each run. Soldiers carry a LootDrop, and LootSystem (a command system) rolls each death once: one in eight leaves a weapon from the soldier table for the gun it carried (loot.station.soldier.: that frame, or now and then a hand cannon, its sidearm), decided from the run's seed and the soldier. Traits (WeaponTraits; their numbers are in content/defs/loot/traits.json, read into a WeaponTraitRules that the host's world and a client's prediction share) are what a weapon does beyond its numbers: each maker's signature on every gun it makes: Kessler steady hand (more damage crouched), Halcyon restoration (a kill heals), Rustline scrapwork (rounds jam now and then), Vashti corrosive or arc, Choir-forged hunger (kills banked as damage, shots cost health); affixes' traits: of the Vigil (more damage while holding the objective), of the Leech (lifesteal); relics' traits: Sixth Bell tolling (a precision kill puts rounds back), Lanternfall lifesteal. They live in WeaponStats.Traits, so they travel with the weapon. Damage changes ride on the shot (WeaponHandling.Fire), and jams come from the shot's hash, so a client can predict them. WeaponTraitSystem, after shots are resolved, does the rest: hunger's price per shot, lifesteal, corrosion (an Afflictions component on soldiers) and arcs on a hit, restoration, banked kills and tolling on a kill, and tracking who's holding the objective. An arc, or a kill by corrosion, is added to the HitLog, so markers, the kill feed and clients see it. Co-op. Weapon drops are sent whole in the snapshot (protocol version 6); a player's own loadout already was. A character's corrosion is sent as a flag. Client. LootContent loads the catalog once and caches rebuilt rolls. The HUD names carried weapons in their rarity's color. WeaponCard shows the drop in reach (stats compared with the weapon in hand, parts, affixes, the hold). Drops spin above where they lie under a beam in their rarity's color. The developer overlay's Loot Lab rolls thousands from a table and level (rarity, maker and frame shares, stat spreads, the power curve), rolls one to inspect, and drops it at your feet. Networking Co-op is a host-authoritative listen server (LastFleet.Networking). The host's machine runs the one simulation, exactly as it does when playing alone. Clients send commands and draw what the host sends back. Simple to reason about, and it's why the simulation never has to agree across platforms (see Simulation rules). Transports. ITransport sends bytes to a peer on channels, either unreliably, unreliably sequenced (stale packets dropped) or reliably in order. There are three: RakNetTransport is the real one (UDP, BRUTAL's RakNet binding). LoopbackNetwork connects transports in memory, with latency, jitter and loss driven by a clock the test controls, so session tests are deterministic and need no sockets. ConditionedTransport wraps a real transport with added latency, jitter and loss (--net-sim), so you can try a LAN game as if it were over the internet. Messages (Protocol/, one record per message) are a type byte followed by little-endian fields written with NetWriter and read with NetReader. A reader that runs off the end throws, and the session drops the message. NetProtocol.Version must match or the host refuses the client. Inputs. Every tick the client sends its next command plus the three before it, unreliably. Why the extra three? So a lost packet doesn't lose a command. The host's InputBuffer for that player runs one per tick. When none has arrived it repeats the last one (without its turning), and it folds a backlog of more than four into one, so a stalled client catches up without losing any of its turning. Snapshots (SnapshotWriter, every SnapshotInterval = 3 ticks, 20 per second, unreliable sequenced) carry the tick, the last input applied for that client, every character's pose, stance, health and flags, grenades, pickups, weapons lying around, the set of broken props and the targets, the mission, the horde near the client, and the recipient's own player in full (exactly where it is and where it's looking, movement state, weapons, loadout, inventory, grenades). The client's ReplicaWorld is a GameWorld with no systems, whose entities keep the host's IDs, so events that name an entity mean the same one on both sides. Packing. Characters are quantized (Quantize): positions to 3 cm as 16 bits, angles to 1/182 of a degree, speed and eye height a byte each, health in halves; how long it's been dead as a byte that's exact up to the last 4 s (the client counts on from when it heard; that way it changes four times a minute, not four times a second); the hit direction as two signed bytes. A character's motion (x, z, yaw, pitch, y, speed, its horizontal velocity in eighths of a meter per second, and which snapshot that was taken in) is stored together, so a moving character is one run in the delta. The client moves each character on from where it was sent, along its velocity (for up to 2 s). So when does a character's position actually need sending? Only when the client's guess goes wrong. CharacterView, kept per client, only sends a character's position again when that guess is off by more than 10 cm at the client's feet (plus 1 cm per meter of distance, and three times that beyond 25 m for one the client can't see: a ray from its eye to the character's chest through the level, checked twice a second). It sends its facing again when it has turned 3 degrees (20 beyond 25 m), and its pace when that changes by a meter per second. In between, the entry repeats what it last said, which the delta makes free. So a soldier walking a corridor or a Stripper running at you is only news when it turns! Characters other than players face to 1/256 of a turn and look up and down to 1/128, so a turn changes one byte. Players are always sent fresh, with no velocity. The Choir's bigger bodies add their kind and what they're doing (CharacterKind.Choir), and the client builds each one from its kind (ChoirBodies), the same as the host. The client's own player has its motion left at zero in the table, since its full block has the exact values. Delta compression (SnapshotDelta, SnapshotHistory). Each input message carries the newest snapshot tick the client has. The host keeps the last 32 snapshots it sent to each client, and sends the next one as its bytes XORed with the acknowledged one, coded as runs of unchanged and changed bytes. The client keeps the last 32 it rebuilt and reverses the process. The codec only knows the layout as sections. A snapshot starts with a table of its section lengths (19: the header, characters, the client's own player, grenades, pickups, weapons, items lying around, containers, cargo crates, cargo pods, supply tanks, broken props, targets, pings, a Spitter's acid in flight and its pools, the mission, the horde's table and its updates), and each section is compared with the same section of the baseline, so a list that grows doesn't shift anything after it. Within a list, each entity keeps its slot from snapshot to snapshot (StableSlots, shared by every client), and one that goes away leaves a hole the size it took (an ID of zero, then how many bytes to skip) for the next one to fill. So an entity that isn't moving is a run of zeros, and a moving one is a few bytes. A snapshot made against a baseline the client no longer has is dropped and counted, and the host sends whole snapshots until an acknowledgment it can use arrives. One gotcha worth knowing: anything that changes is sent again until the client acknowledges it, which takes about a round trip. That means something that changes now and then costs as much as something that changes every snapshot, which is why angles are held to a few degrees and far characters to their steps. Events (TickEvents: shots, hits, explosions, breaks, barks) go with each snapshot. All the ticks since the last one go in one message (each with its tick), reliably in order on channel 1, and they drive the same presentation code on the host and clients: hit markers, kill feed, debris, bark lines. Shots and hits are packed (EventCodec). A hit carries its shot (origin, direction and frame come from the hit), so only launcher rounds in flight are sent on their own. Positions are to 3 cm and directions to a hundredth of a degree. A bite on a character doesn't say where (the client puts it on the character). A client hears every bite on its own player (each one turns its damage indicator), but only one per quarter second on each other character (a sound and a flinch). It gets no shot or hit more than 60 m from its player (except its own and those on it): a fight across the station reaches it in the snapshot (who is dead), not as tracers nobody nearby would see. Of other players' fire, it only gets three pellets of a shotgun round, and beyond 15 m it gets the impacts of every other round (every fourth into a wall; the round's shot is still sent on its own, for its sound and tracer). Kills always come through. Pickups are sent with their timers to the second, and the client's own player with its counting-up timers (time since it last fired, was hurt, stood on the ground) only as precisely as anything reads them. Acid globs are sent as thrown (where from, how fast, when; the client flies them the same way) and pools as left (where, how wide, from when to when), so neither changes once sent. Drawing. Other characters are drawn InterpolationTicks (6, 100 ms: two snapshots) behind the newest snapshot, interpolated between the two snapshots around that time. Prediction (PlayerPrediction). Nobody wants to wait a round trip for their own feet to move, so a client runs its own player in a small world of its own: the host's controller, mantle, loadout, weapon and body systems, in the host's order, against a JoltWorld of the level with broken props switched off the same way the host's are.
