Every other character is in it as a PuppetTag entity, placed from the replica and never moved, so the predicted player bumps into them. Each command runs there the tick it's made. When a snapshot arrives, the predicted player takes the host's state (which reflects the commands up to the snapshot's acknowledged one), the capsule is placed to match (ICollisionWorld.PlaceCharacter), and the newer commands run again. The change in position becomes VisualOffset, which fades by 18% per tick; over 2 m (a respawn) it snaps. Health, grenades, flinch and anything else the host decides come from the host. Mispredictions mostly come from the host holding a late command for a tick (after which it keeps one in hand) and from other characters pushing you. Downed, revive, drag and pings (Simulation). LifeSystem downs a player (with Rescue) at zero health when a teammate is still standing. Their command is cut down to DownedCommand (look, sidearm, reload, ping) and they bleed out. RescueSystem runs next. Holding Interact within reach revives (and holsters the reviver's weapon through WeaponState.Holstered). Drag toggles dragging (MovementState.Burdened slows the dragger in the controller, and the downed player is placed behind them). Both flags are ordinary replicated state, so a client's prediction follows them without running the rescue rules. PingSystem turns a Ping press into a Ping entity (enemy or place), replicated in snapshots. Players' Rescue goes in every character record and in the client's own block. Clock pacing and the jitter buffer. Each snapshot says how many of the client's commands were waiting on the host, and how many it should keep waiting (protocol version 7). A client below that runs its clock 4% fast, and one more than one above it runs 3% slow, so a late packet finds a command already waiting instead of making the host repeat the last one (which the prediction can't know about). So how big should the buffer be? The host sizes it per client from when its input messages arrive (ArrivalJitter). On a perfectly even link, the host tick a message lands on minus its newest command's number would never change. The jitter is the running mean of how much that changes from one message to the next (RFC 3550's estimator, in ticks). Three times the jitter, at least two and at most six commands, is kept waiting. Each one is a tick of input delay, so an ordinary link keeps two, as before. In the soak test at 80 ms of jitter, the host repeated a command 7 times in 120 client-seconds instead of 25. Lag compensation (LagCompensation, Simulation). When hosting, a system after the body system records every character's feet and movement state at the end of each tick, for 24 ticks. Each input message carries the tick the client was drawing others at. NetHost passes it along with the command, and ShotResolutionSystem tests that shooter's shots against characters as they were then (interpolated between ticks, at most MaxRewindTicks = 20 back). Swarmlings aren't recorded. Why not? A client is only sent some of them each snapshot and moves the rest along their paths, so what it shows is a little off from anywhere they actually were. Instead, the host knows where each client was drawing each swarmling (it keeps the same tracks the client draws from: SwarmView.TryShown, through LagCompensation.Horde) and tests that client's shots against those. Other characters work the same way. A client moves each one along the velocity it was last sent, and is only sent it again when it strays (see Packing), so it draws them up to a few tens of centimeters from where they actually were. CharacterView keeps where it told the client each one was at each of the last 16 snapshots, and LagCompensation.Characters tests the client's shots against that, between the two snapshots around its view tick, the way the client draws them (stance and eye height from the history). In the horde soak, the host knows where each client drew every other character to within a millimeter (95th percentile). The host's own player and the soldiers shoot at the present. Predicted hit markers (PredictedHits). A client resolves its own predicted shots the tick it fires them, against the level and the other characters where it draws them (which is where the host's rewind will put them), so a hit on an enemy shows its marker a round trip before the host confirms it: body or precision, and a kill when the shot's damage at that range is at least the health last sent. Teammates and practice targets are left to the host. CombatFeedback remembers the shots it marked, and the host's hit for the same shot (its ShotIndex) shows no second marker, only a kill the prediction missed. A predicted hit that the host calls a miss has already been shown, as in other shooters. The lobby (Lobby/, protocol version 9). Between missions everyone is in a lobby: the host's LobbyHost (alone, or opened on a hosting transport) or a friend's, joined with a LobbyClient. A client's first message is the usual Hello. The lobby checks the version, the content and the four-player limit, and makes names unique, since carried weapons are kept by name. A level travels as its seed, so peers must have the same data. The hello carries the client's ContentFingerprint (a stable hash of the build's content/defs, content/modules and content/props, by path and bytes; GameContent), and a host that sets its own turns away a client with a different one (RejectReason.ContentMismatch; Handshake, shared by the lobby and session hosts; protocol version 40). The game sets it on its lobby host and client. Missions run over the lobby's connection, so the lobby is the gate. After LobbyWelcome, the host sends LobbyState whenever it changes: the mission set up (by level name), whether one is running, a line on how the last one went, and each member's name, ready flag, whether they're in the mission and what they carry. Clients send LobbyReady, and the host starts whenever it wants. The lobby's connection stays open from mission to mission. BeginMission gives the mission's NetHost a RelayTransport on top of it, injects a Connected for each member and sends them MissionStart. Each client's LobbyClient makes its own relay for the mission's NetClient, which then says hello to the mission as if it had just connected. Each lobby passes the mission's messages to its relay (on the host, only after that member's mission hello, so nothing from an older mission slips through) and keeps its own (MissionLeave, MissionRejoin, MissionEnd). EndMission detaches the relay first, so the mission's host, disposed afterwards, doesn't disconnect anyone. A late arrival goes straight into a mission that's running, and a client who leaves it is only a Disconnected as far as the mission is concerned. The hub (HubLevel, Levels.Hub). Between missions the host (or a player alone) plays the ship's hangar deck, built in Blender (content/modules/hub/hangar_deck.gltf, docs/blender/hub.md) and the same everywhere. HubLevel.Load reads it into a HubLayout, and rejects a file where something that collides isn't a box or a marker is missing (Spawn_Player, where the squad comes in; Station_Console, Station_NeedsBoard, Station_Armory and Station_StarMap, where each station is used from). It's a level with no fight (FightSession never calls it clear), started like a mission through the lobby (LobbyHost.BeginMission(level, keepSetUp: true), which plays it without making it the mission that's set up; Playing is what's being played), so friends in the lobby are on the deck too, and late arrivals come straight onto it. Its stations (HubStation, HubLayout.StationAt, 2.2 m): the mission console opens the lobby screen over the deck; the needs board shows the fleet (NeedsBoard: the Scourge, the supplies running shortest, the ships, the last jump and haul, and the refinery; FleetState, saved in fleet.json); the armory opens the inventory. Launching from the console keeps what everyone has on the deck (parts fitted, weapons swapped) and ends the deck for everyone before the mission begins. When a mission ends, or you leave it, you come back to the deck with how it went. Opening the lobby to friends (or closing it) restarts the deck on the new connection. If the deck won't load, you get the plain lobby screen instead. Missions from the lobby, and what players carry. A station's name carries the lobby's GenerationSettings after a slash (station:42/z3-s150-l50-f2-b6): soldiers and loot as shares of the template's, and decks, stories and built rooms, which only the grown raid (grown:) uses; a station is laid out by its plan, so the lobby and the star map set only its soldiers, loot and cargo. They're applied to the template before generating, so every machine builds the same level from the name. The host's LoadoutStore keeps, by player name, the weapons each player got out with (as WeaponIdentity values, rebuilt from the loot data, or a stock weapon's class), saved in loadouts.json beside the settings. A LocalSession arms each player from it as they spawn (SimulationSetup.Arm). So what do you get to keep? When the mission is won, the players still standing keep what they carry (LocalSession.Squad). Anyone else who played it, and everyone when it's lost or abandoned, goes back to the stock kit. A player who dies drops the rolled weapons they carried where they fell, with their ammunition, and respawns with the stock kit (LifeSystem.DropFoundWeapons). Restarting a fight keeps them. The client's sessions. GameClient owns the window, the lobby, the menu and, during a mission, a GameView, which holds one IGameSession and everything drawn from it (models, feedback, debris, HUD, overlay). Starting a mission creates the view, and ending it (the host, eight seconds after the banner, or Back to lobby) disposes it. The host's (or a lone player's) mission goes through a PendingLevel. The level is generated and its LocalSession built (collision, navigation, cover, squads: a few seconds for a station raid) on a worker thread, which reports its stage while the window draws a loading screen. Once that's done, the mesh goes to the GPU and the GameView is created on the main thread. A client's mission goes through a PendingMission. The level loads on a worker thread while the mission's handshake (a PendingJoin over the relay) waits for the host, which answers once its own level is built. With --level, --seed or a smoke run, the first mission builds behind the startup splash. Otherwise the game opens in the lobby. A smoke run builds right away, so its frames are the same every time. The sessions are LocalSession (the simulation, with a NetHost when the lobby is open) and RemoteSession (a NetClient, its replica and the prediction). Only a local session has physics, AI, navigation, the fight's report and restart. Conventions A handful of conventions everyone needs to agree on: Topic Convention Units Meters, seconds, radians Axes Right-handed, +Y up. Yaw 0 looks down −Z Yaw, pitch Positive yaw turns left; positive pitch looks up; pitch is clamped to ±89° Position of a character Its feet Tick rate 60 Hz (SimulationSetup.TicksPerSecond) Color Linear RGB in code; the swapchain is sRGB, so the hardware encodes for display Build output artifacts/ (UseArtifactsOutput), never committed Code layout The source is laid out so you can find a type from its name and its feature. And we don't rely on good intentions here: CodeLayoutTests (in Core's tests) fails the build when a file breaks these rules: One top-level type per file, named after it. Health.cs holds Health. A part of a partial type is Type.Part.cs (DevOverlay.LootLab.cs, SoldierAiSystem.Tactics.cs). Nested types stay with their parent. Namespaces follow folders. src/LastFleet.Loot/Rolling/WeaponRoller.cs is in LastFleet.Loot.Rolling. If you move a file to another folder, its namespace changes to match. Folders by feature, not by kind, once a project outgrows a flat list (about 20 files). Small projects (Ecs, Physics, Platform, Audio) stay flat. A folder is never named like a type it holds (a Hud folder would hide the Hud class behind a Hud namespace). the app and its options at the root The horde So how do you put 300 monsters on screen without melting the CPU? You don't make them characters! The Choir's swarmlings (LastFleet.AI/Horde, design doc "Horde simulation") have no controller, no Jolt body, no brain. A swarmling is a WorldPosition (its feet), ViewAngles (its facing), Health, Faction (Choir) and Swarmling (velocity, the navigation cell under it, what it's doing). docs/horde.md has the tuning. One field for all of them (HordeField). Rather than pathfinding for every swarmling, they all share one field. It has two levels, like the soldiers' NavClusters: Every 12 ticks, a search from the players outwards over clusters (each 4 m square of each floor of the navigation grid) gives each cluster the next one towards the nearest player (downed players count as a little nearer than standing ones). Inside a cluster, a small field, made the first time it's needed and then kept, gives each cell the step towards that next cluster (or the ledge to drop off). The grid is built with the mission's doors open, so each doorway's floor is its own cluster, and a shut door closes it: the field goes around it, and nobody walks through. Movement (HordeSystem, a late system). It runs after CharacterBodySystem, so it moves after everyone else and its bites, logged as hits, survive this tick's clearing of the HitLog. Each swarmling runs down the field, or straight at its target once it's within 8 m and in the open (a clear line on the grid, checked every fourth tick). It keeps 0.7 m from the others using a spatial hash of 1 m squares, and steps from cell to linked cell, sliding along whatever stops it, never leaving the grid. Drops are a short fall. Bites. Within 1.35 m it stops and winds up for 0.3 s (the telegraph: it rears, its blades rise, it shrieks), then bites for 7 if the target is still within 1.9 m. A downed player loses 1.5 s of bleed-out instead. A bite is a HitRecord from the swarmling with no distance (origin and point the same), logged with HitLog.AddMelee so the shot totals only count shots. Clients draw no tracer or whiz for it, and the damage indicator points at the biter. Hits. ShotResolutionSystem tests swarmlings after characters (SwarmVolumes: a low capsule body and the head out in front of it, which takes precision hits) and knocks them back instead of flinching them. 20 damage or more staggers one, breaking its lunge. Grenades damage them, knock them away and stagger them. A client's shots are tested against the swarmlings where that client was drawing them (see Networking, lag compensation). Hordes come when the mission calls them: every 75 s while the squad infiltrates (from 50 s in, and only while the Director is building up); with every hack wave; at the start of the extraction; and as a trickle through the hack and the extraction. Sizes grow with the number of players. They come out of the floor 25 to 55 m away by walking distance, in a cluster no player can see, six per tick. At most 300 are alive at once. HordeSystem.Call sends one at any time (--horde, the F3 overlay's buttons). The field is made while the level loads (Prepare). Through hull breaches. While the field is made, each breach gets a way in (Breachway): where bodies come out (in front of a wall's hole, a third of the way up it, or a body's height under a roof's) and the floor they land on (a step out from the wall, or straight down). A breach with something in front of it or no floor under it gets none. A fresh horde blows one open: every hack wave's horde and the extraction's, and half of the infiltration hordes, at most one every 25 s. It has to land 18 to 55 m from the players by walking distance, with nobody within 6 m of where it lands. The plate breaks (DestructionSystem.BreakOpen, thrown into the room), and a second later the horde comes out one body every 0.07 s, each one hopping out of the wall or dropping from the roof (SwarmlingAction.Fall) to a floor cell around the landing spot. The Choir's bigger bodies don't fit, so they come out of the floor somewhere else. Once open, a breach is a way in for later hordes and trickles (seven in ten of those that have nothing to blow open, if it's in reach), 40 bodies at a time. The client sees the plate break like any prop (debris), and for a breach's plate it also shows a flash, plays the blast's sound and has smoke pour out of the hole for 9 s (CombatFeedback.RecordBreach). --horde --breach sends a horde through breach i right away. Climbers (SwarmSurface). Three in ten of the horde, when their target is more than 10 m away, look now and then (every 16 ticks) for a wall within 3 m, along any of the four directions a station's walls run, that goes all the way up to the ceiling (a ray at waist height and another just under the ceiling find the same face, and nothing sticks out of it on the way up). They make for it and climb it at 3.2 m/s (SwarmSurface.WallEast and the others: the body stands out from the wall, head up). At the top they go over onto the ceiling (SwarmSurface.Ceiling: feet on it, body hanging down) and follow the field along it at 85% speed, cell by cell, as long as each cell has a ceiling (found by a ray up the first time it's asked, then kept; 2.4 to 7.6 m over the floor) within 0.7 m of the last one. They let go within 4.5 m of their target (measured over the floor), but never nearer than 1.8 m: right over someone, they drop off to the side. They also drop where the ceiling ends or the route falls away, when nobody is left to go for, and when a heavy hit staggers them (off a wall, they're pushed away from it). They can't bite until they're down. Shots and grenades find them where they hang (SwarmVolumes.Of takes the surface into account: the body stands out from it), and so do soldiers. The client draws them rotated to the surface (the instance's last float, read by swarm.slang and swarm_shadow.slang). The fleet (FleetState, FleetSim, in LastFleet.AI.Fleet; it's the host's, saved in fleet.json after every mission, with one life). Seven ships (the flagship, a farm, a refinery, a hospital, a fabricator and two transports), four thousand people, morale, and stores of the seven fleet supplies (fuel, food, water, medical supplies, munitions, alloy, electronics; Items.FleetSupplies), starting with eight jumps' worth. Launching a mission, the fleet jumps (see the star map) if it has the fuel (4 per ship), which opens the gap on the Scourge by 1.3, give or take. If it's been caught (the Scourge's distance at or below zero), it makes an emergency jump at double the fuel. Without the fuel it drifts, and the Scourge closes half a mission more. After each mission, won, lost or abandoned, what reached the fleet goes into the stores (a win's haul, plus what cargo pods' drones took, which counts on a loss too). The Scourge closes by the time spent (a mission's worth, depending on difficulty: 0.75, 1 or 1.25, and 3% more each mission), and if it has caught the fleet, its boarders hit a ship. Each jump uses a jump's worth of everything: food (one unit per 160 people), water (one per 200, plus the farm's), medical supplies, munitions (more when caught), alloy (more with damaged ships, which it repairs) and electronics. Shortages kill people (from the transports first), cost morale and wear ships down (a ship with no condition left is lost with everyone aboard), and broken morale causes desertions. The farm grows food when there's water. All of that is each supply's rules, as data in content/defs/loot/supplies.json (SupplyDefinition, in LastFleet.Simulation.Supplies; read by SupplyReader, LootCatalog.Supplies, put in play by FleetSupplies.Use; without data it's FleetSupplies.Shipped, which is the same). The rules say: what a jump costs (Use, parts that add up: per jump, per ship, per damaged ship, so many people rounding up or down, while a kind of ship is flying, while the Scourge is on the fleet; FleetSim.PerJump); what running short does (Shortage, by the units short: people lost to a cause, morale, a ship worn down with a message, or just a message); what having enough does (Stocked: morale, repairs, an item produced, each possibly only while a kind of ship is flying); whether the jump itself burns it (Jumps: fuel; every such supply must have enough to jump); what boarders take, how many jumps' worth a new fleet starts with, and the kinds of station that mostly hold it (the star map's stations are of those kinds, then two of a mix). Which supplies a station keeps in tanks comes from its mission template (its tank kinds' and reservoir's supplies). Every fleet supply item needs rules. FleetState.Version is 3 (a star system's Focus is a supply's item id). If the flagship is lost, or nobody is left, the run is over: you get a new fleet, and the kept weapons go with the old one. Cargo crates now also hold food, and fuel and water come from the stations' tanks. The needs board shows the Scourge, the supplies running shortest (jumps of reserve for each), the ships and what happened at the last jump (FleetSim.Needs). The star map (StarMap, StarSystem). The fleet crosses sectors of ten to fourteen systems, from an entry on the left to a gate on the right. Each system links to its nearest neighbors ahead (and one back), so every system leads on to the gate. Each has a station or a ship to raid (StarSystem.Target, a CampaignTarget of CampaignTuning, content/defs/campaign.json: stations, and frigates, carriers and strike carriers by weight from the sector each turns up in, rolled on a stream of their own; the entry and the gate always stations; a ship is marked with a diamond and named by its kind; Levels.Of plays a station as station:/…, a ship as :/…): its seed, decks (more in later sectors; a plan's level has its plan's), how well it's guarded, and what its cargo mostly holds (a fuel depot, an ice mine, a shipyard, ...). That last part travels in the level's name (GenerationSettings.CargoFocus, a supply's item id, and CargoPercent, -cfuel and -k: two crates in three are that supply, and there are half again as many crates; for a supply kept in tanks, one more tank, holding only that). What a station can hold, each in its item's color, comes from the data (StationSupplies, put in play from the loot data by LootContent). At the ship's star map table the host picks a system one jump away and sets course for it (FleetState.Destination), which sets up that system's station as the mission at the console. Launching a station raid (FleetSim.Launch) jumps the fleet there (fuel, the gap on the Scourge, a jump's worth of everything used). After the mission (FleetSim.AfterMission) the haul is stocked and the Scourge gains by the time it took. A mission at the gate takes the fleet into the next sector (a new map, and the trail half again harder to follow). With no course set, the fleet heads for the system nearest the gate. Knowledge and the Scourge on the map (StarMap.Observe, StarMap.ScourgeSystem). The fleet's sensors reach one jump: its own system and the ones next to it are seen (StarSystem.Seen: their stations are known), and the rest of the sector is just charted lanes. The Scourge follows the fleet's trail (FleetState.Trail, the systems jumped through in this sector). It's as many systems back along the trail as its distance in jumps, or not in the sector yet. When it's in sensor range it's sighted (SeenAt, SeenMission). After that the map shows where it was last seen, in a haze that grows with each mission since, and the board gives a long-range estimate of how far behind it is, rougher the older the sighting (FleetSim.ScourgeText). Here's the sneaky bit: that estimate, and the color of the board's Scourge line, come from the fleet's own reckoning (FleetState.ScourgeGuess), not from where the Scourge really is. The reckoning is set to the truth on a sighting and moved since then by what a jump or a mission is expected to do (FleetSim.ScourgeKnown), so if the Scourge is out of sight and has closed faster than expected, the board doesn't give it away. A run's pacing (RunPacing, set by the host when a mission loads: HordeSystem.Pacing, and the Director's numbers) comes from the fleet (FleetSim.Pacing). The closer the Scourge, the sooner the Choir shows up: While the Scourge is four or more missions behind, there's no Choir. At three, it comes once the hack starts. At two, from a deck before that. Nearer, from earlier still. Once it has caught the fleet, it's aboard from the start. Past coming from the start, the first horde comes 10 s sooner per step (down to 20 s) and the rest more often (down to every 45 s), and every horde is 8% bigger per step (up to half again). The soldiers' Director runs whatever the Scourge does, and every mission of the run makes it 12% quicker (up to twice as quick; twice that on Veteran): shorter quiet before a patrol, between patrols, and in its breathers (DirectorTuning.Escalated). A fight outside a run (tests, tools, the hand-built levels) uses RunPacing.Always: hordes as described above. Three-way fights. The horde goes for anyone who isn't Choir: whoever is nearest, players or soldiers. The field leads it to the players and to soldiers in a fight (alerted, engaging or hunting: the noise draws it), with a soldier counted as 10 m further away than a player (SoldierCost). So a horde called on the squad falls on any squad of soldiers it meets on the way, and soldiers fighting elsewhere draw some of it off. Soldiers see, shout (BarkKind.Choir) and shoot the horde like any enemy, backing off as it comes (a little slower than it runs). Choir Lancers (design doc: the Choir's elite squads). These are soldiers on the Choir's side: the soldier's brain, body and weapon, half again a soldier's health, no loot and no barks (barks are soldiers' words). They're drawn pale, with a white light for a face (with their model, lancer.gltf: bone-pale plate, violet, a crested helm). HordeSystem.CallLancers sends a squad out of sight like a horde, after the nearest player (SoldierSpawner.SpawnLancer, with a squad number of their own). They come with every hack wave from the second one on and at the extraction (two, plus one for every two players), and from the F3 overlay. The horde leaves them alone; soldiers and players fight them. The Choir's bigger bodies (ChoirSystem, ChoirUnit, design doc "Factions"). These are characters like soldiers (controller, body, health, the Choir's side; sizes and health per kind in ChoirBodies) with a simple brain of their own instead of a soldier's (ChoirBrain). Each goes for the nearest non-Choir target, along a path over the grid (two searches per tick at most) or straight at them once within 9 m and in the open, and attacks after a wind-up that warns you (rooted, posed, a sound). Strippers (450 health, 2.25 m tall, 4.3 m/s) close in and strike everyone in front of them within 2.1 m for 32, and every prop there for 220, so cover, crates and breakable walls go in a blow or two. When a breakable prop is between a Stripper and its target (it checks every 0.3 s), it goes to it and strikes it. The mission's locked doors can't be broken. Spitters (110 health, quick) keep 9 to 22 m away with a clear line, sidestepping, and lob a glob of acid (AcidGlob: thrown on an arc to land where the target is heading). It burns whoever it hits squarely for 12 and leaves a pool 2.2 m across for 6 s (AcidPool) that burns any non-Choir standing in it for 5 every half second, so it's ground you need to move off. ChoirSystem is a late system (after the horde). It writes each body's command for the next tick, and its blows and acid are hits logged after this tick's shots have cleared the log. A horde brings a Stripper for every 40 called and a Spitter for every 30, with at most three and four around at once (HordeTuning), and you can send one at a time from the F3 overlay. They're drawn as stand-in boxes like the soldiers, with the Choir's pale plates over dark sinew and its white light (CharacterModels.AddChoir): a hunched Stripper whose bladed arms rise in its wind-up, and a gaunt Spitter rearing back with a glowing sac. Globs are bright blobs and pools are glowing discs. Cost. So did the "not characters" bet pay off? 300 swarmlings with four players take under half a millisecond per tick for the whole world in the AI tests (HordeTests), allocation-free and deterministic. About 0.15 ms of a station's tick is the horde's. Replication (SwarmView on the host, one per client; SwarmReplica on the client; protocol version 13). The snapshot ends with the swarmlings within 70 m of the client's player: a table of their IDs, each in a slot it keeps (cheap to resend: it only changes as they arrive, leave and die); a bit each for the dead; updates for some of them, about 8 bytes each: position, to 3 cm relative to the client's feet; velocity to a quarter meter per second; facing to 1/64 of a turn; its action; and what it's clinging to, three bits (since protocol version 20). How many updates fit is set by the client's budget (SwarmView.Fit): whatever the rest of the fight left of 360 bytes from one snapshot to the next last time (64 kbps is 400), from 2 to 16 per snapshot. The horde takes what's left. Between updates the client draws each swarmling along a curve through its last few updates (Hermite, along their velocities), and on along its velocity for up to half a second past the newest (SwarmTrack). An update that puts it somewhere else is blended in over 6 ticks from the moment it arrives, timed from ticks alone, so the host can keep the same tracks and know exactly where the client is drawing every swarmling. It updates the ones drawn furthest from where they really are first (weighted by how close they are to the client: centimeters at its feet, half a meter 60 m away), sends any that start a lunge within 25 m right away, and sends newcomers right away. How well does it hold up? In the soak test (four players at 150 ms with 2% loss, firing into 300 around them, with the Strippers and Spitters the horde brings and the station's soldiers fighting both), that's about 63 kbps per client in total, with the horde down to its fewest updates. Within 15 m, a swarmling is drawn about 55 cm from where it is (median; 7.5 m at the 95th percentile). Without the soldiers, it's about 26 cm (1.4 m). The host knows where the client drew each one to within a centimeter (95th percentile; more only for a lost snapshot), and that's what the client's shots are tested against, so it hits what it saw however far that was from the truth. One caveat: those numbers are station 3's from before the procgen revamp's shaped rooms. The soak now fights on stations 3 to 10 and judges the budget and the median on their average, which has been 64.8 kbps and 1.16 m since then, over the bounds (64 kbps, 1 m), until the networking work in the roadmap's Phase 4, Step 3 is done. Drawing: instanced, animated on the GPU. The swarmling is a model made and animated in Blender (content/models/swarmling.gltf, docs/blender/creatures.md): an armature, a skinned body, a cheaper body for far away (_LOD1) and six actions (Run, Idle, WindUp, Bite, Stagger, Death). AnimatedModel (Content) bakes it when it's loaded (on the loading thread). Every action is sampled at 30 frames per second and skinned on the CPU once, giving the position of each vertex on each frame, with its face's normal packed into the fourth float (vertex animation, the way textures would hold it, but in a storage buffer: about 2 MB). The renderer uploads it once (SetSwarmModel). Each frame the client (SwarmAnimator) sends one 64-byte SwarmInstance per swarmling: where it stands and faces, two poses (two frames each and how far between them), how far it has faded from one to the other, a hit flash, its glow and how far it has sunk. What it plays follows Swarmling.Action (Run at the speed it covers ground, a loop every 1.1 m; Idle when standing; WindUp; Bite when a wind-up ends; Stagger; Death by how long it's been dead), cross-fading over 0.12 s. The near ones (22 m) are one instanced draw of the full body, and the rest (out to 90 m) are one draw of the far body. They cast shadows with the far body. 300 swarmlings are two draws and 19 KB per frame, where the box stand-ins were 120,000 vertices built on the CPU. Huge win! The dead go dark and sink. They burst (ImpactEffects.AddBurst: chitin shards, glowing motes, a spray and a pool of dark violet ichor), and hits on them bleed ichor. Sounds: a shriek at each wind-up, a squeal at each death, the bite, and the chitter of the crowd near you, louder the more of them there are. Renderer The renderer uses Vulkan 1.3 core features only, so any 1.3 driver works without extensions beyond the swapchain (plus, where the driver has them, the ray tracing extensions, see Ray tracing below, and some presentation extras, see Sleep, wake and a lost GPU below). Why so strict? There are no optional extensions to probe, and dynamic rendering and sync2 keep the renderer short. Here's what that gets us: Dynamic rendering: no render pass or framebuffer objects. Pipelines name their attachment formats instead. synchronization2: vkCmdPipelineBarrier2 and vkQueueSubmit2. Two frames in flight, each with its own command pool, command buffer, image-acquired semaphore, fence, and overlay and effect vertex buffers. Present-wait semaphores are per swapchain image, which avoids a reuse hazard the validation layer reports. VMA (Brutal.Vulkan.Vma) allocates every buffer and image. Static meshes live in device-local memory, filled once through a staging buffer. Per-frame data lives in mapped, host-visible memory. Rebuilds. The swapchain and the frame's images (FrameTargets) are rebuilt when the swapchain is out of date or suboptimal, or the framebuffer size changes, and together with the pipelines when the antialiasing changes. Everything new is created before anything old is destroyed, so a rebuild that fails leaves the old one in place. Frames are skipped while the window is minimized, and while the surface has no area (Swapchain.ChooseExtent). Windows reports that for a window that isn't minimized while its display is asleep or unplugged, and a swapchain can't be that size. Present mode: FIFO with vsync; mailbox, then immediate, without. Window modes. The window can be windowed, exclusive full screen (the display's own resolution and refresh rate) or borderless (an undecorated window covering the display), on whichever display holds most of it (GameWindow.SetMode, from the Display setting or F11). A change resizes the framebuffer, so the swapchain is rebuilt like for any resize. Going back to a window restores its old position. Sleep, wake and a lost GPU. The rule here is simple: no wait in a frame is unbounded. The frame's fence and the next image are waited for in 100 ms slices, with the window's events pumped in between. Why? A display that's asleep can hold on to a FIFO swapchain's images indefinitely, and a window that stops responding holds up Windows' own broadcasts on sleep and wake. Past RendererOptions.FrameWaitLimit (1 s) the frame is skipped and VulkanRenderer.PresentationPaused reports it, and the game and Studio then sleep between frames. Rebuilds wait for the frames in flight (the only GPU work outstanding, since every other submit waits for itself) rather than for the device to go idle. One-off GPU work waits at most GpuWait.HangLimit. A frame's fence is reset right before the submit that signals it, so a frame abandoned part way through never leaves a fence that nothing will signal. When the driver reports the device or surface lost (Windows resets a driver that stops responding, often on waking), or one-off work hangs past its limit, VulkanRenderer destroys everything it created with the device and creates it again on a new one (CreateDeviceObjects, Recover). Then it re-uploads everything it was given: the world mesh, the horde's model, the skinned meshes and the UI textures. TextureStore keeps the textures' pixels and names them by its own IDs, so ImGui's and the icons' texture IDs stay valid. A frame that loses the device is skipped. Losing it more than three times in a minute is treated as fatal, with an error. --lose-device simulates a loss in a smoke run. Where the driver has VK_EXT_swapchain_maintenance1, presents are fenced, so a swapchain's semaphores are only destroyed once presentation is done with them (without it, they're destroyed after the queue goes idle, as usual). Where it has VK_EXT_full_screen_exclusive (Windows), a borderless window forbids the driver from taking over the display, and full screen allows it. Textures (TextureStore, the UI's textures: the logo, ImGui's font atlas, icons) are replaced and destroyed without waiting for the GPU. The old image is retired (RetireQueue) and released once every frame submitted before that has finished. Pacing (FrameLimiter, Core): frames are capped at 180 per second, and at 30 while the window is in the background (unfocused). Waiting sleeps for all but the last 1.5 ms and only spins for that part, so a capped frame uses no CPU while it waits. On Windows the sleep is a high-resolution waitable timer (PreciseSleep), because a plain sleep there rounds up to the 15.6 ms system tick. Validation. --validation enables VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation when it's installed. ValidationMonitor logs its messages and counts errors, which is what fails the GPU smoke test. Each frame is drawn in high dynamic range. Here's the flow: The scene is drawn in linear light into a high-range image (FrameTargets.HdrFormat, RGBA16F), multisampled (RendererOptions.Antialiasing, VulkanRenderer.Antialiasing: 1, 2 or 4 samples, 4 by default, set by the Antialiasing setting or --antialiasing) and resolved at the end of the scene. Next to it is a second target for the indirect light (FrameTargets.Indirect: what the world's fill, its ambient and room bounce lit; also resolved). Its depth is kept, not resolved, because the ambient occlusion reads it (the first sample when multisampled). Then full-screen passes compute its ambient occlusion, add bloom, and bring it into the display's range in the sRGB swapchain, where the overlay and the UI are drawn last. These passes share content/shaders/post_common.slang: one triangle from the vertex index, the images through FrameTargets.CreateLayout's set of four (the pass's source, the bloom, the indirect light and the occlusion), and PostConstants pushed. In order: Pass Pipeline State Reflections ReflectionProbes: rooms whose cube maps are captured this frame (below), each face with world.slang (Pipelines.Capture: one sample, front faces clockwise, since a cube face is mirrored), the staging cube's mips by blits, then reflection_filter.slang (compute) into the room's cube Before the scene; nothing most frames Atmosphere FroxelGrid: froxel_inject.slang gives each cell of a grid of the view (160 × 90 × 64 on High, 80 × 45 × 32 on Low, out to 60 m, its slices spaced by the square of their depth) its haze and the light it scatters towards the eye; froxel_integrate.slang follows each column out from the eye, gathering it and what passes (below) Compute, before the scene; nothing with the atmosphere off World world.slang: flat shading in each vertex's surface material (diffuse and GGX highlights), a sun and sky fill, tiled point lights, reflections of the room's cube map (box projected) or the sky, glow (a color's excess over 1, past white), the air in front of it (the atmosphere, below), a per-draw tint Reverse-Z depth test (Greater), depth write, back faces culled; set 0 is the lights, the shadow maps, the materials, the rooms and their cube maps Horde swarm.slang: one animated body drawn once for each swarmling (instanced), each vertex placed from the body's baked frames (a storage buffer, set 1) by the instance's two poses and fade, then lit as the world is (world_shading.slang, which both include) As the world; the tint's x and y in the push constants say where the body's frames start and how many vertices it has Effects effects.slang: world-space quads with a color and a shape per vertex (impacts, tracers, blood, smoke), seen through the air in front of them as the world is: the whole square, a soft disc, a hard disc, or a blood splat whose lobes and flecks come from a seed Depth test against the world, no depth write, alpha blended, two-sided View model world.slang again, for the weapon in your hands: its own 52° projection (CameraMath.ViewModelFieldOfView), so it neither stretches with the field of view nor swells with aiming's zoom, and no fog The viewport's depth range squeezed into its near end (0.95 to 1): nothing in the world beyond the near plane reaches it, so the gun is drawn over the world and never into a wall Ambient occlusion gtao.slang (gtao_ms.slang when antialiased): ground-truth ambient occlusion (Jimenez et al. 2016) from the depth into FrameTargets.Occlusion (two 16-bit floats: how open, and the distance), at half the screen's size by default: for each pixel, two slices at a turn from interleaved gradient noise, four steps each side within 0.75 m, against the normal from the depth's slopes; the sky and the gun in hand (depth 0.95 and over) left open. Then gtao_blur.slang, 4 by 4 weighed by distance, into FrameTargets.OcclusionBlurred No depth, one sample. Off (the Ambient occlusion setting, --ambient-occlusion off), the blurred image is only made readable; full resolution (AmbientOcclusion.Full) takes four slices Bloom bloom_down.slang into each of the bloom's levels (FrameTargets.Bloom: its mips, the first half the screen, packed 11-11-10 floats where the GPU can draw and filter them), each half the one above with a 13-tap filter, the first taking only what is past the threshold (1, a soft knee of 0.5) with each group of taps weighed down by its brightness (no flashing pixels); then bloom_up.slang adds each level, through a tent filter, into the one above No depth, one sample; up blends by adding. Off (the Bloom setting, --no-bloom), the first level is only made readable Tonemap tonemap.slang: the scene, less its indirect light where the ambient occlusion shuts it out, plus its bloom (0.12), by the exposure (VulkanRenderer.Exposure, 1), through the tone curve (ToneCurve: the game's own neutral one by default, as lit below 0.8 and rolling off above, the curve the world shader had before the frame had range; or AgX), then a step of noise in the display's 8 bits against banding in the dark Into the swapchain, no depth Overlay overlay.slang: flat color per vertex No depth, alpha blended UI ui.slang: textured, vertex color, for Dear ImGui and the splash logo No depth, alpha blended, scissored per draw, plain (Y-down) viewport, drawn last Ray tracing (RayScene, RayTracingSupport: the Ray tracing setting, --ray-tracing off|on, on by default where the GPU supports it; docs/plans/ray-tracing.md). Where the GPU has VK_KHR_acceleration_structure, VK_KHR_ray_query and buffer device addresses (RTX 20 and later, RX 6000 and later, Arc, and Mesa's lavapipe from 25, which is the driver CI and the tests use), the device is created with them whether or not rays are on, so changing the setting doesn't need a restart. Rays are cast as ray queries from the existing compute and fragment shaders, with no ray-tracing pipelines. The level's bottom-level structure is built when it loads (seed 7: 77k triangles, under 2 s on lavapipe). Its drawn parts are merged into as few opaque geometries as the mesh's order allows. Each part that can disappear (a broken prop, a shot-out light's glass, an opened door, a blown hull plate: RayParts.CanGo in the client) gets its own non-opaque geometry, so a ray checks a per-frame flag for whether it's there (FrameGeometry.Gone: a part tint alpha of -1). A room that's out of sight is -2, Unseen, which rays still hit, because things out of sight still cast shadows into what's visible (RayGeometry, traceNearest in ray_common.slang). Each frame, first (the Ray tracing pass), a compute pass poses the skinned bodies (ray_skin.slang, skinning them the same way skinned.slang does) and builds them into two bottom levels, one of them just the viewer's own body. The moving world's triangles go into a third. A top level goes over them, plus one instance per horde body of the horde's far mesh in its first frame, placed the way swarm.slang places it (RayInstances: an instance's kind and number in its custom index, one mask per kind). The debug view (--ray-debug, or the F3 overlay's Ray debug view) draws what a ray from the eye through each pixel hits instead of the scene (ray_debug.slang): the level grey-blue, the moving world yellow, bodies orange, the viewer's own body green, the horde red, without bloom or occlusion. Rays see every room, while the scene only draws the rooms in sight of the player's room, so a camera moved away from the player (--camera) can see rooms in the debug view that the scene leaves out. Shadows by rays (RayLighting, the Ray shadows pass, on wherever rays are traced). This runs after the atmosphere and before the scene, at half the screen's resolution. A pre-pass draws what the scene draws (the level, the moving world, the bodies, the viewer's own body, the horde) as each pixel's surface, normal and distance from the eye (negative on a body or the horde; ray_prepass.slang and ray_prepass_body.slang with the scene's own vertex shaders). Then a compute pass works out, for each pixel, the light its tile's lights give it before any shadow, and traces two rays (one at Medium and Low ray tracing quality, below). Each ray goes to one of those lights, picked by how much light it gives, at a random point on it (anywhere on a rect light's glass, so its shadows are soft). The share of the light that arrives is the picked light's share of the total where the ray is clear (ray_shadow_trace.slang, the ratio estimator of Heitz et al. 2018: only the shadow is noisy, never the light). A body's rays ignore bodies and the horde (they'd shadow the body itself, and the horde's structure isn't posed). A flashlight's and a flash's rays ignore bodies (they start in someone's hands). A ray stops 4 cm short of a rect light's glass and 15 cm short of a point light. The rays are guided (docs/plans/ray-tracing.md phase 6, like MegaLights' visible light list). Each 8 by 8 block of shadow pixels, a compute group, records the lights its clear rays reached by their keys (PointLight.Key, folded into 128 bits). Next frame, a pixel's rays go to the lights its block found clear 80% of the time, with each ray's light weighted by its chance under both picks so the estimate stays unbiased. That share is carried over frames where the same surface was there last frame (ray_shadow_temporal.slang: found with last frame's view-projection, counted as the same if it was as far from the eye then and facing the same way; the new estimate's weight is one over the number of frames held, never under 5%, which is about a third of a second at 60 fps). The accumulated history is clamped to within two standard deviations of this frame's estimates around the pixel (luma and chroma, on similar surfaces in the 3 by 3: a neighborhood clamp, docs/plans/ray-tracing.md phase 7), so a moving body's shadow shows up instead of averaging away. The bounce isn't clamped. Then it's smoothed along surfaces by two passes of an edge-avoiding à-trous filter (ray_shadow_filter.slang). The world shaders, given flag 16, take their tile's lights without their shadow maps and multiply by that share (rayShadowRatio in scene_lights.slang: the four half-resolution pixels around each pixel, weighted by how similar their surfaces are; set 0, bindings 9 and 10, in the general layout, with a placeholder texel where rays aren't traced). The gun in hand keeps its own lights. Every light then reaches through its room's doorways (SceneLights.RaysTraced: its box covers the room and its neighbors, and the lights of rooms next to the visible ones are kept too), since rays keep it off whatever walls hide. At a point in another room, a light only counts where the line from the point to it passes through a doorway between the two rooms (throughDoorway: each room's doorways, from the layout's, RoomLighting.Doorways, up to 12 per room at set 0 binding 15, each a box across its wall grown by the light's size plus 30 cm; if none are recorded between the two rooms, or there are more than fit, the light is kept). This applies in the world shaders, the shadow rays and the rays' hits alike, so the ratio's lights are the ones shaded, and a light no ray could reach costs neither shading nor a ray. The four half-resolution pixels each result is read from, and their weights, are computed once per pixel for all of them (rayTaps). The atmosphere still lights its air with the lights' shadow maps, with each widened light only in its own room (its room is in its box's w, airLight). --ray-shadows, or the F3 overlay's Ray shadow view, draws the share alone: grey where a surface's light arrives, black where it's shadowed. Without rays, a light lit its whole room through anything inside it. The airlock's chamber, walled to the ceiling, now has its own panel. Bounce by rays (RayLighting, the Ray bounce pass, on wherever rays are traced; docs/plans/ray-tracing.md phase 5). From the same pre-pass's surfaces, at half resolution, each pixel casts one ray off its surface in a cosine-weighted direction, up to 30 m (15 m at Low quality; ray_indirect_trace.slang). At Medium and Low only half the pixels do this each frame, in a checkerboard that alternates each frame. The temporal pass keeps a skipped pixel's history as it was, or starts it from its four neighbors when it has none. What the ray hits is lit the way the world shaders would light it: the level's color and material there, read from the level's own vertex and index buffers (set 2) using the hit's geometry and triangle (each geometry's first index is RayGeometry's run), or a neutral grey for anything else; times the lights there. That's its room's lights: each frame LightStore.WriteRoomLights lists, for each room, the frame's lights whose reach touches its box, nearest first, up to 31 (set 0 binding 12), or every light of the frame for a point in no room. One of them is picked by what it gives (a weighted reservoir), with a shadow ray to it; outdoors the sun is among them; plus the sky's fill and that room's bounce, which stands in for the bounces after the first. A ray that hits nothing takes the room's bounce where it ended up (so a short reach doesn't darken a big hall). One that hits the back of a face brings nothing back, and none brings back more than a luminance of 4 (a lone ray under a light would leave a speck). Averaged over the hemisphere, that's the light a white surface receives from all around, the way the world shaders count light. It's carried over frames by the shadows' temporal pass (never under 3% new) and smoothed by four passes of their filter (steps 1 to 8), each result with its own set 1 over the shared guide (RayLighting's chains). The world shaders, given flag 64, use it instead of the room's bounce (rayBounce, set 0 binding 11; the reflection captures keep the room's bounce). --ray-bounce, or the F3 overlay's Ray bounce view, draws it alone. It's darker than the room's bounce on average (the room's bounce is a tuned estimate, RoomBounce.Gain) and varies across a room: lit where light comes through a doorway, dark under a table. Occlusion by rays (RayLighting, the Ray occlusion pass, wherever rays are traced and ambient occlusion is on; docs/plans/ray-tracing.md phase 8). From the same pre-pass's surfaces, at half resolution, each pixel casts two cosine-weighted rays out to 1.5 m (ray_occlusion_trace.slang), each giving how far it got divided by how far it could go. The average is how open the surface is. It's carried over frames and smoothed the same way as the shadows (a third chain, clamped like theirs). The world shaders, given flag 256, apply it (rayOpenness, set 0 binding 13) to the sky's fill and to what a surface reflects (by the reflection's light where it reflects a cube map or the sky, otherwise by the fill). It isn't applied to the bounce by rays, whose own rays already account for occlusion. GTAO and the tonemap's occlusion term are skipped in that case. --ray-occlusion, or the F3 overlay's Ray occlusion view, draws it alone. Reflections by rays (RayLighting, the Ray reflections pass, wherever rays are traced; docs/plans/ray-tracing.md phase 9). The pre-pass writes each pixel's roughness next to its surface (the look, set 1 binding 12). On surfaces smoother than 0.4 (RayLighting.TracedRoughness: glass and bare metal, not painted metal or plastic), each pixel casts one ray along the highlight's lobe (a GGX half vector for the roughness, with the view mirrored about it), up to 40 m (ray_reflection_trace.slang). What it hits is lit the same way as the bounce's hits (ray_hits.slang: the level's color and material, the room's lights with one traced to, the sky's fill and the room's bounce), and its glow is added too, so a panel's glass shows up in a glossy floor. A ray that hits nothing takes the room's cube map along its direction, or the sky. It's carried over frames quickly (at least 20% new), clamped and smoothed twice. The world shaders use it (flag 1024, rayReflection, set 0 binding 14) instead of the cube map: fully up to a roughness of 0.24, and not at all past 0.4. Ambient occlusion only darkens the cube map's share. --ray-reflections, or the F3 overlay's Ray reflection view, draws it alone. Ray tracing quality (RayTracingQuality, the video settings' Ray tracing quality under Ray tracing, or --ray-quality low|medium|high for one run; docs/plans/ray-tracing.md phase 11). It sets everything that affects the rays' cost together (RayQualitySettings.For): High is two shadow rays per pixel and the bounce on every pixel every frame, out to 30 m. Medium, the default, is one shadow ray and the bounce on half the pixels per frame. Low also limits the bounce to 15 m with two filter passes, and uses one occlusion ray. These reach the shaders in the rays' frame constants (quality, and the shadow rays in tuning). A change resets the rays' history. Path tracing and DLSS (RenderPath, PathTracer, Streamline; the video settings' Renderer, or --renderer hybrid|path-traced; docs/plans/path-tracing.md). The Renderer setting chooses how the scene is lit: Hybrid is everything above, raster with rays for shadows, bounce, occlusion and reflections. Path traced is an RTXPT-style path tracer, on any GPU that traces rays. The path tracer shares the frame's start (ray structures, light grid, shadow atlas, atmosphere) and end (bloom, tonemap, HUD) with the hybrid path and replaces what is between: A raster G-buffer drawn by the scene's own vertex shaders (path_gbuffer*.slang: position, normal and roughness, material, albedo, emission, motion in pixels). path_trace.slang traces each pixel's paths (1 to 8 bounces, 1 to 4 a pixel): next-event estimation with a shadow ray to a light picked by resampled importance from the pixel's light-grid cell, its room's panels and the sun, a diffuse or GGX (visible normals) bounce, Russian roulette after the second, a firefly clamp on indirect light, and paths that run out of bounces end in their room's bounce light, which is the engine's radiance cache (the Radiance cache setting; off is unbiased and darker). It writes diffuse and specular light demodulated by their albedos, the guides DLSS Ray Reconstruction needs, and the specular hit distance. Then one of two denoisers: DLSS Ray Reconstruction (NVIDIA RTX, through Streamline), or the built-in one (path_denoise_temporal.slang and path_denoise_filter.slang: reprojected history with depth and normal tests and a moments-based variance, then four à-trous passes guided by depth, normal and luminance, specular filtered for two). path_compose.slang puts light back on its albedo, adds emission and the air in front, and the transparent effects (drawn into their own target, which Ray Reconstruction also takes as its transparency layer). DLSS renders at its mode's share of the display (Quality 67%, Balanced 58%, Performance 50%, Ultra Performance 33%, DLAA 100%), with a Halton(2, 3) jitter of at least 32 phases, and Super Resolution (or Ray Reconstruction) brings it up to the display into the frame's color. Everything in the Path tracing settings applies on the next frame; the path tracer's images are made again when the render size changes. Only loading Streamline is fixed at start (it has to be in place before the Vulkan instance is made), so the menu's "Load NVIDIA DLSS at start" asks for a restart. Streamline (Streamline/, NVIDIA Streamline 2.14.16 in vendor/streamline, Windows only). StreamlineSession loads sl.interposer.dll only once StreamlineSignature has checked that it is signed by NVIDIA (Authenticode, then the Streamline key inside it, as the SDK's sl_security.h does), and starts with manual hooking: the renderer asks for the features' instance and device extensions and Vulkan 1.2 and 1.3 features (VulkanFeatureNames), hands its instance, device and queue to slSetVulkanInfo, and presents through the interposer's vkQueuePresentKHR. Each frame: a frame token, the camera's constants (StreamlineCamera: view to clip and back, clip to previous clip, the jitter, motion vectors in pixels scaled to the render size, reverse depth), the mode's options, the tagged images (StreamlineImage) and slEvaluateFeature on the frame's command buffer. The structures are laid out as the SDK's headers lay them (StreamlineLayoutTests checks every offset against tools/streamline/layout.cpp). Where Streamline cannot run (not Windows, not NVIDIA, an old driver, an unsigned DLL, --no-streamline), DlssSupport says why and the menu shows it; the path tracer then renders at full size with its own denoiser. What the GPU spends (GpuTimer). Timestamps are written between the ray structures, the shadows, the reflections' captures, the atmosphere's grid, the shadows by rays, the bounce by rays, the scene (the G-buffer, when path traced), the path tracing, its denoising, DLSS, the ambient occlusion, the bloom, and the tonemap with the HUD. They're read back when a frame's slot comes round again and smoothed into VulkanRenderer.GpuMilliseconds, which is shown in the F3 overlay and printed by smoke runs (GPU: Ray tracing ... ms, Shadows ... ms, ..., Ray shadows ... ms, Reflections ..., Atmosphere ..., Scene ..., Ambient occlusion ..., Bloom ..., Tonemap and HUD ...). docs/plans/lighting.md asks each of its phases to state its cost in these terms. The client hands each frame a FrameGeometry: overlay triangles, effect triangles, one tint per world part, and the frame's point lights. The world is drawn in runs of consecutive parts with the same tint, pushed at offset 112 of the push constants (128 bytes in total, the most every device allows), so an untinted world stays a single draw and a flashing target adds two. Effects are built on the CPU by EffectBuilder (billboards facing the eye, beams rotated to face it, decals lifted 1 cm off their surface and rotated about it). Each quad carries its corners (-1 to 1) and an EffectShape, which the fragment shader cuts out, so round particles and splats don't need textures. Culling by room (RoomVisibility, stations only). A station is one mesh, drawn by part runs, and it used to be drawn whole: looking towards most of the deck cost every room behind the walls, shaded with its lights. Ouch. So what can we skip? Rooms only see each other through doorways, so each frame the client walks from the camera's room through every doorway that's on screen, narrowing the part of the screen each room is seen through (portals), and hides the parts of rooms it doesn't reach (with a negative tint alpha, the same as broken props). Rooms standing on a visible room are drawn too, since their floors are its ceiling. Only visible rooms' lights are sent. It's conservative: a doorway you're standing in shows everything its room shows, locked doors count as open, and a camera in no room (the death camera under the floor) draws everything. In seed 2026's insertion bay, the four directions drew 446 to 2,930 of the level's 57,534 triangles and 1 to 6 of 136 rooms, with 4 to 19 lights. Renders with and without culling are identical. A test casts rays through a grid of screen points from every fifth room in eight directions on three seeds, and checks that whatever they hit is drawn. F3 shows rooms, triangles and lights drawn. Lighting. Outdoors (a hand-built level) the world is lit by a warm sun and a cool sky fill, as before. Inside a station there's no sun, only the faintest fill (0.018: a room with its lights out is black except for shapes right in front of you, which is a flashlight's job) and a black fog (0.028 per meter). The light comes from the level's fixtures: Point lights. PointLights (position, color, radius and a box) only light what's inside their box, the room, so a light never shines through a wall. Through an opening wider than a door (an open hall's end), the box carries on into the slab of the next room straight beyond it, as wide as the opening (LightReach). Rect lights (PointLight.Rect, LevelLight.HalfU/HalfV). A panel's glass, a hall's floor channel and each wall's floor strip are rectangles shining on one side (the cross product of their half axes), as bright as their glass glows. A panel is twice that (FixtureGlow.LightGain), so rooms keep their light without the glass blooming them away; strips and channels light as they glow (FixtureGlow.LightFor). A surface takes a rectangle's diffuse light by Lambert's formula for the polygon clipped at its horizon (rectIrradiance in scene_lights.slang, each edge by Heitz's fitted angle over its sine; RectLights is the same in C#, tested against the light summed over the glass), or as a point past four half diagonals (RectLights.FarFactor). Its highlight comes from Karis' representative point (where the reflected view meets the glass, with the lobe widened by the glass's narrower half over its distance). Each fades to nothing at its radius from its nearest point, and it's binned by its glass plus its radius, only in front of it. Other lights. Flashes, blasts and alarm beacons are point lights that fade with a gentle inverse square, and flashlights are spotlights. Shadow maps are only for point lights and lights shining down (a hall's floor glow shines up, so what it lights is above it). Bounce (RoomBounce) is the fill. Each frame every live light's strength goes into its room (the panels at their current brightness, flickering or fading, the alarms, the flashes, and a share of each flashlight's: SceneLights.Build). Each room's bounce is that light off its floor (onto faces turned down) and off its walls and ceiling (onto faces turned up), using their colors (RoomSurfaces, averaged from the room's parts) and spread over their area, plus a share of each neighbor's bounce through each doorway, by the opening's area (RoomBounce.OpeningArea). It eases to a change over a fifth of a second and jumps up at once for a flash. The shaders find a point's room in a grid of the layout's cells (RoomLighting: set 0, bindings 5 and 6, with the point moved 10 cm out of its face first) and take that room's bounce. A point in no room (a hand-built level) gets none, only the sky's fill. So a red alarm room is red in its shadows, and a room whose lights are shot out goes dark except for what comes through its doorways. Aged panels. Panels are dimmed (0.5) and aged: each room's light drifts from its role's color towards a sickly fluorescent green or a dirty sodium yellow. 14 in 100 are dead (never a room's first) and 10 flicker. Glow. Color channels above 1 glow: the excess is added unlit, which is how panels, a grenade's blinking light and rarity stripes shine. A light and its fixture are one (FixtureGlow). A panel's glass is its light's color, as bright as the light's strength over the glass (LevelLight.Glow, set when the level is made), so a blue light has a blue panel. A failing panel's glass dims with its light (a part tint), and one that's shot out throws a spark and its light fades over 0.3 s. Alarm lamps, a gun light's lens (on along with its flashlight: WeaponModel.Lamps, Flashlights), a muzzle flash's flame and a hall's floor channels glow the same way, capped (FixtureGlow.MaxGlow) so a small lens doesn't blind you. Bright light rolls off above 0.8 instead of clipping. Gunfire. Every gunshot and every blast adds a brief light (60 ms and 0.45 s), limited to the room it happens in. The light grid. The client (SceneLights) sends the nearest lights whose box is in view, at most 128, flickering the failing ones. The renderer bins them into a light grid each frame on the GPU (LightGrid, light_grid.slang, the Light grid pass, first in the frame; clustered shading). The screen is split into 32 × 18 tiles, each split by distance from the eye into 24 slices (the first up to 1 m, then evenly in log distance up to 100 m, the last one beyond). One thread per cell finds the cell's bounds in the world and takes each light whose reach (its box, cut to its radius, and for a rect light to its lit side) overlaps them and comes within its radius, at most 31 per cell, nearest first (LightGrid.Touches makes the same decision on the CPU, for the tests). Each pixel only tests its cell's lights, found from its distance and screen position (lightCell in scene_lights.slang; the shadow rays and the atmosphere's cells find theirs the same way), so a nearby wall no longer tests the lights of rooms far behind it in the same part of the screen. Until phase 10 of docs/plans/ray-tracing.md the tiles were screen-only and binned on the CPU, 15 per tile and then 31 (0113's black squares were tiles crowded by lights from next door). The view model, which has its own projection, reads the nearest eight lights directly. It keeps a little of the sun outdoors (35%) and a trace of light inside (2%, so in the dark it's a dark shape), but not a flashlight starting within a meter of it (that's its own). Shootable lights and flashlights. A broken panel (see Station dressing) is hidden like any broken prop, and SceneLights leaves out a light whose panel is hidden while its room is visible. A PointLight can be a spotlight: a direction and the cosine of its cone's half angle (80 bytes per light), brightest along its axis, fading to nothing over the cone's outer half, falling off more gently than a bulb (a beam carries), and boxed to the cone's bounds. Flashlights are the first use. CommandButtons.Flashlight (T) switches MovementState.Flashlight, which is predicted like any movement state and replicated as a bit of every character's flags, so everyone sees everyone's flashlight. The client adds a spotlight for each character with theirs on (the viewer's just right of and below the eye, so its shadows show a little; everyone else's from the gun, half a meter ahead of the body), with the viewer's first, ahead of every other light. The first three cast shadows. Each gets a perspective map along the beam, redrawn every frame (it moves) into a cache slot reserved for it, from the rooms it can light (its room, the rooms through its doorways, and the rooms standing on any of them, whose floors are ceilings), and it's boxed to those rooms (the walls of any other room inside that box go into its map too, so the beam stops at them). The rest are boxed to their own room, like a panel. Unlike a panel, a beam sends no bounce light to faces turned away from it, or into its own shadows. Why so careful? A box can include the far side of a wall, and a beam must never show through one (it used to, faintly, which was enough to tell someone was there). A beam belongs to the room its carrier is in, whether standing, crouched or down, and starts inside that room, clear of its walls, however close to one they stand. (It used to be judged from the light's own position, which put a crouched soldier's beam in the story below, or in no room at all on the ground floor, boxed to nothing and shining through every wall.) Soldiers switch theirs on in the dark and while hunting or searching (SoldierAiSystem.Flashlight, kept on for four seconds after the last reason). LightMap (AI) knows each room's working lights from the level (each one a breakable panel, checked every half second for being shot out) and calls a point dark when they barely reach it. The client draws the nearest beams first, and those behind walls last. A character's weapon frame is in every snapshot, and a player's roll is too, so everyone holds their own gun as rolled (CharacterModels). Shadows. The nearest 16 panels in view (not flashes) cast shadows (ShadowAtlas: one 2048² depth image in 512² tiles, filled every frame before the main pass). A panel only shines downwards, so each map is a single view straight down from the light, 140° across, out to its radius, with no cube maps. It draws the light's own room (its parts, minus broken ones; GeneratedLevel.PartRooms) and every character (and the horde, with its far body, swarm_shadow.slang), so props, catwalks and soldiers all cast shadows. A room is a box and a light only lights its inside, so nothing outside the room could shadow it. The pipeline is depth-only, both sides, with slope-scaled bias. The world shader pushes the point 4 cm off its surface and takes four hardware-filtered comparison samples half a texel apart, so edges are soft. A shadow removes the light's direct part, and the room's bounce stays. Points the map doesn't see (above the light, beside the panel) count as lit. Cached. The level part of each map is drawn once into a second atlas, the cache (4096×2048, 32 slots), kept per light (least recently used is evicted) and only redrawn when its room changes (a hash of which of its parts are hidden: a prop broken, a door opened), at most six per frame, so walking into a room full of lights causes no spike (a light still waiting goes unshadowed for a frame or two). Each frame the maps in use are copied from the cache into the atlas, and only lights with a character within reach of their room draw the characters over theirs, so a quiet station draws no shadow geometry at all. Shadows can be turned off in the Video settings (GameSettings.Shadows) for slower cards. Atmosphere (FroxelGrid, Atmosphere: the Atmosphere setting, --atmosphere off|low|high, High by default). The level's haze (FrameParameters.FogDensity: 0.028 per meter in a station, with the clear color as its color, black there) is computed in a froxel grid of the view every frame, before the scene, by two compute passes that read the lights' set (set 0, which compute shaders can see too). Each cell's density is the haze, times its room's factor (RoomLighting.Haze, 0.7 to 1.6 from a hash of the room's position, so some rooms are dustier), plus smoke. Smoke is FogVolumes: what a blast leaves (a cloud that rises, swells and thins over eight seconds) and a breach's smoke while it pours (CombatFeedback.BuildFogVolumes; at most 32). The light it scatters towards the eye is the haze's own color, the room's bounce, and every light of its screen tile (the same tiles the world shader uses) through its shadow map (airLight in scene_lights.slang: like arriving gives a surface, but without facing). It's weighted by Henyey-Greenstein's phase function with g = 0.7, so the air glows when you look towards a light or along a beam, and hardly at all across one. Dust scatters 6% of the light that falls on it, so a lit corridor stays dark rather than milky. Smoke scatters 50%, so a beam through it shows. The second pass follows each column from the eye, gathering what each slice scatters as it dims, and writes what's been gathered and what passes through to each cell's far side. Every world draw and effect (except the gun in hand) reads it at its screen position and distance (set 0, binding 8; atmosphere_common.slang), adding the haze evenly past 60 m. Off, the grid is one cell that's never computed, and draws apply the haze evenly (the distance fog the game always had). Reflection captures always do. On lavapipe the grid costs about 70 ms on High and 11 ms on Low, against a 200 ms scene. CI's three GPU smoke runs take about a fifth longer. Reflections (ReflectionProbes, RoomReflections). Each room has a cube map, 64² per face in high range, with five mips prefiltered by the GGX lobe from roughness 0 (a mirror, the capture itself) to 1, all in one cube-map array (set 0, binding 7; the device's imageCubeArray feature). A room is captured from about eye height in the middle of its box (RoomLighting.CapturePoint), with the world shader. It's lit by its own steady lights and those of the rooms through its doorways (SceneLights.CaptureLights: panels still standing, a failing one at its average, and the beacons on alert, written into the frame's light buffer after its own and read directly, without shadows). It draws its parts and theirs as they stand (nothing broken), and doesn't reflect a cube map itself. Characters, effects, flashlights and flashes are never in a capture. The world shaders find a point's room in the grid, follow the reflected view from the point to the room's box (RoomLighting.Boxes: inside the walls, floor to ceiling), and read the room's cube in the direction of where it hits the box, as seen from the capture point (box projection, eased towards the plain direction as the surface gets rougher), at the mip for its roughness. Outdoors (no rooms) a surface reflects a sky gradient, and in a room that isn't captured yet it reflects the light falling on it, as before. The client (RoomReflections, per level) immediately requests every room the renderer doesn't have captured (RoomLighting.IsCaptured, which the renderer tracks: every room on the level's first frame, and all of them again after the renderer has dropped them for other rooms, as when Studio changes views; ReflectionCapture.Now does all of it in that frame, about two seconds on lavapipe for 134 rooms). After that it requests each room whose light changed (a panel in it or visible from it shot out or repaired, SceneLights.RoomVersion; the alert's stage where it or a neighbor has beacons), nearest to the eye first. The renderer handles those in turn, one face per frame, then fades the room's cube to the new one over eight frames (the prefilter blends into what the mips held), so play never hitches and a shot-out panel's reflection goes dark in about a quarter of a second. Studio's Look room is captured whole whenever it's rebuilt. Its stages have no rooms, so they reflect the sky. Materials (docs/blender/materials.md). Every vertex carries a surface (MeshVertex.Surface, a 32-bit word, VertexSurface): the index of its material in the library (MaterialLibrary: content/defs/materials.json, built into LastFleet.Content as MaterialLibrary.Shipped) and, for a smooth material, a smoothed normal (three signed bytes; SmoothNormals, area-weighted across faces bent less than 50 degrees, within one material). Loaders resolve a glTF material's library id from its extras (lastfleet_material, Blender's custom property; GltfJson.MaterialIds, since BRUTAL's glTF API drops extras), or by its name (MaterialLibrary.Resolve: Glass, Light or anything with an emission, Paint_ slots, and everything else the first material, plastic). GltfMeshLoader, ModelParts (per corner, ModelTriangle.SurfaceA to C), SkinnedModel (SkinnedVertex.Surface, with the smoothed normal in the bind pose, skinned like the normal is) and AnimatedModel (per material, ModelMaterial.Surface) all do this. Code-built geometry is painted metal unless MeshBuilder.Material says otherwise (floors and ducts are worn metal, pipes bare metal), and emissive when its color glows. Placing a model rotates its smoothed normals with it (VertexSurface.Turned). The renderer writes the library each frame into a table at set 0, binding 4 (GpuMaterial, 32 bytes each, at most 64; VulkanRenderer.SetMaterials, which Studio calls as its Look mode, LookMode over a MaterialWorkspace, edits the file). The world shaders light a surface with a diffuse term and a GGX highlight (Smith visibility, Schlick Fresnel) from the sun and every point light and spotlight, using the face normal for lighting and the smoothed normal for highlights. Metal has no diffuse light: its color is what it reflects. What a surface reflects (weighted by Karis' fit of the split-sum integral, taken from its diffuse share) is its room's cube map along the reflected view (using the smoothed normal for a smooth material), or the sky outdoors, or the light falling on it in a room that isn't captured yet. An emissive material's color is light, drawn regardless of what lights it (a color past 1 is lit as before, with its excess glowing). A material with its own color (rubber) replaces the model's color. Windows onto space (docs/plans/structure-first.md, Phase 9). A material marked space (space_window; GpuMaterial.SpaceFlag, 64) is drawn as the sky along the view through it, whatever is behind it: the world shaders, the path tracer's G-buffer, and both tracers' hits (ray_hits.slang, path_trace.slang) all call spaceSky (space_sky.slang). Neat trick: nothing is seen through a window but the sky, so decks never see each other through one, and room culling needs no portal for it. The sky is worked out per pixel from four rows of the material table past its 64 materials (GpuSky, VulkanRenderer.SetSky): the dark of space, two layers of stars (hashed cells on the sphere), a nebula and the galaxy's dust band (value noise), and the sector's sun (a disc with a glow). Its numbers are a SkyLook: a SpaceSky from content/defs/skies.json (SkyLibrary, built into LastFleet.Content; one a sector, ForSector) turned for the fleet's system's place on the sector's map and seeded from the level (SpaceSky.At, LevelSky.For). Studio's Look mode tunes them on its Skies tab, looking out from inside a box faced with the window material. Windows are props (PropKind.Window: a size, a sill, a frame color) a level rule places at anchor hull: back against a stretch of wall wholly on the hull (LevelLayout.Hull, a plan level's HullEdges from each deck's envelope; IPlacementRoom.OnHull, RulePlacer.HullStretches). StationPlacements.BuildWindow sets one into the wall: a frame lining the opening from outside the hull's skin to just proud of the wall, round a pane of glass set back in it (_Pane, solid but not drawn: the client draws its glass, WindowGlass), and returns the opening, which is cut out of the wall and the skin once the skin is on (MeshBuilder.Cut: the pieces of each drawn triangle outside the box, as a part of their own, WindowOpening_; a collided part is left whole for its collision and drawn by the new part instead). The shipped rule (hull_windows) puts them in bridges, crew quarters, lounges, messes and public halls; plan rooms carry their archetype's tags for it (RoomModule.Dressed), as the solver's built rooms do. The outside (a plan's level with windows; LevelAssembler.Outside). What's out there: the hull's skin (HullSkin: a plate a hand's breadth out from every side of a cell facing space, story by story, in two shaded panels with a trim along each deck's floor line, roofs and keels over the envelope's top and bottom cells, LevelLayout.Envelope, and running lights along the top deck; its look is the plan's skin, HullLook); the sky round everything (SkyShell: a box 6 km out, faces turned in, in the window material); the fleet (FleetInView: ships of boxes in space round the level, as the template's fleet says, FleetRule); and the dropship docked outside the airlock (DockedDropship, hidden by the client once it casts off).
