All are drawn only and belong to no room; all but the dropship are PartUsage.Backdrop, left out of the mesh's bounds, so the navigation grid and the rest see only what's playable. Their material, hull_plating, is flagged outside (GpuMaterial.OutsideFlag): lit by the sector's sun (space_sky.slang's rows) and a trace of starlight, not a room's fill; anything out in space (sky or hull) is seen through only the first few meters of a room's haze (VacuumAir in world_shading.slang). Grime. Indoors (the less sun, the more grime), the world shader dirties the level based on where each point is, with no textures: walls dark and brown up from each story's floor, streaks where something ran down them, a stained band under the ceiling, blotches; floors blotched and scuffed; ceilings smudged; everything a little drabber and darker. Each material takes as much as its grime value says (glass none, floors all of it), and grime roughens what it covers. Characters and the gun are drawn clean (a push-constant flag), since fixed grime would slide across anything that moves. Panels stay clean too. What a hit looks like is all presentation, built from each tick's HitRecords on every machine and never fed back to the simulation, with no hitstop: Characters (CharacterModels): a hit flashes the model and knocks its upper body away from the shot, pivoting at the hips (backwards if the direction isn't known), out fast and back slower, further and longer the bigger the hit's share of its health. A headshot also snaps the head back, and the feet shuffle a few centimeters. A headshot kill drops the body where it stands, knees first, then slumps it forward. Any other kill topples it full length away from the shot, or 40° to either side, or towards the shooter, whichever has room (two rays each, once per death). With no room anywhere, it drops where it stands. Bodies lie for 10 s, then sink away. Blood and dust (ImpactEffects): a hit on a character throws a puff of mist back towards the shooter and a heavier one out of the far side, plus a spray of droplets that fall under gravity and spot the floor where they land, and, with one ray along the shot, a splat on any wall within 2.4 m behind. A body that has come to rest leaves a pool that spreads over 5 s. Shots into the level throw a puff of dust and a few chips. Blood darkens as it dries and lasts 30 s (pools 45 s). Everything lives in fixed rings (192 particles, 48 puffs, 96 marks, 16 pools) that overwrite their oldest entries, so a frame allocates nothing and costs a few hundred quads at most. Textures live in TextureStore: RGBA8 images in device memory, each with a combined-image-sampler descriptor set, and identified by that set's handle, which doubles as Dear ImGui's texture ID. Art is uploaded as sRGB so sampling returns linear color; ImGui's font atlas is plain UNORM coverage. The swapchain is sRGB, so the UI shader converts ImGui's vertex colors (authored in sRGB) to linear before writing them. Uploads wait for the GPU, which is fine for textures that rarely change. Why our own ImGui renderer? BRUTAL's own ImGui Vulkan backend needs a render pass object, which this renderer doesn't use, hence the small renderer here. Camera conventions. CameraMath uses row vectors, like System.Numerics (clip = position * ViewProjection). The projection is reverse-Z with an infinite far plane: depth is 1 at the 5 cm near plane and approaches 0 with distance, which keeps a 32-bit float depth buffer precise everywhere. The viewport has a negative height, so clip space is +Y up and glTF's counter-clockwise front faces stay counter-clockwise. The world shader receives the view-projection matrix as four rows in push constants and multiplies them out itself, so no matrix-layout convention can disagree between C# and the shader. Shaders are Slang in content/shaders. The client build runs tools/LastFleet.ShaderCompiler, which compiles each file's vertexMain, fragmentMain or computeMain to .vert.spv, .frag.spv or .comp.spv in the output's shaders folder. Slang errors become build errors with file and line. The game loads SPIR-V only and never ships the Slang compiler. LastFleet.Content.Tests also compiles every shader, so a broken shader fails the tests as well as the build. Meshes. GltfMeshLoader walks a glTF scene, bakes node transforms into world space, gives every triangle a face normal and its material's base color, merges identical vertices and optimizes the result with meshoptimizer. The renderer uploads the resulting MeshData once. Looking at one spot. Want a screenshot of an exact view? --smoke --camera x,y,z,yaw,pitch[,light][,crouch][,aim][,fire] puts the player at that spot instead of running the scripted play (unharmed and still, with the flashlight on with ,light, and holding crouch, aim or fire), so a screenshot shows a chosen view. That's how lighting, shadows and cover were checked. Testing without a GPU. Camera math, overlay geometry, the push-constant layout and the PNG writer are tested in LastFleet.Rendering.Tests. The GPU path is tested by the gpu-smoke CI job: it installs Mesa's software Vulkan driver (lavapipe), the validation layer and a virtual X display, renders 150 frames of scripted play with validation on, fails on any validation error, and uploads a screenshot of frame 140 as the gpu-smoke-screenshot artifact. One Linux gotcha: BRUTAL asks for the Vulkan loader as vulkan, which only resolves to the unversioned libvulkan.so that development packages install. VulkanRenderer.PreloadLoader falls back to libvulkan.so.1, so players only need the runtime package. Sound LastFleet.Audio plays through OpenAL Soft (Brutal.OpenAl) and knows nothing about the game. It has: 48 voices. VoicePool decides who gets one when they're all busy: the cue's own oldest voice, then the lowest priority, but never a loop and never a higher priority. Each voice has a low-pass filter for sounds heard through walls. One reverb they all send to, set from a space-station preset based on the size of the listener's room. Master (the listener's gain, so reverb tails follow it), effects, interface and ambience volumes. Sounds delayed by their distance. With no device it plays nothing. Offline (a loopback device, as the smoke run and its tests use) it mixes into memory. The cues are data (content/defs/sounds.json). A cue's clips are its recordings (content/sounds/.wav, _2.wav) or, until it has any, a placeholder synthesized in code (PlaceholderSounds, about 0.8 s at startup, loaded in the background behind the splash). docs/sound.md is the sound designer's guide. GameAudio (Client) turns what the client sees into sound: Each tick that's the shots (one per shooter, using the weapon's frame on the ShotRecord; yours play the moment you fire), hits (impacts by surface, flesh, rounds whizzing past your head), explosions and breaks. Each frame it's everyone's feet (a step per stride, landings, slides), grenades (thrown, bouncing, beeping with their light), your gun's handling, pickups, flashlight and health, the mission's changes, and the buzz of the nearest failing lights. Sounds in rooms the renderer culls (RoomVisibility) are muffled. The game asks for sounds through ISoundOutput, which tests record, and which an FMOD engine could implement. Decisions Here are the big calls we've made, why we made them, and what would make us think again: Decision Why Revisit if BRUTAL as the foundation, with our own engine layer on top Direct, low-overhead access to Vulkan, GLFW, Jolt, FMOD and RakNet from modern C#, with no editor or scene graph to fight A required native library is missing from BRUTAL Friflo.Engine.ECS behind LastFleet.Ecs Fast archetype ECS with relations, serialization and zero-allocation chunk queries. Consoles aren't a goal, so its LGPL-3.0 JSON dependency (see THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES) is acceptable, shipped as separate DLLs We want Native AOT, which the LGPL dependency rules out. Arch (Apache-2.0) is the fallback Our own ISimulationSystem and GameWorld instead of Friflo's SystemRoot We own update order and scheduling, so systems can move onto BRUTAL's job system later without changes — 60 Hz fixed tick with commands as the only input Stable movement and physics, and the same model the host-authoritative co-op design needs — Host-authoritative listen server for co-op Determinism across physics, hundreds of horde agents and floating-point AI is too fragile for lockstep — Vulkan 1.3 core only No optional extensions to probe; dynamic rendering and sync2 keep the renderer short We need ray tracing or mesh shaders Slang, compiled at build time A modern shader language with modules and generics; SPIR-V is checked on every build and the game ships no compiler Hot reload needs run-time compilation (a dev-only path, not a reason to ship Slang) Reverse-Z, infinite far plane, 32-bit float depth Even depth precision from a 5 cm near plane to kilometers away; no far plane to tune — Grey-box modules as text .gltf They diff and review as text; .glb goes through Git LFS Modules grow past a few hundred kilobytes Collision behind ICollisionWorld The simulation stays engine-free and fast to test; Jolt can be swapped out or stubbed — AI writes PlayerCommands Enemies follow the same movement, weapon and collision rules as players: fair by construction, and one code path to tune — Layered grid navigation from rays, not a navmesh library (DotRecast) Exact match with collision; tiny, deterministic, allocation-free; stacked floors and drops cover the station's verticality, and the cover map and strafe checks work on its cells Large outdoor maps or caves where 0.25 m cells cost too much memory and search time, or crowds that need a navmesh's corridors and avoidance Jolt virtual characters, not rigid bodies Kinematic control exactly as the controller decides, with stairs, slopes and shape swaps handled by Jolt We want physically pushed players xUnit v3 on Microsoft.Testing.Platform The current .NET 10 test stack; dotnet test runs test projects as executables — OpenAL Soft for sound (through Brutal.OpenAl), not FMOD as the design doc planned It ships inside its NuGet package with no account or license, so every clone and CI run plays (or mixes) sound; positional voices, filters and EFX reverb are all the shooter needs so far. LGPL, shipped as its own library Sound designers want FMOD Studio's authoring (events, parameters, music layers): implement ISoundOutput over FMOD Central Package Management and an SDK pinned in global.json One place for versions; reproducible builds on every machine and in CI — Known quirks A few oddities you might trip over: Friflo prints one Assemblies loaded: … line to the console the first time an EntityStore is created. It's scanning loaded assemblies for component types by reflection. That reflection scan is also why Native AOT would need Friflo's explicit NativeAOT schema registration, on top of the license issue above. GLFW on Linux X11: synthetic mouse events (for example from xdotool) don't produce raw-motion events. Real mice do. If you automate input tests on Linux, turn raw motion off.

docs/blender/README.html.title: Art in THE LAST FLEET: start here | The Last Fleet
docs/blender/README.html.summary: Art in THE LAST FLEET: start here (If you're a designer tuning loot and weapons, start at the Studio reference instead. What can be added as data is listed in adding-content.md.) Good news: everything you model goes into the game the same way! You work in a .blend file, export it with one of our Blender add-ons to a glTF file in content/, and the game reads that file when it starts. Reshaping a model doesn't need any code changes, so you never have to wait on a programmer. This page is the overview. Each kind of model has its own guide with the details. What Guide The game reads Your .blend goes in Add-on The ship's hub (the deck between missions) hub.md content/modules/hub/hangar_deck.gltf content/raw/modules/hub/ lastfleet_hub.py Weapon parts weapons.md content/weapons/<frame>.gltf content/raw/weapons/ lastfleet_weapons.py Creatures (the horde) creatures.md content/models/<creature>.gltf content/raw/models/ lastfleet_creatures.py Characters on a rig (soldiers, lancers, players) and their clips rigs.md content/characters/<model>.gltf, content/anim/<rig>.gltf content/raw/characters/ lastfleet_rigs.py Props: loot, containers, crates, the cargo pod and drone props.md content/props/<file>.gltf content/raw/props/ lastfleet_props.py The add-ons are in tools/blender/. Install each one from Edit > Preferences > Add-ons > Install from Disk. They all put their tools on the Last Fleet tab of the 3D view's sidebar (N). Use Blender 4.2 or newer. Whatever you're modeling, install lastfleet_materials.py too. It's how you give each material one of the game's surface materials (materials.md). Had the VANGUARD add-ons installed? That was their name before the game had one. Remove them in Edit > Preferences > Add-ons (they're listed as VANGUARD Creatures, VANGUARD Rigs and so on), then install the lastfleet_*.py files in their place. Your .blend files don't need anything from you: the first time one opens with the new add-ons, its settings and every material's surface material move over to the new names. Save it, and that's done. The game still reads models exported with the old names too. Getting set up (once) Install Git and Git LFS, then run git lfs install once. .blend files, images and sounds go through LFS. Skip it and you'll commit a pointer instead of your file... not great. Clone the repository and install the .NET 10 SDK to build and run the game: dotnet run --project src/LastFleet.Client. Install the add-ons for whatever you'll be working on. The same everywhere These rules hold no matter what you're making: Axes. In Blender, +Y is the game's forward, +Z is up and +X is right. The add-ons export with the axes the game expects, so leave the exporter's settings alone. Scale. One unit is one meter. For a feel of it: a room's walls are 3.6 m high, a cargo crate is 0.44 m high, and a rifle's body is about 0.4 m long. Names. The game finds things by name. An object's name says what it is (Barrel_2_Heavy, Crate, Footlocker_Lid), and empties mark points (Muzzle, Hinge, Door). Blender's .001 suffixes don't matter. Each guide lists the names it uses. Origins. A model's origin matters, because it's the point where the model stands or attaches. Where the model sits in the file usually doesn't matter, so go ahead and lay things out side by side. Apply rotation and scale before you export (Ctrl + A > Rotation & Scale). Materials. Shading is flat: each face is lit by its own normal. A material's Base Color is its color, except for a few material names the game colors itself (a maker's finish on a gun, a rarity's color, a glow), and each guide lists those. How the color reacts to light (paint, bare metal, rubber, glass, a glow) is set by the material's surface material, which you pick from the game's library with the Last Fleet Materials add-on (see materials.md). Textures aren't used. Check before Export. Every add-on has a Check button that tells you what the game would reject or ignore. Export runs it first, so you can't forget. Committing your work Happy with it? Here's how it gets in: Export the .gltf with the add-on, into its folder in content/. Save your .blend into content/raw/... (see the table above). Run the tests: dotnet test --solution LastFleet.slnx. They load every model and check its names, markers and sizes. CI runs the same tests on every pull request, so a broken file can't sneak in without anyone noticing. Look at it in the game. Each guide says how to get to it quickly (--pod, --horde, a level seed). Commit the .blend and the .gltf together, on a branch, and open a pull request. Done! Grey-box starting files Most of the models in the game started out as boxes written by scripts in tools/greybox/. Those scripts made the starting files you edit. Never run one again over files someone has edited, because it would put the boxes back! If you want to start a new weapon frame or room from boxes, each guide says how to make just that one file.

docs/blender/creatures.html.title: Modeling and animating creatures in Blender | The Last Fleet
docs/blender/creatures.html.summary: Modeling and animating creatures in Blender The horde's bodies are models made and animated in Blender. The game draws hundreds of them at once on the GPU, each on its own frame of its own animation. The swarmling is the first one: content/models/swarmling.gltf. So you want to edit or replace it? This page walks you through it in Blender. Reshaping the body or reworking the animations doesn't need any code changes! The file you start from is the grey-box swarmling: a few faceted pieces, each skinned to one bone, with simple keyed animations. tools/blender/generate_swarmling.py made it. Replace it however you like, but don't run that script again over your work, because it'd put the starter model back. Setting up Install the add-on: Edit > Preferences > Add-ons > Install from Disk, and pick tools/blender/lastfleet_creatures.py. Enable Last Fleet Creatures. Its tools are in the 3D view's sidebar (N), on the Last Fleet tab, in the Creature panel. Open the model with the panel's Open button, not File > Import. Why? It sets the scene to 30 frames a second first, which is the rate the game plays animations at. If you import the model into Blender's default 24 fps scene, its keys end up between frames, and exporting it would cut the end off each animation. Folder is where Export writes to (content/models), and Creature is the file name (swarmling). Open fills in both for you. What the game reads What How The rig One armature. The bones can be anything. The starter's are named Root, Hips, Chest, Head, Abdomen, the legs (FrontLeg.L.Upper and so on) and the blades (Arm.L, Blade.L). The near body Meshes skinned to the armature (an Armature modifier, vertex groups named after bones, at most four bones per vertex), with any name that doesn't end in _LOD1 The far body Meshes named <anything>_LOD1. They're drawn beyond 22 m, and for shadows. Give it about a third of the triangles. If there isn't one, the near body gets drawn at every distance. Animations Actions, found by name (see below). Each one is a frame range starting at 0, with keys on whole frames at 30 fps Shading Flat: each face is lit by its own normal. Smooth shading and custom normals are ignored. Colors A material's Base Color. A material named Glow glows in the Choir's violet and dims as the creature dies. Surface materials How each material reacts to light, picked with the Last Fleet Materials add-on (materials.md). The swarmling's chitin is plastic and its Glow is emissive. Size and facing Meters. The creature faces +Y (the game's forward), +Z is up, and its feet are on the origin. Hit volumes. Here's the catch: where a shot hits is decided in code, not by the mesh (Swarmling in src/LastFleet.Simulation). The body is a low capsule 0.72 m tall. The head is a sphere with a 0.17 m radius, 0.42 m forward and 0.6 m up. A shot there counts as a precision hit. So keep the head and body roughly where they are, or ask a programmer to change the numbers to match. The animations Action Played Notes Run A loop, while it runs One stride. The game plays one loop every 1.1 m covered, so the feet keep pace with the ground at any speed. Make it run in place, since the game moves the body. Idle A loop, standing WindUp Once, before the bite 0.3 s, the same as the game's wind-up. This is the telegraph players react to, so make it big and readable! Bite Once, when the wind-up ends Starts from the WindUp's last pose. Stagger Once, when a heavy hit knocks it back Death Once, when it dies It holds the last pose, then the game darkens it and sinks it into the floor. The game fades from one animation to the next over 0.12 s. A couple of gotchas: Loops have to end where they start. Key the last frame the same as the first. Step through them. Use the Play action buttons in the panel to watch each one. Checking and exporting Check reports anything the game wouldn't read: no armature, or more than one; a mesh with no Armature modifier; unweighted vertices, or ones with more than four bones; a missing action; a scene not at 30 fps; an action starting or ending between frames. Export runs the check first, then writes one .gltf with the buffers inside it (no .bin) and every action included. Commit that file. The game bakes it when the first level loads and keeps it, so restart the game to see your change. To see it in the game, run LastFleet --horde 30 (or use F3 > AI > Horde of 30) and let them come to you... they will.

docs/blender/hub.html.title: Building the ship's hub in Blender | The Last Fleet
docs/blender/hub.html.summary: Building the ship's hub in Blender The hub is the hangar deck the squad walks around between missions. It's the ONLY level we build by hand in Blender. It lives at content/modules/hub/hangar_deck.gltf, and its source goes in content/raw/modules/hub/hangar_deck.blend. So what about the rooms in procedural levels? Those aren't built in Blender at all. Each one (the station's insertion bay, corridors and stairwell included) is a room archetype in content/defs/procgen/archetypes.json: a shape, its roles, a style and a furnishing, built from a seed. Its set pieces (a terminal, a reactor's core, the mess's counter) are props placed by its furnishing's rules. Studio's Levels > Archetypes tab edits them and shows each one built. See adding-content.md and the Studio reference. Setup (once) Install Blender 4.2 or newer. In Blender, go to Edit > Preferences > Add-ons. Choose Install from Disk (in the drop-down at the top right), pick tools/blender/lastfleet_hub.py, and tick Last Fleet Ship's Hub. In the 3D view, press N to open the sidebar. You'll find the tools on the Last Fleet tab, in the Ship's hub panel. Building the deck The file you start from is the old deck that code built from boxes, exported box for box (tools/greybox/generate_hub.py). Replace it however you like, just don't run that script again over your work! Here's the flow: Open it. Start an empty file and use File > Import > glTF 2.0 to open hangar_deck.gltf. The deck isn't on the level grid, and it's never joined to another room. Build. Move, add and reshape boxes. Everything that collides has to be a box. You can move, scale and rotate a box freely, but don't edit it into another shape or join several boxes into one object. What about everything else? Name it ..._NoCollision (the lamps, screens and the dropship's glass are), then add plain boxes named ..._CollisionOnly to stand in for its collision. The floor top is at Z = 0. Markers. The panel's buttons place each one at the 3D cursor: Spawn_Player: where the squad comes in, facing the green (+Y) arrow. Station_Console, Station_NeedsBoard, Station_Armory, Station_StarMap: the spot on the deck where each station is used from. A player within 2.2 m of it gets the station's prompt, so put it in front of the desk, board, bench or table, not inside it. If you move a station's furniture, move its marker with it. The game ignores the numbers Blender adds to duplicate names (Station_Console.001), so don't worry about those. Materials. Give each material its surface material with the Last Fleet Materials add-on (see materials.md). A material's Emission is added to its color, which is how you get a screen, a lamp or the engines' glow. Want something brighter than white? Set Emission Strength above 1. Check and export. Set Folder to content/modules/hub/, then press Check and Export. Export runs the check first and refuses if the deck breaks a rule. Otherwise it writes one self-contained hangar_deck.gltf. Commit the .blend (it goes through Git LFS) and the .gltf together. That's it! You don't have to touch the export settings, because the add-on uses the ones the game expects: +Y up, modifiers applied, and Include > Custom Properties ticked (which carries each material's surface material). Then it folds Blender's binary output into a single text .gltf, so a clone without Git LFS still has the deck. The rules When the game loads the hub, it checks the same rules (HubLevel.Load): a box for everything that collides; one Spawn_Player; a marker for every station. If one is broken, it refuses the file and tells you what's wrong. The tests (HubLevelTests, and HubTests, which walks from the way in to every station) run in CI. To see your deck, run LastFleet. The game opens on the ship, and --level hub goes straight there.

docs/blender/materials.html.title: Surface materials | The Last Fleet
docs/blender/materials.html.summary: Surface materials Every model in the game is drawn with one fixed library of surface materials: painted metal, bare metal, rubber, glass and so on. Your model's colors are still yours. The material just says how those colors react to light: is it paint or polished steel, rough or glossy, how dirty does a station make it, and does it glow? Why one library for everything? Because then paint looks like paint on every gun, crate and wall, and changing a material (in Studio) changes every model at once. Tweak painted_metal once and the whole game follows! There are no textures. Faces are flat, and a material is just a few numbers. Material id What it's for Plastic plastic Casings, furniture, anything not covered by another material. Anything with no library material gets drawn as this. Painted metal painted_metal Walls, hulls, crates, a gun's body: metal under paint. Bare metal bare_metal Barrels, rails, pipes, brass. No diffuse light; its color tints what it reflects. Smooth highlights. Worn metal worn_metal Floors, deck plates, ducts: paint worn through to the metal, rough and grimy. Rubber rubber Grips, feet, seals. Always close to black, and rough. Glass glass Windows, visors, screens. Glossy with smooth highlights, and never grimy. Cloth cloth Uniforms, sandbags. Fully rough. Concrete concrete Bunkers, outdoor walls and floors. Rough, and soaks up all the grime. Emissive emissive Light panels, reticles, signal lights, the Choir's eyes. Its color is the light it gives off. Sight glass sight_dot, sight_ring, sight_chevron A red dot's or holographic sight's glass: clear except for its reticle (a dot, a ring or a chevron), drawn in the model's color. Window onto space space_window A window in a ship or station. It shows the sector's sky, whatever its color, and never what's behind it. Hull plating hull_plating A ship's or station's outside, seen from a window. Lit by the sector's sun instead of a room's lights. The library is content/defs/materials.json. Each material has these numbers: roughness: 0 is a mirror, 1 is chalk. Low roughness gives a small bright highlight, and high roughness gives a wide dim one. metalness: 0 for paint, plastic, rubber and glass, which light up in their own color. 1 for bare metal, which is dark except for what it reflects, tinted by its color. Somewhere in between for metal with the paint worn through. smooth: its highlights follow a smoothed surface, so a barrel shows one clean streak along its length instead of a stripe on each face. Its lighting stays faceted, like everything else's. grime: how much of a station's dirt it picks up, from 0 (glass) to 1 (floors). Grime darkens the surface, makes it browner and makes it rougher. Anything that moves (characters, the gun in your hands) stays clean. emissive: its color is light. A color of 1 or less is drawn as is, no matter what's lighting it. A color above 1 (a material with an Emission in Blender) is lit normally, and the excess glows and blooms. color: optional. A color it always has, whatever the model says (rubber is close to black). sight: optional. Makes it a sight's glass: dot, ring or chevron. The reticle is drawn where the eye looks along the aim, the way a real one sits at infinity. space: optional. Makes it a window onto space, drawn as the sector's sky (content/defs/skies.json). outside: optional. It's out in space on a hull: lit by the sector's sun, not a room's fill, and seen through no haze. Reflections Inside a station, a surface reflects its room: the room's walls, props and lit panels, and what you can see through its doorways. We capture the reflection when the level starts, and again whenever one of the room's lights gets shot out or mended, or the alert stage changes. Roughness blurs the reflection, so bare metal shows the room sharply while paint only shows a soft sheen. Outdoors, a surface reflects the sky. Characters, flashlight beams and flashes don't show up in reflections; their light shows up in the highlights instead. Choosing a material in Blender So you've got a model and want its materials to look right in the game? Here's the flow: Install tools/blender/lastfleet_materials.py (Edit > Preferences > Add-ons > Install from Disk, then tick Last Fleet Materials), alongside the add-on you model with. It finds the library on its own when your .blend is in the repository (it looks for content/defs/materials.json in the folders above the file). Otherwise, set Library on the Last Fleet tab of the 3D view's sidebar (N), under Materials. Pick a library material for each of your materials. You can do it in Material Properties, with the Last Fleet panel's Material dropdown, or for all of the file's materials at once in the sidebar's Materials panel. The choice is saved as the material's custom property lastfleet_material, which every Last Fleet add-on exports into the glTF. Run Check materials (in the Materials panel, and in each add-on's own Check while Last Fleet Materials is enabled). It lists every material that has no library material and what it falls back to. It also lists any that names a material the library doesn't have. That one's an error, and the export stops. The kit materials each add-on makes (Kit materials) already have theirs set. A gun's Body is painted metal, its Metal is bare metal, its Grip is rubber and its Reticle is emissive. A room's Floor is worn metal and its Wall is painted metal. Your material keeps its name and Base Color. The names the game colors itself (Paint_ slots, Body, Glint and the rest) still work, because the library material only controls how the color reacts to light, not what color it is. A material with no library material falls back based on its name, the same as models made before the library existed: Glass becomes glass, Light (or any material with an Emission) becomes emissive, a Paint_ slot becomes painted metal, and anything else becomes plastic. Tuning materials in Studio Studio's Look mode (dotnet run --project src/LastFleet.Studio -- --mode look) lists the library down the left. The selected material is shown on a sphere, a crate and a gun barrel, in front of a row of every other material so you can compare. Pick the lighting at the top: Station lights: a station's ceiling panels, warm white, which is how most of the game is lit; Flashlight in the dark: nothing but the beam from your eye, the hardest lighting in the game; Red alarm and Sodium hall: saturated light, which has to stay its own color; Outdoors: the sun and the sky. Drag in the room to look around, and use the mouse wheel to bring it closer. model's color sets the color of the shapes. Every change shows up right away, both there and on every model Studio draws (the Armory's guns, a level played from Missions). Ctrl+Z undoes it and Ctrl+S saves materials.json. Add and Duplicate make a new material at the end of the list, and Remove takes one out (plastic stays). A few rules for the library: An id is lowercase letters, digits and underscores. Never rename one that models use, because they'd fall back by name until they're re-exported. plastic has to be first, because anything with no material is drawn with it. plastic, painted_metal, glass and emissive have to exist, because old models fall back to them. At most 64 materials. Add new materials at the end. Removing or reordering one renumbers the ones after it. The game re-reads models when it starts, but Studio keeps showing models it already loaded with the wrong materials until you restart it. The library is built into the game, so a change to materials.json shows up in the game after the next build.

docs/blender/props.html.title: Modeling props in Blender | The Last Fleet
docs/blender/props.html.summary: Modeling props in Blender Props are the things lying around and standing in the station: the loot on the floor and on desks, the supply cases and footlockers you open, the cargo crates you carry, the cargo pod with its drone, and the station's tanks, reservoir and airlock fittings. Their models are glTF files in content/props/. This page shows you how to edit them in Blender. The game reads the files when it starts, so reshaping a prop doesn't need any code changes! Every top-level object in every file in content/props/ is a model the game's data can refer to, as file/Object (items/Medkit). A new file, or a new object in a file, shows up in LastFleet Studio's model picker with an icon drawn from it, without any code (the Studio reference). The props in the table below are the ones the game currently draws by name. The files you start from are the old grey-box props, exported box for box (tools/greybox/generate_props.py made them). Replace them however you like, just don't run that script again over your work, or it'll put the boxes back. What if a file is missing a prop while you work? The game still draws that prop from its old boxes, so nothing disappears. The station's fixtures are the exception: a station can't be built without them, so keep station.gltf's props in place (the tests tell you which one is missing). The files and their props File Prop What it is Markers items.gltf Medkit, AmmoPack, PodBeacon Quick-slot items lying around Electronics, MedicalSupplies, Munitions, Alloy The fleet's supplies, in piles WeaponPart The case for a loose weapon part containers.gltf Case A supply case on a desk: its body, and the inside you see when it's open Hinge Case_Lid Its lid, with the origin on the hinge Footlocker Only the inside of a footlocker. Its body is part of the level (see below) Hinge Footlocker_Lid Its lid, with the origin on the hinge cargo.gltf Crate A cargo crate, carried in both arms Pod The cargo pod Socket_Lid, Clamp Pod_Lid The pod's lid: on top, or torn off beside an overrun pod Drone The cargo drone that takes the pod away Rotor (one per rotor) Drone_Rotor One rotor blade. The game spins one at each Rotor station.gltf Tank A supply tank against a room's wall (fuel or water) Hose, Gauge, Gauge_Top Reservoir The deep reservoir, deeper in than a hose can reach Valve, Riser Outlet The reservoir's outlet, set on a wall near the airlock Hose, Gauge, Gauge_Top, Pipe Valve A valve's flange, set on the reservoir and on walls along its pipe Wheel, Stand Intake The dropship's intake in the airlock's hull, where a hose connects Port Chute The dropship's cargo chute in the hull Chute furniture.gltf Mess_Table, Chair, Desk, Lab_Bench, Rack, Bunk, Locker, and the rest What the generator furnishes rooms with, referred to in props.json (furniture/Mess_Table) Socket_<Group>_<n>, Attach_<Group>_<n> How the game uses them Items stand on their origin, at any yaw. Lids hinge. A lid's origin is its hinge line, and the closed lid extends from it along the game's forward (Blender's +Y). The body's Hinge empty marks where that origin goes. To open a container, the game swings the lid up around its X axis by about 100°. The footlocker's body is built into the level, so it's solid and soldiers walk around it. Heads up: if you change its size, the lid won't fit anymore. Ask a programmer to change the level's footlocker to match (LockerHalfLength and LockerHalfWidth in ModuleReader, and Container.Height). The pod's lid sits at Socket_Lid. The drone comes down onto Clamp in the last 4 s of the defense, then lifts the pod away. The crate is one model used for a crate standing around, held in a teammate's arms, and seen in your own arms in first person. The station's fixtures and furniture have a bit more to them, so they get their own sections below. The station's fixtures The station's fixtures (station.gltf) are built into the level's mesh by the generator, not drawn as props. Where they go. A tank stands where the data's tank kinds put it (Missions > tankKinds: its model, its supplies, and its radius and height, which have to fit the model). The reservoir, its outlet and its valves go where the reservoir goes, and the intake and chute go in the airlock's hull. Each one faces into the room along Blender's +Y. A tank and the reservoir stand on their origin; for the others, the origin is where they meet their wall. What's solid. They're solid the same way room furniture is: what's solid is set per model in content/props/colliders.json. The shipped fixtures are solid as they're drawn (mesh), so close their meshes, with every face facing out (Studio's Models mode names any holes). Given authored, a mesh named ..._NoCollision is only drawn, one named ..._CollisionOnly is only solid, any other is both, and anything solid has to be a box. What the markers drive. The game draws a gauge's fill between Gauge and Gauge_Top (0.16 m wide), a valve's wheel turning at Wheel, and the hose from Hose. Supply is colored with whatever the tank holds, and Light is its coupling's glow (dark on a tank that's found empty). A couple of gotchas: The reservoir's Riser has to be 3.2 m up, where its pipe runs under the ceilings. Several kinds of tank can share the file (Tank_Small). Name each one in a tank kind. Don't regenerate. The starting file came from tools/greybox/generate_station_props.py. Don't run it again over your work. Furniture Furniture (furniture.gltf) is stamped into the level's mesh wherever the placement rules put it (Studio's Levels > Props names the model, and Levels > Rules places it). It stands on its origin, facing into the room along Blender's +Y. What's solid. What it's collided with is set per model in content/props/colliders.json, kept beside the models: furniture is solid as it's drawn (mesh) unless the file says otherwise; a barrel is a cylinder; a model given authored is solid the same way a station fixture is (..._NoCollision, ..._CollisionOnly, solid meshes must be boxes). Whatever is solid is also what shots hit, so close the drawn mesh with its faces facing out. A piece that breaks (a chair, a glass kiosk) has one solid part (its authored box, or a box or cylinder around it), which disappears when it breaks, along with what's drawn. Markers. Two kinds of empty mark it: Socket_<Group>_<n> is where loot sits on it: Socket_Top_1 to Socket_Top_4 along a mess table's top, Socket_Shelf2_1 on a rack's second shelf. The data gives each group a loot table, a chance and a count. Keep sockets near the front edge, below 1.5 m and 0.55 m apart, so a player can reach them from the floor and loot on one never overlaps another. Attach_<Group>_<n> is where another piece stands: Attach_Chair_1 is where a chair is tucked under a table. The empty's +Y points back toward the piece (the chair faces the table). The data says what stands there and how far it's pulled out. The add-on's Socket and Attach buttons add the next one for the Group you typed, at the 3D cursor. It's forged. Just like the guns, furniture.gltf itself is forged. content/props/forge.json holds each piece's recipe (boxes, bevels, prisms, tubes, rails and vents in the kit's materials, its solid boxes, its markers), and artifacts/bin/LastFleet.WeaponForge/release/LastFleet.WeaponForge content/props writes the file from it, the same way as for guns. Edit a recipe there or in Studio (Levels > Props, Its recipe). So what about a piece you model by hand? It goes in a file of its own (furniture_hand.gltf), because the forge rewrites ALL of furniture.gltf. The data refers to it as furniture_hand/Sofa. Directions and scale In Blender, +Y is the game's forward, +Z is up and +X is right. Units are meters. A prop's origin is the middle of its base, except for a lid (its hinge) and a rotor blade (its hub). Where a prop sits in the file doesn't matter, so we lay the props out side by side to work on. Rotation and scale DO matter, so apply them when you're done (Ctrl + A > Rotation & Scale). Props you walk around, stand next to or carry have to stay within the sizes the game's rules use. Check reports any that are too big: Prop At most (X × Y × Z, meters) Why Items 0.5 × 0.4 × 0.35 They lie on desks and shelves Crate 0.79 × 0.57 × 0.51 It's carried in both arms and set down against walls (CargoCrate: 0.72 × 0.52 × 0.44) Pod 1.08 × 1.08 × 1.08 It's set down in front of a player, short of a wall (CargoPod: 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9) Case 0.6 × 0.4 × 0.3 It sits on a desk Footlocker and its lid 1.0 × 0.55 × 0.5 It has to fit the level's footlocker Colors Most materials keep the Base Color you give them. A few are colored by the game: Material Color in the game Glint A warm glow: an item's tag, a closed container's latch, a crate's corner. It's what you spot in a dark room. On a weapon part's case it glows in the part's rarity color. Rarity A weapon part's rarity color, dimmer than Glint: the band on its case Supply The color of what a crate holds: fuel orange, water blue, food green, and so on Light A pod's or beacon's light. Amber while loading, blinking green while its drone is inbound, flashing red while it's being overrun, dull red once it's smashed. Paint_<Slot> A paint slot. Its color is picked in the game's data for each thing that uses the model (in Studio, a swatch under the model). Its Base Color is the default. anything else Its own Base Color, darkened on an overrun pod Paint slots let one model be used for several things in different colors. Let's say you've got a supply case with Paint_Body and Paint_Stripe: it can be both a blue-striped medical case and an orange-striped fuel case! To add one, select a mesh (or, in Edit Mode, the faces), press Paint slot, and name the slot (Body, Stripe, Trim; letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter). It adds the material Paint_<Slot> and puts it on the selected faces. Its Base Color is the color something gets if its data doesn't pick one. The names above are reserved, because the game colors them. Check reports any that are misused: a paint slot named after one of them (Paint_Glint); a gun's game color on a prop (Body, Accent; on a prop they keep their own color); a reserved name with different capitals (glint). Shading is flat: each face is lit by its own normal. Textures aren't used yet. How each material reacts to light (paint, bare metal, rubber, glass, a glow) is set by its surface material, which you pick with the Last Fleet Materials add-on. The kit materials come with theirs already set (materials.md). Setup (once) Install Blender 4.2 or newer. In Blender, go to Edit > Preferences > Add-ons. Choose Install from Disk, pick tools/blender/lastfleet_props.py, and tick Last Fleet Props. In the 3D view, press N to open the sidebar. The tools are on the Last Fleet tab, under Props. Editing a file So you've got a prop to rework? Here's the flow: Open it. Start an empty file (delete the default cube, camera and light) and use File > Import > glTF 2.0 to open content/props/<file>.gltf. Save the .blend as content/raw/props/<file>.blend (it goes through Git LFS), so the next person starts from your file. Kit materials. Press Kit materials. It adds any game-colored materials the file is missing, and shrinks the imported markers. Paint slot adds a paint slot (see above). Model. Edit the props in Edit mode, or replace them. To replace one, delete it, model a new one, give it the old prop's name and move its origin (Object > Set Origin). Use as many materials as you like. Meshes parented under a prop are part of it. Markers. To add a Hinge, Socket_Lid, Clamp or Rotor, select the prop it belongs to, put the 3D cursor where it goes (Shift + right-click), and press its button. The add-on parents it to the prop for you. Blender's .001 suffixes don't matter, so the drone's four rotor markers can be Rotor, Rotor.001 and so on. Check. Press Check. It lists problems in the status bar and the Info editor: two props with the same name; a misnamed material (see above); a missing marker; a prop that's too big, or isn't standing on its origin; a marker that isn't parented to a prop; anything that isn't a mesh or an empty. It also warns about props the game draws that the file is missing (the game draws those from boxes). A prop it doesn't recognize is a new model: it has no size limit, and the data refers to it by name. Export. Set Id to the file name (items, containers, cargo, station, or a new one; it defaults to the .blend file's name) and Folder to content/props/, then press Export. It runs the check first, then writes one self-contained .gltf. Try it. Run the tests (dotnet test tests/LastFleet.Client.Tests). CI runs them too, so a file that breaks the rules fails the build. PropModelTests checks that every prop is there, the right size, with its markers. Then look at it in the game (below). Commit the .blend and the .gltf together. Seeing a change in the game The cargo pod and drone: LastFleet --seed 7 --pod 3 starts a station raid with a loaded pod in front of you and its drone 3 s away. --pod 0 gives you a pod that's still loading. Items, cases, footlockers and crates: start any station raid (LastFleet --seed 7). Most of them are in the loot rooms. Hold F (Interact) at a container to see it open. The crate in your arms: press F at a crate. Tanks, the reservoir and the airlock's fittings: start any station raid. The airlock's intake and chute are by its hatch, where you start. Studio's Missions mode shows where a seed puts the tanks and the reservoir. A beacon lying around: drop yours from the inventory (Tab). The rules Rule Why Each top-level object is a prop, named as in the table above, or with any name for a new one. The name says what it is. The data refers to it as file/Object. A paint slot is Paint_<Slot>. Glint, Rarity, Supply and Light belong to the game. The data colors paint slots, and the game colors the rest. Containers have a Hinge, the pod has a Socket_Lid and a Clamp, and the drone has a Rotor at each rotor. Lids hinge there, the drone lands there, and the rotors spin there. Markers are empties parented to their prop. Meshes can be parented too. A prop is the object plus everything under it. Only meshes and empties. Modifiers are applied on export; armatures, curves and text aren't exported. The game reads triangles and empties. Crates, pods, containers and items stay within their sizes. The game's rules (carrying, setting down, opening) depend on them. A station fixture is solid only in boxes, and has its markers. The level's collision is boxes, and the generator places the hose, gauge, valves and couplings at the markers. Furniture stands on its origin. Collided with as authored (colliders.json), it's solid only in boxes, and a piece that breaks has one solid box. Its drawn mesh is closed and faces out. Sockets and attach points are named Socket_<Group>_<n> and Attach_<Group>_<n>. Sockets are at least 0.55 m apart, and a piece stays at a few hundred triangles (1,100 at most). Level pieces collided with as boxes have to be boxes, and a breakable prop breaks through one solid part. Rays only hit faces from the front. The data uses the group names to give them loot and pieces.

docs/blender/rigs.html.title: Modeling and animating characters on a rig in Blender | The Last Fleet
docs/blender/rigs.html.summary: Modeling and animating characters on a rig in Blender Soldiers, the Choir's lancers and the players are modeled and animated in Blender on rigs. A rig is a skeleton the game knows about, stored as data in content/rigs/ (the humanoid is the first one: humanoid.json). Why bother with rigs? Every model on a rig shares the rig's animations (its clips). So a new soldier only needs a model, not a new set of animations, and a new kind of body (a rat, a hound, a spider) is a new rig file, not engine code! This is part of the plan in ../plans/animation.md. Soldiers and the Choir's lancers are drawn animated from these files. Each enemy variant names its model in content/defs/ai/enemies.json ("model": "lancer" for lancer.gltf). --box-soldiers draws them from boxes, the old way. How the game blends the clips is set by the rig's animation graph, which is a separate file: see animation-graphs.md. The source files Start from these in Blender (5.2 or later). They're in content/raw/characters/ and go through Git LFS (if a .blend opens as a few lines of text, run git lfs pull once): File What it is Exported to soldier.blend The grey-box soldier: its meshes skinned to the humanoid armature. content/characters/soldier.gltf lancer.blend The Choir Lancer on the same rig. content/characters/lancer.gltf player.blend The players' body (yours in first person, with the head hidden by the rig's firstPersonHides). content/characters/player.gltf humanoid_clips.blend The rig's clips: the armature with every action (Idle, Walk_F, Reload...), plus the soldier on it so you can watch them. content/anim/humanoid.gltf The naming tells you what a file is: <model>.blend is a model, exported as content/characters/<model>.gltf. <rig>_clips.blend holds a rig's clips, exported as content/anim/<rig>.gltf and shared by every model on that rig. Each file knows its rig (Rig file, stored relative to the .blend, so it works wherever the repository is). The game reads the .gltf files, and the .blend files are the source for them. So change the .blend and export it. Never edit the .gltf by hand! They started out as the starter files that tools/blender/generate_soldier.py writes (see below), but now they're the source, so edit them however you like. The script won't overwrite them unless you tell it to (--force). Setting up Install the add-on: Edit > Preferences > Add-ons > Install from Disk, and pick tools/blender/lastfleet_rigs.py. Enable Last Fleet Rigs. Its tools are in the 3D view's sidebar (N), on the Last Fleet tab, in the Rig panel. Set Rig file to the rig the body is built on: content/rigs/humanoid.json in the repository. The add-on reads it for everything below, and writes its output next to it (content/characters, content/anim). Starting fresh? Build rig makes the rig's armature with its bones named and placed as the file says, and sets the scene to 30 frames a second, which is the rate the game plays animations at. Working on the soldier? Set the scene to 30 fps (Output Properties > Frame Rate) before File > Import > glTF, or the keys land between frames. Guides adds back the things that help you fit the model, for example after an import: the sockets: small spheres on their bones that mark where the camera sits and where the hands hold the gun; the body the simulation shoots at: wire capsules for the collision shape and the narrower shape shots hit, small spheres for the eye standing and crouched, and the head sphere that shots hit over each eye. Guides are never exported. What the game reads What How The rig One armature with exactly the rig's bones, under the parents the rig gives. A model's bones can be longer or shorter than the rig's (longer arms, longer legs with a shorter spine). The game keeps each model's own build when the rig's clips play on it (see below). Each bone has to point the same way as the rig's, within 5°, without being turned or rolled (the clips rotate it from there). The root stays on the origin, and the eye stays where the rig has it at rest, within 5 cm up or down and 10 cm sideways (because that's where shots hit the head). The body Meshes skinned to the armature: an Armature modifier and vertex groups named after its bones, at most four bones per vertex. The style is low-poly parts, each weighted fully to one bone. Its size Meters. The body faces +Y, +Z is up, and its feet are on the origin. Fit it to the guides: the simulation's capsule (0.35 m radius, 1.8 m tall) and the head sphere around the eye (1.65 m up when standing). Shots hit those shapes, not the mesh. A designer fits them to the bodies in Studio (Bodies, Rig tab: the rig's body). Shading Flat: each face is lit by its own normal. Colors A material's Base Color. Materials named Paint_<Slot> (Paint_Uniform, Paint_Armor) can be recolored per variant, the same as weapon and prop paint slots. Surface materials How each material reacts to light (cloth, painted metal, glass, a visor, a glowing signal). You pick it with the Last Fleet Materials add-on, and it's exported as the material's custom property (materials.md). The clips Actions on the armature, named the same as the rig's clips (the panel lists them). The humanoid's bones Root (on the ground; it never moves), Hips, Spine, Chest, Neck, Head; Shoulder, UpperArm, LowerArm and Hand on each side; UpperLeg, LowerLeg and Foot on each side. Left is .L (Blender's -X) and right is .R. The rest pose is a T pose. The humanoid's clips Clip Played Notes Idle A loop Standing, with the gun held ready. Walk_F, Walk_B, Walk_L, Walk_R Loops One stride forward, backward, and to each side while facing ahead. The game blends them by the direction of movement, and plays them as fast as the body covers ground, so the feet keep pace. Run_F, Run_B, Run_L, Run_R Loops The same, running. Crouch, CrouchWalk_F (_B, _L, _R) Loops Crouched, standing still and moving. The crouched eye is 1.1 m up. Fire Once, upper body The kick from one shot. Reload Once, upper body Played on top of whatever the legs are doing, so it can run and reload at the same time. Throw Once, upper body A grenade. LeanLeft, LeanRight Held at the last frame Leaning all the way out around cover. The game blends toward it based on how far the body leans. BlindFire Held at the last frame The gun held up over cover, with the head kept down. Downed A loop On the deck, hurt, with the sidearm still up. Death Once Falling dead. It stays in its last pose. Pistol_Idle, Pistol_Fire, Pistol_Reload Same as their rifle clips For a pistol (the pistol grip): held out in both hands, the kick flipping up, the magazine being changed. The arms in Pistol_Idle are also how a pistol is held while walking and running. Clips for a grip. A gun's frame says how it's held (its grip, see animation-graphs.md). A grip plays the rig's clips named after it, <Grip>_<Clip>, instead of the rig's normal ones, and falls back to the normal ones where it has none. So you only make the clips that need to be different (the hold, the kick, the reload), list them in the rig file, and export the clips. Keep the eye where the simulation has it. This one bites people, so here's why it matters. A clip the rig marks as "eye": "standing" (Idle, the walks and runs, Fire, Reload, Throw) or "crouched" (the crouches) has to keep the Eye socket within 5 cm up or down and 10 cm sideways of the eye guide (1.65 m standing, 1.1 m crouched, as far forward as the socket is at rest). That's where the simulation puts the head sphere, so a head drawn higher or further forward gets shot straight through. A bob and a sway are fine. A stride that leans the head well forward, or a crouch that keeps it high, isn't. The fix? Move the hips (down for a deeper crouch, back under a lean) to bring the eye to the guide. Check measures it, and Studio's Bodies mode shows it (Hit shapes). In place. The simulation moves the body; a clip never does. Root is never keyed away from the origin (Check rejects that), and the hips stay over the feet, so a stride is walked on the spot. Loops end where they start: key the last frame the same as the first. Use the panel's clip buttons to step through each one. Models of other builds (retargeting) The clips are animated on the rig's armature, with its bones where the rig puts them. But what if a model is built differently: longer arms, longer legs and a shorter spine, or a stockier frame? The game keeps each model's build while the clips play, the same way Unreal's translation retargeting does. Each bone in the rig has a translation setting (content/rigs/<id>.json): skeleton (the default): the bone keeps the model's own offset from its parent, and the clip only rotates it. A longer forearm stays longer in every clip. scaled: uses the clip's offset, scaled by how much longer the model's bone is than the rig's. The humanoid's hips use this, so a model with higher hips bobs and drops them by the same amount relative to its size. animation: uses the clip's offset unchanged (the humanoid's root, which never moves). The sockets move with the model's own bones, so a longer arm carries its grip further out. There are two things a model can't change: Which way its bones point. The clips rotate each bone from its rest pose, so a bone pointing another way bends another way. Where its eye is. Shots hit the head where the rig has it. So keep the head where the guides put it, and change the body below it and the limbs around it. Studio's Bodies mode can show two models side by side on the same parameters (Compare), and its Rig tab sets each bone's translation. Checking and exporting Check reports anything the game wouldn't read: no armature, or more than one; a bone that's missing, extra, or under the wrong parent; a model's bone pointing away from the rig's (by more than 5°), its root off the origin, or its eye away from the rig's; a bone in a clips armature moved from where the rig puts it; a mesh with no Armature modifier, unweighted vertices, or vertices with more than four bones; a missing clip, a scene that isn't at 30 fps, or a clip starting or ending between frames; a clip keying a bone the rig doesn't have, or moving the root; a loop that ends away from where it started, or a clip that keeps the eye away from the simulation's. There are two export buttons: Export model writes the meshes and the armature, with no animation, to content/characters/<Model>.gltf. Export clips writes the armature and every action, with no meshes, to content/anim/<rig>.gltf (humanoid.gltf). These are the clips every model on the rig plays. Both run the check first, and write one .gltf with its buffers inside it (no .bin). Save the .blend in content/raw/characters/ and commit it together with the .gltf (the .blend goes through Git LFS). Got a pile of files to export? You can do every source file at once, the same way the buttons do (each one checked first, and nothing written if there's a problem): python3 tools/blender/export_characters.py content (or blender --background --python tools/blender/export_characters.py -- content). Name files to export only those (... content soldier humanoid_clips). dotnet test tests/LastFleet.Content.Tests checks the shipped soldier and clips against the rig. Adding clips to the rig List the new clip in the rig file (content/rigs/<id>.json, clips), then make it in <rig>_clips.blend and export (Check names any clip the rig lists that the file is missing). Some clips can be posed by the generator (its CLIPS list in tools/blender/generate_soldier.py, which includes the pistol's). For those, python3 tools/blender/generate_soldier.py content --add-clips adds every listed clip that humanoid_clips.blend is missing, posed the same way as the starter clips, leaves the existing actions alone, and exports the file. Too easy! Making the starter files again python3 tools/blender/generate_soldier.py content (with Blender's Python module, pip install bpy), or blender --background --python tools/blender/generate_soldier.py -- content, builds the rig from its file, the grey-box soldier, the lancer, the player, and every clip. The clips are posed with simple IK: feet planted, hands on a rifle's grips, and the hips moved so the eye is where the simulation has it, on average, through each clip the rig marks with an eye. It saves them as the source files above and exports them. Name a model (... content lancer) to make only that model's file. A couple of gotchas: It stops if the files already exist, which they will once anyone has worked on them. --force writes the starter files back over them. Be sure you mean it! A new model for an enemy One model on a rig can be the look for any number of enemies. Here's the flow: Model it on the rig as above (start from a copy of soldier.blend, saved as content/raw/characters/<model>.blend). Export it to content/characters/<model>.gltf. Set it as the variant's model in content/defs/ai/enemies.json (in Studio: Behavior > Enemies), along with its body (the body type, humanoid). Studio's Bodies mode shows it playing its clips (--mode bodies --body humanoid:<model>). The clips belong to the rig and are shared, so the new model doesn't need any of its own. A new kind of body A rig is just a file! Copy content/rigs/humanoid.json to <id>.json and change it, either in a text editor or in Studio's Bodies mode, Rig tab (which draws the skeleton as you edit). It holds: its bones (a parent comes before its children; head and tail in the rest pose, in the game's axes: +Y up, -Z forward, +X to the body's right); its sockets; its IK chains (a run of bones from root to tip, the direction its middle joint bends, and what it reaches for: grip, ground or look); its masks (from these bones down, except the ones listed); the mask hidden in first person; the body the simulation shoots at; its clips. Build rig then makes its armature. The game checks every rig when it reads it and reports every problem.

docs/blender/weapons.html.title: Modeling weapons in Blender | The Last Fleet
docs/blender/weapons.html.summary: Modeling weapons in Blender Every gun in the game is put together from part models: a receiver for its frame, plus a barrel, magazine, stock, optic and module picked by its roll. The models are glTF files in content/weapons/. This page shows you how to edit them and add more in Blender. The game reads them when it starts, so a new or reshaped part doesn't need any code changes! Forged parts vs. Blender parts Before you open Blender, there's a catch: the shipped part files are forged from recipes (docs/plans/weapons.md phase 5). content/weapons/forge.json holds every part's shapes (chamfered boxes, prisms, tubes, rails, vents, bolts, blocks) and markers, and the weapon forge writes the .gltf files from it. You can run the forge two ways: From Studio's Armory (Part models, tick Recipe): edit a part's shapes one per line, see it rebuilt, then Write files. From the command line with dotnet run --project tools/LastFleet.WeaponForge -- content/weapons (--format also rewrites forge.json in its own layout). A test fails if a part file doesn't match what its recipe makes. So if a part has a recipe, change the recipe, not the Blender file, because the forge would overwrite your Blender edit. Each forged part has two child meshes besides its own: Detail: small things only your own gun shows (rail ridges, vents, bolts). Far: the part without its bevels and detail. Other players' guns are drawn with it, so the frame's moving triangle count stays low. So where does Blender come in? It's still how you make a part that has no recipe. Take its recipe out of forge.json (or don't give a new file one) and model it as described below. The forge replaces the old grey-box kit (tools/greybox/generate_weapon_parts.py). A brand-new frame only needs its file (forged or modeled) and an archetype in Armory > Frames whose model names it. No code needed. Too easy! How a gun is put together The game builds each gun the same way, whether it's in your hands, held by a soldier or lying on the floor: It takes the Receiver from the frame's file. That's the archetype's model in archetypes.json: a frame with "model": "auto_rifle" is built from auto_rifle.gltf, and frames can share a file. The receiver is the gun's body, and its origin is where the hand holds the gun. The receiver has sockets: empties named Socket_Barrel, Socket_Magazine, Socket_Stock, Socket_Optic, Socket_Module and Socket_Grip (the top of the pistol grip). The game attaches one part for that slot at each socket. A muzzle device (Muzzle_…, in shared.gltf) goes on the barrel's Muzzle, scaled to the barrel's thickness at that point, and its own Muzzle marks the new end (where the flash appears). No socket for a slot? Then the frame has no part there. The hand cannon has no Socket_Stock, and the shotgun, hand cannon and grenade launcher have no Socket_Magazine (their pump, cylinder and drum are part of the receiver or barrel). Which part. A slot's options are the parts named after it: Barrel_<anything>, Magazine_<anything>, Stock_<anything>, Module_<anything>, Grip_<anything>, Muzzle_<anything>, in name order. Every part in the loot data (parts.json) names its model, either in full ("model": "Barrel_2_Brake") or by its shape, which is the last word of the name ("model": "Brake"). A shape name picks that look on every frame, and a frame without that shape shows its first one. "None" shows nothing in the slot (a bare rail). A stock (unrolled) weapon uses the first. A part that doesn't name a model gets one picked from its id (and adding a model to the slot reshuffles those), so give it one. Which optic. The optic part decides. Its model names the kind, Iron, RedDot, Holographic or Scope (which picks the first of Optic_Iron, Optic_RedDot, ...), or one specific look in full (Optic_RedDot_Round). A gun with 2× magnification or more (the marksman rifle's frame) ALWAYS carries a scope, whatever optic is fitted. Stretching. A barrel is stretched along its length based on the weapon's range, from 0.85× to 1.15× of the model. A magazine is stretched along its height based on its capacity, so model it 0.16 m long, which is the middle size. Colors. Some materials are colored by the game. The rest keep the Base Color you give them: Material Color in the game Body The maker's finish: its color in manufacturers.json (Kessler olive, Halcyon white...; gunmetal if it has none) BodyDark, BodyShade The maker's finish at 85% and 80% brightness Accent The rarity's color: the stripe along the side Reticle A glowing red, for an optic's dot Lamp A glowing white, for a weapon light's lens Paint_<Slot> A paint slot: a color the part's data picks (its paint in parts.json, by slot), with its Base Color as the default anything else Its own Base Color The names above are reserved, because the game colors them. Paint slot (next to Kit materials) adds a Paint_<Slot> material to the selected faces. A slot name is letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter. Check reports any misused name: a paint slot named after one of them (Paint_Accent); a prop's game color on a gun (Glint, Light; on a gun they keep their own color); a reserved name with different capitals (body). How each material reacts to light is set by its surface material, which you pick with the Last Fleet Materials add-on (materials.md). In the kit, Body and Accent are painted metal, Metal is bare metal (a barrel's clean streak), Grip is rubber, Glass is glass, and Reticle and Lamp are emissive. Shared parts. content/weapons/shared.gltf holds parts any frame can use: the red dot, holographic sight and scope, the modules, and the muzzle devices (brake, flash hider, suppressor). A frame only uses the shared parts for a slot when its own file has none for that slot. So to give the shotgun its own red dot, add an Optic_RedDot to shotgun.gltf, and every other frame keeps the shared one. That's why the hand cannon's file has its own modules: it has no fore grip, so its third module, Module_2_None, is an empty. Markers. Each barrel has an empty named Muzzle where the flash appears. Each optic has an empty named Sight, which is its aim point. When aiming, the game holds the gun so this point is on the eye line. Put it in the middle of the optic's window, or on the tip of the front post for iron sights, and keep everything except the reticle clear of the line through it along the barrel. A red dot's or holographic sight's Reticle triangles aren't drawn. Instead the game puts a pane of sight glass across the window at Sight, and its reticle (the part's reticle: dot, ring or chevron) stays on the aim point however the gun sways, just like a real one does! Keep the window's frame around Sight. The receiver has two more, Grip.R and Grip.L: where the right hand holds the pistol grip and the left hand holds the fore grip (a shotgun's pump; on a pistol the left hand cups the right). Bodies drawn on a rig hold the gun by these. The gun hangs from the right hand, and the left arm reaches for Grip.L. A receiver with no Grip.L is held a third of the way to the muzzle. Parts can mark where hands go on them too (docs/plans/weapons.md): A fore grip module or a barrel (a handguard) can have Hand.L, which the left hand uses instead of the receiver's Grip.L (an unmarked grip module is held around its middle). A magazine can have Grab, where the hand takes it during a reload (unmarked: low on its front). A receiver can have Charge, the charging handle or bolt worked after a reload from empty (unmarked: high on its right side). A module can have Laser, where a laser's beam starts. A scope marks its eyepiece with Eyepiece (the middle of its back window) and EyepieceRim (a point on that window's edge). When aiming, that window is what you look through, and the gun behind it isn't drawn. The magazine goes in at Socket_Magazine and comes out along its -Y. Directions and scale In Blender, the gun points along +Y, +Z is up and +X is the right side. Units are meters, so a rifle's receiver is about 0.4 m long. A part's origin is where it attaches: a barrel's origin is its back end, at the receiver, and it runs forward along +Y; a magazine's origin is its top, where it enters the receiver, and it hangs down; a stock's origin is the receiver's back, and it runs back along −Y; an optic's origin is the bottom of its mount; a module's origin is under the front of the receiver. Where a part sits in the file doesn't matter, so we lay parts out side by side to work on. Rotation and scale DO matter, so apply them (Ctrl + A > Rotation & Scale) when you're done. Want to see a part in place? Move it onto its socket while you work, since its position is ignored on export. Setup (once) Install Blender 4.2 or newer. In Blender, go to Edit > Preferences > Add-ons. Choose Install from Disk, pick tools/blender/lastfleet_weapons.py, and tick Last Fleet Weapon Parts. In the 3D view, press N to open the sidebar. The tools are on the Last Fleet tab, under Weapon parts. Editing a frame So you've got a frame to rework? Here's the flow: Open it. Start an empty file (delete the default cube, camera and light) and use File > Import > glTF 2.0 to open content/weapons/<model>.gltf, for example auto_rifle.gltf. Save the .blend in content/raw/weapons/ (it goes through Git LFS) so the next person starts from your file. Kit materials. Press Kit materials. It adds any of the materials above that the file is missing, and shrinks the imported markers from the meter-wide size Blender shows them at down to 3 cm. Model. Edit the parts in Edit mode, or replace them: delete a part, model a new one, give it the old part's name and move its origin to the attach point (Object > Set Origin). Use as many materials as you like. Meshes parented under a part are part of it. Markers. To add a socket, a Muzzle or a Sight, select the part it belongs to, put the 3D cursor where it goes (Shift + right-click), and press its button. It gets parented to the part for you. Blender's .001 suffixes don't matter, so every barrel can have its own Muzzle. Check. Press Check. It lists problems in the status bar and the Info editor: a name that isn't a part; a barrel with no Muzzle, or an optic with no Sight; a receiver with no barrel or optic socket; a marker that isn't parented to a part; a misnamed material (see above). Export. Set Id to the file name (auto_rifle, or shared for the shared parts; it defaults to the .blend name), set Folder to content/weapons/, and press Export. It runs the check first, then writes one self-contained .gltf with every part, including hidden ones. Try it. Run the tests (dotnet test tests/LastFleet.Client.Tests). They put every frame together and check its sockets, muzzles and aim points, and that aiming looks through the sight. Then play the game: the gun in your hands, the soldiers' guns and the weapons on the floor all use these models. Commit the .blend and the .gltf together. Adding a part Let's say you want an eighth barrel on the auto rifle. Add an object named, for example, Barrel_7_Long to auto_rifle.gltf, with its origin at its back end, pointing along +Y, and a Muzzle empty at its front. Export. That's it! Rolled auto rifles now pick from eight barrels. A couple of gotchas: The shipped auto_rifle.gltf is forged, so for that one you'd add the barrel to its recipe instead. Shared parts lose to a frame's own. For a part every frame can use, put it in shared.gltf, but remember that a frame with its own parts for that slot ignores the shared ones. To make a part in the loot data use it, set that part's model to Barrel_7_Long, or to Long to use that shape on every frame that has one. You can do this in Studio's Armory, where the field opens a 3D picker of the slot's models, or by hand. See it right away in Studio. If LastFleet Studio is open in Armory mode when you export, it picks up the change. Studio reads the repository's content/weapons and reloads a file as soon as it's written (the status line tells you, or tells you why it couldn't load it). Part models on the 3D panel shows every model for a frame's slot on a turntable, along with the data parts that use it. The rolled gun shows the previewed gun put together. The rules Rule Why Each top-level object is a part, named Receiver, Barrel_…, Magazine_…, Stock_…, Module_…, Grip_…, Muzzle_… or Optic_<Iron, RedDot, Holographic or Scope>…. The name says which slot it fills. A frame's file has a Receiver with at least Socket_Barrel and Socket_Optic. Every gun has a barrel and a sight. Every barrel has a Muzzle, and every optic has a Sight. The flash and the aim come from them. Markers are empties parented to their part. Meshes can be parented too. A part is the object plus everything under it. A paint slot is Paint_<Slot>. Body, BodyDark, BodyShade, Accent, Reticle and Lamp belong to the game. The data colors paint slots, and the game colors the rest. Only meshes and empties. Modifiers are applied on export; armatures, curves and text aren't exported. The game reads triangles and empties.

docs/horde.html.title: The horde | The Last Fleet
docs/horde.html.summary: The horde So you want to tune the Choir's swarmlings, or teach them something new? This page walks through how they work. The code is in src/LastFleet.AI/Horde, and how it all fits into the simulation is covered in architecture.md. Trying it The quickest way to get a feel for them is to throw a few hundred at yourself: --horde 300 calls a horde of 300 when the level starts. With --headless <ticks> it prints how many are alive and how long a tick took. Add --breach <i> to have the horde blow open the station's hull breach i and come through it (add --smoke and --camera to watch one). Use --breach near for the nearest breach it can reach you from, or --breach here to have it come into the room you're in. F3, AI section. First pick where the hordes come from: wherever the horde likes; in my room: on the floor 4 to 10 m from you along the path, all at once, whether you can see them or not; through the nearest breach: the one nearest to you along the path, blown open if it's shut, or your room if none can reach you. Then use Horde of 30, Horde of 300, Lancers (a squad of three), Stripper, Spitter and Clear horde (which also clears the Choir's bigger bodies and their acid). The section also shows how many are alive and how many are still coming, and the run's pacing. HordeSystem has its own line in the system timings. Packs What happens when a horde shows up while the squad is still sneaking around (the run's hordes before the hack)? It doesn't come straight down the field at you. That horde is a pack. A pack roams together at a walk (38% of its speed), heading for a spot 8 to 18 m away that it can walk to. The path is found from the spot outward, and each body steps to the next cell closer. Then it picks the next spot, and it gives up on one it hasn't reached within 14 s. Every body looks and listens a few times a second, and ANY of these sets off the whole pack (Swarmling.Pack; HordeSystem.Packs): someone within 3.5 m; a player's gun fired within 28 m (through walls), or a fight there; a suppressed gun only within 7 m; someone in the open within 16 m ahead of it or to the side; a hit on any of its bodies. From then on it hunts like any other horde. Start the hack (or the extraction) and every pack comes for the squad! The hack's own hordes, and hordes called by hand, hunt from the start. F3's AI section can call any horde as a roaming pack too (there's a checkbox next to where it comes from). Tuning Every number lives in HordeTuning. It's a record, so tests and tools can make their own copy with with. Setting Default What it does Speed, SpeedSpread 5.6 m/s, ±12% Running speed. A bit faster than a player runs, and each body gets its own Acceleration 28 m/s² How quickly they turn and get up to speed Health 30 Two auto rifle body hits, or one to the head RoamSpeedScale, RoamMin, RoamMax, RoamGoalSeconds 0.38, 8 m, 18 m, 14 s A roaming pack's walking speed, how far away it picks its next spot, and how long it keeps trying TouchRange, HearRange, SightRange, LoudSeconds 3.5 m, 28 m, 16 m, 0.6 s What a roaming pack notices: anyone within the first range, a gun fired within the second (within the last LoudSeconds), anyone in the open within the third SuppressedHearRange 7 m How far a roaming pack hears a suppressed gun (about a room's width) DirectRange 8 m Closer than this and in the open, they run straight at the player instead of following the field Spacing, SeparationStrength 0.7 m, 9 How far apart they stay, and how hard they push apart AttackRange, BiteReach 1.35 m, 1.9 m A lunge starts within the first. The bite lands if the player is still within the second WindUp 0.3 s The telegraph: rooted, rearing, shrieking BiteDamage, BiteBleed 7, 1.5 s A bite's damage, or the bleed-out time it takes from a downed player AttackCooldown 0.9 s Time between one body's lunges CorpseSeconds 3 s How long the dead stay on the floor FieldTicks 12 How often the field is rebuilt StandingCost 3 m Standing players count as this much further away than downed ones SoldierCost 10 m Soldiers in a fight count as this much further away than downed players SpawnMin, SpawnMax 25 m, 55 m Where hordes spawn, measured along the path to the nearest player SpawnPerTick, SpawnPerPlace 6, 18 How fast they spawn, and how many come from one place before moving to the next MaxAlive 300 The most that can be alive at once FirstHorde, HordeInterval 50 s, 75 s While infiltrating: when the first horde comes, and how often after that (only while the Director is building up). A run's pacing (RunPacing) decides whether hordes come during infiltration at all, from which deck, and how much sooner HordeBase + HordePerPlayer 8 + 5 per player An infiltration horde WaveBase + WavePerPlayer 14 + 7 per player The horde that comes with each hack wave ExtractBase + ExtractPerPlayer 20 + 8 per player The horde at the start of the extraction TrickleBase, TrickleInterval 2 + 1 per player, 10 s The trickle during the hack and the extraction StripperEvery, SpitterEvery 40, 30 A horde brings one Stripper for every this many bodies called, and the same for Spitters
