MaxStrippers, MaxSpitters 3, 4 The most that can be around at once LancersFromWave 2 Choir Lancers come with every hack wave from this one on, and at the extraction LancerBase 2 + 1 for every two players A Lancer squad BreachChance, BreachCooldown 0.5, 25 s The chance an infiltration horde blows a hull breach open (hack waves and the extraction always try), and the minimum time between two breaches BreachMin 18 m A breach is only used if it's at least this far from the players along the path (and at most SpawnMax) BreachClear 6 m Nobody can be this close to where a breach's horde lands OpenBreachShare 0.7 How often a horde with no breach to blow comes through an open one in reach instead BreachDelay, BreachInterval 1 s, 0.07 s Time from the blast to the first body coming out, and from one body to the next BreachPerPlace 40 How many bodies come through one breach before the next place is picked ClimberShare 0.3 The share that climbs walls and crawls across ceilings ClimbSpeed, CeilingSpeedScale 3.2 m/s, 0.85 Speed up a wall, and speed along a ceiling as a fraction of running speed ClimbMinRange 10 m Climbers only go up when their target is at least this far away DropMin, DropMax 1.8 m, 4.5 m A climber lets go within DropMax of its target, but never closer than DropMin (it drops off to the side) CeilingMin, CeilingMax 2.4 m, 7.6 m The range of ceiling heights above the floor it can hang from A couple of gotchas: Hit volumes are constants on Swarmling (Height, Radius, HeadRadius, HeadForward, HeadUp). The model (content/models/swarmling.gltf) is lined up with them, so change both together. Staggering isn't here. 20 damage or more staggers a swarmling for 0.35 s, but that's swarmStaggerDamage and swarmStaggerSeconds in content/defs/loot/impact.json (Studio's Armory > Impact). Strippers and Spitters These are the Choir's bigger bodies. ChoirSystem runs them, and every number is in ChoirTuning. Setting Default What it does StripperReach, StripperWindUp 2.1 m, 0.65 s A Stripper winds up its blow when it's this close, for this long StripperDamage, StripperPropDamage 32, 220 The blow's damage to everyone in front of it, and to the props there StripperCooldown 1.8 s Time between blows SpitterNear, SpitterFar, SpitterRange 9 m, 22 m, 26 m A Spitter stays between the first two distances, and throws at targets within the third SpitterWindUp, SpitterCooldown 0.7 s, 3.4 s How long it rears up to throw, and the time between throws GlobDamage 12 Damage from a glob that hits someone square on PoolRadius, PoolSeconds, PoolDamage 2.2 m, 6 s, 5 The pool it leaves behind, and the damage it does every half second to anyone standing in it Their sizes, speeds and health are in ChoirBodies (Simulation), which clients also use to build their copies. The model The swarmling is content/models/swarmling.gltf, made and animated in Blender (the guide is creatures.md). Its head and body have to stay where the hit volumes are (see above). SwarmAnimator picks which animation it plays: StrideMeters (1.1 m) is how far one loop of Run carries it, so the feet keep up with the ground. NearDistance (22 m) is where the far body takes over. DrawDistance (90 m) is where it stops being drawn. Sounds swarm_screech (the wind-up), swarm_bite, swarm_death and swarm_skitter (a loop for the crowd near you) are cues in content/defs/sounds.json, just like any other. See sound.md to replace the placeholders. Over the network A horde can be hundreds strong, so its updates get their own byte budget per snapshot. SwarmView (on the host, one per client) and SwarmReplica (on the client) send and draw it. How it works is in architecture.md. The numbers to tune are on SwarmView: Range (70 m): which bodies get sent. TargetBytes (360): the client's budget from one snapshot to the next, which the horde's updates are sized to fit. Each update costs about 8 bytes, there are 2 to 16 updates per snapshot, and there are 20 snapshots a second. ExtrapolateSeconds (0.5 s): how far a client keeps moving a body past its last update. The tolerances that decide which bodies get updated first: 6 cm at the client's feet, plus 8 mm for every meter further away. HordeSoakTests measures these on stations 3 to 10. It checks bandwidth and, on average across the stations, how far from its real position the horde is drawn. That second one is over budget for now. It's a networking task on the roadmap, so the check reports the number and is skipped until it's met. It also checks, on each station, how close each client draws the horde to where the host knows it drew it.

docs/releasing.html.title: Cutting a playtest release | The Last Fleet
docs/releasing.html.summary: Cutting a playtest release We want testers to unzip and play, with no setup fuss. So releases are self-contained zips for Windows (x64) and Linux (x64), and the only thing a tester needs to install is a Vulkan 1.3 driver. The Release workflow builds them for us. Steps So you're ready for a round of playtesting? Here's the flow: Make sure main is green in CI and is the build you want tested. Run the Weekly workflow by hand on main (Actions, Weekly, Run workflow) and wait for it to pass. Pull requests only build on Linux and run the fast GPU smoke test, so this is what checks Windows and the ray-traced, path-traced and device-loss renders before testers get the build. Tag it and push the tag. Use a playtest version, numbered per round: git checkout main && git pull git tag v0.1.0-playtest.1 git push origin v0.1.0-playtest.1 The Release workflow takes it from there. It runs the tests and publishes both platforms in Release with ReadyToRun. Then it checks that the published build actually runs (headless on both, plus rendering the outpost under software Vulkan on Linux), zips them, and creates a GitHub pre-release named after the tag with TheLastFleet-0.1.0-playtest.1-win-x64.zip and ...-linux-x64.zip. Send testers the release link. The version comes from the tag (v0.1.0-playtest.1 is version 0.1.0-playtest.1). It shows up in the window title, the first line of the log, and every playtest report (gameVersion), so you can always tell which build a piece of feedback came from. Want to try the packaging without making a release? Run the workflow by hand (Actions, Release, Run workflow). The zips come out as workflow artifacts, versioned 0.1.0-dev.<run>. What is in a zip The game (LastFleet.exe on Windows, LastFleet on Linux) with the .NET runtime. Its native libraries (GLFW, Jolt, meshoptimizer, Dear ImGui, OpenAL Soft). Windows builds also carry NVIDIA Streamline and DLSS (vendor/streamline), because Streamline runs nowhere else. The compiled shaders, and the content folder: the hand-built levels and their encounters, the data in content/defs, the models, animations and sounds, and the BRUTAL logo. The license texts in licenses/. BRUTAL's NOTICE.txt has to ship with every build. PLAYTEST-README.txt for testers, and PLAYTEST-PROTOCOL.md. By hand Want the same build on your own machine? Here's how for one platform: dotnet publish src/LastFleet.Client -c Release -r win-x64 --self-contained -p:Version=0.1.0-playtest.1 -o publish/win-x64 (Use -r linux-x64 for Linux.) Add -p:PublishReadyToRun=true to match the workflow. Notes A couple of gotchas: Builds aren't code-signed, so Windows SmartScreen may warn on first run ("More info", then "Run anyway"). Give testers a heads-up so it doesn't scare them off. Settings and reports live in the user's folder, not next to the game, so a new build keeps a tester's settings. Each tag makes a new release. Delete old pre-releases on GitHub when a round is over.

docs/sound.html.title: Sound | The Last Fleet
docs/sound.html.summary: Sound Everything the game plays is a cue. A cue is just a name (gun_shotgun, step, break_glass), some settings for how it plays (in content/defs/sounds.json), and the recordings behind it (content/sounds/<name>.wav). We didn't want audio blocking us while the game was still grey boxes, so any cue without a recording falls back to a placeholder that's generated in code (PlaceholderSounds in src/LastFleet.Audio). These are synthesized noise bursts, thumps, rings and chimes. They're good enough to play with, but they're meant to be replaced... just like the grey-box rooms! Replacing a placeholder So you've got a sound you want in the game? Here's the flow: Run LastFleet --export-sounds exported. This writes every placeholder out as a .wav file (gun_shotgun.wav, gun_shotgun_2.wav, and so on). Give them a listen so you know what each cue is for and how long it lasts. Record or design your replacement as a mono, 16-bit PCM WAV at 44.1 or 48 kHz. Stereo works, but it gets mixed down to mono anyway. The game positions every sound in the world itself, and it needs a single channel to do that. Interface sounds are mono too. Name it after the cue: gun_shotgun.wav. Want more variety? Add more takes: gun_shotgun_2.wav, gun_shotgun_3.wav. Every time the cue plays it picks one at random, so repeats don't sound robotic. Numbering from 1 (gun_shotgun_1.wav) works too. Drop it in content/sounds/ and start the game. That's it! The cue now plays your recording, and the log tells you how many cues have recordings. If the game can't read a file, the log names it and skips it. Commit it. .wav files go through Git LFS, so run git lfs install once per machine. A couple of gotchas: Trim the silence at the start. The game plays a sound the moment it happens, so any dead air up front makes it feel late. Loops have to loop cleanly. Cues marked "loop": true need to run back into their own start without a click. Tuning a cue content/defs/sounds.json has one line per cue, and the comment at the top of the file explains every field. These are the ones you'll touch the most: Field What it does gain Loudness, where 1 is as recorded. Balance cues against each other here instead of re-recording them. reach Full volume within this many meters. At twice the distance it's half as loud. Big sounds (gunshots, explosions) should reach far. maxDistance Past this distance it stops getting quieter. At twice this distance it doesn't play at all, which frees up a voice. pitchSpread How much each play's pitch wobbles either side of 1. For example, 0.05 means ±5%. priority, maxVoices We only play 48 sounds at once. When they're all in use, a higher priority sound steals a voice from a lower one, so a gunshot never loses to a footstep! If a cue already has maxVoices playing, it cuts off its own oldest one. category effects, interface or ambience. This picks which volume slider in the menu's Audio tab controls it. spatial false for sounds that play "inside your head": your own gun handling, hit markers, pickups. A brand new cue needs a line here and a recording (a cue with neither makes no sound), and then code has to actually play it. What plays when GameAudio (in src/LastFleet.Client/Audio) listens to what the client already sees and turns it into sound. It only listens, though. Nothing it does feeds back into the simulation. Cue When gun_<frame> A shot. Yours plays "inside your head" the moment you fire, while teammates' play at their gun. It's one per tick, no matter how many pellets. gun_soldier A soldier's rifle shot (the auto and pulse rifles' soldier.sound in archetypes.json). A soldier carrying something else (an SMG, a shotgun, a marksman rifle, a machine gun) sounds like that gun: gun_<model>, or the frame's sound. reload_out, reload_in, reload_bolt, weapon_swap Your reload starts, the magazine goes in, the reload finishes, or you switch weapons. impact_concrete, impact_metal, impact_flesh A round hits the level (metal for racks, rails, ducts, pipes, doors and barrels) or hits someone. We cap it at three per shooter per tick. whiz Someone else's round passes within 1.6 m of your head. hit_marker, hit_precision, kill_confirm Your hit markers, as they show up. player_hurt, heartbeat You take damage. Drop below 35% health and you'll hear a heartbeat, which gets louder the lower you go. step, land, slide Everyone's feet. A step plays as each foot lands in the body's animation (the strides' footstep events, more on those below). A body drawn from boxes doesn't have those, so it plays every stride instead (0.8 m walking, 1.15 m sprinting, 0.6 m crouched and quieter). A landing plays after a third of a second in the air, and a slide plays when one starts. grenade_throw, grenade_bounce, grenade_beep, explosion A grenade being thrown, bouncing, blinking (in time with its light), and going off. break_glass, break_wood, break_metal, light_shatter A prop breaking, or a light panel getting shot out. light_buzz The three nearest failing lights hum while they're on. ambience_station, ambience_outdoor The room tone. This is always playing. pickup_ammo, pickup_weapon, pickup_keycard, door_unlock, objective, hack_beep, alarm_wave, pa_chime, mission_success, mission_failed Pickups and the mission: grabbing ammo or a weapon, finding a keycard, opening a lock, the mission moving to its next step, the hack ticking while the room is held, a reinforcement wave (and a breach venting, sealing or being lost), the station's PA as the alert goes up or a breach gets shuttered, and the ending. flashlight_click You toggle your flashlight. door_slide, door_seal, shutter_close, breach_vent A ship's doors and breaches: a room's door sliding open or shut, a door sealing off a breach (a clunk, bolts, then the hiss of the seal), a window's shutter grinding down, and the air roaring out through a breach (a loop at the breach while it vents). swarm_screech, swarm_bite, swarm_death, swarm_skitter The horde (horde.md). The shriek of a swarmling winding up its lunge (it has to carry, because it's your warning!), its bite, its death, and the chitter of the crowd running at you (a loop that gets louder the more of them there are). choir_roar, spit_throw, choir_smash, acid_sizzle The Choir's bigger bodies. A Stripper's roar and a Spitter's gurgle as each winds up its attack (warnings, just like the shriek), a Stripper's blow landing, and a Spitter's acid hitting the deck. dry_fire You pull the trigger on an empty gun and there's no ammo left to reload it. Sounds from animation A body's animation can play sounds on its own. Think footsteps landing, or the click of letting go of a grenade. You put an event on one of the graph's clips or actions, give it a sound cue and a gain, and when the body passes that event the sound plays right where it happens (at the feet, or at one of the rig's sockets). How loud it is depends on how much of the current pose that clip makes up (animation-graphs.md). If strides are blended together, like walking forward and to the side at once, you only hear it once. You place these events in Studio on the clip timeline under the Bodies preview, and pick the sound from this file's cues. The humanoid's strides already play step this way (a run at 1.2 that also kicks up dust, and a crouched step at 0.45), which is why soldiers' and teammates' footsteps line up with their feet. A body drawn from boxes, or yours with the floating gun, still steps by distance. How it sounds in the world Positioned and faded. A sound out in the world plays where it happens. It falls off with OpenAL's inverse distance model based on its reach, and it gets duller the farther away it is, as the air absorbs it. Delayed by distance. Sound travels at the speed of sound (who knew?), so an explosion 34 m away is heard a tenth of a second after you see it. Muffled through walls. A sound in a room you can't see (RoomVisibility, the same rooms the renderer culls) is quieter and duller, like it's coming through the wall. Reverb by room size. Reverb uses OpenAL's space-station presets, picked by the room you're standing in: a closet, a corridor, a room, a big room, or a hall (two stories, or 16 cells or more). Outdoors there's barely any. Headphones. The Headphones setting in the Audio tab turns on OpenAL Soft's head-related filtering, so you can tell what's above, below or behind you. The engine LastFleet.Audio plays through OpenAL Soft (by way of Brutal.OpenAl). It has 48 voices, each with a low-pass filter for muffling, one shared reverb they all send to, and four volumes (master, effects, interface, ambience). If there's no sound device it plays nothing and the game keeps running. A smoke run mixes into memory instead, so it behaves the same on every machine, and its report counts the sounds that started. The game asks for sounds through ISoundOutput, so we can swap a different engine in behind it later. Why not FMOD? The design doc planned on FMOD, so why didn't we start there? OpenAL Soft Pros: Ships inside its NuGet package. No account, no license, every clone builds and plays sound Good enough for positioned sound, muffling and reverb, which is everything we need right now Cons: Sound designers can't author anything in a tool. It's all cues and settings in our own files FMOD Studio Pros: Sound designers get events, parameters and music layers, authored in FMOD's own tool Cons: The libraries have to be downloaded from fmod.com, and they need a license for a commercial release Someone has to write an FMOD version of ISoundOutput, with the cues as events So OpenAL Soft came first. If we want what FMOD gives sound designers, the swap is just a new ISoundOutput.

docs/studio/README.html.title: Studio guides | The Last Fleet
docs/studio/README.html.summary: Studio guides Step-by-step tutorials for LastFleet Studio. Where the reference covers every field and every button, these walk you through real tasks, one step at a time, with a screenshot of what you should see along the way. Every screenshot here is Studio itself, doing the step it shows. So if your screen doesn't match... either Studio has changed since the guide was written, or something's gone wrong! Either way, it's worth a look. Studio New to Studio? Start with Getting started: opening it, finding your way around, editing a field, undo, saving, and seeing your change in the game. Then pick the mode for what you want to change: Guide Use it to... Loot Tune what drops: rarities, loot tables, relics, and the odds in the Loot Lab. Armory Tune the guns: frames, makers, parts, traits and impact. Check one in 3D or try it on the range. Items Tune everything else you carry: medkits and other effects, supplies, the refinery and the bench. Flow See how materials, recipes, items and loot connect, and find broken names. Missions Walk through generated levels, ask a room why it's there, run checks over many seeds, and tune breaches, doors and the campaign. Levels Change what levels are built from: tags, styles, archetypes, rules, props, networks, loot, typing, plans and districts. Bodies Check animation on the turntable, edit the graph and the rig, tune reloads and fit hit shapes. Behavior Make enemies fight differently: the sandbox, cover, the behavior tree, intent scoring, difficulty and variants. Look Tune surface materials under each light, and the skies. Models Pick what each prop model is collided with, and fix what Studio flags. A couple of tips that hold for every mode: Nothing is written until you save. Edit freely: the status bar at the bottom tells you what's not saved, and Ctrl+Z takes it back. Studio can open straight into a step. Most guides show the command line for where they start (--mode, --select, --tab and friends). Run dotnet run --project src/LastFleet.Studio -- --help for the full list.

docs/studio/armory.html.title: Studio: Armory | The Last Fleet
docs/studio/armory.html.summary: Studio: Armory Armory mode is where the guns live. Every gun the game rolls is a frame (a pulse rifle, a shotgun...) made by a maker, built from one part in each slot, with a rarity and maybe an affix or two on top. Armory mode edits all of those, plus the trait rules (the numbers behind each trait) and impact (what a round's push does to whatever it hits). Why tune guns here and not in the JSON? Because a gun is the sum of a lot of small numbers, and it's hard to know what "rate of fire 150, burst of 3, falloff from 22 m" feels like. Armory mode rolls a real gun from the data as it stands, shows its numbers in play next to what they were before your change, spins it in 3D, and puts it in your hands on the range. All without saving a thing! How to open it Click Armory along the top, or start Studio in it: dotnet run --project src/LastFleet.Studio -- --mode armory Add --select pulse_rifle (or any frame, maker or part id) to open with it picked. Here's the tour: On the left are the lists: Frames (archetypes.json), Makers (manufacturers.json), Parts (parts.json), Affixes (affixes.json), and at the very bottom Trait rules (traits.json) and Impact (impact.json). In the middle is the editor for what you've picked. Top right is the 3D panel. The rolled gun spins the previewed gun, put together from its part models the way the game does it. Part models browses every model in a frame's file instead. Bottom right is the Preview: a gun rolled from the current data. Pick its Frame, Maker and Rarity (or leave them on Any), its Item level and Seed. Under that is its card and its numbers in play. New to Studio? getting-started.md covers editing, saving and undoing. Tune a frame's damage over distance So the pulse rifle falls off too early? Let's push its range out and see what that does. Pick pulse_rifle under Frames. The Preview follows whatever frame you're editing, so it switches to a Pulse Rifle. Above the fields is Damage over distance (falloff): damage (as a fraction of full) over meters. There's a line for a gun with range stat 0, one for range 100, and one for the rolled gun in the Preview. Damage is full out to where the line starts falling, drops in a straight line to its lowest, then stays flat. Drag the range 0 key (the dot where that line starts falling) to the right. That's falloffStart for a gun with range 0. The other keys work the same way: the range 100 key moves the start for range 100, and the end key moves sideways for falloffSpan and up or down for falloffMinimumMultiplier. Hover over the curve to read it. At 34 m, our pulse rifle now does 18.4 a hit at range 0, and its full 21 at range 100. Now let's speed it up too. Drag roundsPerMinute (under frameStats) from 150 to about 169. Scroll down the Preview to In play. Now is the rolled gun with your changes, Saved is the same roll with the data on disk. Anything that got better is green: rounds a minute 150 to 169, damage a second 50 to 57, and the falloff now 34 to 52 m instead of 31 to 49 m. Anything worse would be red. Like what you see? Ctrl+S. Or try it out first... Try a gun on the range Numbers are one thing, but how does it feel? Let's take that faster pulse rifle out for a spin. In the Preview, click Try it on the range. You're dropped onto the game's range with the previewed gun in your hands, edits and all, playing just like the game. The card top left has its numbers: our 169 rounds a minute and 57 damage a second are right there. Shoot! The card counts your shots and how many hit the targets. Press Esc to come back to Studio, right where you left off. Not happy with how it handles? Tweak a number, hit Try it on the range again. Too easy! When you're done experimenting, Ctrl+Z takes the changes back (or Ctrl+S keeps them). Check a gun in 3D The 3D panel shows the gun exactly the way the game puts it together, so it's the place to catch a part sitting in the wrong spot or a sight that doesn't line up. Pick marksman_rifle under Frames. The Preview and the 3D panel switch to a Marksman Rifle. Untick Turn to stop the turntable, then drag the gun to turn it yourself. The mouse wheel brings it closer. Hand points marks where hands go on it: the pistol grip (Grip.R), the Fore grip, the magazine's Grab and Well, the Charge handle, and the Muzzle. These come from the parts' markers in Blender (see weapons.md), so if a hand point is off, it's the model that needs fixing. On the left, Through the sight shows what you'd see aimed: here the marksman rifle's scope reticle. A sight with a second zoom shows that one beside it. Now pick Part models at the top. This lists every model in the frame's file (here marksman_rifle.gltf) for one slot. Pick Barrel in Slot, then click Barrel_5_Coil. It spins on its own, and the panel says which data parts use it (Named by: part.barrel.halcyon.coil_01) and what markers it has. The models come straight from content/weapons. Export from Blender and Studio reloads the file right away, so you can keep the 3D panel open while you work on a model. Recipe, next to the list, opens the part's recipe from content/weapons/forge.json. Pick the model a part shows as Parts are the pieces each gun is built from, one per slot. Each one changes the gun's stats (its mods) and shows as a model from its frame's file. Pick part.barrel.halcyon.coil_01 under Parts. It's a barrel (slot), only made by Halcyon (manufacturer), starts at military rarity, and its model is Coil. Click the model button (Coil +). The picker opens below it, with every barrel model for each frame, each with its icon. Type in filter by name to narrow them down. Rest the mouse on a model and it spins in 3D on the right, with its paint slots and markers in the tooltip. Click one to pick it. (the game's choice) at the top leaves it to the game. Click the model button again (now Coil -) to close the picker. Heads up: right now Studio marks a part's short model name (like Coil, the end of Barrel_5_Coil) as not found in red, even though the game finds it just fine. The Part models panel is the one to trust here: it shows the model Named by the part. Give a maker a new gun name Makers are who builds the guns. Each has a paint color, a bias on every gun's stats, a signature trait, and the names its guns go by. Pick kessler under Makers. The Preview switches to Kessler Armory, and its card shows the maker's signature (Steady hand) and its bias (Kessler Armory: Stability +6, Recoil dir. +7). Open models. There's a row for each frame Kessler builds: the frame on the right, and the names players see on the left. A frame with no row here is one this maker doesn't build. Under marksman_rifle, click + add. A new empty name shows up. Click it and type Longwatch MR-12. The Preview rolls again, and this seed now comes out as the Longwatch MR-12! Ctrl+S to keep it, or Ctrl+Z to take it back. These are only names. The gun's look comes from the frame's models and the maker's color. Make a trait stronger Kessler's signature is Steady hand: more damage while crouched. What a trait does is code, but how strong it is lives in the Trait rules. With the Preview still on a Kessler gun, scroll down the left list and pick Trait rules. Every trait is here with its numbers: steadyHand, restoration, scrapwork, hunger, tolling and the rest. Drag steadyHand's crouchedDamage up from 1.12 to about 1.27. The Preview's card follows: Steady hand: +27% damage while crouched. Affixes, just above, work the same way as parts: each has a kind (prefix or suffix), the rarity it starts at, its mods, and any traits it brings. Tune what a round's push does What happens when a round hits someone? It pushes them. Hard enough and they slide off their feet, harder still and they're knocked down, and a killing round throws the body. Impact sets those thresholds for everyone. Scroll to the bottom of the left list and pick Impact. Pushes are in meters a second. Each frame's own impact and impactRange say how hard and how far its rounds push. Rest the mouse on knockdownPush: at this push or above, the body is knocked down (no moving or firing, the downed pose). Want knockdowns rarer? Drag knockdownPush up a little, from 6 to about 7. Keep it under maxPush (9), or nothing could ever knock anyone down! The scales below it (playerScale, soldierScale, swarmScale) say how much each kind of body is pushed. Players aren't pushed at all (0). The status bar lists every file you've changed. Ctrl+S saves them all. Impact doesn't show in the Preview, so this is one to try in the game: save, then start a mission and shoot someone. Where to next The reference covers every field. Armory is described at the top, and the Preview, the falloff curve, the 3D panel, the model picker and the range under seeing a change. loot.md: the loot tables, rarities and relics that decide which of these guns drop. weapons.md: making the part models, and the markers the hand points come from. adding-content.md: what to set when you add a frame, maker, part or affix.

docs/studio/behavior.html.title: Studio: Behavior | The Last Fleet
docs/studio/behavior.html.summary: Studio: Behavior How do you make an enemy smarter, or meaner, or just different, without a programmer in the loop? You do it here. Behavior mode is where enemies get their brains: the behavior tree that decides what a soldier does each moment, the scoring that picks an intent in a fight, the squad personalities, the soldiers' difficulty (content/defs/ai/tuning.json) and the enemy variants (enemies.json) that the levels, the mission and the director spawn. The best part? You never tune blind. The whole mode sits on top of a sandbox: the game's grey-box range, with real soldiers fighting in it, using your data the moment you change it (saved or not). How to open it Click Behavior on the mode bar at the top, or start Studio straight in it: dotnet run --project src/LastFleet.Studio -- --mode behavior Here's the tour: The panel on the left has four tabs: Sandbox (what a click in the world puts in, and the fight's controls), Behaviors (the tree editor and the scoring graph), Enemies (the variants) and Tuning (the difficulty). Drag its right edge to make it wider. The Behaviors tab is a lot happier with room to breathe! The world behind it is the sandbox, seen from a free camera. Hold the right mouse button to look around, and fly with W, A, S and D. The rings on the floor are cover points (more on those below). The soldier panel pops up on the right when you click a soldier. Put a squad in and read a soldier's mind So you want to see why a soldier does what it does? Drop a squad in and ask it. On the Sandbox tab, leave A click in the world puts in on A squad. The settings under it are for the squad: its Squad size, the Enemy variant, what it Thinks as, whether it's Hunting the target, and its Personality (By share (as in the game) picks one the way a level does). Click the floor across the range. The squad appears and goes Hunting the target. Over each soldier is what it's doing, with its squad's personality and its role underneath (Steady Suppressor, Steady Rifleman). Tick Paused under Running so they hold still for you. Click a soldier. The Soldier panel opens on the right and "reads its mind": its squad, personality and role, what it's doing and why (Hold, because nothing pressing), its inputs (health, the target, range), each intent's score (with the stickiness, +0.10, on the one it's already doing), and what every personality would choose in its place right now. Nothing here is saved, it's just for watching. Clear the soldiers and the horde empties the range when you're done. Test cover Soldiers pick their cover from cover points, so if a crate gets ignored in a level, this is where to find out why. Pick Cover next to A click in the world puts in. Leave it on Low (crouch behind), and keep Show the cover points soldiers choose from ticked. Click the floor. A box goes down with its broad side to the target, and yellow rings show up around it: those are the spots a soldier can crouch behind it. The panel now has the box's exact Base, Width, height, depth and Turn, so you can line it up exactly. Click Make it high. The box grows to 2 m and the rings turn blue: now a soldier stands behind it and leans out. Soldiers treat these boxes just like the level's own walls and crates, as soon as you let go. They're only for trying out the AI though, so they're never saved. Read and edit the behavior tree A behavior's tree runs from its root every tick. Flow nodes run their children top to bottom, conditions check things, and actions do things. If you've used Unreal's behavior trees, you'll feel right at home. Click the Behaviors tab, and drag the panel's right edge across so the canvas has room. Pick the behavior in the box at the top left (Soldier (soldier.json)). Next to it is what it Needs of a body (fire, reload, throw, crouch, lean, blindFire), and the toolbar has + New behavior, Duplicate, Delete, Tree or Scoring, Tidy and Fit. Click the Bound forward action. The panel on the right says what it does in plain words, then its settings: the action (picked from a list, never typed), a Note, its id, and Make it the root, Take it from its parent, Duplicate and Delete. Click the Note field, type Leapfrog: back soldier first and press Enter. The note shows up on the node itself, and the status bar says 1 file not saved (Ctrl+S): soldier.json. Notes are just for designers; the game never reads them. Now see it live. Pick a soldier in the sandbox (see above) and come back to this tab. The view on the right follows that soldier, and tells you who it is and what it's thinking as (Soldier 28: Soldier, thinking as Soldier). Every edit reaches the soldiers right away, before you save. Ctrl+S keeps it, Ctrl+Z undoes it (the status bar says Undid a change to soldier.json). Wiring new nodes in (right-click for the palette, drag from a pin) is covered in the tree editor reference. Score an intent Choose intent is the one action that weighs things up. It scores four intents (hold, advance, push, fall back) and the soldier does the best one. That's utility AI, and its numbers live in the scoring graph. Still on Behaviors, pick Scoring on the toolbar. It reads left to right: the inputs (ownHealth, range, suppressed...), then the conditions, terms and factors with their curves drawn, then the four intents, then the personalities. Click the outOfRange term. Its curve is drawn large on the right, along with what it does in plain words: it adds to ADVANCE's score, 0 at 20 m or less, rising evenly to its weight (0.35) at 30 m and beyond. Under the curve are the reason shown over a soldier's head when this term wins, and adds at most (its weight). Pick a soldier in the sandbox, and the graph lights up with its numbers: the inputs show its values (range 21.82, role suppressor), each term shows what it adds right now, the conditions say whether they hold, and the intents show their scores (HOLD 0.50, ADVANCE 0.34). Click the Cautious personality on the right. A squad's personality scales each intent's score, sets how many go around the side (go around the side), and how far apart they keep (keep within (m)). Here you can see why a cautious squad holds and falls back: hold ×1.2, fall back ×1.4, push ×0.6. how often (weight) is its share of the squads. Edits here save with Ctrl+S and undo with Ctrl+Z, like the tree. Click a curve's key and its exact input and value show up under the curve, ready to edit. Adding terms, wiring them in and shaping curves are all in the scoring graph reference. Tune how hard a side is Difficulty comes from reactions, aim and coordination, never from health. No bullet sponges here! These are the same values as the game's F3 AI overlay, as data. Click the Tuning tab. Shared is what every side's soldiers fight with, grouped into Awareness, Lethality, Tactics and the rest. Hover over any value to see what it does. Pick Station next to Editing (the garrison). Every value now has a checkbox in front of it. Tick Settled aim error (deg), then click its number, type 2.5 and press Enter. It turns amber: that's Station changing it for itself. Station (1) counts the values it changes, and tuning.json is flagged as not saved. Tick Only what this side changes to see just the values this side overrides. Spawn a station squad in the Sandbox to feel the difference. To undo it all, Share every value puts the side back on the shared values. Ctrl+S writes tuning.json, and the game reads it when it starts. Look at an enemy variant A squad is all one variant: what it looks like, what it carries, where it spawns and how it thinks. Click the Enemies tab and pick lancer. Its behavior and faction are picked from lists, then its body: health, damageScale, grenades, runSpeed, sprintSpeed and dropsLoot. Under weapons is how often it carries each frame (the Armory's frames), and + add frame... adds another. Scroll down. spawns is how often a squad from each source is this variant (the lancer only comes with the choir), and clips are the body's clips it plays its own versions of (none here, so set to add some). Want a brand new enemy? That's + New enemy at the top of the list, and the enemy variants reference walks through it. Then pick it under Enemy on the Sandbox tab to watch it fight, and look at it in Bodies mode under Variant. Where to next The full reference is Behavior: how enemies fight: the behavior tree, tuning, scoring and personalities, the tree editor, enemy variants and the sandbox. To see a variant's model and clips on a turntable, head to bodies.md.

docs/studio/bodies.html.title: Studio: Bodies | The Last Fleet
docs/studio/bodies.html.summary: Studio: Bodies Ever had a soldier's feet skate across the floor, or a hand pop off the gun halfway through a reload, and had to start the whole game just to see it again? That's what Bodies mode is for. It puts a body type (an animation graph in content/anim) on a model of its rig (content/characters) and plays the rig's clips the same way the game blends them. You drive it with the graph's own parameters, so you can check a blend, a pop or a foot sliding in seconds. It's also where the body's data gets edited: the graph itself (its nodes on a canvas), the rig (content/rigs), the footstep events on each clip, the shapes shots actually hit, and the reloads' steps (content/defs/reloads.json). Everything except the Reloads tab saves with Ctrl+S and undoes with Ctrl+Z, like the rest of Studio. The preview's sliders are never saved. They're just for looking! How to open it Click Bodies on the mode bar at the top, or start Studio straight in it: dotnet run --project src/LastFleet.Studio -- --mode bodies Here's the tour: The bar along the top picks what you're looking at. From left to right: the Body type (humanoid), the Model it's drawn as (soldier), an enemy Variant, a model to Compare it with, and the gun it's Holding (auto_rifle). The row under it has the view's toggles: Turn, Body, Bones, IK targets, Hit shapes, Pause, Time and Step. The tabs: Preview (what you see here), Graph, Rig and Reloads. The turntable in the middle, with the clip timeline under it. The parameters on the right: every parameter the graph declares, as a slider or a checkbox, then the graph's Actions, then the Events the clips have passed (footsteps). Check a run on the turntable So you want to know whether the run blend looks right? In the game, the client sets the graph's parameters from what the body is doing. Here, you set them. Double-click the speed slider on the right, type 4.5 and press Enter. The soldier breaks into a run, and the Events list starts filling up with footstep (Run_F, 1.00) as each foot lands. Tick Bones and IK targets on the second row, and untick Body to hide the mesh. Now you see the skeleton itself. Bones in an IK chain are orange, and the yellow marks are what the IK reaches for: the floor under each foot. If a foot slides, this is where you'll see it. Try the other sliders while you're here (hover over one to see what it means). Defaults puts every slider back. None of this is saved, so go nuts! Move a footstep on the clip timeline Footsteps (and any other sound or effect a body makes as it moves) are events on the graph's clips. If a step sound plays a frame before the foot actually hits the floor, here's the flow: Pick the clip in the box above the timeline. Here it's Run_F, 2 events. The timeline shows its frames, the playhead, and each event as a diamond. Tick Clip alone. The body now poses in just that clip at the playhead (no blending, no IK), so you can see exactly where the event falls. Click the second footstep diamond. The body jumps to it, and the row under the timeline shows what the event does: the Sound it plays (step), its gain, the Effect it shows (dust) and At, where on the body it happens (the feet). Drag the diamond to the right. It snaps to frames (the clips are keyed at 30 a second), so here it lands on frame 11, at 0.367 s. The status bar now says 1 file not saved (Ctrl+S): humanoid.json, because events belong to the graph. Happy with it? Ctrl+S keeps it. Changed your mind? Ctrl+Z puts it back (the status bar says Undid a change to humanoid.json). Adding and removing events is covered in the reference. Find your way around the graph The Graph tab is the body's animation graph, wired up like Unreal's anim graph. Poses flow left to right into the Output Pose, which is what the body is drawn in. Click the Graph tab. On the left is the canvas, with the Output Pose fed by a Select between dead, downed and alive. On the right, the body plays the graph with the parameters under Try it, and under that is the selected node. Here it's the Select, with its three states, tried in order. Use the mouse wheel on the canvas to zoom, and follow the chain leftwards. Hover over a node to read what it does. Click the Reach Arm.L node. That's the IK that puts the left hand on the gun's fore grip. Its fields show up on the right: the Chain (Arm.L), the Target (leftGrip), the Socket (Grip.L), its Weight (the leftHandOnGun parameter), and its fade and swing. Open The body's actions (played into the slot), then actions, then throw. Each action has its game name, the rig clip it plays, the mask it covers (upperBody), its fadeIn and fadeOut, and its events. Drag fadeIn to the right to make the throw ease in slower. Here it went from 0.100 to 0.315, and the status bar flags humanoid.json as not saved. That's it! Ctrl+S to keep it, Ctrl+Z to undo it. Wiring nodes, wrapping one inside another and adding new ones are all covered in the graph editor reference. Play a reload and tune its steps A reload is two things: the reload action (the arms' clip, played into the slot), and the reload's steps (where the left hand and the magazine go, and when). Let's watch one, then tweak it. Back on Preview, tick Pause so it holds still, then click Play reload. A reload slider shows up under the actions. Drag the slider to about 0.39. The left hand has the magazine out and is holding it down by the hip. Click the Reloads tab. Each reload is a table of steps for the frames it names (here auto_rifle, pulse_rifle, smg, marksman_rifle, machine_gun). to is where the hand goes, until is the share of the reload that step ends at, magazine is where the magazine is meanwhile, and from empty marks a step only done after the last round (the charging handle). Drag the pouch step's until from 0.52 to 0.56, so the hand lingers at the pouch a little longer. Every change plays right away on the Preview tab's body. One gotcha though: this tab isn't part of Ctrl+S or Ctrl+Z. It has its own Save to write reloads.json, and Read again to throw your changes away and read the file back in. Fit the shapes shots hit Shots never hit the mesh. They hit the simulation's shapes: a head sphere around the eye and a body capsule under it. Those come from the humanoid rig's body, so if a helmet sticks out past the head sphere, this is where you fix it. Click the Rig tab. It's the rig file next to its skeleton: the bones (orange where they're in an IK chain), the sockets and eyes in yellow, and the shapes shots hit in red, standing and crouched side by side. The rig's numbers are under body: headRadius, headAbove, crouchHeadAbove and hitRadius are the ones for the shapes. Pick upperBody in the first box over the skeleton (Mask). Its bones turn green, so you can see what a mask covers before an action uses it. Drag headRadius to the right. Both head spheres grow as you drag (here to 0.270, which is way too big, but it shows up nicely). Ctrl+Z that, and let's do it the hands-on way. Go back to Preview and tick Hit shapes. The shapes are drawn over the playing body, the eye from the animation is a cyan ring, and the game's eye is an orange diamond. Under the parameters, Hit shapes has the same numbers as sliders. Hover over the dot on the head sphere's edge. It turns orange and tells you to drag it in or out. Drag it out a little: the sphere grows, Head size turns red as the selected number (0.215 here), and humanoid.json is flagged as not saved. Every change goes into the rig, so it applies to every humanoid (soldiers, lancers and players), and Studio's sandbox shoots at the new shape right away. Ctrl+S keeps it, Ctrl+Z undoes it. Heads up: the shapes are for the size of the head and helmet. If the drawn eye and the game's eye drift apart (Eye drawn ... cm up at the top of the parameters), fix the clip, not the shapes! Compare models and enemy variants Does a clip still look right on a lankier body? Put them side by side. Open the Compare box on the bar and pick lancer. The lancer stands next to the soldier, playing the same graph with the same sliders and the same gun. Each keeps its own build, so you see the clip on both bodies at once. Here both are crouched. Set Compare back to none, then open Variant and pick lancer. Now the body is the enemy variant itself: its model, playing its own clips (from Behavior > Enemies) in place of the body's. The model box switches to lancer along with it, and the header on the right says lancer.gltf. These are just for looking, so there's nothing to save. To change what a variant is drawn as, or which clips it swaps, head to the Enemies tab in Behavior mode. Where to next The full reference for this mode is Bodies: animation on a turntable, the graph and the rig, with the graph editor, the rig editor, Reloads and fitting the shapes shots hit. How the graph's nodes work is in animation-graphs.md. The enemy variants and the behaviors they think with are in behavior.md.

docs/studio/flow.html.title: Studio: Flow | The Last Fleet
docs/studio/flow.html.summary: Studio: Flow The loot data lives in a handful of files: the item tables, the items, the refinery's recipes, the fleet's supplies, the grades, the refinery tiers, the fabrications and the loot tables. Each one makes sense on its own, but the interesting question crosses all of them. How does a lump of scrap you pick up on deck 2 end up as a gun on the armory bench? That's what Flow mode is for. It draws the whole chain as boxes and arrows, read left to right, and it's live: click a box and edit it right next to the chart, and the chart redraws as you go. It's the place to sanity check the economy before you go digging through the other modes. How to open it Click Flow on the mode bar at the top, or start Studio straight into it: dotnet run --project src/LastFleet.Studio -- --mode flow There are two panels: The chart (left): six columns, each with its title along the top. Where it is found (the item tables, with the missions that roll from them), Items, What they become (the refinery's recipes, and the fleet's supplies below them), Grades and the refinery, What the armory makes and What that rolls. The bar above it says what the arrow colors mean: white gives, amber costs, blue unlocks and green is the fleet's. The edit panel (right): empty until you click a box. Then it's the same editor you'd get in Items or Loot mode, for whatever that box is. Drag the chart to move it, turn the wheel to zoom, and press See it all (or double-click an empty spot) to fit the whole thing back on screen. Follow a material to a gun So you want to know where scrap comes from and what it turns into? Here's the flow: Turn the mouse wheel over the left side of the chart to zoom in. Once you're close enough, every arrow shows its amount. Drag an empty spot of the chart to move it, until the first two columns are on screen. Rest the mouse on Scrap metal. Its arrows light up, with their amounts, and everything else dims. Read it left to right. The white arrows coming in are the item tables that give scrap, with the share of their rolls (11% of a station pile, 9% of a footlocker). The amber arrows going out are what it costs: x10 scrap into each of the two recipes that take it. Want to keep going? Rest the mouse on the recipe, then on the grade it gives, and you'll walk the whole way to the armory's fabrications and the loot table they roll from. That's it! Change what a recipe makes Say the Scrap into Mk I recipe feels too generous, and you want it to make Mk II instead. You don't need to go find it in Items mode. Just do it from the chart: Click the Scrap into Mk I box. It gets a white outline, and the edit panel shows the recipe: its id, name, inputs, grade and gives. Open the grade list and pick mk2. The chart redraws right away: the recipe's white arrow now runs to Mk II, and Mk I drops down the column, since nothing refines into it anymore. Now let's make it cost something rarer too. Open + add inputs... under the inputs. It only offers the raw materials the recipe doesn't take yet (ore, circuitry, crystal). Pick crystal. A new amber arrow runs from Choir crystal into the recipe, x10, and the panel has a row for it with an open button (jump to that item) and an x (take it out again). The panel's title now says (not saved), and the bottom line says "1 file not saved (Ctrl+S): crafting.json". Happy with it? Ctrl+S writes it. Not so sure? Ctrl+Z takes back one change at a time. Find and fix a broken name Everything in the loot data refers to everything else by id. So what happens when an id changes and something still uses the old one? Flow makes it really obvious. Click the Choir crystal box. The panel shows the item, with its id (crystal) at the top. Click the id field, select it all (Ctrl+A), type crystl and press Enter. Typo on purpose! The chart goes red where things broke. The recipe that takes crystal now points at a red box, crystal, "no such item", with red arrows. The bar above the chart counts them ("2 broken links, in red: each names something that is not there"), and the bottom of the window lists the game's own errors: the station.case table and the mk4_crystal recipe both name a crystal that's gone. The chart is read straight from the files, so it still shows when the data doesn't build. The rest of Studio shows the last version that built until you fix it, and the game would refuse the data as it stands, so don't save it like this. Fix the name: here, Ctrl+Z puts the id back. In real life, the red box tells you which name to fix, and where. The red is gone, the broken links are gone, and the bottom line says "Saved." again. Point a fabrication at a different loot table The armory bench fabricates weapons and parts, and each fabrication says which loot table its weapon rolls from. Want the Mk I weapon to come out of a different table? Here's how: Drag the chart left until the last two columns, What the armory makes and What that rolls, are on screen. Click Weapon (Mk I). The panel shows what it makes, the table it rolls from, its grade and its cost. Open table and pick another one, e.g. loot.station.soldier.shotgun. The fabrication's rolls arrow now runs to a new box for that table on the right. Every reference in the panel has an open button next to it. Click the one beside grade and the panel jumps to the mk1 grade: its itemLevel, and on the chart, every fabrication it pays for, with how many. As always, Ctrl+S keeps the change and Ctrl+Z takes it back. Where to next The reference for this mode is Flow: how it all connects. The fields you edit here are the same ones as in Items mode (items, item tables, supplies, crafting) and Loot mode (loot tables). Flow is just a different way in. What a mission rolls its piles, footlockers and crates from is set in the mission template. See missions.md.

docs/studio/getting-started.html.title: Getting started with Studio | The Last Fleet
docs/studio/getting-started.html.summary: Getting started with Studio LastFleet Studio is where we tune the game's data. Rarities, guns, items, missions, levels, enemies... nearly everything you'd want to tweak is a JSON file under content/, and Studio is the friendly way into those files. Why not just open the JSON? You can, but you'd be guessing. Studio runs the game's own code right next to the data, so you see what a change does the moment you make it: across thousands of loot rolls, on a gun's numbers, or in your own hands on the range. And nothing touches the files until you save! This guide covers what's the same in every mode: opening Studio, finding your way around, editing a field, saving and undoing. The other guides go mode by mode. How to open it From the repository: dotnet run --project src/LastFleet.Studio Studio edits the content/ of whichever repository you run it from. It finds the repository by looking for LastFleet.slnx above the program, or above the folder you're in. Want to skip the clicking? Flags go after a --: --mode <name> opens straight into a mode: loot (the default), armory, items, flow, missions, levels, bodies, behavior, look or models. --select <id> opens with that definition already picked (--select standard for the Standard rarity). Use <list>:<id> when the same id lives in more than one list (--select supplies:water). --help lists the rest. Many modes have their own, like --range or --graph, and the mode guides cover them. So dotnet run --project src/LastFleet.Studio -- --mode loot --select standard opens right where the next section starts. A quick tour Here's what you get with no flags at all: Along the top: File, Edit and View are the menus. More on those below. Then the mode tabs: Loot, Armory, Items, Flow, Missions, Levels, Bodies, Behavior, Look and Models. The highlighted one is the mode you're in. Click another to switch. Most modes are laid out the same way: The left column lists every definition the mode edits, grouped by file (here: Rarities, Loot tables and Relics). Each group has a + New button under its title. The middle is the editor for whatever you've picked on the left. The right is the mode's preview. In Loot mode that's the Loot Lab. Other modes have a 3D view, a sandbox, a map... The status bar along the bottom says whether everything's saved, and which folder you're editing. Every pane can be resized by dragging the bar between them (there's a faint grip in the middle of each bar). Studio remembers your sizes for next time. Switching modes is just a click. Here's Items, with its own lists down the left and its own previews on the right: Edit a field So you want to change something? Here's the flow: Pick a definition on the left. We'll click standard under Rarities. The middle fills in. At the top is the definition's id and the file it lives in (rarities.json), with Duplicate and Delete. Under that is a short note on what this list is for and how to add to it, and then the fields themselves. Not sure what a field does? Rest the mouse on it. Every field has a tooltip, and they're written for designers, not programmers. Here's perLevel: Want the bigger picture? Click About these fields. It opens the notes from the top of the file itself, so they're always the notes the team wrote alongside the data. Click it again to fold them away. Now change something. Number fields work like sliders: drag left or right on weight to change it (or double-click it to type a number). Text fields, like name, you just click and type in. The moment you change it, two things happen. The header says rarities.json (not saved), and the status bar turns orange: 1 file not saved (Ctrl+S): rarities.json. A few more things about fields that are worth knowing up front: A field that refers to something else (a rarity, a maker, a frame, a part...) is picked from a list of what exists, so you can't make a typo. A name Studio doesn't recognize is marked in red. A field that's been left out of the file uses its default. It shows greyed out, with set to write a value in. Lists (a table's entries, a rarity's mods) open as a tree. x removes a row and + add adds one. + New adds a copy of the selected entry at the end of the list, with the id new. Duplicate copies it right after itself. Delete removes it, and anything that refers to it will stop loading. What if a change breaks the data, like a table naming a frame that doesn't exist? The bottom of the window tells you what's wrong, using the game's own error message, and the previews keep showing the last version that worked. The game would refuse the data in that state, so fix it before you save. Undo and redo Changed your mind? Ctrl+Z undoes the last change, in any mode and any file. Ctrl+Y (or Ctrl+Shift+Z) redoes it. Open the Edit menu. Undo names the file the change was in, so you always know what you're about to undo. Click Undo (or press Ctrl+Z). The weight goes back to 62, and the status bar says what happened: Undid a change to rarities.json. Since that's exactly what's on disk, it's back to Saved. too! What counts as one change? A whole drag, from grabbing the field to letting go, or a whole bout of typing in a field. While you're still typing in a field, Ctrl+Z undoes just your typing. Studio keeps the last 200 changes. Save your work Nothing's written to the files until you save. When you're happy: Press Ctrl+S, or open File and click Save all. Revert to saved is in there too, for throwing away every change since the last save. The status bar goes back to green: Saved. Editing and the folder. Studio writes each file in the same layout it was already in, comments and all, so a save only changes the lines you edited. That keeps the diff small and easy to review. One heads up: only the comment block at the top of a file (the one About these fields shows) survives a save. Comments anywhere else in the file are lost. Edited a file by hand while Studio was open? Studio reads it again as soon as it changes on disk, and the status bar says so. If you had unsaved changes in that file, yours are kept: save to keep them, or Revert to saved to take the version on disk. Closing with unsaved changes What if you forget to save? Studio has your back. Close it (or File > Quit) with changes still pending, and it asks first: Save and quit saves everything, then closes. Quit without saving throws the changes away. Stay takes you back to where you were. Seeing a change Editing numbers blind isn't much fun, so every mode has a way to show you what a change actually does. Here's a taste in Loot mode: In the Loot Lab on the right, pick loot.station.soldier (what a station soldier drops) and click Roll 10,000. Standard comes out at 62.5% of the drops. Now drag the standard rarity's weight up, from 62 to about 77. The Lab rolls the same 10,000 again on its own, and Standard climbs to 67.4%, with every other rarity a little rarer. That's it! Every mode has its own version of this: Armory's Preview and range, Items' What a table gives, Behavior's sandbox, and so on. The mode guides walk through each one. What about the game itself? The running game doesn't pick up a save, so save in Studio, then start the game (or restart the mission) to play with your new data. The grey-box range is a quick place to try a gun: dotnet run --project src/LastFleet.Client -- --level range Where to next The reference covers every field. The sections on running it, editing and seeing a change go deeper on everything above. loot.md: rarities, loot tables, relics and the Loot Lab. armory.md: the guns, their parts, the 3D preview and the range. items.md: items, effects, supplies and crafting. Not sure whether something is data or code? adding-content.md covers what you can add in Studio, and what still needs a programmer.

docs/studio/items.html.title: Studio: Items | The Last Fleet
docs/studio/items.html.summary: Studio: Items Guns aren't the only thing lying around a station. There are medkits and ammo packs, armor plates and stims, raw materials for the fleet's refinery, and the fleet's own supplies: fuel, food, water and the rest. Items mode is where all of that lives, along with what each item does when you use it, how the fleet burns through its supplies, and what the refinery and the armory bench make out of the raw stuff. Why bother with a mode for it? Because items touch everything. A medkit is an item, an effect, an entry in four item tables and part of every player's starting kit. Items mode shows you all of those links, lets you jump between them, and rolls the tables 10,000 times after every change so you can see what a supply pile actually gives. How to open it Click Items along the top, or start Studio in it: dotnet run --project src/LastFleet.Studio -- --mode items --select medkit Use --select supplies:water to open on an entry whose id is in more than one list (water is both an item and a supply). Here's what you're looking at: On the left, top to bottom: Items (items.json), Effects (effects.json), Supplies (supplies.json), Item tables (also items.json), and further down the crafting lists from crafting.json: Grades, Refinery tiers, Recipes and Fabrication. In the middle is the editor. Above an item's fields is Used by: the tables it's found in (and how often), the recipes that refine it, and what the game's own rules do with it. Each one is a button that takes you there. On the right, What a table gives rolls a table 10,000 times at the Deck you pick, and again after every change. Under it, The items in play lists every item the way the game has it right now: its stack, how long it takes to use, and what it gives. New to Studio? getting-started.md covers editing, saving and undoing. Make a medkit heal more So the medkit feels weak? An item doesn't heal on its own: it runs an effect. Here's the flow: Pick medkit under Items. It's consumable, so it has a useSeconds (1.4) and an effect (patch_up). Click open next to the effect. That takes you to patch_up under Effects. Its trigger is use (it runs when the item is used from a quick slot), and Used by lists the items that run it. Open actions and then heal: one action, healing by an amount of 60. Drag amount up. The items in play follows along: at about 87, the medkit's Gives column reads 87 health. Want it to do something else too? An effect runs its actions in order, so: Click + add under the actions. A copy of the last one shows up. Open it, then open its do list. Every kind of action is here: heal, giveArmor, shield, changeStat, refillAmmo, callPod, placeDevice, sound and flash. Pick giveArmor. Its fields swap to the new kind's: an amount and a max. Drag amount down to something modest. Now the medkit gives 87 health; 13 armor. Happy with it? Ctrl+S. Otherwise Ctrl+Z a few times, until the status bar says Saved. again. An effect only fires an action when it would actually do something (healing only when you're hurt, and so on). A passive effect (one that works while the item is held, like the shield cell's) can only shield and change stats. Change what a supply pile holds Every supply pile, footlocker, case and cargo crate in a level rolls from an item table. A mission names the tables its level uses. Let's look at the pile. Pick station.pile under Item tables. Its shares are drawn above its fields, and What a table gives on the right switches to it too. Open entries, then the first one, scrap. Each entry has an item (with open to jump to it), a weight (how often it's picked against the others), a count ([fewest, most]) and perDeck (how many more for each deck deeper in). Drag Deck on the right up to 3. Scrap now comes in stacks of 6 to 9, and the supplies 5 to 7, while medkits stay at 1 or 2. That's perDeck at work: only entries with one grow as you go deeper. Drag scrap's weight up from 14 to about 20. Scrap goes from 11.6% of the picks to 16.1%, and everything else gives up a little. Ctrl+S to keep it, or Ctrl+Z to put it back. A brand new table is + New item table: give it an id and entries, then name it in a mission (see missions.md). Follow scrap to the refinery Raw materials like scrap are what the fleet's refinery turns into graded material, and the armory bench turns that into guns. How do you find your way around all that? Follow the links! Click open next to the scrap entry's item (or pick scrap under Items). It's refinable, and its Used by says it's Found in the footlocker (9%) and the pile (11%), and Refined by two recipes: mk1_scrap and mk2_ore, 10 a batch. Click mk1_scrap (10 a batch). That's a recipe: a batch takes its inputs (10 scrap) and gives so many (1) of a grade (mk1). Want the recipe to need circuitry too? Open + add inputs.... It only offers raw materials (the items marked refinable) that the recipe doesn't already take. Pick circuitry, and it's added at 10. Ctrl+Z that one away (it was just to show you!) and click open next to grade. Grades go lowest first, and each one's itemLevel is the item level of whatever's fabricated from it. Mk I makes item level 2. Tune the refinery and the bench Scroll down the left list to the rest of crafting.json. Pick plant under Refinery tiers. A fleet starts at the first tier (field) and upgrades at the needs board. Each tier has the cost of the upgrade in the fleet's supplies (30 alloy and 10 electronics here), the grades it can make (Mk I and Mk II), and how many batches it refines a jump. Pick weapon_mk1 under Fabrication. This is what the armory bench on the ship makes: a weapon rolled from a loot table (loot.station.cache), at its grade's item level, for a cost of 3 Mk I. The others, like sight_mk1, make a part of one slot instead. Every number here is a drag away, and Ctrl+S saves crafting.json like any other file. Want to see the whole chain in one picture, from where things are found to what the bench makes? That's what Flow mode is for (see flow.md). Make fuel run out faster The fleet's supplies get used up every jump. How fast, and what happens when they run short, is in Supplies. Pick fuel under Supplies. At the top, For a new fleet sums it up: a jump takes 28 fuel (7 ships, 4,000 people), and a new fleet starts with 224. Below that, the stations that mostly hold it. Open use, then ship. A jump costs fuel in parts that add up, each one per something (jump, ship, damagedShip, people, shipAlive, contact) with an amount. Fuel is 4 per ship. Drag amount up by one, to 5. For a new fleet now says a jump takes 35, and a new fleet starts with 280 (it starts with 8 jumps' worth unless startJumps says otherwise). Other supplies have more to them. Food, water and the rest also have short (what happens when you run short: peopleLost, morale, shipWorn, a message) and stocked (what having enough does: morale, repairShips, produce). Picking a different kind of row swaps its fields, the same as an effect's actions. Ctrl+S to keep it, or Ctrl+Z to take it back. Where to next The reference covers every field of Items mode. loot.md: the loot tables the armory bench fabricates guns from. armory.md: the guns and parts themselves. adding-content.md: what to set when you add an item (and why new items go at the end of the list).

docs/studio/levels.html.title: Studio: Levels | The Last Fleet
docs/studio/levels.html.summary: Studio: Levels Missions mode says how big a level is and what's in it. Levels mode is where the pieces it's built from live: the words rules use to say where things go, how rooms look, the kinds of room, the furniture and what places it, the pipes, where the loot goes, how rooms get their types, and the ship plans and districts that the structure-first levels are laid out by. It's all in content/defs/procgen, one file per tab. It's the biggest mode in Studio, so this guide is a bit longer. The good news? Every tab works the same way: a list on the left, the picked entry on the right, and a preview that's redrawn after every change. How to open it Click Levels on the mode bar at the top, or start Studio straight into it: dotnet run --project src/LastFleet.Studio -- --mode levels Add --select <name> to open on something: a tag, or failing that the style, archetype, rule (mess/tables for a furnishing's rule), prop, network, loot assignment, typing rule, plan or district with that id. --mode levels --select frigate opens on the frigate plan, for example. The layout: The tabs (top left): Tags, Styles, Archetypes, Rules, Props, Networks, Loot, Typing, Plans and Districts. There are more tabs than fit, so the bar scrolls along to keep the one you pick in view. The list (left): everything in the tab's file, with + New ... and Copy above it. The editor (right): the picked entry. A card at the top says in plain words what it does, then its previews, then its fields. Fields it can leave out show greyed out with set to add them. Every change is in memory until you save. The bottom line counts the files not saved, Ctrl+S writes them and Ctrl+Z takes back the last change. File > Revert to saved throws all of it away. Name a new kind of room, and keep rooms apart Tags are how everything else in this mode says where. A rule places its props in rooms tagged room.office, an assignment hides a stash in rooms tagged role.key, and so on. Tags nest: a rule asking for room.storage also matches room.storage.cold. So you want cold stores? Here's the flow: On the Tags tab, press + New tag. A tag called new_tag is added to tags.json and picked. Click its name, select it all (Ctrl+A) and type room.storage.cold. Then click description and say what it means: it's for whoever writes the next rule with it. The list puts it under room.storage straight away, and the right side says what it's Nested under. Click a dimmed tag in the list, like room.crew. Nobody listed it: it's a tag because others are nested under it (an implied tag). It shows what's nested under it, and Describe it adds it to tags.json so it can have a description too. The ones marked (built in) are set by the generator itself (role.*, layout.*, deck.*). Tags are also how rooms get their types. Each room in a mission becomes one of the kit's own rooms or one of the mission's archetypes, and the Typing tab's rules say what can go where. Open the Typing tab. At the top is the kit's own share (0.70), then + count, + adjacent and + distance to add a rule of each kind, then the rules themselves. Click offices_not_side_by_side. The card says what it asks for: "No room with any of room.office is joined to one with any of room.office." Below it are its two sides, a and b, each a set of tags. Now click Adjacency table. It's every archetype's tags (and type.kit) against each other. Want crew quarters kept away from the reactor? Tick the cell where the room.crew.quarters row meets the room.industrial.reactor column. That's it! It writes an adjacency rule for you, apart_room_crew_quarters_room_industrial_reactor, and unticking takes it out again. Ctrl+Z takes the tick back, as it did here. Give rooms a new look Who models the walls? Nobody! The generator works out a room's walls from its shape and builds them in the room's surface style. A style only lists what's different from its base, which is another style, and ultimately station. Open the Styles tab and pick industrial. On the right is the style as it builds: a stretch of a room's wall with a doorway, and a hall built in the style, seen down its length. deck and room pick which deck's and room role's colors the trims are drawn in. Below that are its base (station), id, description and every part it changes: here the wall, the floor and the hall (its structure is arches, its floor trim, and its glow). Drag the wall's R to the right and its G to the left. Both previews are redrawn in the new color as you go. Want a part it currently takes from station? Open Say how it differs... and pick stripe. The stripe is added just as the base has it (low, high, depth, shade, material, and its color following the room's role), so you can change it. Take from its base... removes a part again. What if you go too far? Drag the stripe's high way up. The style goes red, with what's wrong right under its name ("stripe.high: 7.35 is outside 0 to 3.6"), and the previews say "As it last built". The bottom of the window says the same, in the game's own words. Press Ctrl+Z and it's fine again. Tick Graph next to + New style to see the styles as a graph instead: each style with the parts it sets, wired to everything that's built in it on the right (the archetypes, and each mission's hall themes). Click a style to edit it. A style decides how a room looks, never where people and shots can go. Wall positions, thicknesses, doorway heights and the like aren't in it. Build a two-story room A room archetype is a kind of room the generator builds: its shape, tags, roles, style, furniture, and how many stories tall it is. Let's make the crew commons taller. Open the Archetypes tab and pick crew_commons (plus). At the top are six footprints its recipe makes from seeds (Reroll for others). Click one to build it below: from above, with its doorways in yellow, and on a turntable next to it. Drag the turntable to turn it and use the wheel to come nearer. Its form has the shape (plus, 3 to 5 cells across and deep), its tags, its roles, its furniture (plaza) and, greyed out, the style it takes by default. Press set next to style and you can pick another, like industrial. Drag the stories slider to 2. Uh oh! It goes red: "a tall room with a floor up it is 4 cells or more each way, for its stairs; this may be 3 by 3." The previews keep showing the room as it last built. Fix what it says. Drag the smallest width and depth from 3 to 4. Now it builds: the plan shows the stairs, a story slider appears under it (on ground here), and the turntable shows the floor up above. Happy with it? Ctrl+S. This was just a test, so here it went back with File > Revert to saved. Furnish a mess hall What goes in rooms is two tabs working together. Rules (rules.json) say what's placed where, and Props (props.json) are the things they place. Start on the rule: --mode levels --select mess/tables, or open Rules and pick tables under Furnishing: mess. The rules are split into each furnishing's rules (how a built room with that furnishing is furnished; archetypes name a furnishing) and then the level's own rules. The card says what it does in plain words: it places mess_table as near the middle as it fits, keeps 1.2 m clear round each, stands in the way (so it leaves every way through open), and is laid out together, "1 to 4 rows of 1 to 3, 0.4 m apart in a row, 2 m aisles between rows". Next to it is the table's footprint from above and from the side. Too cramped? Drag aisle to the right. The card follows: "3.85 m aisles between rows". Press Ctrl+Z, and now open the Props tab and pick mess_table. A furniture prop with a model spins on the stage, with its loot sockets and attach points marked: here 6 sockets for items on top (Top) and 6 places for other pieces (Seat, where the chairs go). Under it is the prop from above and from the side, which rule places it (mess/tables), and its form. Open sockets and its group (Top). That's the loot on the table: how many sockets get it (fill), the chance it holds anything, and the table it rolls from (room, the room's own). The line above the footprint sums it up: "a piece holds 0.12 piles from room on average". Drag chance up. At 0.53, a table holds 0.53 piles on average. That's a well-stocked galley! Route a pipe and hide the loot Two of the smaller tabs, but both change a level a lot. Networks are what connect parts of a level. reservoir_feed is the pipe the generator lays from a deep reservoir to its outlet. So how do you tell a pipe where to go? You don't, exactly. You tell it what each way costs, and the cheapest route wins. Open Networks and pick reservoir_feed. Under What its route pays is a slider for each way the route can run (along a wall, over a doorway, the ceiling's edge, standing off, across an open ceiling, a riser, through a wall, through a lintel, a service cell) and one for each bend. Don't want pipes strung across open ceilings? Drag Open ceiling up, here from 30 to 124. The sliders stop at 200; Ctrl-click one to type more. Below are its limits and the pipe itself (size, color, material, bracket spacing). A level's route, and the route it didn't take, are drawn on the Missions mode map. Loot (loot.json) says where a level's loot goes: which rooms hold a cache, which may hide a stash, and the item tables piles, footlockers, cases and cargo roll from. Open Loot. On the left are the Assignments, in order, Each deck's stashes and every table a level's loot is rolled from. Every assignment that matches a room applies, and the first cache and the first of each table win, so the order matters (the arrows next to Copy are for moving the picked one). Pick stashes_key_rooms. The card says: "Applies to rooms with any of role.key. May hold a stash, weight 0.6, 0.25 more each soldier holding it (two at most), from the mission's stash table." Drag the stash's weight up, to 0.86 here, and the card follows. Keycard rooms are now likelier to hide a stash than the deck's other rooms. Pick loot.station.stash under Tables. It says what kind of table it is (a weapons table, edited in Loot mode) and who rolls from it: the stashes of all three missions. Draw a ship The ship raids aren't grown room by room. They're laid out structure first, from a plan: the shape of the ship, the halls carved into it, and the bulkheads that cut it into sections, each section a district of rooms. Start on a plan: --mode levels --select frigate, or open Plans and pick frigate. At the top are its skin (how its outside looks from the windows), its description, its decks and its stair cores. Under Its envelope are four seeds of it (Reroll for others), and one drawn big: seed 1 is 168 × 68 m, with 4 sections, 12 compartments and 16 pressure doors and hatches. The sections are tinted, the halls white, bulkheads red, pressure doors yellow and hatches orange. deck switches between the Main deck and the Crew deck. The show list draws a check over it. Pick the way through: in at the airlock, each gate's keycard, the hack, and out, in yellow. The others are the compartments, what could be lost to a breach, and rooms per corridor. Now let's draw! Pick Paint instead of Look. The view widens so you can paint out past the hull, and paint into offers a new mask (adds). Drag along the top of the hull to paint cells in (right-drag rubs them out). Your first stroke makes a new part, part 3, a mask, and the list now says frigate (3 parts). Each stroke after that paints into it. Paint along the edge a few times, and there's a new strip of rooms along the frigate's flank: 8,672 m² inside now, up from 8,352. Scroll down to Its rooms. This is the whole level for that seed: 88 rooms and 45 stretches of hall, its doorways and void cells, and how long each stage took. Any problem is in red; here, "2 rooms (12 cells) had no way in from a hall and were left empty." Below, the level stands on a stage. Drag it to turn it and use the wheel to come nearer. Under the stage are Its parts (here the hull, a box and your new mask, each with up, down and remove, and Add a part for every kind) and Its halls. Which rooms go in a section comes from its district. Open Districts and pick crew, then open rooms and crew_quarters. A district has an anchor, the set piece its section is built round (a mess_hall 4 to 5 cells wide), and its rooms, each an archetype with how many cells it takes along its hall, a weight, whether it runs (several in a row, like cabins) and whether it's private. Plans that use it lists the plans whose sections are crew. Click frigate to jump back to the plan. Done drawing? Ctrl+S keeps your ship. Here it went back with File > Revert to saved.
