A plan's picture, without the window Want to check a plan without opening Studio at all, say on a build machine? Ask for a picture of it: dotnet run --project src/LastFleet.Studio -- --mode levels --select frigate --seed 1 --plan-png frigate.png It builds that seed, prints what it made ("frigate for seed 1: 168 × 68 m, 522 cells in 1 piece(s), 4 sections, 12 compartments, 88 rooms..."), lists its problems and exits. The picture is the plan's structure, one per deck: the first in the file you named and the second next to it with _deck2 on the end. It exits with code 1 if the plan has a problem or its envelope is in more than one piece. This frigate does, with the same "2 rooms had no way in" as above, so it's a handy check to script. Where to next The reference for this mode is Levels: what levels are made from, with a section for every tab. To see all of this in a generated level (a room's type and why, how each placement rule did, the pipe's route), see missions.md. The tables loot rolls from are edited in Loot and Items mode; flow.md shows how they connect.

docs/studio/look.html.title: Studio: Look | The Last Fleet
docs/studio/look.html.summary: Studio: Look Every model in the game is drawn with one of a small library of surface materials: painted metal, bare metal, glass, rubber and the rest (content/defs/materials.json). Tweak one and every crate, gun and wall that uses it changes with it. That's a lot of reach for a couple of numbers, so you want to see what you're doing! Look mode puts the material on a few test shapes in a test room and lets you switch the room's lighting, so a material that looks great under the station's lights doesn't turn into a mirror under a flashlight. It also has the Skies tab, for the skies you see through a ship's windows (content/defs/skies.json). What each number in a material means is in materials.md. How to open it Click Look on the mode bar at the top, or start Studio straight in it: dotnet run --project src/LastFleet.Studio -- --mode look Here's the tour: The panel on the left has two tabs, Materials and Skies. On Materials, the top has the Light the room's in and the shapes' model's color. Under them is the list of materials, with Add, Duplicate and Remove, and under that the picked material's fields. The test room on the right: a big sphere, a crate and a gun barrel in the picked material, and a row of every other material behind them to compare it with. Drag in the room to look around, and use the wheel to get closer. Tune a material under each light So the bare metal on the guns looks too shiny in the dark? Here's the flow: Click Bare metal in the list. The shapes switch over to it: roughness 0.30, metalness 1.00, smooth ticked and a little grime. Under the station's lights it reflects the room nicely. Open the Light box and pick Flashlight in the dark. The room goes black except for the beam, and there's that hot pinpoint on the sphere. That's what a player sees when he points a flashlight at a gun on the floor. Click the roughness slider at about its middle, to 0.50. The highlight spreads out and softens right away, on the shapes and on every model Studio draws. The status bar now says 1 file not saved (Ctrl+S): materials.json. Now check it under the other lights before you call it done. Pick Red alarm in the Light box. Same material, same numbers, a very different room! There's also Sodium hall and Outdoors in that box. Happy with it everywhere? Ctrl+S writes materials.json. Not happy? Ctrl+Z puts the roughness back (the status bar says Undid a change to materials.json). One heads up: under the flashlight, a mirror-smooth metal reflects a dark room, because the beam isn't part of the reflections. Tune a sky The Skies tab is what you see out of a window: stars, a nebula, the galaxy's band and the sector's sun, drawn by the game's own shader. Click the Skies tab. The list at the top has the skies (Ember Reach, Cold Drift, Violet Shoal, The Hollow), and the room is replaced by the sky itself. Drag to look around, and use the wheel to narrow the view. Pick Violet Shoal. Under Seen from are the preview's own settings: where across and down the sector's map you are (the sun moves with it), and the seed the clouds and stars come from. These aren't saved. Under them are the sky's own fields: its Stars, Nebula, Band and Sun, as sliders and color pickers. Click the sun size slider near its right end. The sun swells right there in the view (here to 8.02, which is huge, but you can't miss it), and skies.json is flagged as not saved. Scroll down the panel to Sectors. That's the order the fleet meets the skies in, one a sector, going round again past the last. up moves one up the order, remove takes it out, and Add the selected sky puts the picked sky on the end. Ctrl+S writes skies.json, and Ctrl+Z backs out the change. Want a new sky? Duplicate one that's close, rename it, and tweak away. Where to next The reference is Look: the surface materials and Skies. What every material number does is in materials.md. To see which collider a model gets (and the models themselves on a turntable), see models.md.

docs/studio/loot.html.title: Studio: Loot | The Last Fleet
docs/studio/loot.html.summary: Studio: Loot Every gun in The Last Fleet is rolled. When a soldier drops its rifle or you crack open a cache, the game picks a frame, a maker and a rarity from a loot table, then builds the gun from parts. Loot mode is where we tune those odds: how rare each tier is, what each source drops, which makers it favors, and where the hand-made relics come from. Why does this need a tool? Because odds are hard to feel from a JSON file! Is a weight of 26 a lot? What does a perLevel of 0.04 do ten decks down? The Loot Lab answers that by rolling thousands of drops with the game's own code, and rolling them again every time you change something. How to open it Loot is the first mode tab along the top, and it's where Studio opens by default. From the command line: dotnet run --project src/LastFleet.Studio -- --mode loot --select loot.station.soldier Here's the mode with the station soldier's table picked and the Lab rolled: On the left are the three lists Loot mode edits: Rarities (rarities.json), Loot tables (tables.json) and Relics (relics.json), each with its own + New button. In the middle is the editor for whatever you've picked. On the right is the Loot Lab. Pick a table, an Item level, and roll 1,000 or 10,000 drops. It shows the rarity shares, Makers and frames, every stat's spread and the power curve. Roll one shows a single gun in full. New to Studio? Start with getting-started.md for the basics of editing, saving and undoing. Make a table favor a maker So you want station soldiers to drop more Vashti Labs guns? A loot table can bias the makers it rolls, without touching the makers themselves. Here's the flow: Pick loot.station.soldier under Loot tables. Its manufacturers map is at the top: kessler at 2 (twice as likely) and rustline at 0.5 (half as likely). Under that, its entries are the frames it drops, each with a weight. In the Lab, pick loot.station.soldier, click Roll 10,000, then open Makers and frames. Kessler Armory is 63% of the drops, and Vashti Labs just 4.3%. Open + add maker... under the map. It only offers the makers the table doesn't have yet. Pick vashti. vashti shows up in the map. Drag its number up. At about 1.4, the Lab (which re-rolled on its own) has Vashti Labs at 5.8%, with everyone else giving up a little. The table's entries work the same way, just for frames. Expand one and its archetype is picked from a list of every frame. Swap the first entry from pulse_rifle to machine_gun and the Lab's frame shares follow right away: Heads up! A gun is rebuilt from its seed, its table and its item level, so changing a table that's already shipped changes guns players are carrying. Happy with it? Ctrl+S. Just experimenting? Ctrl+Z until the status bar says Saved. again. Make a new rarity Want a tier rarer than Prototype? Rarities live in rarities.json, lowest first, and the order in the file is the order of the tiers. Pick the tier you want to copy (we'll use prototype), then click + New rarity. A copy called new shows up at the end of the list, and it's already in the Lab: New, at 2.6% of the soldier table's drops. Click the id field, select it all and type elite. Do the same with name: Elite. The name is what players see. Click the color swatch next to color. The color picker opens, and you can drag around in it or type a hex code into the field at the bottom (we used #FF4F7A). Click anywhere else to close it. Now tune it. Each field has a tooltip, but here's the gist: weight is how often it comes up against the other tiers. We dragged it down to about 1.1. perLevel is how its chance changes with item level. Above 0 it gets likelier deeper in. affixes is how many affixes roll on it, as [fewest, most]. statBonus is added to all five 0 to 100 stats. mods roll onto every gun of the tier. Expand mods and its damage mod: mul is the damage band, [lowest, highest]. Each tier's band should sit above the last one, so a rarer gun hits harder. The Lab has Elite at 1.3% now, in its own color: Ctrl+S to keep it. A rarity that's never picked isn't much use, so check the tables too. A table's rarity map can favor (or snub) your new tier, just like the manufacturers map above. Check the odds deeper in Does Elite stay rare all game, or does it take over later on? That's what Item level in the Lab is for. Deeper decks drop higher item levels, and every tier's perLevel moves its odds as the level goes up. With loot.station.soldier picked in the Lab, drag Item level to 17. Click Roll 10,000 (moving the slider doesn't re-roll on its own). Standard has dropped from 62% to 31%, Refined is now the most common, and Elite (with its perLevel of 0.12) has gone from 1.3% to 3.2%. Scroll down the Lab. Under the stats table is the Power curve: how the guns' power spreads across the batch. Under that, set a Seed and click Roll one to see a single gun in full: its name, rarity, frame and maker, its stats, its traits, what its rarity and maker added, and every part with what it changes. Next seed rolls another. Nothing here changes the data, so there's nothing to save. It's just a better look at what you've got! Make a relic drop more often Relics are the hand-made uniques. They have fixed parts, roll at their best, and carry traits of their own on top of their maker's signature. They never drop by chance: only a loot table entry that names them can drop one. Pick relic.sixth_bell under Relics. It has a name, its frame (archetype) and manufacturer, a line of flavor text, its traits, its eight parts (one per slot) and its affixes. Each of those is picked from a list of what exists, with x to remove one and + add... for another. Now where does it drop from? Pick loot.relics under Loot tables. Its entries name a relic instead of a frame: the Sixth Bell and Lanternfall, one each. And who rolls loot.relics? Pick loot.station.cache. Its last entry names a whole table (loot.relics), at a weight of 0.15, and only from item level 2 up (minLevel). In the Lab, pick loot.station.cache and Roll 10,000: relics are 0.9% of a cache's drops. Drag that entry's weight up to about 1.1. Relics jump to 5.7%, and the status bar lists both files you've changed so far. Making a brand new relic is the same flow as a rarity: + New relic, give it an id and a name, set its frame, maker, parts and traits, then add an entry naming it to loot.relics (or any table you like). When the data doesn't build What happens if you rename something another file points at? Let's find out. Pick relic.sixth_bell and take the last letter off its id. Studio rebuilds the loot data after every change, and this time it can't. The bottom of the window says so in red, with the game's own error message: loot.relics names a relic that doesn't exist anymore. The previews keep showing the last version that built. The game would refuse the data like this, so fix it before you save. Here that's just Ctrl+Z, and the message goes away. Too easy! Where to next The reference covers every field. Loot mode is described at the top, and the Loot Lab under seeing a change. armory.md: the frames, makers and parts the tables roll from. items.md: crafting, where the armory fabricates guns from these same loot tables. adding-content.md: what to set when you add a rarity, table or relic.

docs/studio/missions.html.title: Studio: Missions | The Last Fleet
docs/studio/missions.html.summary: Studio: Missions Every level in the game is generated from a mission template, one file each in content/defs/missions. A template says how many decks there are, how the way through is grown, how many soldiers and rooms and loops, which room archetypes it draws from, what the loot rolls from, and a whole lot more. Reading those numbers tells you very little about what a level actually feels like. So Missions mode generates a level from the template right there, draws it from above, and regenerates it after every change. You can click through it room by room, ask it why a room is what it is, and then make a dozen more seeds and count them. Under the templates are the things every mission shares: how windows break (breaches.json), how rooms' doors behave (doors.json) and what the fleet finds to raid on the star map (campaign.json). How to open it Click Missions on the mode bar at the top, or start Studio straight into it: dotnet run --project src/LastFleet.Studio -- --mode missions Add --seed <n> to open on a particular seed. The first level takes a few seconds to make ("Making the level..."), so give it a moment. There are three panels: The list (left): the mission templates (grown_raid, ship_raid, station_raid), then Every mission: Breaches, Doors and Campaign. + New mission (a copy) starts a new template from the selected one. The level and the template (middle): at the top, the level's Seed (with -, +, Next and Random) and the Lobby settings a lobby would apply. Below that, every field of the template, in plain words. Rest the mouse on one to see what it does. At the very bottom are the Checks. The map (right): the level from above. The two lines above it sum the level up (rooms, soldiers, weapons, piles, containers, crates, keycards, how long it took to make), and say how linear it is: the share of rooms on a loop against what the template wanted, and the share of dead ends. Then the buttons: the stories, Map, Types and Recipe, Fit, Show... and Play it. Walk through a level Is this template any good? One level won't tell you, but it's where you start. Here's the flow: Pick grown_raid in the list. Press Next to go to the next seed. The level is made again and the lines above the map update: seed 2 has 155 rooms, 80 soldiers, 66% of its rooms on a loop (wanted 65%) and 10% dead ends (at most 10%). Phew! This template's levels are two stories tall. Pick Story 2 to see the upper floors. Rooms on other stories are drawn as outlines, so you can tell what's under what. Go back to Story 1 and turn the mouse wheel over the map to zoom in. Once you're close, each room is labeled with what it's for and its deck (E d2 is a room on deck 2), and the marks are easy to read: red dots are soldiers, orange triangles weapons, the yellow diamond a keycard, the purple rings hull breaches. Drag to move the map, and Fit brings it all back on screen. Ask a room why it's there Generated levels make a lot of decisions. When one looks wrong, you want to know why it happened, not just what happened. So click on it! Click a room on the map. It gets a yellow outline, and the panel under the map says what it is: its archetype, its size, how many stories, its deck and the deck's theme, and what's in it. It also says why it got its type. This one was typed maintenance_bay, "drawn by weight from those the rules left", and lists what else it could have been and how likely (kit 70%, cargo_hold 2%...), and why each other type was ruled out. Scroll down the panel. Under Placement rules here is how each placement rule did in this room, as "placed out of wanted". This room wanted a tank and got none, and it says why the spots it tried didn't work: "the mission's condition 81, something there 38, a spawn or item there 8". The Rule button next to each one opens that rule in Levels mode. Now click a mark instead, like a weapon's orange triangle. The panel shows the weapon that was rolled (here a Bailiff HC-44 of the Hunt, a hand cannon from loot.station.stash at item level 3). Below it, you can pick the table everything of its kind in this mission rolls from (that changes the template's loot), and there's an Edit button for the table itself. Press Close, then pick Types above the map. Now the rooms are drawn as they're connected, from the insertion on, each colored by the type it was given (the kit's own rooms grey, each archetype its own color, gates in red). Rest the mouse on one to see why it got its type, and click it to see it below. Change how a level grows A template like grown_raid grows its level in steps: first the main path, then the keycards, the side rooms, the loot rooms, then loops and typing. That's its recipe, and you can see each step as it goes. It's a great way to see exactly where something went sideways! Pick Recipe above the map. The steps show as nodes, left to right: Main path, Keycards, Side rooms, Loot rooms, then Loops, Type rooms and The level. Each says what it adds and on which decks. The first one is picked, so you see its fields below (5 to 7 rooms a deck, half of them on the last deck) and the mission's graph after it: 27 rooms and no keycards yet. Click 3. Side rooms. Now you see its fields (count 4 to 6, deeperChance 0.35) and the graph after three steps: 54 rooms and both keycards. Want more loot rooms? Press + loot rooms. A new step, 4. Loot rooms, goes in after the picked one, and the level is made again. The line above the map tells the story: 163 rooms now, and 28 weapons instead of 18. The template shows (not saved) and the list marks it with a *. < Earlier and Later > move the picked step, and Remove the step takes it out (the main path and the keycard stay). Keep it with Ctrl+S, or take it back with Ctrl+Z. Count a dozen levels One good level doesn't mean much. What about the next eleven? That's what the Checks are for. Scroll the template all the way down to Checks. The first line says whether every table the template names exists ("Every table it names is there."). Pick 12 (or 100 or 1000, if you've got the time) and press Make 12 levels and count. A bar shows how far it's got, and Stop keeps what's been made so far. When it's done, you get a table: a row for each seed, starting from the one shown, with its rooms, soldiers, guns, piles, boxes, crates, keys, loop and dead end percentages and one-way shortcuts. Above them are the fewest, the average and the most. The green line says every level meets the template's loop rules. Drag the bar between the template and the map to make the template wider, and the table gets roomier. Look over a ship raid ship_raid works differently from grown_raid. It's laid out by a plan: the level is the inside of a ship whose shape comes from Levels mode's Plans, with the mission read into it. Pick ship_raid in the list and Map above the map. The template has a laid out by a plan section at the top: its plans, the exits it boards by, how many zones, how long the way through must be, the room tags keycards go in, the objective, the exits it's taken off by, its escape pods, and more further down. Tick Threat above the map. Each room is shaded by how hard it's defended, cool to red. The red end is where the last zones are. Click a room. The panel names its threat (this one is 1.10), along with what's in it and its placement rules. Tune what every mission shares Some things are the same in every mission: how windows onto space break, how doors behave, and what the fleet finds to raid on the star map. They're under Every mission in the list. Click Breaches. Here's how a window takes damage (toughness, and the shares of it at which its cracks show and spread), the pull of a breach, its timers and its look. The line under the fields sums it up: "A window takes 600 (about 4 grenades). Blown out, its doors seal after 8 s; its shutter closes at 20 s; the doors unseal 6 s later." Drag toughness to the right to make windows tougher. The summary follows along: at 756 it takes about 5 grenades. Click Doors. Sliding doors (auto), doors opened by hand (byHand) and how the swarm batters them (swarm), summed up in a line again. Which rooms get hand-opened doors is up to each archetype's roomDoor, in Levels mode. Click Campaign, and open targets. Each target has its id, the name the star map gives a ship of it, the mission it's raided with, the plan a ship raid is laid out by, its weight and the sector it turns up from. Under them is the share of each sector's systems each target gets. Open carrier and drag its weight up. The shares redraw right away: at a weight of about 1.06, carriers go from 14% to 19% of sector 2's systems. These three files show as not saved like any other. Ctrl+S writes them, and File > Revert to saved throws the change away. Where to next The reference for this mode is Missions: the procedural levels. What levels are built from (the archetypes, rules, props, networks, typing and plans; the Rule buttons jump there) is in levels.md. The loot tables a mission rolls from are edited in Loot and Items mode, and you can see how they all connect in flow.md.

docs/studio/models.html.title: Studio: Models | The Last Fleet
docs/studio/models.html.summary: Studio: Models When a player bumps into a desk, a soldier hides behind a crate or a round goes through a planter, what are they actually hitting? Not the drawn model. They hit its collider, and every prop model gets one, set in content/props/colliders.json. Characters, shots, sight, cover and the navigation grid all use the same one. Models mode is where you pick it. You see the collider's outline over the model as it turns, built exactly the way the level generator sets it into a level, along with anything worth fixing. The plan behind it is in plans/model-colliders.md. There are five kinds of collider: authored: the boxes in the model's file (..._CollisionOnly). The default. mesh: exactly what's drawn. Good for irregular furniture, like a desk's hutch or a terminal's screen. box and cylinder: one box, or one upright cylinder, around what's drawn. A cylinder suits barrels and drums. none: nothing at all; walked and shot through. How to open it Click Models on the mode bar at the top, or start Studio straight in it: dotnet run --project src/LastFleet.Studio -- --mode models Want to land right on one model? --select furniture/Desk opens on the desk. Here's the tour: The list on the left has every prop model, grouped by file (cargo, containers, furniture (mesh), items...). The file's default collider is in brackets after its name. Each model shows its collider, with (file's) when it's using the file's default, and not placed when nothing sets it into a level (it isn't furniture or a station fixture). There's a filter by name box at the top. The stage on the right shows the picked model, once you pick one. Pick a model's collider So the desk is a pain to walk around? Let's see what it's collided with. Click Desk under furniture (mesh). The top of the stage tells you how it's placed (Placed as furniture by desk.), then two boxes: Every model in furniture.gltf (the file's default, mesh) and This model (as its file (mesh)). The cyan outline is the collider: every leg, drawer and the monitor, exactly as drawn. Under the stage is what it's made of (216 solid triangles (216 drawn), 1.7 × 0.8 m, 1.35 m high.) and Nothing to fix. Open This model and pick box. The outline becomes one box around the whole desk, the solid triangles drop from 216 to 12, and the list says Desk box. The status bar says 1 file not saved (Ctrl+S): colliders.json. Every change reaches the furniture Studio builds levels from right away, saved or not. Ctrl+S writes colliders.json, and Ctrl+Z puts it back (the status bar says Undid a change to colliders.json). Too easy! See what Studio flags Not every collider works for every model, and Studio tells you when one won't do. Breakable props are a good example. Click Crate_Stack. It's Placed as furniture by crate_stack (breaks). and it's collided with its authored box. Open This model and pick mesh. Studio flags it in orange under the stage: It breaks, so it keeps its authored box: a piece that breaks takes damage through one solid part, and shots hit a mesh, not the part. The outline stays the authored box, because that's what the game would really use. Ctrl+Z that one. Studio flags a few other things in the same spot: why a collider won't do (an authored model whose solid isn't a box), surfaces characters step up onto (drawn in orange on the outline), and a mesh that isn't closed (shots and sight only hit a face from the front, so they slip through a hole). When there's nothing, it says Nothing to fix. Find a model and compare its colliders The list is long, so use the filter. Click filter by name and type planter. The list narrows to Planter and Planter_Bed. Click Planter_Bed. It's on its file's mesh, so every plant and both lamps are solid. Open This model and pick authored to compare. Now only the bed itself is solid, and the plants and lamps above it aren't collided with at all. Which one's right? That's a design call: whether a soldier should see over the plants, and whether rounds should pass through them. Pick it, then Ctrl+S to keep it or Ctrl+Z to go back. Where to next The reference is Models: what each model is collided with. How prop models are made and exported (including the _CollisionOnly boxes) is in props.md. For the materials those models are drawn with, see look.md.

docs/studio/reference.html.title: LastFleet Studio | The Last Fleet
docs/studio/reference.html.summary: LastFleet Studio LastFleet Studio is the designers' tool. It's its own program, separate from the game, and it edits the game's data files right there in the repository. Why not just edit the JSON by hand? You could, but you'd be guessing. Studio runs the game's own code alongside the data, so a change shows up right away: across thousands of rolls, in a weapon's numbers in play, and in your hands on the range! And nothing gets written to the files until you save. What you can add as data, and what still needs a programmer, is covered in adding-content.md. This page is the reference. Want to learn it by doing? The Studio guides walk you through real tasks in every mode, step by step, with screenshots. There are ten modes, on the bar at the top: Loot: what drops and how rare it is. Rarities (their odds, how they scale with item level, their bonuses), loot tables (what each source drops, with weights, and how it favors makers and rarities) and relics. Armory: the guns. Frames (archetypes: the models file each one is built from, how it fires, rate of fire, magazine, damage and the rest of its numbers, base stats and clamps, whether it's in the stock kit, and how an enemy soldier fights with it), makers (their paint, bias, model names and signature traits), parts (and the model each one shows as), affixes, the trait rules, and impact (what a round's push does to what it hits, impact.json). A 3D panel shows the gun, and every part model, as exported from Blender. Items: everything else that lies around. The items themselves (medkits, ammo packs, armor plates, stims, shield cells, breaching charges, the cargo pod beacon, weapon parts, raw materials for the refinery, and the fleet's supplies: fuel, food, water, medical supplies, munitions, alloy, electronics), and the item tables that a level's supply piles, footlockers, cases and cargo crates roll from (content/defs/loot/items.json). Plus what the items do (effects.json), how the fleet uses its supplies (supplies.json), and crafting: the grades, refinery tiers, recipes and fabrication (crafting.json). Flow: the loot data as one big picture, read left to right: where things are found, the items, what the refinery and the fleet make from them, the grades, what the armory fabricates and what that rolls. Click a box to edit it right next to the chart. Missions: the mission templates (content/defs/missions). Every setting for the procedural levels, with a level generated from the template and drawn from above so you can click through it, plus many seeds generated and counted. Below the templates is what's the same for every mission: how windows break (breaches.json), how rooms' doors behave (doors.json) and what the fleet finds to raid on the star map (campaign.json). Levels: what levels are generated from (content/defs/procgen). Its tags (the words rules use to say where things go), its surface styles (how rooms and halls are built and how they look, drawn as they build), its room archetypes (the kinds of room built in generated shapes, or a hand-drawn one, each built on a turntable), its placement rules and the props they place, its networks, where a level's loot goes, how rooms are typed, the plans that structure-first levels are laid out by, and the districts their rooms come from. Bodies: a body type's model playing its animation graph (content/anim), driven by the graph's parameters as sliders. You can check blends, pops, foot sliding and the IK without ever starting the game. It also has the editors for the graph (its nodes on a canvas), the rig (content/rigs) and the reloads' steps (content/defs/reloads.json). Behavior: how enemies fight. Their behavior trees (content/defs/ai/soldier.json and any you add), the scoring that picks an intent in a fight, the squad personalities, the soldiers' difficulty (tuning.json), and the enemy variants (enemies.json) that the levels, the mission and the director spawn. You try all of it out while watching soldiers fight in a sandbox. Look: the surface materials every model is drawn with (content/defs/materials.json): painted metal, bare metal, glass and the rest. You tune them on test shapes in a test room, under a station's lights, a flashlight in the dark, an alarm's red, a sodium hall's orange or the sun. See materials.md. It also tunes the skies that windows show (content/defs/skies.json). Models: what each prop model is collided with wherever it's placed (content/props/colliders.json): its drawn mesh, its authored boxes, one box or cylinder around it, or nothing. You see the collider's outline over the model as it turns, along with what's worth fixing. Running it From the repository: dotnet run --project src/LastFleet.Studio Studio edits content/defs/loot, content/defs/ai, content/defs/missions and the rest of content it has editors for (content/defs/procgen, content/anim, content/rigs, materials.json...) in whichever repository it's run from. How does it find the repository? It looks for LastFleet.slnx above the program, or above the folder you run it in. A few handy flags: A different copy: to edit a different copy of the first three, pass --loot <folder>, --ai <folder> and --missions <folder>. Open in a mode: --mode armory (or items, flow, missions, levels, bodies, behavior, look, models) opens in that mode. Open on something: --select <id> opens with that definition selected (a part, a rarity, a loot table...; use supplies:water to select it in its own list). --pick model then opens the model picker on its model. Everything else: --help lists the rest. Editing F11 (or View > Full screen) goes full screen. Press it again to go back to a window. Every pane can be resized. Drag the bar between two panes to change how the space is split between them. A faint grip marks the middle of the bar, and the cursor changes when you're over it. This works in every mode: lists against their editors, previews against what's next to or under them, the Bodies timeline against the turntable. The panels pinned to an edge (Look's, Behavior's and the selected soldier's) get wider and narrower by dragging that edge. The model picker's and a prop's preview get taller by dragging the bar under them. Double-click a bar to reset it. Sizes are stored as fractions of the window, so they still fit when the window changes size. They're saved next to the game's settings (studio-layout.json), so Studio opens just the way you left it. A smoke run ignores them. Ctrl+Z undoes the last change, in any mode and any file (Edit > Undo shows which file). Ctrl+Y or Ctrl+Shift+Z redoes it. What counts as "one change"? A drag (a node, a curve's key, a slider) or typing in a field, from when you grab it to when you let go. A few more details: While you're typing in a field, Ctrl+Z undoes your typing in that field. Undoing all the way back to what's on disk counts as saved. The last 200 changes are kept. Revert, or a file being reloaded from disk, clears the changes for that file. An undo or redo clears the selection in a graph. The left column lists every definition by its id. Pick one and you edit it in the middle. Above its fields it tells you what the list is for and how to add to it. Hover over a field to see what it does. About these fields shows the comment at the top of the file (right after its opening brace), line for line: // lines, or a /* ... */ block (with the leading * on each line dropped), keeping blank lines and indentation. Studio writes it back unchanged. Heads up though: comments anywhere else in a file are lost when Studio saves it. Here's how each kind of field works: Numbers: drag left and right, or double-click to type. Counts (a magazine, a stat's points) stay whole numbers. Text is typed, except where it refers to something defined elsewhere. A rarity, a maker, a frame, a part, an affix, a relic, a table, a trait, a stat, a slot or a part's model is picked from a list of what exists. A list of those names (a maker's signature traits, a relic's parts, a tank's supplies, a hall style's accents) has a picker for each one and + add for another. A name the data doesn't recognize is marked in red. A color (#rrggbb, or three numbers where Studio knows the field is a color) gets a color picker. A pair [min, max] is two fields side by side. A list of names that don't refer to anything (a maker's weapon names) has a field for each one, x to remove one and + add for another. It's never one text box you split with commas! Fields left out use a default. Studio shows them greyed out, with set to write a value in (a maker's color, a part's model, a frame's frameStats). Lists of things (a table's entries, a part's mods) open as a tree. x removes a row, and + add adds one like the last. Maps (a table's maker and rarity bias, a maker's model names) take new keys: type the key and press + add. About these fields shows the file's own notes on what each field means. + New under each list's title adds an entry at the end of the list. It starts as a copy of the selected one (or the first one), with the id new. Give it an id and a name, then change whatever makes it different. Duplicate copies the selected entry right after itself with its own id (..._2). Delete removes it, and anything that refers to it will stop loading. After every change, Studio rebuilds the game's loot data. What if it doesn't build anymore (a table naming a frame that doesn't exist, a part with no slot, a missing field)? The bottom of the window tells you what's wrong, using the game's own error messages. Until you fix it, the previews show the last version that built. The game would refuse the data in that state, so fix it before saving. File > Save all (Ctrl+S) writes the changed files. File > Revert to saved throws your changes away. The bottom line shows which files have changes, and if you close Studio with unsaved changes, it asks first. Studio writes the files in the same layout they're already in, comments included, so a save only changes the lines you edited and the diff is easy to review. Edited a file by hand? Run LastFleetStudio --format (or dotnet run --project src/LastFleet.Studio -- --format) to put it back in that layout. The tests check that every file is in it. Seeing a change Editing numbers blind isn't much fun, so Studio gives you a bunch of ways to see what a change actually does: Loot Lab (Loot mode, on the right): pick a loot table and an item level and roll 1,000 or 10,000. It shows rarity, maker and frame shares, each stat's spread and the power curve. After every change it re-rolls the same batch automatically, so you can watch the odds move as you drag a weight. Roll one shows a single weapon in full. Preview (Armory mode, on the right): a weapon rolled from the current data. Pick its frame, maker and rarity, or leave them on Any. When you're editing a frame or a maker, it previews that one. The card shows its name, stats, traits, parts and affixes. Below that are its numbers in play: damage per shot, precision, rate of fire, damage per second (with and without reloads), magazine, reload, falloff, zoom, spread, kick, aim and swap times. Next to each number is what the same roll gave with the saved data, in green where it got better and red where it got worse. Next seed rolls another one. Damage over distance (Armory, above a frame's fields): the frame's falloff drawn as a curve of damage (as a fraction of full) over meters. It's full out to where the falloff starts, drops in a straight line to its lowest, and stays flat after that. It's drawn for a gun with range stat 0 and with 100 (the start point moves with range), and for the previewed gun if it uses this frame. You can drag its keys: where it starts at range 0 or 100 (falloffStart), or where it ends, sideways for falloffSpan and up or down for falloffMinimumMultiplier. Hover over the curve to read how much damage a hit does at that distance. The 3D panel (Armory, top right): The rolled gun spins the previewed weapon on a turntable, put together from its part models the way the game does it. Hand points marks where hands go on it (the pistol grip, the fore grip, the magazine's grab and well, the charging handle) and its muzzle. A gun with an optic also shows Through the sight: the reticle as it looks aimed (the part's reticle), and its second zoom beside it if it has one (secondZoom). Part models lists every model for the previewed frame's slot (Receiver, Barrel, Magazine...) and shows the selected one, along with the data parts that use it. Drag to rotate it, and use the mouse wheel to bring it closer. The models come from the repository's content/weapons, so when you export from Blender, Studio reloads the file right away. Recipe shows the part's recipe under it (content/weapons/forge.json), one shape per line, in millimeters. You edit it the same way as furniture recipes (Levels > Props, Its recipe, with the gizmo on the stage; see below). Picking a model: a field that refers to a model (a part's model) shows the model's icon and name. Click it to open the list of models it can use, below it. They're grouped by file, each with its icon, and there's a filter to narrow them down. Next to the list, the model spins in 3D (the one under the mouse, or else the selected one; drag to rotate it, and use the mouse wheel to bring it closer). Under it are the model's paint slots (materials named Paint_<Slot> in Blender, see props.md). If the thing picks its own colors, each slot gets a swatch, saved by slot name in a paint map next to the field (as in Blender sets a slot back to its color in the file). Otherwise the slots are shown the way Blender colored them. Every top-level object in every file in content/props and content/weapons is listed, named file/Object (items/Medkit), and a new file shows up without any code. Too easy! A part's model names just the object (the game finds its frame's file), and the picker offers that slot's models. Icons are drawn from the models (architecture.md), never by hand. Files changed outside Studio (an exported model, a data file edited by hand or pulled from Git) are reloaded as soon as they're written. The status line says what was reloaded. If a data file has unsaved changes in Studio, your version is kept. Save to keep yours, or Revert to take the version on disk. Try it on the range: puts you on the game's range with that weapon in your hands, playing just like the game, with targets to shoot (no soldiers). A card shows its numbers, your shots and your target hits. Esc takes you back to Studio. Items: what lies about Items mode edits content/defs/loot/items.json, effects.json, supplies.json and crafting.json: Items: every item, including the fleet's supplies and raw materials. Each one has: an id; a name (as the HUD shows it); a model (picked from content/props, with its paint); a color (its swatch and the band on its crates; color (pick) above the fields picks it); a stack (how many fit in a slot); flags for what it's for: consumable (with useSeconds and the effect it runs, picked from the effects), an optional passive (an effect you get while it's held: set it under the fields, then pick one), fleetSupply, refinable (a raw material for the refinery), weaponPart (with fitSeconds) and carried (held in both arms, like a crate). Each flag is a checkbox, and the editor only shows the fields that the item's flags turn on. Tick consumable and its use time and effect appear with their defaults; untick it and they're removed from the data. The list and The items in play show each item's icon, drawn from its model in its paint. Wondering where an item ends up? Above it, Used by says what uses it: the item tables it's found in (and how often), the recipes that refine it, the refinery upgrades it pays for (each one a button that takes you there), and what the game's own rules do with it (the starting kit, a soldier's drop, the stations' tanks, the fleet's needs). Links: a field that refers to another entry (an item table's item, a recipe's or a fabrication's grade, a refinery tier's grades, the items in a recipe's inputs or a tier's cost) has an open button next to it that takes you to that entry. Effects (effects.json): what an item does, and when. Each effect has a trigger (use: when its item is used from a quick slot; passive: for as long as its item is held) and its actions, in order. Each action does one thing, picked in do: heal (by its amount); giveArmor (amount, up to max); shield (amount, regenerating at perSecond after delaySeconds without taking damage); changeStat (stat: moveSpeed, damageTaken or reloadSpeed, changed by a fraction, for seconds); refillAmmo (magazines, added to every weapon's reserve); callPod (sets a cargo pod down in front of you, if the mission is still going); placeDevice (a charge placed on whatever the player is looking at, which goes off after fuseSeconds like a grenade: blastDamage over blastRadius, breaking anything breakable); sound (a cue, picked from content/defs/sounds.json); flash (a burst of light: color, brightness, radius, seconds). A passive effect can only shield and change stats. Picking a different kind of action swaps its fields for the new kind's, at their defaults. An effect is only used when one of its actions would actually do something (healing only when hurt, and so on). Used by lists the items that have it, and The items in play says what each one gives (a held item's passive shows as "held: ..."). Supplies (supplies.json): how the fleet uses each fleet supply. Every item with fleetSupply has rules here: use: what a jump costs, in parts that add up (each a per: jump, ship, damagedShip, people, shipAlive, contact, with its amount); short: what happens when you run short, in order (peopleLost, morale, shipWorn, message); stocked: what having enough does (morale, repairShips, produce); jumps (used up by the jump itself), boarders, startJumps and stations (the star map's stations that mostly hold this supply; which ones a station keeps in tanks is set by its mission's tankKinds). Picking a different kind swaps its fields, the same as an effect's actions. For a new fleet shows what a jump currently costs of it and what a fleet starts with. An item with rules links to them under Used by. Item tables: what a supply pile, a footlocker, a case or a cargo crate holds. Each roll picks one entry, by weight, with a count ([fewest, most]) and perDeck extra for each deck deeper. A mission names the tables its level uses (pileTable, footlockerTable, caseTable, cargoTable in its loot). Each table's shares are drawn above its fields. Crafting (crafting.json): what the fleet makes of raw materials, and what the armory makes of that. Grades of refined material, lowest first, each with the itemLevel of what's fabricated from it. Refinery tiers (a fleet starts at the first), each with its cost in the fleet's supplies, the grades it can make and its batches a jump. Recipes, a batch taking its inputs (raw materials) and giving so many of a grade. Fabrication, what the armory bench makes (a weapon rolled from a loot table, or a part of a slot) for cost of its grade. Flow mode draws all of it. What a table gives (on the right): a table rolled 10,000 times at the deck you pick, and rolled again after every change. It shows how often each item comes up, and how many. Selecting a table on the left shows it here. The items in play lists every item as the game currently has it. Each time a fight starts, every pile, container and crate is rolled fresh from its table (a weapon part at the deck's item level), the same as the weapons. Flow: how it all connects The loot data is spread across a handful of files, and it's hard to keep the whole chain in your head. So how does a raw material you pick up turn into a gun? Flow mode draws it for you, as boxes and arrows in columns from left to right: Where it is found: the item tables, each with the missions that roll their piles, footlockers, cases and cargo crates from it. Items, each with what it's for (used in the field, a weapon part, a fleet supply, raw material...). What they become: the refinery's recipes, and below them the fleet's supplies, each with what the fleet uses of it (per ship, per people, the jump itself). Grades of material, and below them the refinery tiers. What the armory makes: the fabrications. What that rolls: the loot table a fabricated weapon is rolled from (and the tables missions roll weapons from), or the kind of part. Arrows go from what's found, paid or used to what it gives, buys or makes. The colors mean: white: gives (a table gives its items, with their share; a recipe gives its grade); amber: costs (a recipe's inputs, a fabrication's grade, a refinery tier's supplies, each with how many); blue: unlocks (a refinery tier unlocks the grades it's the first to refine); green: the fleet's (an item to its supply's needs; water growing food). Hover over a box to highlight its arrows with their amounts, and everything else dims. Click it to edit it in the panel on the right, where every change shows up on the chart right away. A name that doesn't exist (a recipe naming an item nobody defined, a fabrication with a misspelled grade) shows as a red box with red arrows, and the bar above the chart counts them. The chart is read straight from the files, so it still shows even when the data doesn't build. Find the red, fix the name, and the rest of Studio builds again! Drag the chart to move it, use the mouse wheel to zoom, and double-click an empty spot (or See it all) to fit it on screen. Amounts show on every arrow once you zoom in close. Missions: the procedural levels Missions mode edits the mission templates, one file each in content/defs/missions. A level is generated from the current template, using the current procgen data from Levels mode, and drawn on the right. It's regenerated after every change to either, so you're never looking at a stale level. A deck theme (hallThemes) says how big and open its halls are, and names the surface style they're built in (style). How they look is edited in Levels mode's Styles. The template (in the middle): every setting the generator reads, in plain words (hover over one to see what it does). Decks (zones), rooms along the way, side rooms and loot rooms per deck, loops, soldiers, stories, the rooms built from the seed, and the loot: the weapon tables and how many, and the item tables for supply piles, footlockers, cases and cargo. + New mission (a copy) starts a new template from the selected one. The station's fixtures are props picked in 3D, the same way as an item's model: each of the tankKinds (its model, the supplies it can hold, its radius and height, a weight), the reservoir's model, outlet and valve, and the airlock's intake and chute (docs/blender/props.md, station.gltf). If a model is missing or doesn't have its empties, the level can't be generated, and Studio tells you why. The level: its seed (Next, Random), and the lobby settings a lobby applies to the template (decks, soldiers %, weapons %, stories, built rooms, what the cargo is mostly made of, cargo %). They aren't saved; they just show what a lobby would get. --mode missions --seed <n> opens Studio on that seed. Above the map: If the level had to be regenerated because its template requires reservoirs it couldn't place, it says so, along with how many it has (red if it's still short). A line on how linear it is: the share of its rooms on a loop and the share of dead ends (compared against the template's loopRules, red when it falls short), the longest chain of dead ends, its one-way shortcuts, and how long the mission's route is and how much of it you walk twice. The map (on the right): the level from above, one story at a time (rooms on other stories are drawn as outlines). Rooms are colored by what they're for and labeled with their deck (L d2 is a loot room on deck 2). Doorways are white, gates red, and one-way shortcuts blue, with a dot on the side they open from. The marks are: insertion (I), objective (O), extraction (X); keycards (yellow diamonds), soldiers (red), weapons (orange triangles); supply piles (dots in the color of what they hold), footlockers and cases (brown), cargo crates (in the color of their supply); hull breaches (purple rings), a deep reservoir's valves (red squares) and the reservoir (a ring); and networks. Each network route is orange (faint when it's off the story shown, with a dot where it goes up or down), the cheapest route it didn't take is grey beside it, and there's an orange diamond at its middle. Show... hides any kind of mark. Drag to move, use the mouse wheel to zoom, and Fit to see it all. Map, Types and Recipe pick what's shown. Recipe shows the mission's recipe as nodes, left to right. First its steps (Main path, Keycards, Side rooms, Loot rooms, each saying what it adds and on which decks), then Loops, Type rooms and The level. Click a node to edit it below (a step's fields: rooms, the last deck's share, the detour chance, how many, how often two deep, which decks) and to see the level as it is after that node: the mission's graph after a step, the map after the loops, the room types after typing, and the finished map at the end. It's a great way to see exactly where something went sideways! Under the nodes, + side rooms and + loot rooms add a step after the selected one, < Earlier and Later > move it, and Remove the step deletes it (the main path and the keycard stay). A template that grows from its room counts shows the recipe those counts produce, and Write the recipe writes it into the template so you can change it. Types instead shows the mission's rooms as they're connected (the insertion first, each room to the right of the one you reach it from, gates in red), each colored by the type it was given (the kit's own rooms grey, each archetype its own color, with a legend on the left). Hover over one to see why, and click it to see it below. Click a mark (or a room) to see it below the map: what it is, its deck and the deck's theme (a hall built in the theme is marked as such), and what the fight rolls for it (on Run 0, the first run; each restart rolls fresh), for example a footlocker's piles or a crate's supply and amount. A room says why it got its type (drawn by weight, or the only one the rules left), what else it could have been and how likely, and what ruled out each other type, with a Rule button that opens a typing rule in Levels mode. A room also lists how each placement rule did there: how many it placed out of how many it wanted, and if it fell short, why the spots it tried didn't work (too tall, something already there, it would block the path, it can't be reached...). A Rule button opens the rule in Levels mode. Hovering over the Rule button shows the sub-seed it drew from: the level's seed, the placement stage, the room and the rule. A network says how long its pipe is, what it cost and what it runs along, and what the route it didn't take would have cost, with a Network button that opens it in Levels mode. For a pile, a container, a crate or a weapon, you can pick the table that everything of its kind in this mission rolls from (this changes the template's loot; a loot assignment that names its own table wins, see Levels > Loot), or Edit the table, which opens it in Items mode (or Loot mode for a weapon's table). Play it (above the map): plays the level shown just like the game, with the loot, items and AI as they currently are in Studio, saved or not. Esc brings you back. Checks (under the template): whether every table named by the template and the loot assignments exists, and Make 12, 100 or 1000 levels and count. One level looking good doesn't tell you much, so this generates that many seeds starting from the one shown, with the lobby settings (a bar shows progress, and Stop keeps what's been made so far). Each level is counted (rooms, soldiers, weapons, piles, containers, crates, keycards, the percent of rooms on a loop and of dead ends, one-way shortcuts), with the fewest, average and most. It also shows whether every level meets the loop rules, and any that can't be generated (the first 100 seeds are listed; click one to show it). A heat map under it shows where placement rules fell short: rules down the side, kinds of room (an archetype, or what a room is for) across the top, and each cell showing how often, hotter meaning more. A template laid out by a plan (plan, as ship_raid.json is) works a bit differently: It has its plans and their weights, how many zones, how long the way through should be, where keycards go (room tags, doors off the way through, the chance of a long detour), the objective (its kind, the room tags it can be in, and the archetype a room is made into when none has them; or objectives, the kinds a level picks among by weight, each with how long it takes and, for a self-destruct, its countdown and how often a compartment seals, added filled in with the three kinds' defaults), the exits extraction tries in order, and spawn closets per zone. The map then draws the plan's level with the mission read into it: the airlock's vestibule (I), each zone's rooms labeled with their deck, the gates through the bulkheads in red, the keycards, the objective (O), the arena, extraction (X) and escape pods (orange squares). The recipe, room counts, loops and stories above aren't used by such a template. Its threat says how hard its places are defended: the first and last zones' threat, scales by district and by room tag, and the patrols it sets (seconds between them and soldiers in one, at threat 0 and at 1), with the room tags patrols would rather come from beside. The map's Threat box shades each room by its threat, cool to red, and picking a room names its threat and whether patrols would rather come from it. Its breaches say how a window blown out goes: the chance (permanentChance) it seals its compartment for good, when the mission can still be finished without it and every compartment already lost (else the shutter closes and the doors unseal), and the districts (never) whose compartments are never lost. Its fleet is the rest of the fleet seen from the windows: how many ships, how far off and how long. Breaches (under Every mission, at the bottom of the list): how windows onto space break and what a breach does, the same for every mission (content/defs/breaches.json). A window's toughness, and the shares of it taken when its cracks show and spread. The pull: how fast it drags someone at the breach, how far it reaches, how near someone is caught in it and what that does to them a second, and how near a dropped weapon or item is pulled out. The timers (the doors sealing, the shutter closing, the air coming back). Its look: how long the shutter takes to slide down, how much mist streams out, and how fast the lamps over sealed doors flash. A line under it sums it up: how many hits of a grenade a window takes, and how long a breach lasts. Want to see it for real? In play, the developer overlay's Blow out window breaks the window nearest you. Doors (under Every mission, after Breaches): how rooms' own doors behave in a ship's level (content/defs/doors.json). A sliding door's reach (how near anyone comes for it to open), how long it waits to shut, and how near its middle anyone keeps it open. A door opened by hand: its reach for a player, and how near and how long a soldier stands at it to open it. How much battering the swarm does to one, and how much it takes before it's broken open for good (and can no longer seal). Which rooms' doors open by hand is each archetype's roomDoor (Levels > Archetypes). Campaign (under Every mission, after Doors): what the fleet finds to raid in each system of the star map (content/defs/campaign.json). Each target has its id (one must be station), the name the map gives a ship of it, the mission it's raided with (station_raid, or ship_raid with the plan it's laid out by, picked from Levels > Plans), its weight and the first sector it turns up in. Below, each target's share of a sector's systems in sectors 1, 2, 3 and 5. A sector's first system and its gate are always stations. The template's loops and dead ends (loopRules): how far apart a loop's ends are, the longest corridor that can be routed around corners for one, the share of rooms that should be on a loop and the most that should be dead ends (loops are added until both are met, or no more fit), and how many one-way shortcuts cross each gate. Levels: what levels are made from Levels mode edits the designers' procgen data in content/defs/procgen. It grows along with the procgen revamp (../plans/procgen-revamp.md). Each of these is a tab on the left: the tags (tags.json); the surface styles (styles.json); the room archetypes (archetypes.json); the placement rules and the props they place (rules.json, props.json); the networks (networks.json); the loot assignments (loot.json); the room typing (typing.json); the level plans (plans.json); and the districts their rooms come from (districts.json). Tags Tags are how rules say where things go. A tag is a dotted name made of lowercase letters, digits and underscores, such as room.storage.cold. Tags nest: a rule asking for room.storage also matches a room tagged room.storage.cold. Every parent a name implies (room, room.storage) counts as a tag even if it isn't listed. The list (on the left): every tag as a tree, filtered by what you type. Built-in tags are marked and dimmed, because the generator sets them itself (role.*, what a room is for in the mission; layout.main_path, layout.dead_end, layout.on_loop). Implied tags are dimmed too. A tag with a problem (a bad name, defined twice, using a built-in's name) is red. Hover over it to see why. + New tag adds one to tags.json as new_tag. Rename it and describe what it means on the right. The tag picked (on the right): where it comes from, its name and description (editable only for your own tags), Remove the tag, and what it's nested under and what's nested under it (click one to go to it). An implied tag has Describe it, which adds it to tags.json so it can have a description. Styles A surface style is how the generator builds a room and how the room looks: its walls, floor and ceiling, the bands around its walls, the duct and pipes under its ceiling, its light panels, and, for a hall built in the style, what stands along the hall and the lights in its floor. So who models the walls? Nobody! The generator works out a room's walls from its shape and builds them in the room's style. A style only lists what's different from its base, which is another style, and ultimately station. The list: every style. The ones styles.json doesn't list are built in (station, plus service, public, industrial and research for the default deck themes' halls), and they're dimmed, shown the way the game builds them. A style based on another one shows < base. A style with a problem is red. Hover over it to see why. + New style adds one to styles.json as new_style, based on the selected style. Graph shows the styles as a graph instead. Each style sits to the right of its base, with the room parts it sets itself, wired to what's built in it on the right (the archetypes, and each mission's deck themes). Click a style to edit it. The style picked: drawn as it builds, and redrawn with every change. It shows a stretch of a room's wall (a doorway and its lintel, the baseboard and stripe, the duct, pipes and panels) and a hall built in the style, seen down its length. Pick the deck and room to see the trims in that deck's color or that room role's color. Below that are its base, id, description and every part it changes, all editable. Colors have a picker; materials and a hall's structure and floor are picked from what exists; a trim's color is either fixed or follows the deck or the role; a hall's accents are picked, any of them. Say how it differs... adds a part it currently inherits from its base, copied as the base has it, so you can change it. Take from its base... removes one again. Remove the style deletes it. A built-in style has List it in styles.json, which writes it out in full, as built in, so you can change it. One thing a style doesn't touch: sizes the game depends on (where walls stand, how thick and tall they are, a doorway's height, a panel's size). A style decides how a room looks, not where people and shots can go. Archetypes A room archetype is a kind of room the generator builds from the level's seed. It sets: the shape the room is built in; its tags, and which parts of a mission it can play; the style it's built in, and its furniture; whether its corners are cut, and whether pillars hold up its ceiling; how many stories tall it is, with a floor (or none) on each; and (roomDoor) the door its doorways onto halls get in a ship's level: auto, sliding open for whoever comes near, or interact, opened and shut by hand (quarters, offices, storage, security and server rooms ship as interact). bay makes it a hangar ships come and go from (flight_hangar ships so). In a ship's level each of its walls wholly on the hull is a ship entrance, open the room's full height behind a faint field you see space through but can't walk through, with the lane from it to the dropship's pad kept clear of furniture, props, loot and crates. Two walls across from each other make a hangar a dropship flies straight through (the strike carrier's). A mission template names the archetypes its built rooms are drawn from (Missions mode, archetypes, picked from the list). Every room is an archetype. The station's kit (the insertion bay, the corridors and stairwell, the spawn closet, the keycard, objective and extraction rooms, and the rest that every level has) is the set of archetypes whose kit is station, each built once from its id. A kit's archetypes aren't offered to templates. The list: every archetype in archetypes.json, with its shape. + New archetype adds a plain room with two to four cells per side. Copy adds a new one like the selected one. The archetype picked: six footprints its recipe makes from seeds in turn (Reroll for different ones). Click one to build it below the way the generator does: seen from above, with its doorways in yellow and its cut corners, and on a turntable next to it (drag to rotate it, and use the mouse wheel to get closer). A tall room has a story slider under the plan. Each story shows its floor, its railings, the doorways onto it, and the stairs climbing from it or through it (with a bridge where they cross open space to the floor). Its form: its shape's kind and ranges (cells across and deep, how much a cut takes, a blob's lumps, the corner cut); its tags (the content's own, picked), roles, style and furniture (picked); its stories (a slider from 1 to 4: raising it adds open stories at the top, lowering it removes the top ones); each story's floor above the ground (vertical.floors: its kind, none for an open story, its depth and the stairs' kind; a stairwell's landing); its weight; for a kit room, its kit and, for a rectangle of a fixed size, its doors (each a side, a cell and a level). Fields it can leave out are offered with their defaults. A stamp is drawn by hand: a grid of the largest size a room can be appears above the form, and clicking a cell adds or removes it. The cells have to touch side by side, with two or more each way. Remove the archetype deletes it. Rules What goes in rooms lives in rules.json. It's split in two: First, each furnishing's rules: how a built room with that furnishing gets furnished as it's built. Archetypes name a furnishing. Then the level's rules, in the order they place (highest priority first). + New rule adds one to the level's rules (a footlocker against a wall now and then). + New furnishing adds a furnishing with one rule. + rule under a furnishing adds one of its rules. Copy adds one like the selected one. The rule picked: a card that says in plain words what it does: what it places (each prop's share), in which rooms, where in them, how many, the clear space around each one and the spacing between them, whether it blocks the way (if so it leaves every path through open), the floor space it keeps clear in front for using it, and whether it's required. Next to it is its first prop's footprint, the same as on the Props tab. Its form: what (props picked from props.json, each with a weight), where (tags picked: any, all, none, including the generator's role.* and layout.*), its anchor and fallback (picked), count, clear, spacing, priority, blocks, interaction and required. Fields it can leave out are offered with their defaults. Remove the rule deletes it (a furnishing left with no rules is deleted too). arrange: places a furniture rule's props as a group, rather than one at a time. It can be a row (columns: a range for how many pieces) or a grid (columns and rows). gap is the meters between pieces in a row (0 for a run of server racks). aisle is the meters between rows (at least 1.1 m, so a player and a soldier can pass). along sets the room's length, across it, or its wall. backToBack pairs rows facing away from each other (lab benches). fill places as many as fit instead of a drawn number. A galley, for example, is a grid of mess tables with chairs attached. The group is placed whole or not at all: if any piece would block off a doorway, none of them are placed. Each group counts once toward the rule's count. The card says what it makes (a grid of 2–3 by 1–4, 0.4 m apart, 2 m aisles, along the room). Props What rules place lives in props.json, each with its kind. The selected prop is drawn to scale from above (its front, the side facing into the room, in yellow; on the Rules tab, its rule's clear space shaded around it; plus the half-meter grid props are placed on) and from the side (against a room's 3.6 m walls and the highest a prop can reach, 0.6 m below the ceiling to leave room for ducts and lights). Next to that are the rules that place it, and its form: kind (picked), size, and for furniture its color, what it breaks into (picked) and its piece's name. A tank's size comes from its kind in the mission template. A window (onto space, on a plan level's hull walls) has a color (its frame's), its size (its top over the floor as its height) and a sill, how high its glass starts; a rule places windows alone, at anchor hull. + New prop, Copy and Remove the prop work as elsewhere. Furniture can use a model (picked from the models in every prop file, furniture/Mess_Table). Its size then comes from the model, and the model spins on the stage with its loot sockets and attach points marked, each group in its own color. A model with paint slots takes a color for each one (paint). A furniture model's problems (a solid part that isn't a box, a breakable piece with more than one box, a base that's off its origin) show as the prop's problem in the list. sockets: loot for a group of the model's sockets (Top, Shelf2). You set the chance it holds anything, the fewest and most sockets that get loot, the item table, the weapon table and the share of weapons, and item levels on top of the level's own. Setting a table to room uses the room's own table (a stash room's weapons, a deck's piles), as loot.json assigns them. The line under it says what one piece yields on average. A group with no loot is a surface other rules place things on (a case on a desk). Loot on furniture that breaks falls to the floor. attach: a prop that stands at a group of the model's attach points (a chair at each Chair). You set its chance, the share that get pulled out, how far (up to 1.5 m), and a turn of up to 45° either way. A piece that would block a path, poke through a wall or stand in the aisle is left out. Its recipe: a forged model (furniture.gltf) can be edited here the same way a gun is in Armory mode: its parts, their shapes and materials, and its solid boxes. Write files re-forges the file, and the stage shows the change. On the stage: pick a line (with the button on its left, or by clicking into it), a marker or a solid box (the buttons under the lines). It's outlined in yellow, with a gizmo. Move (W) shows arrows along x (red), y (green) and z (blue); drag one to move it that way. Scale (E) shows a handle at the end of each axis it can grow along. Drag one out to make it longer in that direction, with both ends moving equally (a rotated box scales along its own axes; a prism, tube or rail scales its length and, across, its radius). Drag the white box in the middle to scale it as a whole. Markers can only move. Vents and bolts can only move too (a bolt's head scales as a whole). The line updates as you drag, and so does the model. Drags snap to 5 mm (1 mm for a gun part). Hold Shift for finer steps or Ctrl for coarser ones. Escape or the right mouse button cancels a drag. Undo reverts the last drag, or the last line added or removed. While something is selected, the stage stays still and keeps its view as the model changes. Drag on the stage, away from the gizmo, to rotate it. Nothing is saved until you press Write files. Read again throws away every change. Networks Networks are what connect parts of a level, in networks.json, each with its kind. reservoir_feed is the one the generator lays, from a deep reservoir to its outlet, and it can't be removed. So how do you tell a pipe where to go? You don't, exactly: you tell it what each way costs. The selected network shows what its route pays: a slider for each way the route can run (along a wall's band, over a doorway, under the ceiling, standing off a wall, across an open ceiling, up a wall, through a wall, through a lintel, through a service cell) and one for each bend. The cheapest route wins, so raising a cost keeps the pipe from running that way (ctrl-click to type a value above the slider's 200). Below that is its form: its kind, its limits (the longest open span, the most service cells), its pipe (size, color, material, bracket spacing) and how far apart bundled pipes run. A level's route, and the route it didn't take, are shown on the Missions mode map. + New network, Copy and Remove the network work as elsewhere. Loot Where a level's loot goes, in loot.json. On the left are the assignments in the order they apply (each showing what it gives: cache, stash, tables, levels), Each deck's stashes, and every table a level's loot is rolled from. The selected assignment shows a card (the rooms it applies to, and in words what they get), then its form: where: tags picked (any, all, none; deck.1 to deck.6 for a deck); cache: its weapons table and count (if left out, the mission's); stash: its weight against the deck's other rooms, with more per room deeper off the main path and per soldier holding it, and its table; tables: the item tables its piles, footlockers, cases and cargo roll from; levels: item levels added to its caches, stashes, piles and containers. Every assignment that matches a room applies. The first cache and the first of each table win, while weights and levels add up, so the order matters (the arrows move the selected one). Each deck's stashes gives the first decks their own counts (the rest use the mission's stashesPerZone). A table shows what's rolled from it, and the assignments (with the rooms they name) and missions that use it. It's red if the loot data has no table by that name. No loot.json? Then the generator uses its built-in assignments (the same as the shipped file). Write loot.json or + New assignment writes the file with them. + New assignment, Copy and Remove the assignment work as elsewhere. Typing How a level's rooms are given types before they're laid out, in typing.json. Each room in the mission becomes either one of the kit's own rooms or one of the mission's archetypes. On the left are: the kit's own share (of the rooms that could be an archetype, before the rules apply); + count, + adjacent and + distance to add a rule of that kind (Copy copies the selected one); the rules; and the Adjacency table. A selected rule shows a card saying what it asks for, then its form: a count: where (tags picked), per (deck or level), min and max; an adjacency: a and b; a distance: a, b, min and max steps along the mission's paths (no limit unless set). Here, a room's tags are its role, its deck, layout.main_path, and its type's tags: an archetype's tags or type.kit. The Adjacency table lists every archetype's tags and type.kit against each other. Tick a cell to keep rooms of those two from being connected (it writes a simple adjacency rule; unticking removes it). If a rule set can't be satisfied, the level stops, and Missions mode shows why. Plans Plans are the shapes of structure-first levels, in plans.json (../plans/structure-first.md): a frigate, a carrier, a station of hub and spokes, an accreted station (spokes, bolted-on modules and an arm bending to a second hub), a ring station, or one of your own. A plan is a list of parts, applied in order, each adding cells (4 m) to its envelope or cutting them out. Plan coordinates run along a ship from its bow (x) and across it (z), with the centerline at z = 0; north is toward −z, the top of the picture. A plan can have decks, bottom to top a story apart, each with a name and, if not the plan's, its sections' districts; every deck is cut into the same sections. With more than one, each part and hall has a tick box per deck it's on (all ticked: every deck), the previews have a deck picker, and stairs show in light purple. Its cores are stair cores between a deck and the one above: a frame along a part (on, at, across) and the deck it climbs from. Each is built as near there as two by three cells fit clear of both decks' halls, its foot and landing joined to corridors. Its skin (+ skin) is how its outside looks from its windows: the plating's color and trim, how much its panels vary, how often a running light shows along its top deck, and the lights' two colors. Left out, it's grey plating with green and red lights. The kinds of part: hull: a ship's hull from its bow's tip, its length and beam picked from their ranges, and its profile: how wide it is from the bow (0) to the stern (1). Each point is a row of sliders (along, width); + point adds one in the widest gap, and the outline below shows the shape. box: a rectangle from its corner (or its middle, if centered), mirrored across the centerline if ticked (a pair of sponsons from one part). arm: a straight run out from a cell, east, south, west or north, staying on its line however long it's drawn: a station's arm, a ring station's bridge. bridge: a straight run out from a center at any angle (degrees from east toward south), from, to cells out: a ring station's bridge from its core to its ring. A spine laid on it runs smooth along its line on any slant. ring: a ring round its center; as wide as its radius, it's a disc. mask: cells painted as rows of # (a cell) and . (none), or painted on the preview (see Paint below). Every part has adds or cuts and a chance, for parts some ships have and others don't. up, down and remove reorder and take out parts, and Add a part adds one of each kind. Its halls Its halls are carved into the envelope in order, corridors first and then service ways round them. Each is laid on a part and follows the shape that part was drawn at, so a spine runs the length of whatever hull the seed drew. Its tier is primary (a main corridor), secondary (a passageway, a cross passage) or service (a service way, its own compartment, joined to the corridors by hatches). Its width is how many cells across it is. Its style is the surface style it's built in (Levels > Styles; the plan's own if left as it is). A hall two or more cells across gets what that style's halls have standing along them, at every cell along it: frames across it (posts against both walls and a beam), arches, a colonnade down the middle (two rows from three cells across) or pillars against the walls, frames if the style has none, each with a lamp etched up its faces toward the hall in the style's hall glow. Nothing stands in a doorway or cuts the way through. The carrier's and strike carrier's main passages are two cells wide (frames, and arches in industrial), and so is the spoke station's hub concourse (a colonnade, in public). The kinds of hall: spine: along the part's line, from from to to (shares of its length; past 0 or 1 reaches into the parts beside it), at an offset across it (+ is right of it looking along it), or counted in from the edge (1 the outermost row). mirrored adds a second at the opposite offset: a pair of passageways. inset keeps that many cells of envelope either side for rooms, so a passageway stops where the hull narrows. meets halls runs on past its ends to meet a hall carved before it: a bridge to the rings either end. shortest leaves it out when it would be shorter than that share of its part, so a passageway that has room only beside a sponson isn't left stranded. cross: straight across the part at a share of its length, out to its reach either side, or (unticked) as far as the envelope allows less its inset. ring: round a ring part, from outside cells in from its outside, or (unticked) the middle of its width, and across meters between its walls. It's built smooth round its bend rather than stepped on the grid, on every cell the bend touches, so a wider ring hall takes more cells; rooms beside it open onto it through a short throat. Its sections Its sections are where the bulkheads cut it. There are two ways to do it: bulkheads across a part: sliders for where each is along it (a share of its length), + bulkhead halfway along the longest section, and how many cells each may jitter by seed. each part its own section: a station's hub, each arm, each bridge.
