With each part its own section, a ring can be cut at east, south, west or north (tick two or more): bulkheads out from its center where it runs square to the grid, each piece after the first a section of its own with the ring's district. districts say what each section is, in order. The preview tints each section, and draws the halls (main corridors palest, service ways brown), bulkheads in red, pressure doors (where a corridor crosses a bulkhead) in yellow and hatches in orange. Every section a service way passes gets a hatch onto one of its corridors, through a short stub if need be. Below the size are the plan's problems for that seed: a section with no corridor, halls that don't join the rest, a service way with no corridor near enough for a hatch. Its envelope Its envelope shows what the plan makes for four seeds. Click one to see it bigger, with its size, floor area, sections, compartments and doors. Reroll shows other seeds. Hover over a part to outline its cells (green where it adds, red where it cuts), or over a hall to outline it in blue. An envelope in more than one piece, or one more than 800 m across, shows in red. + New plan starts from a plain hull; Copy and Remove the plan work as elsewhere. Over the bigger one, you pick what a press does: Look: nothing; just look. Paint: draw a hull freehand! Pick the mask to paint into (one on the deck shown, or a new mask that adds or cuts, made with your first stroke on that deck alone). Drag to paint cells in, right-drag to rub them out; the stroke is one change, one undo. A mirrored mask paints both sides of the centerline at once. The view widens while painting, so you can paint out past the hull; it grows to follow. Pins: drag a pin where it goes. It holds to the part under it, the way a stair core does (along a line part as a share of its length and cells across; round a ring as cells from its center, growing with it), so it follows the part however a seed draws it. show draws a check over it, on the level built for that seed: sections: as above. compartments: each its own tint: what a breach seals, between pressure doors. could be lost: green for a compartment a breach could seal for good (the mission can still be finished without it), red for one it can't (the way through, a keycard, the airlock), grey for one in a district the recipe never loses. rooms per corridor: each corridor run (the stretches of one hall) by the rooms opening onto it, the count on it: red none, amber one or two, green three or more, so a bare passage stands out. the way through: the mission's route, in at the airlock, each gate's keycard (key n), the hack, and out. Which mission does it build with? The first mission laid out by plans that names this plan (else the first laid out by plans, made to use it), so its airlock, keycards and way through are the game's. If the mission can't be laid out by it that seed, the checks that need one say why. Its pins and rooms Its pins are set pieces held in place. A room pin cuts a room of its archetype round the plot cell nearest it: the bridge at the bow, the hangar across the stern. One naming its district's anchor's archetype is that section's anchor. The boarding pin boards the squad at the airlock (or hangar) nearest it, rather than the one nearest an end. + room pin and + boarding pin add one halfway along part 1 on the deck shown and switch to Pins so you can drag it. Each lists its kind, part and deck, and a room pin its archetype. Its rooms builds the picked seed's level: the space the halls leave in each section is cut into rooms from its district (see Districts), each room's doors facing its hall, and every room and stretch of hall built as a room module. It says how many rooms, stretches of hall and doorways it has, how many cells are left as void (too small for a room, or with no way in from a hall), and how long each stage took. The plan above draws the rooms' walls, doors in white and suite doors (through the room in front) in grey. Below, the whole level stands on a stage, looked at from above with the ceilings open. A level with more than a stage can draw at once leaves out its smallest pieces (furniture, fittings), and says how many. Want to check a plan without opening the window? --mode levels --select <plan> --seed <n> --plan-png <file.png> draws its structure as a picture, prints its problems and exits (exit code 1 if it has any, or its envelope is in more than one piece). Districts What each district of a plan is made of, in districts.json. A plan's section names its district. Its rooms are cut from the space its halls leave, across each plot's length so their walls line up along the hall, each picked from the district's rooms by weight. anchor: the set piece the section is built round (a mess, a cargo hold, the bridge), put in the section's biggest plot where it's deepest. Its width can go up to 16 cells, and it isn't split across either way below that, so a hangar can fill a band from the hull to a passageway (a carrier's is [16, 16]: its whole plot). It may be a tall archetype (the hangar, two stories open to its ceiling): it stands its full height where no deck is over it, and a story tall, with a problem saying so, where one is. rooms: each an archetype (picked from those one story high: its style, furnishing and tags; its shape comes from the plot), its width (the fewest and most cells it takes along its hall), its weight, whether it runs (three to six in a row the same width, like cabins), and whether it's private (somewhere you go into rather than through, so it rarely gets a second door onto another hall; a shared room usually does). Below the form are the plans whose sections use it (click one to go to it). + New district, Copy and Remove the district work as elsewhere. --mode levels --select <name> opens Studio on the tag with that name. If there's no such tag, it opens the style, archetype, rule (a furnishing's rule as furnishing/rule), prop, network, loot assignment, typing rule, plan or district with that id. Bodies: animation on a turntable, the graph and the rig Want to check a blend, a pop or a foot sliding without starting the game? That's what this mode is for. Bodies mode puts a body type (an animation graph, content/anim/<id>.json; see animation-graphs.md) on a model of its rig (content/characters), playing the rig's clips the way the game blends them. It has four tabs: Preview to watch it; Graph to edit its graph; Rig to edit its rig; Reloads to edit the reloads' steps. The graph and the rig are data like everything else: saved with Ctrl+S, undone with Ctrl+Z, and reloaded when they change on disk (unless you have unsaved changes to them here). The preview's sliders aren't saved; they're just for looking. The bar: the body type, the model, an enemy Variant of the body type (its model, playing its own clips: Behavior > Enemies, clips), a model to Compare it with, and the gun it's holding. The gun's grips come from the receiver's markers (weapons.md), and its frame's grip picks the clips (a hand cannon uses its Pistol_ ones, see animation-graphs.md). The view's toggles are on the row below. Compare stands a second model of the rig next to the first, playing the same graph with the same sliders and gun. Each one keeps its own build as the clips play (the rig's translation per bone, see rigs.md), so you can see a clip on a soldier and a lankier body side by side. Turn spins it (drag to rotate it by hand, and use the mouse wheel to get closer). Body hides the mesh. Bones draws the skeleton (bones in an IK chain are orange). IK targets draws what the IK reaches for in yellow: the gun's fore grip, the floor under each foot. Hit shapes draws the shapes shots hit on top of the body, so you can select and drag them (see below). Pause and Time slow it down so you can look closely. Step raises (or lowers) the floor under the left foot, so you can see the foot land on it and the hips drop. The parameters (on the right): every parameter the graph declares, as a slider over its range or a checkbox for a flag (hover over one to see what it means). In the game, the client sets them from what the body is doing. Here YOU set them, so the left hand only lets go when leftHandOnGun is off. Below them are the graph's Actions. Play one to see it once over its length (a reload lasts as long as the held gun's reload), drag its slider to hold it at a point, or Stop it. While an action plays, the left hand lets go of the gun the same way it does in the game (or follows the gun's reload steps). Defaults resets them. Above the parameters are the clips being played in place of the graph's (Pistol_Idle for Idle), if the gun's grip or the variant swaps any. Below, the events its clips passed (footsteps), with when they happened and how heavy they were. The clip timeline (under the body): shows one of the graph's clip nodes or actions, picked above it. A clip the graph plays in two places counts as two nodes, each with its own events. An action is shown on its clip, with its events stored as a fraction of it so they stay in place however long it lasts. The timeline shows the frames (a long tick every five), the playhead, and the clip node's events (a footstep) as diamonds. Click or drag on it to move the playhead. Tick Clip alone to pose the body in just that clip at the playhead (no blending, no IK, so you can see exactly where an event falls), or Play it. Drag an event to another frame. It snaps to 30 frames a second, the rate the clips are keyed at, and is written when you let go, as one change to undo. Right-click an event to remove it. Click it to rename it or type its time in seconds. + Event adds an event with the name next to it at the playhead. A selected event also shows what it does: the Sound it plays (from the game's cues), its gain, the Effect it shows (dust, sparks) and At, where on the body it happens (one of the rig's sockets, or the feet). The game plays these as bodies pass the event. Events belong to the graph, so a change to one is a change to the graph file, saved with Ctrl+S and undone with Ctrl+Z. Read again: the graph, the rig, the clips and the models are reloaded when they change on disk (exported from Blender, or the graph's file edited), and the sliders are kept. If a file doesn't load, Studio says why. You can open straight onto what you want to look at, too. --mode bodies --body humanoid --set speed=4.5 --action reload=0.4 opens on a body running and reloading, held at four tenths of the way through (--action reload plays it instead). A few more: --body humanoid:lancer shows it on the lancer's model; --compare player puts the players' body next to it; --holding hand_cannon puts a gun in its hands (none for nothing); --variant lancer shows an enemy variant; --tab graph (or rig) opens on that tab; --hit-shapes ticks Hit shapes. The graph editor If you've used Unreal's anim graph, you'll feel right at home: the Graph tab lets you wire the graph the same way. Poses flow left to right into the Output Pose, which is the pose the body is drawn in. Each node is a box with its output on the right and its inputs down its left side. Each input is named for what it takes: a layer's Base pose and Layered pose, an additive's Base, Additive and Reference pose, IK's Pose, a select's states when dead ... otherwise, a blend's points at 1.8. A select or blend has a + to add a new state or point. Next to the canvas, the body plays the graph and shows every change right away, with the parameters as sliders beside it (Try it) and the actions you can play, so you can see what each one does. Below them is the selected node, for editing. If the graph can't be read (for example an input left empty, shown in orange), it says why, and the body keeps playing the last version that worked. So how do you read the humanoid's graph? From the right: The Output Pose is fed by the select between dead, downed and alive. Alive is the hands on the gun (reach), fed by the aim (look), fed by the feet planted on the floor (ground), fed by the added leans, fed by the slot where the body's actions play (a reload over the legs), fed by blind fire's layer and the arms' hold, fed by the legs' walk and run blends. Each step works on the pose from the one to its left. Placing: drag a node to put it anywhere. Its position is saved in the file (pos), but the game doesn't read it. A node you've never placed sits to the left of the node it feeds and follows it around. Right-click empty canvas and pick Tidy up to lay them all out again. Wiring: drag from a node's output onto another node's input to plug it in. Whatever was plugged in there before comes out and is left loose where it was, and the spot the moved node came from is left empty. You can also drag from an input onto a node to plug that node in. A wire turns green where it's allowed and red where it isn't (a node can never feed itself). Alt-click an input to unplug it. New nodes: right-click empty canvas to add a loose node there. It's faded and marked "not plugged in", and kept in the file (loose) until you plug it in or delete it. To add one already plugged in, drop a wire from an input onto empty canvas, or click an empty input or a +. Dropping a wire from an output onto empty canvas wraps that node inside a new one (a layer over it, IK on it...). Right-click a node to wrap it inside another kind, unwrap it (its first input takes its place), unplug its output, delete it (or press Delete; whatever fed it is left loose), copy it, or paste over it. Drag empty canvas (or use the middle mouse button) to pan, use the wheel to zoom, and double-click empty canvas to see everything. The selected node, next to the canvas: Its fields: a clip node's clip (from the rig), its time (its clock, the ground covered, its end, a number or a parameter) and the rest; a layer's mask; IK's chain, target and socket; and any weight, axis, pitch or yaw, as a number or a parameter. Its points or states: each point's position on the axis, and each state's condition (a parameter on or off, or otherwise for the last one). You can edit them (Edit selects one), move them up or down, or remove them. + Point or + State adds one. Put inside...: wraps the node inside a new layer, additive, reach, look, ground, select or blend, with the node underneath and the rest at defaults for you to set. Take out does the reverse: the first node under it takes its place. Make a clip replaces it, and everything under it, with a clip. The graph: what its body can do, its parameters and targets (above): the graph's own fields. Its rig, its clips file and its groundSpeed are picked from what exists, not typed. Its capabilities are what a body of this type can visibly do, picked from fire, reload, throw, crouch, lean and blindFire. An enemy variant's behavior can only need these, and fire, reload and throw also need an action with that name. Then its parameters (with their ranges for the sliders) and the targets its IK reaches for. The body's actions (played into the slot): its actions, each with a name (the game's name: reload, throw, fire, use), the rig clip it plays and the mask it covers (picked, not typed), and its fadeIn and fadeOut. The graph's single Slot (actions) node is where they play. If the game asks for an action the graph doesn't have, nothing shows. A gun's grip can play its own clip for one (Pistol_Reload). The rig editor The Rig tab edits the body type's rig (content/rigs/<id>.json) next to its skeleton as the file describes it. Each bone is drawn from its head to its tail (bones in an IK chain are orange), its sockets and eyes are yellow, its size is shown as grey rings, and the shapes shots hit are red (see below). Pick a mask to see its bones in green, or a bone to see it in white. Its fields are: the bones, each listed after its parent, with a name, parent, head and tail, and its translation. The translation is where the bone's offset from its parent comes from when a clip plays on a model: skeleton (the model's own; the default, shown until you set one), scaled (the clip's, scaled to the model; used for the hips) or animation (the clip's, unchanged); sockets; IK chains (their bones, pole and target); masks (from some bones, except others); the mask hidden in first person; the body's numbers; the clips. Models made on the rig still have to match it: the same bones under the same parents, each pointing the same way as the rig's, and the eye where the rig has it (the bones can be longer or shorter). The Blender add-on builds the armature from this file and checks models against it (rigs.md). Want a second kind of body, like a quadruped? That's a new rig file and a new graph, made here or by copying the humanoid's. Reloads The Reloads tab edits content/defs/reloads.json: what the left hand and the magazine do over a reload, for every gun of the frames it names (the frames' model, typed with a comma between), whatever its parts. Each reload is a table of steps: to is where the hand goes (grip, grab, out, drop, pouch, belowWell, well, charge); until is the share of the reload it ends at (0 to 1, so a faster reload speeds all of it); magazine is where the magazine is meanwhile (in, hand, gone); from empty marks a step only done after the last round (the bolt pulled). + adds a step after one, the same, and - removes it. Every change plays right away on the Preview tab's body (with its reloading and reloadProgress sliders). One gotcha: this tab has its own Save and Read again. It isn't saved with Ctrl+S or undone with Ctrl+Z. Fitting the shapes shots hit Shots hit the simulation's shapes, never the mesh: a head sphere around the eye and a body capsule under it, standing or crouched. They come from the humanoid rig's body, so a designer fits them here. The settings are: headRadius (the sphere's size); headAbove and crouchHeadAbove (how far the sphere's center is above the eye, standing and crouched); hitRadius (the capsule's radius, no wider than radius). The Rig tab draws them in red, standing, with the crouched version beside it. The game, Studio's sandbox and Studio's level play all use the shapes as you edit them (once saved, the game reads them when it starts). On the Preview tab, tick Hit shapes to see them on the playing body, standing or crouched and leaning according to the sliders. They're drawn on top of the body, so they show through it. The head sphere and body capsule are red, the eye from the animation is a cyan ring, and the game's eye is an orange diamond (they sit on top of each other when the clip is right). Hover over one to highlight it, and click to select it: The head sphere: drag its center (or its outline) up or down to set how far above the eye it sits, standing or crouched depending on what's shown. Drag the dot on its edge in or out to resize it. The body capsule: drag the dot on its edge (or its outline) in or out to set its radius. The eyes: when selected, they say what they are. You can't drag either one (the game's eye belongs to the simulation, and the drawn one comes from the clip). The numbers are also under the parameters (Hit shapes), as sliders, with the selected one highlighted. Every change goes into the rig (content/rigs/humanoid.json, saved with Ctrl+S and undone with Ctrl+Z), so it applies to every humanoid, and Studio starts shooting at the new shape right away. Selecting a shape stops the turntable; tick Turn to start it again. Under the parameters, Eye drawn ... cm up, ... cm across shows how far apart the two eyes are. It turns orange past 5 cm up or 10 cm across. Why does that matter? A clip marked "eye": "standing" or "crouched" in the rig has to keep the eye there (the client's tests and the Blender add-on's Check both measure it), because a head drawn away from the simulation's eye gets shot where it isn't drawn. So fix the clip (move its hips), not the shapes. The shapes are for setting the size of the head and helmet. Behavior: how enemies fight An enemy is a variant (Soldier, Lancer...) that thinks using a behavior. Both are data in content/defs/ai. A variant's body and model are what it's drawn as (Bodies mode shows them). The behavior tree A behavior's tree decides what a soldier does at each moment. Every tick, the soldier runs it from the root. Each node either succeeds or fails: Flow nodes run their children top to bottom. A Selector stops at the first child that succeeds ("the first one that works"). A Sequence stops at the first child that fails ("all of them, in order"). Put conditions first and an action after them, and it reads as if this, then do that. Do all runs every child no matter what each one returns. Not flips its one child's result. Conditions check things and don't change anything. For example: the soldier's awareness (idle, alerted, engaging, hunting, searching), whether it sees an enemy, its distance to the enemy, a value it weighs (its health, the range...), how many of its squad are still standing, whether the level has cover, and its current intent. Actions do things, using the game's own code: Roam (at the start of the level, soldiers wander around their post), Watch the enemy, Choose intent, Hold cover, Bound forward, Push the enemy, Fall back, Fight in the open, Clear rooms, Go to the enemy, Search where he went, Look around, Top up the magazine, Throw a grenade and Dodge grenades. (Fight from cover combines the four cover actions in one node, for a short tree.) An action can fail: Clear rooms when there are no rooms to clear, Bound forward when it isn't the soldier's turn or there's no cover ahead, Search where he went when there's nowhere left to look. When that happens, a selector just moves on to its next child. How a soldier notices the enemy (idle, then alerted, engaging, hunting, searching) is handled by the game's code, and the tree reads it with Awareness is. Searching for a lost enemy So the squad has lost track of you. Where do they look? Going straight to where you were last seen is the obvious answer, but you're probably not there anymore! Search where he went looks for him where he most likely went, not just where he was. From where he was last seen and the direction he was moving, the squad guesses places: just past each doorway around him (more likely the more it lies in his direction, and the closer it is); straight ahead along his path; and where he was. Its setting, rooms out (2), is how far from where he was it guesses: 1 for the neighboring rooms, 2 for those plus the rooms past them. The squad splits up the guesses. Each soldier takes the most likely one near it that no squadmate has taken, goes there with its gun up, and looks around before marking it checked. The node fails once every guess has been checked. In the shipped tree, the soldier then looks around and stands down after a while. Seeing him ends the search, and hearing a shot restarts it from where the shot was. A Check a value on searchLeads (the places left to check) branches on whether the squad still has somewhere to look. How long a soldier looks around once its squad has nothing left to check, and the longest it searches at all, are tuning values (the Tuning tab, below: "Look round after search", "Search at most"). Tuning: how hard each side is The Tuning tab is the soldiers' difficulty (content/defs/ai/tuning.json). It shows every value, grouped (Awareness, Lethality, Tactics, Searching, Indoors, Taking hits, At ease), and hovering over one tells you what it does. These are all of the game's F3 overlay AI sliders, as data. Difficulty comes from reactions, aim and coordination, never from health. No bullet sponges here! Tuning is per side. Shared holds the values every side's soldiers fight with. Pick Station (the garrison: enemy variants with faction hostile) or Choir (the lancers, who fight alongside the horde) to see that side's values. Tick a value to change it for that side only (it turns amber), and untick it to go back to the shared value. "Only what this side changes" lists just those, and "Share every value" resets them all. In the file, soldiers holds the shared values and factions holds what each side changes. Every edit is saved and undone like any other, and the Sandbox tab's soldiers use it right away, so spawn an enemy from the side you're tuning to try it. The game reads the file when it starts. Its F3 overlay (AI) tunes a side live while it fights. Copy AI values copies what that side changes to the clipboard, in the same format as the file, so you can paste it under factions. Scoring: choosing an intent Choose intent is the one action that weighs things up. It scores four things a soldier could do from its cover and picks the best: hold it; advance to cover closer to the enemy; push the enemy while he's vulnerable; or fall back. It doesn't move the soldier or change the tree's flow. It only records the intent, about every half second, and always succeeds. The nodes after it act on the intent. In the shipped tree that's a selector of Intent is push then Push the enemy, Intent is advance then Bound forward, Intent is fall back then Fall back, and finally Hold cover. In Unreal's terms, Choose intent is a service writing to the blackboard, and Intent is is a decorator reading it. Scoring is utility AI. Its numbers are the behavior's scoring, under Scoring on the toolbar. Here's how a score gets built: Each intent starts at its base (or its baseByRole: a rifleman advances more readily than a suppressor). It adds its terms. These are weighted votes, not if-blocks. A term is a weight times a curve over one input (for example range from 20 to 30 m: nothing at 20, the full weight at 30 and beyond), or a weight by role. A term only counts when its when conditions are true (targetHealth < 0.6). It's multiplied by its factors. These are curves too (when pinned, a soldier advances at 0.4 of its score), or values by role. An intent whose gates aren't all true scores 0 (nobody pushes an enemy they can't see). The highest score wins. The soldier's current intent gets the stickiness (0.1) added on top, so it doesn't keep flipping between two close scores. The term that added the most is the reason shown over its head. The inputs a curve or condition can read are: ownHealth and targetHealth, from 0 to 1 (the target's is -1 when it's out of sight); range, in meters, and sinceSeen, in seconds; suppressed, coveringFire, targetReloading and squadPushing, each 0 or 1; advanceBlocked, which is 1 when the soldier isn't allowed to bound forward right now: either the soldiers further back go first, or it recently found no cover ahead. The shipped advance has a gate advanceBlocked < 1, so a soldier that can't move up holds instead, and its label says so. It also has a gate range > 12, so a soldier that's close enough to fight from where it is holds there (a push at a vulnerable enemy still closes in); searchLeads, how many of the squad's guesses about where a lost enemy went haven't been checked yet (0 when they've all been checked, or none were made); role; score, the intent's total so far, for a term that only adds to something already there. Personalities Each squad gets a personality, so no two squads have to fight quite the same. It sets: a scale on each intent's score; how many soldiers in a squad of three or more go around the side (flankers); cohesion: how far, in meters toward the enemy, its soldiers can get ahead of or behind the rest of the squad when they take cover (10 unless set). The game picks one for each squad by share, based on the squad's number and the level. The shipped ones are: steady: half the squads; the scores unchanged, cohesion 10; aggressive: cohesion 14; cautious: no flankers, cohesion 7; flanking: two flankers, cohesion 12. How a squad moves up So how does Bound forward actually work? The squad leapfrogs: The soldier furthest back goes first, to cover near or a little ahead of the squad's lead (a dash of up to 16 m, or however far it takes to catch up to the lead), while the rest cover it. The suppressor stays back as the base of fire and doesn't take a turn, and a soldier that finds no cover ahead passes its turn to the next one. Then the next soldier furthest back goes, and so on. A few rules keep it tidy: At most a third of the squad is moving at once. Nobody takes cover further ahead of the rest than the cohesion allows, though a bound can always come up level with the lead. A soldier that doesn't have a turn, or has no cover ahead, holds. One that has just bounded (and so isn't at the back anymore) holds where it ended up. A soldier on its way to cover gets there before it thinks again. A new role or intent doesn't turn it around halfway; only the cover no longer protecting it, getting stuck, or falling back does. Within 12 m of the enemy, the squad stops advancing and fights from where it is. Push the enemy is the only thing that deliberately leaves the squad. Afterwards the soldier takes the cover closest to the squad that it can. Roles (who suppresses, who flanks) rotate every roleSeconds (6), set in the scoring's general settings. A flanker that's still on its way around keeps its role until it gets there, and only calls out "Flanking left/right!" as it sets off. The scoring graph The scoring graph reads left to right, the same way a score is built: the inputs; the conditions, terms and factors, with their curves drawn; the four intents, each with three pins: requires all of (its conditions), adds (its terms) and multiplied by (its factors); the personalities, and the choice. A term's or factor's own conditions go on its only if all of pin. Hover over a node to read what it does in plain words ("adds 0.35 while covering fire is 1"). Double-click a Choose intent node in the tree to open its scoring. A behavior made from scratch has no scoring until its tree uses Choose intent. Give it scoring starts it as a copy of the soldier's. It's put together the same way as the tree: Right-click the canvas for the palette: a term, factor, condition or personality. A new term, factor or condition starts loose: dimmed, marked "not wired", and doing nothing in the game. Wire it in. Drag from its right-hand pin onto an intent's or term's pin. Drag from an input onto a curve or condition to make it read that input. Let go on empty canvas to add a node that reads it. Edit a curve by its keys, like in Unreal's curve editor. Click a term or factor and its curve is drawn large in the panel. Drag a key to move it, double-click to add a key at the mouse, right-click a key to remove it (a curve always keeps at least two), and click a key to type its exact input and value. The curve runs in a straight line between keys and stays flat past the first and last. Two keys at the same input make a step. In the file, a keyed curve is keys ([[20, 0], [25, 0.1], [30, 1]]). A curve written as from, to, low and high still works, and turns into keys the first time you edit it. Take it out (leave it loose), on a node's buttons, unwires it without deleting it. Remove the curve turns a term into just its weight. Click a node to edit it. The panel uses plain names for fields ("how often" for a personality's share, "value at end" for a curve's high), and each field's help gives its name in the file. What a node reads is set by its wire, not picked from a list. Drag a node to move it. Node positions are saved in the file. Once you change anything, every node stays where it is. Tidy up (on the right-click menu) lays everything out again and routes the wires like a circuit diagram. Each input's wires leave it horizontally and run down a lane of their own (the top input's lane is furthest right, so no wire crosses another input's lane to reach its own), then turn off horizontally at the pin they feed, going around any node in the way. The intents' wires into the choice share one lane next to it. The top of each lane is a reroute you can branch more wires from, and a wire's corners show up when the mouse is near, so you can drag them. Ctrl+Z undoes a Tidy up. Double-click a wire to put a reroute node on it, then drag the node to lead the wire around other nodes. Like in Unreal's blueprints, you can drag from a reroute's small pin on its right to wire what it carries into something else too, so one input can feed several curves and conditions through one reroute. Right-click a reroute to remove it (the wires through it go straight again). Node positions, reroutes and loose nodes are stored in the behavior file (x, y, via, inputVia, reroutes, layout, loose) only for Studio. The game never reads them, and they cost nothing while the AI runs. The tree editor The Behaviors tab is the editor. It shows the tree on a canvas, and on the right a view of the sandbox that follows the selected soldier. Right-click the canvas for the palette of nodes, grouped into Flow, Conditions and Actions. Type to search, and Enter picks the first match. Drag from a flow node's right-hand pin to another node's left pin to make it a child. If you let go on empty canvas, the palette opens so you can add a new child there. Children run top to bottom: drag a node up or down to change its order. The small number next to each wire is its position. Click a node to edit it on the right: what it does, and its settings. Settings are picked from lists, never typed: an awareness, a value and a comparison, a distance, an action. You can also give it a note, or rename its id. The buttons, also on a node's right-click menu, are Add a child, Make it the root, Take it from its parent, Duplicate and Delete. The Delete key removes the selected node, and its children stay behind, loose. Loose nodes do nothing until they're wired in under the root. Drag the background (or use the middle mouse button) to pan, and use the wheel to zoom. Tidy lays the tree out again, and Fit brings all of it into view. Node positions are saved with the nodes. Next to the selected behavior, Studio shows what it needs of a body: the things its tree's actions make a soldier do that a body has to be able to show (Hold cover: fire, reload, crouch, lean and fire blind; Throw grenade: throw). An enemy variant that thinks with it needs a body type that can do those things (Bodies, Graph tab: what its body can do). The Enemies tab flags a variant whose body can't, and the game logs it. + New behavior makes one from scratch. Give it a name, and you get a root with nothing under it yet. Duplicate copies the one shown. Delete removes it at the next save. The soldier's own behavior can't be deleted, and Studio warns you if a variant still uses the one you're deleting. See it live. This is the fun part! Select a soldier, either in the Sandbox tab or by clicking it in the view. The view follows it, and the editor shows the tree that soldier is running, lit up with what it's doing at each moment: green for succeeded, red for failed, grey for not reached. Think as this behavior gives the selected soldier the behavior shown, so you can try a tree on it right away. In the Sandbox tab, Thinks as spawns a whole squad with a given behavior. Every edit reaches the soldiers immediately, before you save. Enemy variants The Enemies tab lists the variants (enemies.json). Each one has: a behavior and a faction, picked from lists (hostile soldiers, or the choir that fights everyone); a body: health, the damage it deals, grenades, run and sprint speeds, and whether it drops loot; weapons: how often it carries each frame (the archetypes in Armory; a new frame shows up as an option as soon as it exists); spawns: how often a squad from each source is this variant. The sources are a level's squads, the mission's reinforcements, the director's patrols, and the choir that comes with the horde; its body type and model, and its own clips: each of the body's clips it replaces (picked from the rigs' clips) and the clip it plays instead, all from the rig's clips made in Blender. A gun's grip is applied first, so to change how the variant holds a pistol, replace Pistol_Idle, not Idle. Bodies mode shows it under Variant. The tab flags a clip name no rig has, and a behavior that needs something its body can't show (a behavior that throws grenades on a body that can't throw). A squad is all one variant, picked by those weights. So you want to add an enemy? Click + New, give it an id and a name, pick its behavior (make a new one under Behaviors first, if you want), then set its guns and where it spawns. That's it! In the Sandbox tab, Enemy spawns a squad of any variant. The sandbox The sandbox is the game's grey-box range, seen from a free camera. Hold the right mouse button to look around. W, A, S and D fly, Q and E go down and up, and Shift goes faster. On the left, the Sandbox tab says what a click in the world places: a squad with the selected size, enemy variant, behavior and personality (or picked by share, as in the game). It hunts the target, or stands at ease like at the start of a level (untick Hunting); a horde of the selected size, coming up out of the floor around the click (it fights everyone); the target: the player, standing where you click, who can't be hurt. Tick The target strafes to give the soldiers a moving enemy; cover: a box, either low (a soldier crouches behind it and rises over it to shoot) or high (he stands and leans out), placed with its broad side facing the target. Click a box to select it, and drag to move it. R rotates it (Shift: the other way) and Delete removes it. The panel sets its exact position, size and rotation, switches it between low and high, or duplicates it. Soldiers treat the boxes like the level's own walls and crates. They're solid, block sight, get walked around, and are used as cover as soon as you let go. Show the cover points marks every spot a soldier can choose: a yellow ring for low cover, blue for high, with a tick pointing toward the cover, brighter where a soldier is using it. The test cover isn't saved. It's for trying out the AI, not for making levels. Paused and Speed slow the fight down so you can watch it. Clear the soldiers and the horde removes everyone. Over every soldier is what it's doing and why (in the intent's color), along with its squad's personality and its role. Click one to "read its mind" on the right: its inputs, each intent's score (and the stickiness), and what each personality would choose in its place at that moment. Save writes the behavior files, enemies.json and tuning.json, and the game reads them when it starts. Shipped copies of the soldier's behavior and the variants are also built into the game, in case a file is missing or broken. Look: the surface materials The library of surface materials, and what each number does, is described in materials.md. Look mode lists the library down the left. Pick a material to see it on the sphere, the crate and the gun barrel, with a row of every material behind them to compare it with. Change its numbers and it updates right away, both there and on every model Studio draws. Light picks the room's lighting, and model's color sets the shapes' color. The room's reflections are re-captured whenever the shapes change, so a mirror-smooth metal shows the room right away. Under the flashlight, though, the room it reflects is dark, because the beam isn't included in reflections. Drag in the room to look around, and use the wheel to get closer. --mode look --select bare_metal --light flashlight opens on bare metal in the dark (station, flashlight, alarm, sodium or outdoors). A material ticked space is a window onto space: it shows the sky (below) whatever its color. One ticked outside is out in space, on a ship's or station's outside (hull_plating, the skin seen from a window): it's lit by the sector's sun, not a room's fill, and no room's haze lies over it. Skies The Skies tab tunes the skies windows show (content/defs/skies.json), looked at from inside, drawn by the game's own shader. Pick a sky on the left, and these are all sliders and color pickers: its stars (density, brightness, color); its nebula (strength, scale, the color of its thick parts and of its thin edges); its band, the galaxy's disc (strength, width, tilt, color); its sun (intensity, size, glow, elevation, color). Seen from is the preview's own, not saved: where across and down the sector's map the system is (the sun goes once round the sky across the map, and swings up or down 10 degrees down it) and the level seed its clouds and stars come from. Sectors is the order the fleet meets them in, one a sector from the first, going round again past the last: move one up, remove it, or add the selected sky. Add, Duplicate and Remove work as elsewhere; renaming a sky renames it in the sector order. Drag to look round, and use the wheel to narrow the view. --mode look --sky violet_shoal opens on the Skies tab looking at Violet Shoal. Models: what each model is collided with What a placed model is collided with (by characters, and by shots, sight, cover and the navigation grid alike) is set per model in content/props/colliders.json, beside the models; see ../plans/model-colliders.md. Models mode lists the prop models down the left by file, each with its collider ((file's) when it comes from its file's default). It also marks a model not placed when it's neither furniture (a prop in props.json names it) nor a station fixture (a mission template names it as a tank kind, the reservoir, its outlet or valve, or the airlock's intake or chute), so nothing sets it into a level. Pick one to set Every model in its file (the file's default) and This model (its own, or as its file): authored: the boxes in its file (..._CollisionOnly). The default. mesh: what's drawn, exactly: for irregular furniture (a desk's hutch, a terminal's screen). box and cylinder: one box, or one upright cylinder, around what's drawn: a cylinder for barrels and drums. none: nothing; walked and shot through. The model turns on the stage with its collider's outline over it in cyan, built exactly as the generator sets it into the level, as furniture or as a fixture. Orange marks surfaces characters step up onto: walkable, no higher than a step (0.4 m), and with room above them for a crouching character. Under it, it says what it's made of and what's worth fixing: why it won't do (an authored model whose solid isn't a box); surfaces to step up onto; a mesh that isn't closed (shots and sight only hit a face from the front, so they pass through a hole); and a piece that breaks given a mesh, which keeps its box (it breaks through one solid part). Every change reaches the furniture Studio builds levels from right away, saved or not, and Save writes colliders.json. --mode models --select furniture/Desk opens on the desk. What it does not do yet Studio covers a lot, but not everything. A few things still live outside it: What a soldier drops besides its gun (a medkit or an ammo pack, one time in five, and a weapon part, 6% of the time) is still code. The full list of what's still code is in adding-content.md. The running game doesn't pick up a save. Restart the mission (or the game) to play with the new data. Behavior mode builds trees from the actions and conditions that already exist. A new kind of action (a new way to move or fight) needs code. The horde's behavior is still tuned in code (HordeTuning). The soldiers' (how they notice the enemy, their aim, reactions and perception) is data, in the Tuning tab. There's no mode for the sound data yet.

index.html.summary: The Last Fleet A co-op, procedurally generated sci-fi FPS, built on the BRUTAL C# framework, .NET 10 and Vulkan 1.3. These pages are for the people who make what's in it: the models, the materials, the loot, the levels and the enemies. Where to start You make models. Start at Art in THE LAST FLEET. It covers what every model has in common (axes, scale, names, origins, materials) and links to a guide for each kind: the ship's hub, weapons, creatures, characters on a rig, and props. Every model's look comes from its surface materials. You tune the game. Start at LastFleet Studio, the designers' tool: loot, guns, items, missions, levels, bodies, enemy behavior and materials, each edited with the game's own code running beside it. New to Studio? The Studio tutorials walk through real tasks in each mode, with a screenshot of every step. Adding content says what you can add as data and what still needs a programmer. You write code. Architecture explains how the projects fit together, and the API reference is generated from the code's documentation comments. How these pages are made Every page is a Markdown file in the game's repository, under docs/, and the API reference comes from the source. The site is rebuilt whenever a change to either is merged, so what you read here matches the game on main.
